exp.0:1:
This verse says that Elkanah had two wives: Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah could not have any. The names are spelled as "Hannah" and "Peninnah" here.

Context: the one telling the story is the narrator of the book, not a character. He introduces Elkanah's family, a man from the region of Ephraim who went every year to worship at Shiloh. The Bible only describes that he had two wives; it does not say that God approved of it. This painful situation prepares the story of Hannah and her prayer, which will lead to the birth of Samuel.

For today: if you live with a lack or a comparison that hurts, remember that God sees what others overlook. Bring your pain to Him in prayer with sincerity, as Hannah will do, and seek the support of people who listen to you with respect.
exp.0:2:
This verse tells how Elkanah went up year by year from his city to Shiloh. There he worshiped God and offered sacrifices. The phrase "the Lord of hosts" speaks of God as the Lord of all power. The Hebrew-era term for the place is simply rendered here as "Shiloh," the same name used in the verse. Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, are also mentioned, since they served as priests in that place.

Here the narrator of the book introduces Elkanah's family. Shiloh was then a center of worship for Israel. The sons of Eli are named because the story will later show that their conduct was wrong. For now, the text only sets the scene, and it shows that Elkanah was steady in his faith.

For today: Elkanah worshiped God regularly, even in a setting where the religious leadership was not an example. We can follow his example by being faithful in prayer and worship, without depending on how well or how poorly others do theirs.
exp.0:10:
Hannah makes a promise to God. She asks him to look upon her suffering, not to forget her, and to give her a male child. If God does this, she will give him back to the Lord for his whole life.

Ana habla con el corazón roto is rendered as: Hannah speaks with a broken heart. She was barren and suffered mockery, and she went to Shiloh, where the sanctuary was. Her promise resembles the Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), which included not cutting the hair, although the text of this verse does not use that word. She prayed silently, with tears, and Eli, the priest, mistook her for a drunken woman.

For today: bring your pain to God honestly, without pretending to be strong. And if you make him a promise, think carefully about what you say and be faithful to it. Hannah not only asked; she was also willing to give up what she wanted most.
exp.0:12:
Hannah was praying silently. Her lips were moving, but no word could be heard, because she was speaking from the deepest part of her heart. Eli, the priest, saw her and thought she was drunk.

Hannah had no children and suffered greatly. She was at the sanctuary in Shiloh, and she had just made a vow: if God gave her a son, she would dedicate him to the Lord for his whole life. Eli watched her and misunderstood the way she was praying, since perhaps he was not used to seeing a prayer so quiet and so intense.

For today: God hears the prayers that no one else understands. When pain keeps you from finding words, you can pour out your heart before Him. And if someone misreads your faith, remember that God knows what is within you.
exp.0:13:
Eli asks Anna how much longer she is going to stay drunk, and tells her to let her wine go, that is, to let the drunkenness wear off. Here "put away" means to get rid of it, so that she becomes sober again.

Eli, the priest, was watching Anna's mouth in the sanctuary. She was praying in silence, only moving her lips, and he judged her wrongly. Anna was deeply distressed because she had no children, and that is why she prayed with such pain. Afterward she explains to him that she has not drunk anything and that she was only pouring out her soul before God.

Today we can learn not to judge by appearances. Before drawing conclusions about someone who is suffering, it is wise to approach them with respect and to listen. And if you are anguished, you can pray with sincerity, even when others do not understand you.
exp.0:15:
Anna asks Eli not to think of her as a wicked woman or as someone without reverence for God. Her words mean she is not an evil person and does not lack the fear of God. She explains that she has been praying for so long because her sorrow was overwhelming.

It is Anna speaking, a woman who could not have children and suffered greatly because of it. She was praying silently in the sanctuary, moving her lips without her voice being heard. The priest Eli thought she was drunk and rebuked her. She answers him with humility and sincerity, and he blesses her.

For today: when you are deeply troubled, you can tell God everything you feel, even when others do not understand you or judge you wrongly. Anna poured out her soul before God, and afterward she left in peace. Do the same with your burdens.
exp.0:23:
This verse tells us that Hannah, once her son Samuel had been weaned, brought him up to the house of the Lord in Shiloh. She also brought three young bulls, an ephah of flour (a large measure of ground grain), and a bottle of wine, to offer as a sacrifice. Being weaned means he no longer nursed. The verse also makes clear that the child was young.

This is the narrator's account. Hannah had promised God that, if he gave her a son, she would give him back to serve him. Now she keeps her promise. The exact age of Samuel is not known; in that time weaning could happen at two or three years old, though this is not certain.

When we make a promise to God, Hannah encourages us to keep it faithfully and gratefully, even when it costs us. She also reminds us that what God gives us, we can return to him with trust.
exp.0:24:
It says they killed the bullock, that is, a young bull, to offer it as a sacrifice. Then they brought the boy Samuel before the priest Eli. Some scholars note that the older text varies at this point (three bullocks or a three-year-old bull), but the central idea is the same.

The narrator tells that Hannah, after weaning her son, went with her husband Elkanah to Shiloh. Years earlier she had promised God to give him the son he granted her. Now she keeps her word: she offers the sacrifice and presents the child to the priest, and right away she will remind Eli who she is.

For today: if you promised something to God in a difficult moment, do not forget it when the answer comes. A simple way to keep it is to thank him, and to give back with joy the time, gifts, or goods he has entrusted to you.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that there is none holy like the Lord, that there is no other God beside him, and that there is no refuge as secure as our God. "Holy" means set apart, pure, unique in his goodness. The word translated here as "rock" in the Hebrew is an image of firm and steady protection.

Speaking is Hannah, who for years could not have children and had asked God for a son. Now she has left her son Samuel in the service of the Lord at the sanctuary. Her prayer is one of gratitude. She praises God because he sustained her in the face of those who despised her, and she sets this against the human arrogance she mentions next.

When you face a difficult situation, do not place your security only in your own strength, your money, or other people. Go to God in prayer, as Hannah did, and rest in the fact that he is a firm rock who does not fail.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that God lifts the poor and the needy out of their humiliation and seats them among princes, giving them a place of honor. Needy is the word for those in want, and the lowest place is a heap of rubbish or the ground in the dust. An inheritance is a possession that is received. At the end it states that the earth belongs to God, who holds it up as though on pillars.

The one speaking is Hannah, in a prayer of thanksgiving. She had been barren and humbled, and God gave her Samuel. She sees in her own case an example of how God works in the world. Her song also points toward a king, the anointed one, although Israel still had no king.

Today we can trust that God sees the humble and the forgotten. If you are going through a time of discouragement, pray sincerely and wait on Him. And if you are in a high position, do not forget that everything belongs to God.
exp.1:8:
He will watch over the steps of those who belong to him, whom the verse calls his holy ones because they are set apart for him. The wicked, those who live without God, fall into darkness, that is, into ruin and confusion. It ends with a clear truth: no one truly succeeds by their own strength alone.

The one speaking is Hannah, in a prayer of thanksgiving. She had been barren and humiliated, but God gave her a son, Samuel, and she dedicated him to serve in the sanctuary. Her song celebrates that God changes circumstances: he lifts up the humble and brings down the proud. That is why this verse speaks of trusting in God and not in oneself.

For today: when you feel weak or insecure, do not depend only on your own abilities. Pray and entrust your steps to God, trusting that he sustains and guides you.
exp.1:9:
Verse 10 says that those who oppose God will be broken before Him, and that God will make His power heard like thunder from heaven. He will judge the whole earth, even to its farthest places. He will also give strength to His King and lift up the horn of His anointed one; the horn was a sign of power and victory, and "anointed" means one who has been set apart with oil.

Hannah speaks in her prayer of thanksgiving, after giving her son Samuel to serve God. She celebrates that God lifts up the humble and brings down the proud. There is not yet a king in Israel, so many see here a look forward: to anointed kings and, for Christians, to Jesus.

Today we can trust that God does justice, even when we do not see it right away. If you feel small or unfairly treated, bring your situation to God in prayer, without depending only on your own strength.
exp.1:12:
This verse describes how the priests in Shiloh treated the people who brought sacrifices. When someone offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant came while the meat was boiling. He carried a large fork with three prongs to take meat out of the pot.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He has just said that the sons of Eli did not know the LORD. For this reason he explains how they abused their position. What follows shows that they took the meat by force, with no respect for what belonged to God. This contrasts with the young Samuel, who served faithfully.

For today: if we serve in the church or in any responsibility, let us not use that place for our own benefit. Serving God calls for a humble heart and honesty with what belongs to Him and to others.
exp.1:13:
The verse tells how the priest's servant would thrust a three-pronged fork into the pot where the meat of the sacrifice was cooking. Whatever the fork brought up, the priest kept for himself. This was not a one-time event: it was done to every Israelite who came to Shiloh.

Here the narrator of the book describes the conduct of Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas. The text says they were wicked and did not know the LORD. Shiloh was the place where the sanctuary stood, and the people went there to offer sacrifices. They took by force what did not belong to them and treated what was holy as if it were their own.

For today: when we serve in the church or in any position of responsibility, let us not use that position for our own benefit. Serving God means giving with honesty and respect, not taking advantage of others.
exp.1:14:
This verse tells how, before the fat of the animal was burned, which belonged to God, the servant of the priest came and demanded raw meat to roast. He would not accept boiled meat. He wanted the best, and he wanted it first, without waiting.

The one speaking is the servant of Eli's sons, who were priests in Shiloh. The law stated that the fat was burned for God and that the priest received a set portion. But these men used their position to take more than they were due, and by force. The text says that in this way they despised the offerings of the LORD.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use spiritual things for our own benefit. Whoever serves God or others should do so with humility, giving God first place and never taking advantage of the trust of others.
exp.1:18:
This verse tells us that Hannah, Samuel's mother, made him a small robe every year. She would bring it to him when she went up with her husband Elkanah to the sanctuary to offer the yearly sacrifice. The verse's wording refers to making the robe and bringing it, so the sentences about the old phrasing are removed. The robe was an everyday garment, different from the linen ephod that Samuel wore while serving.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, without attributing the words to any character. Hannah had dedicated Samuel to the Lord while he was a child, and he lived with the priest Eli. While the sons of Eli despised the offerings, the account shows Samuel serving faithfully and his mother caring for him with constant love.

For today: love is shown through simple, sustained acts. Although Hannah could not have her son near her, she cared for him with thoughtful details year after year. We can do the same for the people God has entrusted to us, giving them attention, prayer, and practical help faithfully.
exp.1:21:
Eli was very old at this point, and this verse says that he heard about everything his sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were doing to all of Israel. He also learned that they lay with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, that is, the women who gathered at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

The narrator tells us this to show the corruption of Eli's sons, who were priests. They abused their office and the people, while the young Samuel grew faithfully before God. Eli is the one who hears the complaints, and in the verses that follow he rebukes them, though with gentle words. Scholars agree that the sin was serious, though they do not all explain in the same way who those women were or what their service involved.

For today: whoever has authority, in the family, the church, or the workplace, must not ignore the wrong he sees. Correcting it in time and with firmness, but with love, protects others and honors God.
exp.1:22:
Eli asks his sons why they act this way. He tells them that he has heard, from the mouth of all the people, the wicked things they are doing.

Eli speaks as the priest, now very old. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were also priests, but they abused their office and sinned at the entrance of the tabernacle. Eli rebukes them because their bad example was leading the people away from God. The following verses show that they would not listen. Some scholars point out that his correction was weak for the seriousness of the case.

Those who hold some responsibility over others, such as parents, leaders, or teachers, must correct wrongdoing firmly and lovingly, and in time. And all of us should listen to correction before our hearts become hardened.
exp.1:23:
Eli tells his sons to stop this behavior. He explains that what people are saying about them is not good news, because through their conduct they are leading God's people into sin.

The speaker is Eli, an elderly priest and the father of Hophni and Phinehas. These sons were abusing their position at the tabernacle, and all of Israel was talking about it. Eli rebukes them, but his tone seems gentle, and they did not listen to him. The text says that God had already decided to judge them.

For today: our example influences others, especially if we carry some responsibility. Let us be careful how we live and, if we correct someone, let us do it with clarity and firmness, without putting it off.
exp.1:27:
God says he chose the family of Levi, the family Eli came from, to serve him as priests. He gave them important duties: to offer sacrifices on his altar, to burn incense, and to wear the ephod, a priestly garment used for seeking God's guidance. He also gave them a share of the people's offerings for their support.

A prophet, described as a man of God, speaks to Eli on behalf of the LORD. Eli was a priest, but his sons were abusing their office and taking the best of the offerings. God reminds him of everything he had given them before rebuking him for honoring his sons more than him.

All service to God is a privilege received, not a right to be used for our own gain. If we have any responsibility in the church or in the family, let us ask God to help us serve with humility and always put him first.
exp.1:32:
God says he will not completely remove all of Eli's descendants from service at the altar. But great sorrow awaits Eli: his eyes will grow dim with grief, and his heart will be filled with sorrow. Many of his descendants will die young, in the prime of their adult lives.

A man of God speaks to Eli, the priest. God rebukes him because he allowed his sons to treat the offerings with contempt, and because he honored them more than God. Many believe the survivor who is announced refers to Abiathar, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: God is merciful, but he also takes obedience seriously. If you have authority at home or in the church, do not ignore what is wrong in order to avoid conflict. Correct with love, and put God first.
exp.1:33:
This verse says that God would give Eli a sign: his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, would die on the same day. A "sign" is a proof that what was announced would come to pass. In this way Eli would know that the rest of the message was also true.

A man of God, sent to Eli, speaks on God's behalf. Eli was a priest, but he did not correct his sons firmly, though they abused their office and despised the offerings. God announces judgment on that household. The fulfillment appears afterward, in 1 Samuel 4, when both of them die in battle.

For today: God takes sacred service and the responsibility of those who lead seriously, whether in the church or in the family. If we guide others, let us ask God for the courage to correct with love and to live with integrity, because our example matters greatly.
exp.1:35:
It says that whoever survives from Eli's family will have to come and humble himself before the faithful priest whom God will raise up. He will come to ask him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread. He will beg to be put into one of the priests' offices, only so that he may have something to eat.

The one speaking is a prophet, a man of God sent to Eli. His message announces God's judgment on his house, because his sons Hophni and Phinehas dishonored the service of God and Eli did not correct them. Many believe the faithful priest is fulfilled first in Samuel or in Zadok, though interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: serving God is a privilege, not a business. Examine your motives and ask him to give you a faithful heart, one that honors him even when it is hard to correct what is wrong.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that the young Samuel served God under the guidance of the priest Eli. In those days the word of the Lord was rare, that is, scarce and uncommon, and for that reason very precious. There was also no open vision, meaning that it was not common for God to communicate clearly and openly.

This is the beginning of the story of Samuel's calling. The narrator is the author of the book, who is not named. He describes a spiritually difficult time in Israel, when Eli's priesthood was weakened by the sin of his sons. Some scholars understand that God spoke little as a consequence of that condition of the people, although the text only says that it was rare.

Even when God seems silent, we can keep serving him faithfully in what is simple, as Samuel did. Keep your ear attentive to his Word, which we have within our reach today, and do not stop seeking him with humility.
exp.2:2:
This verse tells us that Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, near the ark of God. The lamp of God had not yet gone out, meaning it was still before dawn. "Temple" here refers to the sanctuary at Shiloh, which was a tent with structures built around it.

The writer describes a difficult time: the word of the Lord was rare and visions were not frequent. Eli, the priest, was already old and nearly blind. The young Samuel served him. The lamp was probably the lampstand of the holy place, which burned through the night. Some think the mention marks the hour, just before dawn, and others that it emphasizes the faint light in dark times. The text does not fully make this clear.

God often speaks when we are available and in stillness. Set aside a quiet moment each day, perhaps at dawn, to read the Bible and listen with humility.
exp.2:18:
It says that Samuel grew up and that God was with him. It also says that God did not let any of his words "fall to the ground." That expression means that nothing Samuel announced went unfulfilled. Samuel's words proved to be true.

The narrator is the author of the book. Samuel was a young man who served at Shiloh, alongside the priest Eli. God had given him a hard message of judgment against Eli's house, and Samuel delivered it honestly. This verse shows the result: God backed Samuel, and soon all Israel recognized him as a faithful prophet.

For today: God values those who speak the truth with humility, even when it costs them. Ask Him to be with you, and be honest in what you say, trusting that He cares for your witness over time.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that Samuel spoke to all the Israelites, and that in those days Israel went out to fight against the Philistines. The Israelites camped near Ebenezer, and the Philistines set up their camp at Aphek. The phrase about setting up camp means putting the military camp in place.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Samuel was already recognized as a prophet in Israel. The verse does not say what message he gave, nor whether Israel sought God's guidance before the battle. What follows shows a defeat and an attempt to use the ark as if it were a charm. Some understand that there is a lack of true trust in God in this.

For today: before facing a struggle, it is not enough to have religious symbols or customs. Let us seek God sincerely, listen to his Word, and ask for his direction, instead of trusting in formulas or outward appearances.
exp.3:1:
This verse tells that the Philistines attacked Israel. The battle broke out and the Israelites lost. About four thousand men died on the battlefield. The phrase about the Philistines starting the battle means they began the attack, and the phrase about Israel being struck down means they were defeated.

The one telling the story is the writer of the book, who does not identify himself. He recounts the start of a war between Israel and the Philistines, a neighboring people and an enemy. What follows shows that the leaders asked why God had let them lose. But instead of examining their hearts, they decided to bring the ark of the covenant, as if it were a charm. This sets up an even greater defeat.

When something goes wrong for us, it is good to stop and humbly ask God what He wants to teach us. Let us not use symbols, customs, or religious formulas as a shortcut. What God seeks is a sincere heart that trusts in Him.
exp.3:5:
The Philistines heard a great shout of joy coming from the camp of Israel. Puzzled, they asked what all that noise meant. Soon they learned that the ark of the Lord, the sacred chest of the covenant, had arrived in the camp. The shout here is the loud cry of the Israelites, and it reveals how intense their rejoicing was.

The Philistines were Israel's enemies and were in the middle of a war. Israel had just lost a battle and, instead of seeking God with humility, they sent for the ark, as though it were a charm that would guarantee them victory. The Philistines speak here, and their reaction shows that they knew the reputation of Israel's God, though they understood him in their own way.

For today: we should not confuse religious symbols with the presence of God. He is not to be handled like an object of luck; he seeks a repentant and obedient heart, not merely emotion or ritual.
exp.3:7:
The Philistines are frightened when they learn that the ark of Israel has come into the camp. They think the God of the Hebrews is there, and they ask who will rescue them from these mighty gods. They say that it was these gods who struck Egypt with every kind of plague in the wilderness. "Struck" means hit or punished; a "plague" is a terrible punishment or blow.

The speakers are Philistine soldiers, enemies of Israel. They speak out of fear, because the Israelites shouted with joy when the ark arrived. The Philistines speak of "gods" in the plural, which shows that they did not know the God of Israel well. They also mix in some details from the story of the exodus. Even so, they knew the reputation of what God did in Egypt. Afterward they take courage and defeat Israel, which reminds us that God is not bound to act because of a sacred object.

For today: let us not trust in symbols, customs, or rituals as if they were a charm. Let us trust in God himself and seek to live in obedience and sincerity before him.
exp.3:11:
This verse tells that a man of the tribe of Benjamin ran away from the battlefield and arrived at Shiloh that same day. He had torn clothes and dirt on his head. In that time these were well-known signs of mourning, deep sorrow, or tragedy. Shiloh was the place where the sanctuary stood and where the priest Eli lived.

It is the narrator who speaks, and he introduces us to the messenger who will bring the news of Israel's defeat. The ark of God had been captured and Eli's sons had died. Before the man says a word, his appearance already announces the disaster. The text does not give his name, so we know nothing more about him.

For today: when hard news arrives, we should not hide it behind false calm. It is healthy to weep sincerely and to bring our pain before God, who listens even when everything seems lost.
exp.3:12:
This verse shows Eli, the aged priest, sitting in a seat by the road, watching in the distance. He was keeping watch, alert to see who was coming. His heart was trembling with fear for the ark of God, which had gone out to battle. When the messenger entered Shiloh and gave the news, the whole city cried out in grief.

The narrator tells what happened after Israel lost to the Philistines. The ark was captured, and Hophni and Phinehas, Eli's sons, died. Eli did not yet know anything, but his unease showed that the ark mattered to him more than anything else. The Bible does not explain all his thoughts, so it is not wise to assume too much.

For today: when we feel fear for something we love, we can bring it to God in prayer before the news arrives. And if bad news has already come, we are not alone in facing it.
exp.3:17:
This verse tells of the death of Eli. When the messenger mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat, beside the gate. He broke his neck and died, because he was an old man and heavy. It also says that he had judged Israel for forty years.

The one speaking is the narrator, who recounts what happened after the news of the defeat by the Philistines. The messenger brought four pieces of news: Israel fled, many had died, Eli's sons had died, and the ark had been taken. What struck Eli most deeply was the loss of the ark, which symbolized God's presence among his people.

For today: Eli was more shaken by the ark than by his sons, and this shows that the most precious thing is the presence of God. We can ask ourselves what matters most to us, and ask God to always hold first place in our hearts.
exp.4:0:
This verse tells that the Philistines, after capturing the ark of God, carried it from Eben-ezer to Ashdod, one of their main cities. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among Israel.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had defeated Israel in battle and took the ark as a war trophy. They thought their god was stronger. The verses that follow show that this was not so: the image of Dagon fell face down before the ark. God did not need an army to defend his honor.

For today: sometimes it seems that circumstances or people defeat what belongs to God. But He remains sovereign even when everything seems lost. Trust that God works with power, even in silence, and do not be carried away only by appearances.
exp.4:1:
The Philistines, who had captured the ark of God in battle, brought it into the temple of their god Dagon and placed it beside him. The wording in the verse is plain: the ark was brought in and set down by the idol.

The narrator tells what happened after Israel lost the ark to the Philistines. They thought their god had defeated the God of Israel, so they put the ark on display as a trophy of war. Dagon was a deity highly honored in the region, although scholars debate the details of his origin. The verses that follow show that God needs no one to defend him.

Today we can remember that God shares his place with nothing. When we place something beside him, such as money, success, or pride, sooner or later it becomes clear that they are not equals. Let us ask him to occupy first place.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that the next day, the people of Ashdod got up early and found their god Dagon fallen, face down on the ground, in front of the ark of the Lord. Lying face down means lying flat on the ground. They lifted the statue and set it back in its place.

The book of Samuel tells what happened without any character speaking. The Philistines had defeated Israel and taken the ark, believing that their god was stronger. Dagon was a deity greatly honored by them. Here the account shows that the Lord does not depend on a temple or an army to show who He is.

Today we can remember that nothing can take the place of God. If something, such as money, success, or the approval of others, tries to sit on the throne of our heart, it is good to put it in its place and let God be God.
exp.4:8:
It says that when the Philistines carried the ark to Gath, God acted against that city with a very great destruction. He struck everyone, from the least to the greatest, and they had painful swellings, which were probably tumors or sores.

The narrator tells what happened after the Philistines captured the ark. In Ashdod they had already suffered, and their leaders decided to move it to Gath, thinking that this way they would escape the problem. But the punishment followed them. Some scholars debate exactly what the disease was.

For today: we cannot treat God as an object that can be moved from place to place to avoid his consequences. When God confronts us, the best thing is to humble ourselves, acknowledge the truth, and seek him, instead of running away.
exp.4:9:
This verse says that the Philistines sent the ark of God to Ekron, another of their cities. When it arrived, the people cried out in fear: "They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to us, to slay us and our people!"

The one speaking is the people of Ekron. They had already seen that the ark had caused great harm in Ashdod and Gath, so they were afraid before anything happened to them. The Philistines had captured the ark in battle, but they did not know what to do with it. They wanted to move it away from their cities, not to obey God.

For today: it is possible to recognize that God is powerful and still try to keep Him at a distance. Today we can stop running from God and come near to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy.
exp.5:1:
The Philistines call for their priests and diviners, that is, their religious guides, and ask them what they should do with the ark of the Lord. They want to know how to send it back to its place.

The rulers and the people of the Philistines are speaking. They had captured the ark in battle, but for seven months they suffered plagues and troubles wherever they kept it. Now they understand that they cannot keep it without consequences. Since they do not know the Lord well, they turn to their own religious experts. Some scholars see here a sincere fear; others see only an attempt to appease a powerful god.

When something troubles our conscience, we can look for advice everywhere except to God. Today, instead of running away or making excuses, it is wise to acknowledge his authority, seek his direction in the Bible, and correct what is wrong.
exp.5:8:
It says the Philistines would make a test. If the cows carried the ark along the road toward Beth-shemesh, which was Israelite territory, then the God of Israel had caused them that great disaster. If they did not head that way, they would know that it was not God's hand that punished them, but a chance event, a mere coincidence.

The speakers are the priests and diviners of the Philistines. They had captured the ark and were suffering plagues. They wanted to know whether the evil came from the God of Israel. They chose cows with calves, which would naturally want to return to their young. If even so the cows turned away from them and kept straight on, it would be a clear sign.

Today we can learn not to attribute everything to luck. Even those who doubt can be led to recognize God. Let us ask him for open eyes to see his hand, and for humility to answer him.
exp.5:9:
The Philistines did what their priests and diviners had told them. They took two cows that had just given birth and were still nursing, hitched them to the cart, and shut their calves up at home. The verse says the men did so, took two milch cows, and tied them to the cart while shutting up their calves at home.

The Philistines had captured the ark of God and suffered plagues. They wanted to know whether the suffering came from the God of Israel or was just a coincidence. The cows, by instinct, would return to their calves; if instead they went toward Beth-shemesh, it would be a clear sign that God was at work. This test was their idea, not a command from God.

God can speak to us even when we do not seek him in the right way. But we do not need to ask for strange signs: today we have his Word. When you are in doubt, look for him in it and in prayer, and obey what he has already shown you.
exp.5:11:
The verse tells that the two cows, which had been yoked to the cart carrying the ark, went straight toward Beth-shemesh. They were lowing, that is, mooing, and they did not turn aside to the right or to the left. The Philistine lords followed them at a distance as far as the border of the town.

The narrator recounts what happened after the Philistines, punished with plagues for having taken the ark, decided to return it. To test whether the punishment came from God, they placed the ark on a cart pulled by cows that had just given birth, which would normally have stayed with their calves. That they went straight into Israelite territory was taken as a sign. The text does not explain how this happened; it presents it simply as the work of God.

Today we can remember that God guides us even when circumstances seem against us. Let us trust in Him and move forward with firmness, without turning aside.
exp.5:13:
The cart carrying the ark came to the field of a man named Joshua, from Beth-shemesh, and stopped beside a large stone. The people split the wood of the cart for fuel and offered the cows that had pulled it as a burnt offering, meaning a sacrifice burned completely for God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had captured the ark and suffered plagues, so they decided to send it back on a cart pulled by cows. The cows went straight toward Israel, and this was understood as a sign that God was directing everything. The people of Beth-shemesh, upon seeing it, rejoiced and worshiped.

For today: when God gives us back something or brings us out of a trouble, let us respond with gratitude and devotion. We can offer to Him from the heart what we have, holding nothing back.
exp.5:14:
The Levites, who were in charge of the sacred service, lifted the ark of the Lord down from the cart. They also took down the chest that held the golden jewels, and placed them on the great stone. The men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings, which were sacrifices burned up completely, and other sacrifices to the Lord that same day.

This is historical narrative. The Philistines had returned the ark with a gift of gold to make up for their offense. The cows had carried the cart as far as Beth-shemesh, and the people, who were harvesting wheat, rejoiced when they saw it. They respond with worship, and the Levites care for the ark as the law required.

For today: when God gives us back something good or gives us joy, our first response can be to thank him and worship him. We can set aside a moment to thank him before going on with our tasks.
exp.5:16:
This verse lists the gold offerings that the Philistines sent to the Lord as a repayment. There was one gold figure for each of the five main cities: Ashdod, Gaza, Askelon, Gath and Ekron.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had captured the ark of God, and they suffered a plague. Their priests advised returning it with gifts of gold to acknowledge the Lord. The people of Beth-shemesh received it and offered sacrifices. The five Philistine rulers saw all this and went back to their land.

For today: when we recognize that we have failed, fear alone is not enough; God looks for a humble heart that honors him. Let us ask forgiveness sincerely and treat what belongs to God with reverence.
exp.5:17:
This verse says that the Philistines also sent golden mice, as many as the cities they had under their five lords, both the fortified cities and the villages without walls. It also mentions the great stone where they set down the ark of the Lord, and that this stone was still there to this day, in the field of Joshua, a man of Beth-shemesh.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, and he writes after the events took place. The Philistines had captured the ark and suffered plagues. Their priests advised them to return it with a guilt offering of repayment, in the form of tumors and golden mice. The stone served as a sign that all of this really happened.

For today: when we recognize that we have failed, fear alone is not enough. God wants us to take it seriously, to honor Him with humility, and to seek to be reconciled to Him, who is holy and also merciful.
exp.5:18:
God punished the people of Beth-shemesh because they looked into the ark of the Lord, that is, they opened it or looked into it without proper respect. Many died, and the people mourned (they lamented) over that great blow.

The narrator tells what happened when the Philistines sent the ark back, the ark that represented God's holy presence. The people of Beth-shemesh treated it lightly. The figure of 50,070 is difficult: some scholars believe there was a copying error and that far fewer died. This cannot be stated with certainty. Even so, the central message is clear: God is holy.

Today we can approach God with confidence, but also with reverence. Before praying or reading the Bible, pause and remember who God is.
exp.5:20:
This verse tells how the people of Beth-shemesh sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kirjath-jearim. They told them that the Philistines had brought back the ark of the Lord, and they invited them to come down and take it away.

The people speaking here were the ones who had just suffered a terrible punishment for looking inside the ark. They were frightened and mourning, and they asked who is able to stand before such a holy God. That is why they wanted the ark to leave their town. The number of those who died (50,070) is much debated among scholars because of the way it is written in the Hebrew, and some think the original figure was smaller.

For today: God is to be approached with respect and humility, not with careless curiosity. His holiness is not meant to push us away, but so that we seek him with reverence and obedience.
exp.6:0:
The men of Kiriath-jearim went and took the ark of the Lord and placed it in the house of Abinadab, which stood on a hill. There they set apart his son Eleazar to take care of the ark.

The account is told by the book's narrator, who does not name himself. The Philistines had sent the ark back, and the people of Beth-shemesh could no longer keep it (chapter 6). That is why it was brought to Kiriath-jearim. The text does not say that Eleazar was a Levite, so we cannot claim it.

Today, when God entrusts us with something sacred, we care for it with reverence and responsibility. We might ask ourselves what room we give God in our home and our daily routine.
exp.6:2:
Samuel tells all the people of Israel that if they truly want to return to God with all their hearts, they must put away the foreign gods, including Ashtaroth, a goddess worshiped by the neighboring peoples. They must give their hearts fully to the Lord and serve him alone. Then God would deliver them from the power of the Philistines.

Samuel, prophet and judge of Israel, speaks here. About twenty years had passed since the ark arrived at Kiriath-jearim, and the people felt sorrow and longing for God. The Philistines held them in subjection. Samuel shows them that repentance is not only feeling sorry but also changing how one lives. Afterward, the people removed their idols.

For today: returning to God truly means letting go of whatever has taken his place in our hearts, such as money, pride, or an addiction. Ask God to show you what you should let go of today.
exp.6:3:
This verse tells that the people of Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtoreths, which were false gods of the neighboring peoples, and served the Lord only, the true God. "Put away" means they removed them from among themselves, and "served" means they worshiped and obeyed him.

The writer then describes what happened after Samuel's appeal. For twenty years the people had been sorrowful and seeking God, while the Philistines held power over them. Samuel told them that if they truly returned to God with all their heart, they must put away those idols. The verse shows that they listened to him. Afterward they gathered at Mizpah to pray and to acknowledge their sin.

For today: returning to God is not only feeling sorrow, but also removing from our lives whatever takes his place. Today we can ask ourselves what we are putting above God, and with his help, let it go.
exp.6:5:
This verse tells that the people of Israel gathered at Mizpah. They drew water and poured it out before the Lord, fasted the whole day, and confessed, "We have sinned against the Lord." Also, Samuel judged them, that is, he led them and settled their affairs as their leader. Pouring out water probably expressed repentance and surrender, although scholars explain it in several ways.

This is an account from the time of Samuel. Israel had worshiped the Baals and Ashtaroth, false gods, and now was turning back to the Lord. Samuel called them together to pray for them. Afterward, the Philistines threatened the people, and they asked Samuel to keep crying out to God.

For today: returning to God begins with sincerely acknowledging our sin. It is not enough to feel sorry; we must say it before God, leave behind whatever draws us away from Him, and trust in His forgiveness.
exp.6:6:
The verse tells that the Philistines learned that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah. Then their lords went up to attack Israel. When the Israelites heard it, they were afraid.

The narrator describes what happened after Israel had repented at Mizpah. Samuel had gathered them to pray, and they fasted and confessed their sin. Perhaps the Philistines saw the gathering as an opportunity to attack. What follows shows that the people, frightened, sought help from God through Samuel.

Turning back to God does not always remove problems right away; sometimes they arrive just after. But fear can lead us to cry out to God, as Israel did. When something frightens us, we can pray and turn to Him, without waiting to have everything resolved.
exp.6:8:
Samuel took a young lamb that was still nursing, meaning a very small one, and offered it to God whole as a burnt offering, a sacrifice that was burned completely. While he offers it, he prays earnestly for Israel, and God hears him.

The people had gathered at Mizpah to return to the Lord, and the Philistines, powerful enemies, came up to attack them. The Israelites were afraid and asked Samuel not to stop praying for them. So Samuel presents the sacrifice and cries out. Shortly afterward, God answers with a great thunder that throws the Philistines into confusion.

When you are afraid, come to God with humility and sincerity, and also ask for the prayers of other believers. We do not always know how he will respond, but he listens to those who trust in him.
exp.6:14:
This verse says that Samuel was judge over Israel for all the days of his life. The word "judged" does not refer only to handing down sentences in a court. In that time, a judge also guided, corrected and defended the people. "All the days of his life" means that Samuel served until the end of his days.

The narrator of the book tells this, summarizing Samuel's leadership. It comes after Israel returned to God and the Philistines were defeated. The verses that follow explain how he worked: each year he traveled through Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah, and then returned to Ramah, where he built an altar to the LORD.

For today: serving God and others with steadiness, not only in special moments. A faithful life, day after day, leaves a lasting mark.
exp.7:0:
And it came to pass, when Samuel was old, that he appointed his sons as judges over Israel. Judges were leaders who settled disputes and governed the people with justice.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not Samuel. Samuel had been a faithful prophet and judge for many years. This verse opens the account of how Israel ended up asking for a king. The verses that follow explain that the sons, Joel and Abijah, did not follow their father's example: they pursued gain and twisted justice. The Bible does not say why Samuel gave them that role, so it is better not to guess his reasons.

For today: faith and good character are not inherited automatically. If we have children, students, or people under our care, let us teach them by example and pray for them. And when choosing leaders, let us look more at their integrity than at their family name or their closeness to us.
exp.7:1:
This verse says that Samuel's two sons were named Joel, the firstborn, and Abiah, the second. Both of them served as judges in Beersheba, a city in the south of Israel. The word "firstborn" means the eldest son.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samuel was already old, and he appointed his sons as judges to help him. But the text that follows makes clear that they did not follow their father's good example: they sought unjust gain and perverted justice. This led the leaders of the people to ask for a king.

For today: having a godly family or a godly father does not guarantee that children will share the same faith. Each person must seek God for themselves, and those who serve in positions of responsibility must guard their integrity.
exp.7:2:
It says that Samuel's sons, Joel and Abijah, did not follow their father's good example. They let themselves be carried away by the love of money, accepted bribes, and twisted justice, that is, they judged without integrity. The sons turned aside from the right path.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samuel was already old and had appointed his sons as judges in Beersheba, in the south of Israel. Their wrongdoing led the elders of the people to ask for a king. This is how the shift toward the monarchy in Israel begins.

For today: faith is not passed down automatically, and positions of responsibility must not be used for personal gain. If we have authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, let us ask God for integrity and reject all unjust profit.
exp.7:4:
The elders of Israel tell Samuel that he is now old and that his sons do not follow his example. So they ask him to appoint a king to rule over them, just like the other nations.

The leaders of the people speak, gathered in Ramah, where Samuel lived. His sons, who were judges, took bribes and twisted justice. Their complaint had some merit, but the desire to be like all the other nations showed that they wanted to stop depending on God as their king. God Himself made this clear to Samuel shortly afterward.

For today: when we face real problems, such as injustice or the failures of leaders, let us first seek God's guidance in prayer, and not thoughtlessly copy the world's solutions.
exp.7:5:
This verse says that the request for a king displeased Samuel, or sat badly with him, because the people asked for a king to govern and judge them. The verse says the thing displeased Samuel, so the word used there is the one that matters here. Faced with that displeasure, Samuel did not argue or become angry with the people; instead he prayed to the Lord, that is, to God.

The elders of Israel speak with Samuel, who is now old, in Ramah. His sons were not following his example, and that is why they ask for a king like those of the other nations. Samuel felt rejected, but God explains to him that the one truly rejected is Him.

When something hurts us or offends us, the first thing we can do is bring it to God in prayer. In this way we avoid reacting in anger, and we give God room to clarify our hearts and guide us.
exp.7:8:
In this verse God tells Samuel to listen to the people and give them a king. But first he must warn them with seriousness, and explain to them the rights the king would claim over them, which here means the customs and demands a king would place on them.

God speaks to Samuel. The Israelites asked for a king like the other nations. God explains that they are rejecting not only Samuel, but Him as their King. Even so, He allows them to choose, but He wants them to know what it will cost them, for the king would take their sons, their goods, and their labor.

God respects our freedom, but He does not hide the consequences from us. Before asking for something that seems like a good idea, it is wise to pray and ask ourselves what it will cost us and whether we are putting God in second place.
exp.7:11:
It says the king will appoint some of the people's sons as commanders over thousands and commanders over fifties, that is, officers of the army. Others he will force to plow his fields and reap his harvests (the wheat or barley crops). They will also have to make weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots, that is, the gear and parts for the battle chariots.

Samuel, the prophet and judge, is speaking. The people had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. God told Samuel to warn them clearly what the king's demands on them would be. It was a warning, not a command.

For today: before we place our trust in any leader, system, or human security, let us consider the cost. Only God deserves our complete trust, and He never charges us too much.
exp.7:12:
This verse says the king would take the daughters of the Israelites to put them to his service. The ones who prepared perfumes and ointments, the cooks who prepared the food, and the bakers who made the bread were all tasks for the king's household and court.

The prophet Samuel is speaking. The people had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. God told him to warn them how a king would act. Samuel lists what the king would demand: sons, daughters, lands, and a share of the harvests. It is a warning, not a command from God for kings.

For today: before we insist on getting something, let us think about what it will cost us. And let us remember that no human leader can take the place of God in our lives.
exp.7:13:
It says that the king the people ask for will take their fields, their vineyards, and their best olive groves, and give them to his servants, that is, to his attendants and officials. The olive groves are orchards of olive trees, an important source of food and wealth.

The speaker is the prophet Samuel. Israel asked for a king so as to be like the other nations, and this grieved Samuel. God told him to warn them how a king would act. This list of abuses shows the cost of placing trust in a human ruler instead of in God. Some scholars see here a general warning about human power; others see a description of what later happened in the monarchy.

For today: before we place all our hope in a person, a leader, or a system, let us remember that none of them can take the place of God. Let us pray for those who govern, and trust Him first.
exp.7:15:
Here the text says that the king will take for himself the workers and servants of the people, their best young men, and their donkeys, to use in the king's labor. The people who worked in the households are the ones it describes as servants, and the strong young men are the ones it calls the young men. Donkeys were very valuable beasts of burden.

Samuel speaks to the people of Israel, who had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. God told him to warn them plainly about what it would cost. Samuel describes how a human king, with so much power, would demand much from them. Many understand this as a serious warning and not as a simple list of rules.

For today: before we trust someone or something to give us security, let us think about what it will ask of us in return. Let us place our trust first in God, who serves his people with love.
exp.7:16:
It says the king would take a tenth of the people's sheep and goats. "Will take a tenth" means taking one out of every ten. In the end, the people would no longer be free and would live as servants of the king, working for him.

Samuel is the one speaking. The people had asked for a king so that they would be like the other nations, and Samuel was saddened. God told him to warn them clearly about how a king would rule. Even so, the people did not want to listen and kept demanding a king. Some see here a rejection of God being their King.

For today: before we insist on getting something, let us think about what it will cost us. What we desire can end up controlling us. Let us ask God for wisdom and trust that He cares for us better than any human power.
exp.7:17:
It says the people will cry out in pain because of the king they chose for themselves. And on that day the Lord will not listen to them. Samuel is the one speaking. Israel asked for a king to be like the other nations, and Samuel warns them what it would cost: the king would take their sons, servants, animals and part of their possessions. Samuel speaks this way because God told him to warn them. Many understand that God's silence would speak of the consequences of their decision, not of a total rejection of them.

Before making an important decision, ask yourself what it might cost you and whether you are seeking God's guidance or just copying what others do. God loves us, but decisions have consequences.
exp.8:1:
This verse introduces Saul, the son of Kish. He is described as a young man, and as very handsome and good-looking. It is said that no one in Israel surpassed him in attractiveness, and that he stood taller than all the others, head and shoulders above them. Saying he surpassed the others means that he stood out above them.

The narrator introduces Saul just as Israel is asking for a king. His family has been mentioned before, and later we will see him set out to look for some lost donkeys. The description highlights his outward appearance, something the people valued in a leader. Later the story will show that appearance is not what matters most.

Today we can remember that beauty, talent, or height are not enough to form character. Let us ask God for a humble and obedient heart, rather than seeking only what is seen on the outside.
exp.8:2:
This verse tells us that the donkeys belonging to Kish, Saul's father, had been lost. Kish then told his son to take one of the servants and go out to look for them. The female donkeys are the she-asses in the verse, animals very valuable for work and transport.

Kish speaks here. He is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, described as a man of substance, that is, of good standing and respect. Before this moment, Israel had asked for a king, and the text presents Saul, a tall and handsome young man. This ordinary task, searching for lost animals, becomes the way by which Saul will come to meet Samuel. The Bible does not explain this here, but the account shows how God can work through everyday events.

For today: do not despise small tasks or setbacks. Do them with responsibility and trust in God, because he can use the ordinary to guide your life.
exp.8:4:
It says that Saul and his servant reached the land of Zuph, and that Saul wanted to turn back. He thought that his father, Kish, would no longer be worried about the lost donkeys but would be anxious about them instead. Saul is speaking, a young man whom his father sent to look for some lost donkeys. After searching several regions without success, he grows tired of looking and thinks about his family. What follows shows that the servant suggests consulting a man of God, and so the meeting with Samuel begins. We do not know for certain the exact location of Zuph.

Saul was concerned about how his father was feeling. Sometimes, when things do not turn out as we hope, it is good to think also of those who love us and are waiting for us. And, as happened here, sometimes a simple piece of advice from someone else leads us to seek God.
exp.8:5:
The servant of Saul answers that there is a man of God in that city who is held in high regard. He says that everything this man declares comes true, so he proposes that they go to see him. Perhaps he will show them the way they should go.

The servant of Saul is speaking. They have searched through several regions for the lost donkeys of Kish, the father of Saul, and have not found them. Saul wants to turn back so as not to worry his father. The servant proposes that they seek out this man of God, who, according to the text, is Samuel. His name is not yet mentioned here, but the account confirms it later on.

When we do not know which path to take, it is wise to seek counsel from people who live close to God and know his Word. It is also good to listen to someone who speaks to us with humility, like this servant. And while we ask for counsel, let us pray that God himself will guide us.
exp.8:7:
Here the servant of Saul answers that he has in his hand a fourth part of a shekel of silver. The word "answered" carries the sense of replying again, and "man of God" means a man of God, a prophet. The servant offers that money to the prophet so that he may tell them which way to take.

Saul and his servant were looking for the donkeys of Saul's father that had been lost. They had no more bread, and they thought they could not appear empty-handed before the man of God. It was customary to bring a gift to the one being consulted. The servant, practical and attentive, solves the problem.

For today: when we seek direction from God, let us do it with humility and generosity. Also, God can use ordinary people, like this servant, to guide others toward his will.
exp.8:9:
Saul agrees that his servant has a good idea, and the two of them set out for the city where the man of God lived.

Saul is looking for his father Kish's donkeys, which have wandered off, and he does not know what to do next. The servant suggests they consult the seer, the prophet, and offers to give a small amount of silver as a gift. Saul accepts the advice. The seer here is Samuel, although the text does not yet name him.

For today: Saul was the leader, yet he was willing to listen to good advice from someone under his authority. When we are lost or have no answers, it is wise to listen to those who counsel us with good sense and to seek God's guidance, without letting pride get in the way.
exp.8:11:
The young women answer Saul that yes, the seer is right there in front of them. They tell him to hurry, because the man came to the city today, and the people have a sacrifice today at the high place.

These young women were going out to draw water from the well. Saul and his servant had been looking for his father's donkeys that had been lost, and they had come to ask about Samuel, who was called the seer. The women give them precise and urgent information, since Samuel was about to go up and bless the meal of the sacrifice. Without knowing it, Saul is about to meet the one whom God will use to anoint him as king.

For today: God often guides our steps through simple things, like an ordinary conversation with someone on the way. Pay attention to the opportunities that come your way and act with diligence, trusting that God works even in the everyday.
exp.8:13:
Saul and his servant went up into the city. As they were entering, right in the middle of it, they came upon Samuel, who was coming toward them to go up to the high place. The high place was an elevated site where sacrifices were offered and religious ceremonies were held.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys, and he went to ask about the seer. Some young women told him that Samuel was about to arrive. The meeting seems accidental, but the text that follows shows that God had already announced it to Samuel.

God can guide our steps even in ordinary things, such as searching for something lost. We do not always notice it at the time, but we can trust that he is at work. Live each day with attention and with faith.
exp.8:15:
God tells Samuel that the next day, at this same time, he will send him a man from the land of Benjamin. Samuel was to anoint him (pour oil on him as a sign that God had chosen him) as ruler, that is, leader of Israel. This man would deliver the people from the Philistines. God says he has looked upon his people because their cry has come up to him.

This speaks on the day before Saul arrived. Israel was suffering under Philistine oppression and had asked for a king. Saul was searching for his father's lost donkeys, without knowing that God was guiding him toward Samuel. God already had a plan in place.

For today: God hears the cry of those who suffer and acts in his own time, often in ways we do not see. You can pray with confidence, knowing that he sees you and cares for you.
exp.8:17:
Saul meets Samuel at the entrance of the city, at the gate, and politely asks him to tell him where the seer lives. "Seer" was another name for the prophet, someone to whom God showed things. Saul does not know that he is already speaking with the very person he is looking for.

Saul, a young man from Benjamin, is searching for his father's lost donkeys. God had already told Samuel that on that day the man who would be prince over Israel would arrive. Saul comes without knowing any of this, but God is guiding him in the middle of an ordinary task.

God can work in our everyday days, even in small problems, to lead us toward something greater. It is wise to faithfully do what is before us and to trust that He directs our steps, even when we cannot yet see all of his plan.
exp.8:20:
Saul answers Samuel with amazement and humility. He says that he is from Benjamin, one of the smallest tribes of Israel, and that his family is the least important of that tribe. That is why he does not understand why Samuel speaks to him about something so great. The phrase "such a thing" refers to Samuel's statement that all of Israel's desire is set on him.

Here Saul speaks, a young man who was looking for his father's lost donkeys. Samuel, the prophet, already knew that God had chosen him as the future king. That Benjamin was "small" probably alludes to its size or little influence, and the Bible suggests something of this in Judges 20–21. Saul sees himself as unimportant.

For today: God does not look at what we appear to be, small or unimportant. We can accept his calling with humility, without boasting and without making excuses out of fear, trusting that He equips us.
exp.8:21:
Samuel took Saul by the hand and brought him and his servant into the dining hall where the meal was being served. He gave them the place of honor, at the head of the table, among about thirty guests.

Samuel is a prophet and judge of Israel. Saul had been searching for some lost donkeys, and God had already told Samuel that this young man would be the first king. Saul had just said that he came from a small tribe and a small family. Samuel answers by honoring him, though he does not yet tell him everything.

For today: God often honors people who are simple and humble, even when they do not see themselves as important. We can receive others with respect and trust that God knows what he is preparing for us, even when we do not yet understand it.
exp.8:24:
This verse tells that Samuel and Saul came down from the high place, a raised spot where sacrifices and meals were held, into the city. There Samuel talked with Saul upon the top of the house, that is, the flat roof of the house, a quiet and secluded place.

The narrator now relates what followed the feast. Samuel already knew, because God had shown him, that Saul would be the first king of Israel. The text does not say what they talked about that night; some think Samuel was preparing him for what was coming, but that is a guess.

For today: before major decisions or callings, God often uses moments of calm and conversation. Look for quiet spaces to listen, and surround yourself with wise people who speak to you with patience.
exp.8:26:
Samuel and Saul were walking down to the edge of the town. Then Samuel asked Saul to tell the young servant to go on ahead. The servant went on ahead, and Samuel asked Saul to stay behind for a moment so he could tell him a word from God.

Samuel speaks here as the prophet and judge of Israel. Saul had come looking for his father's lost donkeys, and God had already told Samuel that this man would lead the people. Samuel wants a private moment, with no one else present, to give him the message. Soon he will anoint him, as the next chapter describes.

For today: sometimes God speaks best when we stop. Pause, turn off the noise, and stop rushing, even for a few minutes, so you can listen to his Word calmly, without hurry or distraction.
exp.9:0:
Samuel takes a small flask of oil and pours it on Saul's head. Then he kisses him and asks whether it is not the Lord who has anointed him as leader over his people.

Samuel speaks as a prophet and judge of Israel. Israel had asked for a king, and God allowed Saul to be the first. Samuel anoints him privately, and the kiss was probably a sign of respect and affection. Afterward he gives him signs to confirm that God was with him. Scholars debate how to understand that first anointing, but the text stresses that the calling comes from God.

God can call us to a task without our seeking it. If we receive a responsibility, let us remember that it is not ours: we serve in what belongs to God, and we should do so with humility and depending on Him.
exp.9:1:
Here Samuel tells Saul that on that same day, as he leaves Samuel's side, he will meet two men near Rachel's grave, in the territory of Benjamin. They will bring him news: the lost female donkeys have been found, and his father has stopped worrying about them, but now he is distressed about him and asks what he will do for his son.

Samuel has just anointed Saul as leader of Israel. To confirm that all of this comes from God, he gives him concrete signs that will come true along the way. The exact location of Zelzah is not known with certainty.

God can show us that He knows our small worries and our great ones. While we go around and around a problem, He is already at work somewhere else. We can trust that He cares for us and for those we love, even when we cannot see how.
exp.9:2:
Samuel goes on telling Saul what will happen to him on his way home. When he reaches the plain of Tabor, he will meet three men going up to God at Bethel. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and the third a bottle of wine. "Going up to God" means they are heading to a place of worship, probably to offer sacrifices.

Samuel has just anointed Saul with oil, a sign that God chose him to lead Israel. These specific signs, which would happen one after another, would confirm that Saul was not acting on his own impulse but that God was guiding him. The exact location of this plain of Tabor is not known with certainty.

God often gives us small, concrete signs to encourage us when He calls us to something great. We can pay attention to those everyday details and remember that He watches over our steps, even in the ordinary parts of the road.
exp.9:7:
Here Samuel tells Saul to go down ahead of him to Gilgal. Samuel would come afterward to offer sacrifices: the burnt offerings, which were wholly burned up for God, and the peace offerings, which were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving. Saul was to wait seven days, until Samuel came to tell him what to do.

Samuel, the prophet, has just anointed Saul as future king and has given him signs to confirm that God was with him. This command was a test of obedience at the beginning of his reign. Later, in 1 Samuel 13, Saul did not wait for the appointed time, although interpreters debate exactly how that scene relates to this command.

For today: God calls us to obey, and also to wait. Even when we have a good opportunity or a lot of pressure, trusting his timing protects our hearts from hasty decisions.
exp.9:9:
It says that Saul came to the hill, that is, to a height or hill. There he met a group of prophets coming toward him. Then the Spirit of God came upon him with power, and Saul prophesied among them. Here "prophesied" means speaking or praising under the influence of God.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, and he relates what Samuel had announced to Saul after anointing him as future king. Samuel gave him several signs to confirm that God was with him. This was the last one. The text says that God changed his heart, preparing him for his new task. The verses that follow show that the people were amazed.

For today: God is the one who equips those he calls. If you feel that a task is too big for you, ask him for his Spirit and trust that he sustains you. But remember that a powerful experience does not replace a life of continual obedience.
exp.9:13:
It says that Saul's uncle asked him and his servant where they had gone. Saul answered that they went out to look for the lost donkeys, and that when they saw the donkeys were nowhere to be found, they went to Samuel. The word "were" appears in the verse itself, so no note is needed on it.

Saul had just been anointed in secret by Samuel as the future king, and he had experienced signs that confirmed it, including prophesying with a group of prophets. His uncle, curious, asks him about the trip. Saul answers, but according to the verses that follow, he keeps silent about the matter of the kingdom. The Bible does not explain why; some think it was humility or prudence, others that it was fear or insecurity.

For today: not everything God entrusts to us must be told right away. Ask him for wisdom to know when to speak and when to keep silent, and treat with respect what God is only beginning to do in your life.
exp.9:15:
Saul tells his uncle what happened with the donkeys: that Samuel had assured them the animals had already been found. Saul did not tell him anything about the kingdom, that is, that Samuel had anointed him as the future king.

Saul had gone out to look for his father's lost donkeys and ended up with the prophet Samuel. There he received an enormous piece of news: God had chosen him to rule Israel. His uncle asks him with curiosity, and Saul answers only part of it. The Bible does not explain why he kept quiet; it could have been humility, prudence, or fear, and this cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: not everything God entrusts to us must be shared right away. Asking God for wisdom helps us know when to speak and when to wait, with humility and without boasting.
exp.9:21:
The Israelites inquired of God again to find out whether Saul, the chosen man, had yet arrived. God answered that Saul was hidden among the baggage, that is, among the luggage and supplies of the people gathered there.

Samuel had called the people together at Mizpah to present the first king of Israel. The choice was made by lot, tribe by tribe, until it came to Saul, but they could not find him. Then the people asked the Lord, and He Himself showed where he was. The text does not say why he hid himself; many think it was out of fear or humility, but the passage does not make this clear.

For today: sometimes we feel small or afraid in the face of what God calls us to do. We can come to Him with sincerity, and remember that He knows where we are and can encourage us to move forward.
exp.9:22:
They ran and brought him out from where he was hiding, and set him in front of everyone. He looked very tall: he stood head and shoulders above anyone else.

Samuel gathered Israel at Mizpah to present the first king. By casting lots, God pointed out the tribe, then the family, and finally Saul. The account does not explain why he hid; many think he felt fear or humility before such a responsibility. His height caught the people's attention, though it was God who chose him.

For today: not everything that impresses the eye is the most important. God calls people who feel small or unsure, and invites us not to hide from what He asks of us, but to trust Him.
exp.9:23:
Samuel speaks to all the people and asks them to look at Saul, the man whom the Lord chose. He says there is no one like him among all Israel. The people answer with shouts of joy: "Long live the king!" Here the word "shouted" means calling out loudly, and "like" means alike or the same.

Samuel, the prophet and judge of Israel, has just cast lots to point out the first king. Saul was chosen, but he was hiding among the baggage. Samuel presents him as God's choice, not the people's idea. Also, Saul stood out for his height, and the people are excited because of it.

For today: God chooses and uses people who sometimes feel small or doubt themselves. We can trust his calling, and at the same time remember that looking only at outward appearance is not enough; what matters is obeying God.
exp.10:0:
This verse tells that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, came up with his army and pitched his camp against Jabesh-gilead, an Israelite town. Afraid, the people of the town asked him to make a peace agreement with them, and they offered to serve him, that is, to put themselves under his rule.

Here the men of Jabesh are speaking. They were in a weak position and were seeking to save their lives. This happens at the beginning of Saul's reign, at a time when Israel had no leader who could defend it clearly. What follows shows that Nahash's offer was cruel and humiliating.

For today: when we feel fear, it is easy to accept quick solutions that cost us our dignity or our faith. Before giving in, it is wise to stop, ask God for help, and seek the counsel of other believers.
exp.10:1:
Nahash, king of the Ammonites, tells the men of Jabesh that he will make a treaty with them only if each one agrees to have his right eye gouged out. He says that this will bring a public shame, a humiliation, upon all of Israel.

The people of Jabesh Gilead were surrounded by the Ammonite army, and they offered to surrender and serve him. Nahash was not seeking peace, but cruelly intended to humiliate the whole people of Israel. For this reason the elders ask for seven days to look for help. This happens before Saul rescues them.

For today: there are people who offer agreements that in reality aim to harm and humiliate. Before accepting any deal, it is wise to examine their intentions and to seek help from others, as the elders of Jabesh did. God invites us to seek counsel and support within the community.
exp.10:9:
The men of Jabesh tell their enemies, the Ammonites, that they will come out to them the next day. They offer to let the Ammonites do with them whatever seems good to them. The phrase about what seems good to them is simply that: whatever seems good to you.

The people of Jabesh of Gilead were surrounded by the Ammonites. They had already sent word asking for help from Saul and from Israel, and news had reached them that they would be delivered. Many understand that their words sounded like surrender, but they concealed their hope of rescue. The text does not explain this, so it is one possible interpretation.

For today: when you find yourself surrounded by a problem, do not lose hope. If God has already given you a promise or help is on its way, wait with confidence, and be wise in what you say and do.
exp.10:10:
It says that Saul organized Israel's army into three groups. The next day, during the last part of the night (the watch just before dawn, near sunrise), they entered the Ammonite camp by surprise. They attacked them until the sun grew hot, that is, until close to midday. The Ammonites who survived were so scattered that not even two of them were left together.

Here the narrator tells how Saul rescued Jabesh-gilead. The Ammonites had laid siege to it and had threatened its people with great shame. Saul had gathered Israel, and the messengers had already promised deliverance for tomorrow, by the time the sun grew hot. The plan was carried out, and then Saul gives the victory to the LORD.

For today: God often works where there is courage, order, and unity. Do diligently what is yours to do, and then acknowledge that the victory comes from God, without boasting.
exp.10:12:
Saul says that no one is going to be put to death that day. The reason he gives is that the Lord has brought salvation to Israel. Saul does not take credit for the victory himself but gives the glory to God.

Saul is speaking just after being proclaimed king, following his defeat of the Ammonites who were threatening Jabesh Gilead. Some of the people had doubted that he could reign, and now they wanted to put them to death. Saul stops that revenge. Then Samuel leads the people to Gilgal to renew the kingdom and to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving to God.

For today: when God gives us a victory, we can respond with humility and mercy, not with pride or revenge. Giving thanks to God and forgiving those who doubted us shows a heart that has received grace.
exp.11:1:
Samuel tells the Israelites that they now have a king to lead them. He himself is old and gray-headed, and his sons are among the people. He has lived before them from his youth until this day.

Samuel speaks at an assembly in Gilgal, after Saul had been made king. The people had asked for a king, and Samuel lays down his role as judge. Before he steps aside, he reminds them of his conduct over his whole life, so that they can examine it. The verses that follow show that he submits himself to their testimony.

For today: live in such a way that your conduct over the years can speak for you. Integrity is built day by day, and whoever has been honest can give an account with calm and humility.
exp.11:2:
Samuel stands before all the people and invites them to accuse him, if they can, of any wrong.
