He asks whether he has taken anyone's ox or donkey, whether he has cheated or oppressed anyone, or whether he has accepted a bribe to look the other way. A bribe is what is meant by the bribe he asks about, and to look the other way is to let an injustice pass in exchange for money. If there were anything like that, he promises to make it right.

Samuel speaks at the end of his time as judge. Israel had just asked for a king, and he now presents them to the new king, Saul. Now elderly, he wants to make it clear that he exercised his authority with honesty. The anointed one here refers to the king. All the people acknowledge that Samuel was upright.

For today: live in such a way that we can be held accountable without fear. Let us take care with the small decisions about money, work, and how we treat others, so that our conscience and our witness are clean before God and before people.
exp.11:7:
When Jacob and his family arrived in Egypt, their descendants suffered and asked God for help. Then God sent Moses and Aaron, who brought them out of Egypt and settled them in the promised land (the phrase "this place" in the original). Some old words: "cried out" means they asked for help at the top of their voices; the small word "to" is just a plain connecting word.

The prophet Samuel speaks at an assembly in Gilgal, after Saul had already been confirmed as king. Samuel reminds the people of the story of God's faithfulness. He wants to show them that God always rescued them when they cried out, and that their true king and savior is the LORD. Then he mentions how the people forgot God again and again.

Today, this verse invites us to remember how God has helped us in the past. Take a few minutes this week to recall the times He sustained you, thank Him, and trust that He will also hear you when you cry out to Him today.
exp.11:9:
This verse recalls what the people of Israel did when they were oppressed: they cried out to God, acknowledged their sin, and promised to serve him again. The gods Baalim and Ashtaroth were false gods of the neighboring peoples.

Samuel, now an old man, speaks at the close of his leadership. He reviews their history to show them that God always responded when they repented. Through this he wants them to see that asking for a human king revealed little trust in God, their true King.

For today: when you realize you have drifted away from God, do not wait until you are in a bigger crisis. Return to him with sincerity, name what you did wrong, and ask him for help. His mercy remains open to anyone who comes back with a sincere heart.
exp.11:10:
God answered the cry of his people and sent them deliverers: Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel. Through them he rescued them from the enemies all around, and they lived in safety. "Jerubbaal" is another name for Gideon. About Bedan we are not certain: some think it is a copying error or a little-known name for one of the judges.

In his farewell speech to Israel, Samuel reminds them that every time they turned back to God, he saved them. He says this because they are now asking for a king, as if God were not enough to protect them.

For today: when you feel threatened, remember how God has helped you before. Before looking for security in other things, return to him sincerely and trust that he is still faithful.
exp.11:12:
Here Samuel says to the people: "Look, this is the king you chose and asked for." But he adds that the Lord is the one who set him over them. That is, the people asked for him, and God allowed it.

Samuel speaks at an assembly in Gilgal, when Saul had already been confirmed as king. Samuel is about to step down from leadership. He reminds them that, facing the threat of Nahash the Ammonite, they asked for a human king, even though God was already their King. Right after this he calls them to obey God, both the people and the king.

For today: our decisions have consequences, even when God permits them. Before asking for something out of anxiety or fear, it is good to pray and ask ourselves whether we trust God. And after deciding, the best course is to keep obeying him with humility.
exp.11:15:
This verse says that Samuel invites the people to stand still and carefully watch something great that God is about to do before their own eyes.

Samuel, the prophet and judge who is now an old man, is speaking. Israel had asked for a king, and Samuel reminds them that what matters is obeying God, both the people and the king. Since it was the season of the wheat harvest, normally a dry time, God sent thunder and rain. That sign showed them that asking for a king, for the reasons they had, had been a mistake before God.

Today, God remains the one who deserves our trust more than any human leader or plan. Before we seek security in other things, we can stop, listen to his voice, and obey him with humility.
exp.11:16:
Samuel reminds them that it is wheat harvest time, when normally it does not rain. He tells them that he will pray to God and that God will send thunder and rain. This will serve as a sign so that they understand that their wickedness was great in asking for a king.

Samuel speaks in his farewell as judge of Israel. The people already have Saul as king, but Samuel wants them to understand that, in asking for one, they distrusted that God was their true king. The storm out of season confirmed his word, and the people acknowledged their sin.

Today, this passage invites us to humbly recognize when we have placed our trust in something other than God. He does not reject us for it; He calls us to return to Him and to follow Him with all our heart.
exp.11:17:
Samuel prayed to God, and that same day God sent thunder and rain. When the people saw it, they felt a great fear of God and also of Samuel. The phrase about their fear, meaning that they felt a deep reverence and dread, is the point of the verse.

Samuel is speaking to the Israelites, who had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. He sees that request as a rejection of God being their King. It was the time of the wheat harvest, when it normally did not rain, so the storm was a clear sign that God was speaking.

For today: when you recognize a mistake, do not stay with only fear or guilt. As the context shows, return to God with sincerity and keep serving him with all your heart, because his forgiveness and his guidance are still available.
exp.11:19:
Samuel tells the people not to be afraid. He acknowledges that they did wrong, but he asks them not to turn away from God. Instead of running from Him out of shame, they should serve Him with all their heart. The phrase "do not turn aside from following the Lord" means not stopping in your following of the Lord.

Samuel speaks after God sent thunder and rain as a sign. The people were frightened, because they had asked for a king like the other nations, and that showed little trust in God. Samuel does not downplay their sin, but neither does he condemn them without hope. He invites them to return to God.

When we fail, guilt can pull us away from God. This verse encourages us to do the opposite: to admit our mistake, draw near to Him, and keep serving Him today with sincerity.
exp.11:23:
It says that the people should revere and honor God, and serve him sincerely and with all their heart. The reason is that they should remember the great things he has done for them. "Fear" here means to reverence with respect and trust, not to live in dread. Serving him truly means serving him honestly, without pretense.

Samuel, now old, speaks in his farewell address. Israel had just asked for a king, and Samuel reminds them that God will not abandon them. He calls them not to turn away from him, and then warns them of the consequences if they insist on doing evil.

For today: when you feel tempted to serve God out of habit or just to fulfill an obligation, stop and call to mind what he has done in your life. Giving thanks for what you have received awakens a sincere desire to obey him and serve him with joy, not out of duty.
exp.12:0:
The verse says that Saul had already been king for a year, and that after he had reigned two years over Israel, what follows happened. The phrasing looks odd in the text, and with reason: in the Hebrew the numbers seem incomplete or damaged. For that reason modern translations present it in different ways, and scholars do not agree on how many years Saul reigned at this point.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of the book. He wants to place us in time before telling of Saul's first great war against the Philistines, enemies who dominated the region.

For today: power and success are not permanent, and they are not measured only by years. What matters is how we live each stage. Let us ask God for obedience and humility from the beginning, because Saul's early days show us how fragile a good start can be.
exp.12:1:
Saul chose three thousand men of Israel to form a small army. Two thousand stayed with him at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with his son Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. He sent the rest of the people home, each man to his own house.

The narrator of the book speaks here, describing how Saul organized his army at the beginning of his reign. Israel lived under pressure from the Philistines, their enemies. This step prepares for Jonathan's attack that comes later and for the whole conflict that follows. The figures for Saul's reign in the previous verse are difficult, and scholars explain them in different ways.

For today: great challenges are met with concrete, orderly steps, but without forgetting that victory depends on God, not only on our preparation. Let us plan wisely and trust in Him.
exp.12:3:
What it says: All Israel heard that Saul had defeated the Philistine outpost. They also learned that the Philistines now despised them. Then the people gathered to Saul at Gilgal.

Context: This is the narrator's account. Although the text says that Saul struck the garrison, the previous verse says it was Jonathan. Some think Saul received the credit as king, and others think he blew the trumpets and claimed the victory. It is not certain. The attack provoked Philistine fury and put Israel in danger.

For today: A brave action can bring harsh and unexpected consequences. Before acting, let us seek God's guidance and not only the applause of people. And when pressure comes, let us trust in Him, not in our pride.
exp.12:4:
The Philistines gathered together to fight against Israel: thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and soldiers as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They came up and set up camp at Michmash, east of Beth-aven. The sand of the seashore is a comparison meaning an uncountable crowd.

The narrator is the author of the book, who tells what happened after Jonathan attacked a Philistine garrison. Saul blew the trumpets to call Israel together, and the Philistines responded with great force. Some scholars think the number of chariots is very large, or that the text may have been copied differently, but the point is that Israel was greatly outmatched.

When we face problems that seem bigger than we are, fear can paralyze us, as it did Israel. Today we can bring that fear to God in prayer before we act, and trust that he continues to care for us.
exp.12:5:
This verse tells us that the Israelites realized they were in great danger. Seeing the enemy so numerous, the people became frightened and looked for places to hide: in caves, holes, cliffs, rocks, and cisterns (pits used to store water).

The narrator of the book speaks here. Saul, the first king of Israel, had attacked a Philistine garrison, and the Philistines responded with an enormous army. The Israelites gathered at Gilgal, but fear took over them, and some fled across the Jordan. Samuel had not yet arrived.

For today: when fear closes in on us, we are tempted to hide or to act on impulse. It is better to stop, pray, and trust God, waiting patiently for his direction.
exp.12:6:
This verse says that, facing the threat of the Philistines, some Hebrews fled across the Jordan River to the lands of Gad and Gilead. Saul stayed in Gilgal, but the people who were still with him were trembling, that is, filled with great fear.

This is a moment of crisis early in Saul's reign. The narrator is the author of the book, who describes how the Israelite army was falling apart out of fear. Samuel had told Saul to wait in Gilgal, and the next verse shows the pressure he was under: the people were scattering, and Saul ended up offering the sacrifice without waiting for Samuel.

For today: when fear presses in, it is tempting to act quickly and in our own way. Before deciding, stop, pray, and ask whether you are obeying God or only reacting to pressure.
exp.12:7:
Verse 8 tells us that Saul waited seven days in Gilgal, as Samuel had instructed him. But Samuel did not come, and the people were scattered from him, that is, they left him, abandoning him little by little.

The narrator describes the pressure Saul was under. The Philistines threatened Israel, the people hid in caves, and others fled across the Jordan. Those who stayed with Saul trembled with fear. Saul had been commanded to wait for Samuel, who would offer the sacrifice. Seeing the army fall apart, Saul grew desperate and offered the burnt offering himself. The following passage recounts this.

When God asks us to wait and everything seems to be falling apart, it is tempting to take shortcuts. Obedience includes trusting God's timing, even when pressure is screaming at us to act now.
exp.12:8:
Saul orders that the complete offering be brought to him, called a "burnt offering" (an animal burned entirely for God), along with the "peace offerings" (offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving). Then he himself offers the burnt offering.

Saul is the first king of Israel. He was at Gilgal, with the Philistines preparing to attack and his people fleeing in fear. Samuel, the prophet, had told him to wait seven days, but he was taking a long time. Saul grew impatient and offered the sacrifice himself, something that was Samuel's task to do as priest and prophet. The verses that follow show that this was a serious mistake.

For today: when the pressure rises and God seems slow, it is tempting to act on our own. Let us learn to wait and obey, trusting that God knows the right time.
exp.12:12:
Samuel tells Saul that he acted foolishly. The phrase about acting foolishly means that he did not act with wisdom. To be commanded means to have been given an order or charge. Saul did not obey God's command, and because of this he lost the chance for his kingdom to be secure over Israel forever.

Samuel, a prophet and judge, speaks to Saul, the first king. Saul had waited for Samuel in Gilgal, but when he saw the people scattering and the Philistines gathering, he offered the burnt offering himself. That was something that was not his to do. Saul justified it by fear and pressure, but Samuel calls it disobedience.

Today, when pressure builds, it is tempting to take shortcuts and give reasons that sound good. But trusting God includes waiting and obeying, even when we do not see results. Before deciding under pressure, ask yourself: does this honor what God has already told me?
exp.12:21:
It tells us that when the day of battle came, the soldiers of Israel had no swords or spears. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Earlier, it is explained that the Philistines did not allow any blacksmiths to remain in Israel, so that the Israelites could not make weapons. The people depended on them even to sharpen their farming tools. In this way the text shows how weak and subjugated the nation was.

For today: sometimes we feel without resources in the face of a big problem. This verse reminds us that a lack of means is not the end of the story. God can work even when we see ourselves as small, so we can pray, trust, and take the next step with humility, without relying only on what we have.
exp.13:1:
This verse tells where King Saul was while his son Jonathan went out to attack. Saul was on the outskirts of Gibeah, resting under a pomegranate tree, close to a place called Migron. With him were about six hundred men, a very small army.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He wants us to see the contrast: Saul, the king, is still and without a plan, while Jonathan, without telling him, takes a risk in faith. Some scholars think the pomegranate tree shows Saul's passivity, although the text does not say this clearly.

For today: sometimes we expect others to take the first step. God can use the one who trusts in Him and acts with courage and humility. Ask Him for wisdom to know when to leave comfort behind and obey Him.
exp.13:2:
Here is the verse: Ahiah, the son of Ahitub, the brother of Ichabod, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli, the Lord's priest in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. And the people knew not that Jonathan was gone.

This passage introduces Ahiah, the priest who was with Saul and wore the ephod, a priestly garment used to seek guidance from God. It explains that he was the son of Ahitub and a descendant of Eli, the priest of Shiloh. It also says that the people did not know Jonathan had left.

The narrator tells this as Jonathan secretly heads out toward the Philistine camp. Israel was weak, and Saul had about six hundred men. The mention of Eli's family recalls a priestly line under judgment, and the name Ichabod evokes the loss of God's glory. Some think Ahiah is the same person as Ahimelech, but this is not certain.

For today: God can work even when the outlook seems bleak and no one notices. Before taking a step of faith, let us seek his direction with humility, and act with courage and wisdom.
exp.13:4:
This verse describes the location of two rocky cliffs or crags in the pass where Jonathan wanted to cross. One stood to the north, facing Michmash, where the Philistine garrison was. The other stood to the south, facing Gibeah, where the Israelite side was.

Here the book's narrator speaks. He wants the reader to picture the difficult terrain over which Jonathan and his armor-bearer took their risk. Israel was at a disadvantage against the Philistines. Jonathan acts without telling the people, trusting that God could work. The names Bozez and Seneh appear in the context, but their exact meaning is not certain.

For today: sometimes the path God sets before us is narrow and difficult. Even so, we can take a step of faith, with prudence and prayer, trusting that it is no trouble for God to help, whether we have much or little.
exp.13:8:
Jonathan tells his armor-bearer how they will recognize what God wants them to do. If the Philistines call out to them, "Wait until we come to you," then they will stand still in their place and will not go up to them.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, is speaking during the war against the Philistines. He and his armor-bearer approach the enemy outpost alone. Jonathan does not want to act on impulse but proposes a sign: the Philistines' reaction would show whether God is giving them the victory. If the enemies come down, they will wait; if they invite them to come up, they will go.

For today: before taking an important step, we can pray and calmly look for clear signs of God's guidance, without rushing ahead. It is also wise to know how to wait when doors do not open.
exp.13:11:
The Philistine soldiers of the garrison, that is, the outpost, call out to Jonathan and his armourbearer (the one who carried his weapons) and say, "Come up to us, and we will shew you a thing." It was a mocking challenge. Jonathan tells his armourbearer to climb up after him, because the Lord has already given the Philistines into the hand of Israel.

Jonathan and his armourbearer had agreed on a sign: if the Philistines invited them to come up, they would take it as a sign that God was giving them the victory. Israel was weak and afraid, and Jonathan acted in faith, not knowing how everything would turn out.

For today: faith can take a concrete step when we see an open door, and trust that God is at work, even when we feel few or weak.
exp.13:12:
This verse tells how Jonathan climbed up a steep slope, using both his hands and his feet, and his armorbearer, the young man who carried his weapons, followed closely behind him. Jonathan struck down the enemies he met at the front, and the young man coming behind finished them off. The armorbearer is the helper or attendant who serves a soldier.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonathan and his armorbearer had come near a Philistine outpost, and the Philistines challenged them to come up. Jonathan took this as a sign and said that the LORD had delivered the enemies into the hands of Israel. They were only two men against a garrison, but Jonathan trusted in God.

For today: when you feel God calling you to take a difficult step, do not expect it to be easy. Move forward with faith, effort, and companionship, as Jonathan did, who climbed up and was not alone.
exp.13:19:
This verse tells how Saul gathered the soldiers who were with him and went to the place of the battle. There they saw that the Philistines, confused, were fighting among themselves: each one used his sword against his companion, and there was a very great slaughter. Saul's men were the ones who came together to face them.

Earlier, Jonathan and his armor-bearer had attacked a Philistine outpost, and God sent great fear and trembling over the enemy camp. Saul, noticing the uproar, stopped consulting the priest and went out to fight. The text presents this victory as the work of God, not only of men. Afterward, even Israelites who had been hiding decided to join in.

Today we can learn that God can change situations that seem impossible. When a person takes a step of faith, as Jonathan did, God can do more than we imagine. Trust, act in faith, and do not forget to give the glory to Him.
exp.13:22:
It was the Lord who gave Israel the victory that day. This verse says he rescued them from the enemy. The pursuit of the fleeing Philistines reached as far as Beth-aven, a place west of the hill country of Michmash. Its exact location is not known for certain.

The narrator is the one speaking. Jonathan had attacked a Philistine outpost with his armor-bearer, and God sent panic into the enemy army. When the Israelites who had been hiding or scattered joined together, the battle turned. The narrator makes clear that the victory came from God, not only from human effort or from Saul's leadership.

For today: when you see progress in your life, give thanks to God and recognize his hand. He can use small, brave actions to open the way, and he also reminds us not to trust only in our own strength.
exp.13:24:
All the people of the land came to a forest, and there was honey on the ground, right where everyone could see it. The phrase about the ground refers to the honey lying on the earth, within easy reach of the hand. In this passage, the people of the land are the Israelite soldiers who were pursuing the Philistines.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had just come out of a victory that God had given them, but they were tired and hungry. Saul, their king, had made a hasty oath: no one was to eat until evening, or they would be cursed. So, although the honey was there, the people did not touch it.

For today: before making promises or giving orders, it is wise to think carefully. A decision made in haste, even when it seems zealous, can burden others with needless weight. Let us ask God for wisdom and calm.
exp.13:28:
Jonathan replies that his father, King Saul, has troubled the land, meaning he has brought serious trouble upon the whole nation. He says that his eyes have been enlightened, that is, he regained strength and spirit after tasting a little honey.

Jonathan speaks with a soldier who told him about Saul's oath, which he had not heard. Israel was pursuing the Philistines, and the people were exhausted and hungry. Jonathan thinks the order was unwise, since it weakened the army just when it most needed strength. The Bible does not say here that God had asked for that fast.

For today: before imposing harsh rules, let us consider whether they truly help or whether they burden others needlessly. Religious zeal needs wisdom and compassion.
exp.13:29:
Jonathan says that if the people had eaten today of the spoil they found among their enemies, the defeat of the Philistines would have been even greater.

Jonathan speaks after his father, King Saul, had made the people swear that no one would eat anything during the battle. Jonathan had not heard that oath and ate a little honey, and his eyes brightened, that is, he regained his strength. He sees that his father's command left the army weak and tired, and for that reason he criticizes the decision.

For today: The decisions of a leader, even when well intended, can harm others if they are made in haste or without wisdom. Before imposing rules or vows, think about how they will affect those who depend on you, and ask God for prudence.
exp.13:31:
This verse tells that the people, very tired and hungry after the battle, rushed upon the spoil. They took sheep, oxen and calves, killed them right there on the ground, and ate the meat with the blood.

The narrator is the author of the book. Saul had made the people swear that they would not eat all day, and they were left worn out. As evening came, hunger pushed them to eat carelessly. The law of Moses forbade eating blood (Leviticus 17:10-14), since life was in it. That is why they reported to Saul that the people were sinning.

Today, pressure and exhaustion can lead us to disobey God. Orders given without wisdom can also push others to fail. Let us seek to decide calmly and lead with prudence, without burdening anyone with unnecessary demands.
exp.13:34:
This verse says that Saul built an altar to the Lord, and that it was the first altar he built. The word "built" is the ordinary sense of the verb here, and "altar" refers to the place where sacrifices were offered to God.

The narrator tells this after the people, hungry following the battle against the Philistines, slaughtered animals and ate the meat with the blood still in it, something the law of Moses forbade. Saul ordered them to slaughter the animals over a large stone. Then he built the altar. Some think it was a sincere act of devotion; others, a hasty act. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when we fail, it is not enough to fix the outward situation quickly. It is wise to return to God with humility and listen to his voice before deciding what to do next.
exp.13:42:
Saul asks Jonathan to tell him what he has done. Jonathan answers honestly: he tasted a little honey with the end of the rod he was carrying in his hand. Then he asks, with grief and amazement, whether for that he has to die.

Saul had made a rash vow: no one was to eat that day while they pursued the enemy. Jonathan did not know about it, because he was not there when it was made. Since Saul received no answer from God, he cast lots to find the guilty one, and the lot fell on his own son. Here Saul questions him, and Jonathan answers without hiding anything.

Jonathan teaches us to tell the truth even when it costs us. The scene also reminds us to think carefully before promising something so forcefully, because hasty decisions can hurt the people we love.
exp.13:44:
Here the people speak up for Jonathan in front of Saul. They ask whether Jonathan, the one who brought such a great victory to Israel, should really be put to death. They swear by the name of the Lord that not one hair of his head will fall to the ground, because that day he acted with God's help. The word for "rescued" here means saved or set free. So the people rescued Jonathan from death.

The speaker is the people of Israel, Saul's army. Saul had made a hasty vow that no one should eat during the battle. Jonathan did not know about it and tasted a little honey. Saul wanted to keep his word at any cost, but the people saw that God was with Jonathan.

For today: it is not enough to be firm in what we say; we also need wisdom and mercy. Before promising something with great force, it is wise to think carefully. And if we realize that a decision is unjust, we should have the courage to speak up with respect.
exp.13:48:
This verse gives the names of Saul's sons: Jonathan, Ishui and Melchi-shua. It also names his two daughters: the older was called Merab, and the younger, Michal. The spellings "Jonathan" and "Michal" are simply older forms of these names. Some scholars note that other passages in the Bible mention slightly different names for Saul's sons, and it is not entirely clear why.

The narrator of the book makes a brief summary of Saul's reign here. After recounting his military victories, he presents his family: his sons, his wife, and his commander Abner. This works like a snapshot of the kingdom. Later on, Jonathan and Michal will play an important role in the story of David.

For today: God pays attention to families and to people's names, not only to great achievements. Care for your family with as much dedication as you give to your work, because that is also where your faith is lived out and where you leave your mark.
exp.13:49:
This verse says that the wife of King Saul was named Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz. It also says that the commander of his army was Abner, son of Ner, who was Saul's uncle. "Commander of his army" means the chief commander of the soldiers.

Here the narrator is not speaking through a character; the author of the book gives a brief summary of Saul's family and closest helpers. It comes after the account of his military victories and before a reminder that the war against the Philistines was still fierce. With these details, the story shows who surrounded the king. Abner will appear later as an important figure in the kingdom.

God uses people with names and family ties, not only famous leaders. Today we can value our families and those who walk with us at work or in service, praying for them and thanking them for their support.
exp.13:50:
This verse gives family information. It says that Kish, the father of Saul, and Ner, the father of Abner, were sons of Abiel. In other words, Saul and Abner were close relatives. The previous verse already said that Abner was Saul's uncle, although some understand the word to mean a close relative in general. Also, other passages (such as 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:36-39) present the names of this family somewhat differently, and scholars explain this in several ways.

The narrator of the book, whose author is unknown, pauses the story to introduce the family of King Saul and his military commander. In this way he makes clear who the most important men of the kingdom were at its beginning.

For today: God works through royal families, with names and roots. Value your family and pray for it, knowing that God can use those who are close to you.
exp.13:51:
He says that throughout Saul's reign there was fierce war against the Philistines. He also says that whenever Saul saw a strong or valiant man, he took him to be with him.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator of the book, who closes his summary of Saul's reign after naming his family and his general Abner. It shows that Israel lived under constant military pressure and that Saul sought to strengthen his army. The text does not say whether this was wise or not; it only describes it. Later, David would be one of those valiant men who came to his court.

For today: surrounding ourselves with capable and committed people helps us face struggles. But, more than strength, we need to seek God's guidance and companions who draw us closer to Him.
exp.14:4:
He says that Saul came to the city of Amalek and set an ambush in the valley. An ambush is a hiding place used to attack by surprise. The text does not explain more details of the plan.

God, through the prophet Samuel, had commanded Saul to punish Amalek, a people who had attacked Israel when Israel came out of Egypt. Here the narrator tells how Saul began the campaign. It is a difficult passage, and many understand it within the ancient context of God's judgment on a nation. Later, Saul obeys only in part.

For today: obedience to God is tested in the details, and it must be complete, not half-done. We can ask ourselves whether we are sincerely carrying out what God asks of us, or only what is convenient for us.
exp.14:5:
Saul speaks to the Kenites, a people who lived among the Amalekites. He tells them to go away and separate themselves from them, so that they will not be destroyed along with Amalek. He gives them this chance because they had shown kindness to the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt. The Kenites heeded the warning and departed.

God had commanded Saul to judge Amalek for its attack against Israel in the wilderness. Before the battle, Saul gathers the army and prepares an ambush. Then he warns the Kenites in order to protect them. The Bible does not say in detail how that kindness had been shown, but it is remembered that it was not forgotten.

For today: God remembers and honors the good we do, even when it seems small. And if we find ourselves in a place that pulls us away from God, it is worth heeding the warning and leaving in time.
exp.14:11:
This verse tells how Samuel got up very early to go and meet Saul. Someone brought him word that Saul had come to Carmel, that he had set up a monument there to his own victory, and that afterward he had moved on to Gilgal. The verse says Samuel rose early in the morning, and the word "told" shows that he was given the news.

God had just told Samuel that he regretted making Saul king, because Saul had not obeyed. Samuel spent the whole night crying out to God, deeply troubled. Now he is going to confront the king. While Samuel prays, Saul is busy setting up a monument for himself. Some understand this as a sign of pride; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when we fail, God asks us for obedience and humility, not applause. It is worth asking ourselves whether we seek to honor God or to be recognized ourselves.
exp.14:16:
Samuel reminds Saul of something important: although he once saw himself as small, God made him leader of all the tribes of Israel. The word "head" means chief or leader, and "anointed" means that he was set apart by God to be king, with oil as the sign.

Samuel speaks after Saul did not obey the command to destroy the Amalekites completely. Saul excused himself by saying the people kept the best of the flock to sacrifice to God. Samuel confronts him with firm affection, reminding him where God took him from and why He put him there.

For today: when God gives us responsibility, blessing, or influence, let us not use it to do whatever seems right to us. Let us remember that everything we have comes from Him, and respond with humble and complete obedience, without excuses.
exp.14:18:
Samuel asks King Saul a pointed question: why did you not obey the Lord? Instead of carrying out the command, Saul rushed upon the plunder (the goods taken from the enemy) and did what God considered wrong.

Samuel speaks as God's prophet. God had commanded that Amalek be completely destroyed, but Saul spared King Agag and kept the best of the livestock. Earlier, Samuel reminds him that God had raised him up as king when he felt small. It is a rebuke for his ingratitude and disobedience. This passage is harsh, and many read it carefully because of the war it describes.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I obey God completely, or only in the things that suit me? Partial obedience is often a way of justifying what we want. Let us ask for humility to listen and to do his will.
exp.14:20:
Saul says it was the people who kept the best of the plunder: sheep and oxen. He describes them as "the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed," meaning the best of what God had commanded to be completely destroyed. He says it was to offer them in sacrifice to the Lord in Gilgal.

Saul is speaking with Samuel, who confronts him for not having obeyed. God had ordered him to destroy everything belonging to the Amalekites, but Saul spared King Agag and the best of the livestock. Here he puts the blame on the people and presents his disobedience as something religious. Samuel will answer that obedience is worth more than sacrifice.

For today: we should not dress up disobedience in good religious intentions. God does not want us to offer him things to cover up what we refuse to obey. If he has already spoken to us, let us start by obeying, acknowledge our wrong without excuses, and ask his forgiveness with humility.
exp.14:21:
Samuel asks whether the Lord takes as much pleasure in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obeying his voice. He answers that obeying is better than sacrifice, and paying attention is better than offering the fat of rams.

Samuel speaks to Saul, the first king of Israel. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites, but Saul spared King Agag, and the people kept the best of the livestock. Saul justifies himself by saying it was to sacrifice them to God. Samuel shows him that religion without obedience is worth nothing.

For today: it is not enough to sing, attend church, or give offerings if we ignore what God has already asked of us. Ask yourself: is there something God has shown you that you keep postponing or changing for some excuse that sounds pious? Obeying him simply pleases him more.
exp.14:22:
It says that rebelling against God is as serious as divination, which looked for guidance apart from God. And that stubbornness, or deliberately disobeying, is as serious as idolatry, which is putting something else in the place of God. Because Saul rejected the word of the Lord, God rejected him as king.

The prophet Samuel speaks to Saul. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but Saul and the people kept the best of the spoils. Saul said it was to sacrifice to God. Samuel explains to him that God cares more about obedience than about religious offerings.

For today: we cannot replace obedience with religious acts or good intentions. Today you can ask yourself in what area you know what God asks of you, and give him your sincere yes, even when it costs you.
exp.14:25:
Samuel tells Saul that he will not go back with him. The reason is clear: Saul rejected the word of God, that is, he set it aside and did not take it seriously. For that reason God also rejected him from being king.

Samuel, the prophet, speaks with Saul after Saul disobeyed a command from God. Saul had already admitted his sin and asked for forgiveness, but he explained that he acted out of fear of the people. Samuel answers firmly, and many understand that the passage is speaking of the loss of the kingdom, not necessarily of the loss of personal forgiveness. The Bible does not fully spell this out.

For today: obeying God matters more than pleasing people. If fear of others takes control of us, let us ask God for the courage to do what is right and to obey him from the heart.
exp.14:26:
As Samuel turned to leave, someone caught hold of the hem of his robe, and it tore. The hem is the edge of the garment, and the robe is the cloak. The text does not say who grabbed it, but most readers understand that it was Saul, trying to stop Samuel.

Samuel had just told Saul that God had rejected him as king because he did not obey God's word. Saul was begging Samuel to come back with him. Right away, Samuel uses the torn robe as a sign: in the same way, God was tearing the kingdom out of Saul's hands.

For today: it is not enough to grieve once we already see the consequences. It is better to obey God in time and with sincerity. If we have failed, let us come to Him with humility and without excuses, not only out of fear of losing something.
exp.14:33:
It says that Samuel went to his town, Ramah, and that King Saul returned to his house in Gibeah, his city. The words "went up" indicate that Saul went back to a higher place, as Gibeah was. The two men part ways after a very tense day.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul had disobeyed God by not completely destroying the Amalekites, nor their king Agag, as he had been commanded. Samuel put Agag to death and broke with Saul. The verses that follow say that Samuel never saw Saul again and that he mourned for him, while God regretted having made him king.

For today: obedience to God is not replaced by excuses or good intentions. And when someone strays from the path, we can grieve for that person and pray for them, without excusing the wrong.
exp.14:34:
This verse says that Samuel never saw Saul again for the rest of Saul's life. Even so, Samuel grieved over him and mourned for him. God, for his part, is described as having regretted making Saul king. That wording does not mean God made a mistake, but that he was grieved by the direction Saul had taken and changed how he dealt with him.

This is the close of chapter 15. Saul had disobeyed God's command concerning the Amalekites, and Samuel, the prophet, told him that God was rejecting him as king. Afterward Samuel went to Ramah and Saul went home to Gibeah. The relationship between them was broken.

For today: disobedience has painful consequences, even for those who love us. Still, we can follow Samuel's example: to mourn for someone who has gone wrong, rather than to rejoice in their fall.
exp.15:0:
God speaks to Samuel and asks him how long he will keep mourning for Saul, since God has already rejected him as king over Israel. He tells Samuel to fill his horn with oil and go to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, because among Jesse's sons God has already chosen the new king.

The Lord speaks with the prophet Samuel. Saul had disobeyed God, and Samuel was very sad about it. The oil in the horn was used for anointing, that is, setting someone apart for a special task. Samuel is afraid, but God gives him a simple plan so that he can go safely.

For today: it is good to grieve our losses, but God does not want us to stay stuck. When one door closes, he already has a next step prepared. We can obey even when we feel afraid, trusting that he guides us step by step.
exp.15:4:
Samuel answers the elders of Bethlehem that he has come in peace, to offer a sacrifice to the Lord. He asks them to sanctify themselves, that is, to prepare and cleanse themselves to present themselves before God. He himself sanctifies Jesse and his sons, and invites them to the sacrifice.

The prophet Samuel is speaking. The elders were afraid, perhaps because Saul was king and Samuel was coming with a delicate errand. God had commanded him to anoint a new king among the sons of Jesse. The text does not explain why Samuel does not state his whole purpose; God himself had shown him how to proceed.

For today: before we draw near to God, it is good to prepare the heart with humility and sincerity. We can set aside a few minutes to pray, confess what weighs on us, and listen, knowing that God looks at what is within us.
exp.15:6:
It says that God spoke to Samuel and asked him not to look at Eliab's appearance or his great height, because God had rejected him. People look at what can be seen on the outside, but God looks at the heart.

Samuel had been sent to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, because God had rejected Saul. Seeing Eliab, tall and impressive in appearance, Samuel thought he was the chosen one. God corrects him. Then Jesse presents other sons, and God does not choose any of them either.

Today we can remember that we should not judge people, or ourselves, only by appearance, success, or what others think. Let us ask God for a sincere and humble heart, and learn to value others for who they are on the inside.
exp.15:7:
This verse tells how Jesse, David's father, made his son Abinadab pass before the prophet Samuel. Samuel understood that God had not chosen this young man either.

Samuel had been sent by God to Bethlehem to anoint a new king over Israel, because Saul had been rejected. Jesse presented his sons one by one. Earlier, Samuel had been impressed by Eliab because of his appearance, but God reminded him that He looks at the heart.

For today: let us not judge people, or ourselves, only by what is seen on the outside. Let us ask God to teach us to value character, faith, and humility, which is what He looks at.
exp.15:11:
What it says: David, the youngest son of Jesse, was called in from the field and brought before Samuel. He is described as ruddy, and also as having a beautiful countenance and being goodly to look at. Then God told Samuel to anoint him, because this was the chosen one. To anoint is to pour oil on someone to set them apart for a task.

Context: Samuel was looking for Israel's new king, because God had rejected Saul. Samuel had examined seven sons of Jesse, and God had chosen none of them. David was tending the sheep, and no one had considered him. A few verses earlier, God had told Samuel that He does not look at the outward appearance but at the heart.

For today: God sees and calls people whom others overlook. If you feel unimportant, remember that God knows you. And when you judge others, try to look more deeply than appearances.
exp.15:16:
Saul accepts the suggestion of his servants and asks them to find someone who can play an instrument well. The word "play" here is the verb used for playing a stringed instrument, and the verse asks for someone who can do it skillfully.

The king himself is speaking. His attendants had seen that an evil spirit, allowed by God, was tormenting him, and they proposed that music might bring him relief. Interpreters explain that spirit in different ways, but the text says it truly troubled him. Saul asks for someone skilled, and in this way the path opens for David to arrive.

Today we can learn to listen to the good advice of those around us when we are distressed. Accepting help, whether music, companionship, or counsel, is not weakness. And God can use simple things, such as a song, to bring rest to a weary heart.
exp.16:1:
Saul and the men of Israel were also gathered together, the text says. They set up their camp in the valley of the Oak (other versions call it the valley of Elah) and lined up in formation to fight against the Philistines. The phrase "were gathered together, and pitched... and set the battle in array" means that they took their positions in rows, ready for combat.

The narrator of the book tells how the Philistines, Israel's enemies, had invaded territory belonging to Judah. Israel responds, and both armies end up facing each other, separated by a valley. This is the setting where Goliath will appear and, afterward, David. The verse prepares the scene of a great conflict that seems to have no way out.

For today: we often face big problems that leave us paralyzed, as if we were standing in a valley waiting. This verse reminds us that God works in the middle of those situations of waiting and tension. While you carry out your part responsibly, trust that He can intervene in ways you do not expect.
exp.16:4:
He says that Goliath wore a helmet of bronze or strong metal on his head and a suit of armor made of plates or scales. That body armor weighed five thousand shekels, which according to many scholars would be about 57 kilograms, although the exact calculation may vary. The helmet is the covering for the head, and the armor is what covered the chest and body.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book. He describes Goliath so that the reader feels how imposing he was. Israel and the Philistines stand face to face, and this giant appears as a threat that paralyzes everyone. The story sets up the contrast with David.

For today: sometimes problems look enormous and well protected, and they frighten us. This description reminds us not to measure everything by what we see. We can pray and face our fears trusting in God, not in our own strength.
exp.16:10:
This verse says that when Saul and all the people of Israel heard the challenge of the Philistine, they were dismayed and felt great fear. "Dismayed" means being very disturbed and left without courage. "Philistine" refers to Goliath, the warrior of the enemy army.

Goliath has been challenging Israel for days. He proposes that one man fight him alone, and that the losing side serve the winner. Saul was the king and was supposed to lead the army, but he and everyone else were paralyzed. The text does not say that they prayed or sought God at that moment; it only shows the fear. This sets the scene for David's arrival.

For today: when a great problem speaks loudly to us and fills us with fear, it is easy to look only at its size. We can stop, pray, and remember who God is before deciding how to respond. Fear is human, but it does not have to rule over us.
exp.16:11:
This verse introduces David and his family. It says that David was the son of Jesse, a man from Ephrath in Bethlehem of Judah, who had eight sons. "Ephrathite" means from the region or clan of Ephrath, which is connected with Bethlehem. Jesse was already an old man in the time of King Saul, very advanced in years for his generation.

The narrator interrupts the scene of the Philistine giant to introduce David and his origins once again. Israel is paralyzed by fear before Goliath's challenge. At that moment, a young man from an ordinary family, from a small town, appears. Some scholars think this repetition is due to how the ancient accounts were joined together, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God often works through ordinary people and in places that go unnoticed. Do not be discouraged if you feel small; trust that God can use your life right where you are.
exp.16:12:
This verse says that the three eldest sons of Jesse, a man of Bethlehem, had gone with King Saul to the war. Their names were Eliab (the firstborn), Abinadab, and Shammah. "Followed Saul" means joining his army.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. After describing Israel's fear before the Philistine giant, he introduces David's family. The names of his brothers prepare what follows: David, the youngest, went back and forth between the camp and his father's sheep. Later, Eliab will be the one who rebukes him (17:28).

For today: God often works through people who seem small or little noticed, like David among his brothers. Do not look down on your own place or the place of others. Be faithful in everyday things, because God can use them for something great.
exp.16:13:
This verse says that David was the youngest son of Jesse, and that his three older brothers had gone with King Saul to war. The word "youngest" means the smallest in age. "Followed Saul" means they joined his army.

Here the narrator of the book introduces David's family while Israel faces the Philistines. The brothers are on the battle front, and David, being the youngest, stays behind to tend his father's sheep. So the account sets the scene in which Goliath challenges Israel and David appears.

For today: God can use the one others overlook. If you are given a simple, little-noticed task today, do it faithfully. That is where the character is formed that God can later use in important moments.
exp.16:14:
This verse says that David went back and forth from Saul's camp to look after his father's sheep in Bethlehem. The words "But" and "to tend" are used in the old wording, and "to tend" means to lead the sheep to eat and to take care of them.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. He has just said that David's three older brothers went off to the war with Saul. Now he makes clear that David was not always at the front, but went back and forth between serving Saul and caring for the flock. This detail prepares the next scene, when his father will send him to bring food to his brothers and David will come to see the giant Goliath.

For today: David was faithful in the small and everyday things, caring for sheep, before he faced something great. Do your daily work with care, even when it seems unimportant; God often shapes our character right there.
exp.16:16:
Jesse asks his son David to take his brothers an ephah of this parched grain and these ten loaves. An ephah was a measure of capacity for grain, about twenty liters, although estimates vary.

Jesse is a father who cares about his three oldest sons, who were serving in Saul's army. Meanwhile, the Philistine Goliath had been challenging Israel for forty days. Jesse does not know that this journey will change David's story. He only wants to know whether his sons are well.

God often uses small, everyday tasks to lead us to great things. Today we can faithfully do what is asked of us, such as caring for our family, without despising it, because we never know what door God may open through it.
exp.16:18:
This verse tells us where Israel's army was. Saul, his soldiers, and all the Israelite people were in the valley of the oak tree (other versions call it the valley of Elah), facing the Philistines. The word "fighting" here describes more the fact that they were at war and in battle position, as the following verses show.

It is the narrator's explanation. Jesse has just sent David with food for his brothers, and this verse makes clear where he would go: to the front line of battle. This sets up the scene where David will arrive and meet Goliath.

For today: while others live through moments of tension or struggle, God often uses small, everyday tasks, like carrying food or asking how others are doing. Serve faithfully in simple things; that is where something great can begin.
exp.16:19:
He says that David got up early in the morning, left the sheep in the care of a keeper, and set out carrying the food that his father Jesse had asked him to take. He arrived at the camp just as the army was going out in formation and giving the war cry. The fortified camp is the place where the army was gathered; the battle line is the formation for fighting; the keeper is the one who looked after the sheep; and what David carried was the supplies he had brought.

The narrator is the author of the book, and he tells us that Jesse sent David to visit his older brothers, who were soldiers in Saul's army. David was to take them provisions, greet the commander, and come back with news of them. David was not going to fight; he was obeying a simple errand from his father.

For today: God often uses the person who is faithful in small things. David cared for the flock responsibly and carried out his father's errand without complaint. Let us do our daily tasks with care, because in them God may be preparing us for greater things.
exp.16:22:
This verse tells us that while David was talking with his brothers, Goliath came up, the Philistine champion from Gath, who stood between the two camps. He came out from the Philistine ranks and repeated the same challenge as always, and David heard it.

The narrator sets the scene. David, a young shepherd, had come to the battlefield to bring supplies to his brothers and see how they were doing. Goliath had been issuing his challenge for days, and the people of Israel lived full of fear. This is the first time David hears the challenge in person, and that prepares what he will do next.

For today: when everyone freezes before a giant problem, we can stop and listen carefully and ask ourselves what God thinks about it. Other people's fear does not have to decide how we respond.
exp.16:23:
This verse says that all the men of Israel, when they saw Goliath, ran away to get away from him, and felt great fear. The word "men" in the verse simply means men, and "fled from him" means that they moved away from where he was standing.

The narrator describes what was happening in the camp of Israel. Goliath had been challenging the army for days, and no one dared to face him. David had just arrived to visit his brothers and heard the challenge for the first time. His reaction, in the verses that follow, contrasts with the fear of the others, because he focuses on the fact that Goliath is defying the living God.

Today we too can become paralyzed when we look only at the size of a problem. This passage invites us to remember who God is before deciding how to respond. When you feel afraid, pray and fix your eyes on Him, not only on the difficulty.
exp.16:25:
Here David asks the soldiers what will be given to the man who defeats the Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel. Then he says that this man is uncircumcised, meaning he does not belong to the covenant people of God, and yet he dares to defy the armies of the living God.

David has just arrived at the camp, sent by his father to bring food to his brothers. He sees that everyone is running away from Goliath out of fear. David is not thinking only about the reward; he is angered that God is being insulted. His brother Eliab misreads his motives and rebukes him, but David presses on.

For today: when everyone freezes in fear, remember that God is real and present. See your problems from God's perspective, not only from their size, and be brave even when others discourage you.
exp.16:26:
The people of Israel repeated to David what had already been said before: whoever defeated the Philistine would receive a reward.

David had just arrived at the camp to visit his brothers. He asked what would be given to the one who struck down Goliath, and the soldiers answered him with the reward King Saul had promised. David was not asking only about the prize. It grieved him that this man was mocking the armies of the living God. His brother Eliab became angry when he heard it, but David kept asking.

For today: when something stirs you because it dishonors God, do not let criticism or fear silence you. Ask questions, look for what you can do, and act with humility, trusting that God works through ordinary people.
exp.16:27:
Eliab, David's eldest brother, overhears him speaking with the soldiers and becomes very angry. He confronts him with harsh questions: why he came down, and with whom he left the few sheep. He accuses him of pride, meaning arrogance, and of having a wicked heart, that is, bad intentions. He says David came down only to watch the battle.

Eliab speaks in the camp of Israel, where the army is afraid of Goliath. David, who had arrived sent by his father with supplies, asks what reward there will be for the one who defeats the Philistine. Eliab may have felt embarrassed or annoyed, but the text does not state his exact reasons. What we do see is that he judges David without knowing his heart.

For today: when someone criticizes you harshly, do not respond with the same anger. David answered with calm and went on with what God placed on his heart. And we too must be careful not to judge the intentions of others.
exp.16:33:
David answers King Saul by telling about his experience: he was looking after his father's sheep, and when a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock, he did not stand still.

The words "your servant" are a respectful way of speaking to the king. Here "flock" refers to the sheep being kept together.

David speaks before Saul, who doubted him because he was young, while the giant Goliath was defying Israel. David does not boast of his strength; he is building his argument. The verses that follow show that he trusted God had protected him in private and would protect him now.

For today: God often prepares our character through small and unseen tasks. Be faithful in everyday things, without waiting for applause, and trust that God uses those experiences to prepare us for greater challenges.
exp.16:34:
He says that David would go out after the animal that carried off a sheep, strike it, and rescue the lamb from its mouth. If the beast turned on him, he would seize it by the jaw (the lower jaw) and strike it until it died.

David speaks with King Saul. Saul doubted that a young man without experience could face Goliath, a seasoned warrior. David does not boast of his own strength; he tells how he cared for his father's sheep with courage and faithfulness. Then he says that the LORD, who delivered him from the lion and the bear, would deliver him from the Philistine as well.

For today: God often prepares our trust through small and hidden tasks. Be faithful in everyday matters, and remember how God has helped you before; that strengthens faith for the great challenges.
exp.16:35:
David says that he had already killed both lions and bears while he was looking after his father's sheep. According to him, the Philistine will be just like those animals, because this uncircumcised man, meaning someone outside God's covenant with Israel, has defied and insulted the armies of the living God, that is, the real and active God, not an idol.

David speaks to King Saul. Everyone in the army feared Goliath, and Saul doubted that a young man could fight. David does not boast of his strength; he offers his experience as proof. Then he says that the LORD, who delivered him from the lion and the bear, will also deliver him from this Philistine.

For today: God often prepares us in small and hidden places, such as daily work or caring for others. When a great challenge comes, remember how God helped you before, and trust that he will remain with you.
exp.16:37:
Saul, the verse says, put his own war clothing on David. He placed on his head a strong metal helmet, and he fitted him with a breastplate, a protective covering for the chest. Saul wanted David to be well armed.

David had just told Saul that he trusted God to defeat Goliath, just as God had delivered him from the lion and the bear while he was caring for sheep. Saul gave him his blessing, but then wanted to help him in his own way, with the armor that Saul knew. Because Saul was king, his equipment was the safest that could be offered. Afterward David took it off, because he was not used to wearing it.

We can receive the help of others with gratitude, but what works for them does not always suit us. God has guided us through our own story, and we should trust Him by humbly using what we really know how to do.
exp.16:39:
He took his staff, the shepherd's rod, and chose five smooth stones from the brook. He put them in his shepherd's bag, the pouch he carried for his things. With the sling in his hand, which is a strip for hurling stones, he drew near to the Philistine, Goliath.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul, the king, had lent David his armor, but David was not used to it, so he took it off. The soldiers of Israel were afraid of the giant, and David, a young shepherd, offered to fight. Why he chose five stones, the Bible does not explain, and several ideas have been suggested.

Today we can learn to serve God with what we already have and know how to do, without copying others. God can use your simple tools when you trust Him.
exp.16:40:
This verse says that Goliath, the Philistine, kept coming forward toward David, drawing closer little by little. In front of him went his shield-bearer, that is, the helper who carried his shield.

The narrator describes the moment just before the battle. David had just turned down Saul's armor because he was not used to it, and he went out with his staff, five stones, and his sling. The contrast is strong: a giant protected by a helper and his weapons, facing a young shepherd with simple tools. Later David will say that he trusts in the name of the Lord.

For today: you do not need to look strong or have the resources of others to face your giants. Use faithfully what God has already given you, and trust in Him.
exp.16:41:
When the Philistine Goliath looked closely at David, he looked down on him. He saw him as someone of no importance.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. Goliath was an experienced warrior and expected a rival who was armed and strong. Instead, he saw a young shepherd with a staff, a sling, and some stones. So he judged him only by what he saw on the outside.

For today: do not let yourself be measured by appearances, and do not measure others by them either. God often works through people whom the world underestimates. If you feel small or unprepared, trust that God can use you when you are faithful to him.
exp.16:42:
Goliath asks David if he is a dog, that he comes to fight him with sticks. Goliath then curses David by calling on his gods, that is, the Philistine gods.

Goliath, the Philistine champion, speaks here. He feels insulted because he sees David as a young man without weapons of war. The "sticks" most likely refer to the shepherd's staff David was carrying, and he also had his sling. Goliath trusts in his strength and in his gods, but David will answer by trusting in the God of Israel.

Today, others sometimes mock our faith or our strength. We do not have to defend ourselves with pride or respond in kind. We can face our problems with humility, trusting that God is the one who gives the victory, even when we feel small.
exp.16:43:
Goliath tells David to come closer, because he is going to leave his dead body for the birds of the air and the beasts of the field to eat. It is a very harsh threat.

Goliath is the Philistine giant who defied the army of Israel. Seeing David, young, good-looking, and without weapons of war, he despised him and even cursed him in the name of his gods. He mocked because he trusted in his strength and his armor. David, in contrast, answers that he comes in the name of the Lord.

For today: do not let yourself be intimidated by words of mockery or threats that seem bigger than you. When you face something difficult, do what is right and trust in God, not only in your own strength or in what others think of you.
exp.16:44:
Here David answers Goliath. He tells him that Goliath comes with a sword, a spear, and a shield, that is, with human weapons. David, on the other hand, comes "in the name of the Lord of hosts," meaning he trusts in the authority and power of God, who commands the armies of Israel. He says that Goliath has defied him, that is, he has challenged and insulted him.

David speaks in the valley of Elah, in front of the Philistine army. Goliath had just mocked him, cursed him, and threatened to leave his body for the birds. David does not see this battle as a personal matter, but as an offense against God and his people.

Today, when problems seem enormous, we can do what David did: not rely only on our own strength or resources, but pray and act trusting in God, doing what is right with humility.
exp.16:49:
This verse sums up the battle: David defeated the Philistine Goliath using only a sling and a stone. He struck him and killed him, though he had no sword in his hand.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks here, summarizing how the encounter ended. The verses that follow clarify one detail: David then took the giant's sword to cut off his head. Before the battle, David had said that the fight belonged to the Lord and that God would give the victory without the need for sword or spear (v. 47).

For today: God can work through what seems small or even ridiculous in the face of great problems. Do with faith what you have at hand, however simple it may be, and trust that the outcome is in God's hands.
exp.16:50:
This verse says that David ran toward the fallen Philistine and stood over him. He drew the giant's sword from its sheath, finished him off, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.

This is part of the account where the narrator describes the duel between David, a young shepherd, and Goliath. David had turned down Saul's armor and trusted in God, not in weapons. He had already won with the stone from his sling; this final act secured the victory. For the Philistines, the defeat of their champion meant the defeat of their whole army, which is why they fled.

When God places you before an enormous problem, take the step in faith and do not freeze. Use what you have, persist until the end, and trust that God is the one who gives the victory.
exp.16:53:
David took the head of the Philistine Goliath and brought it to Jerusalem. The giant's weapons, on the other hand, he kept in his own tent. The word that translates as "brought" is a plain word meaning he carried it there, and the word for his tent is his own tent or dwelling.

This is part of the account of David's victory over Goliath. The narrator summarizes what happened after the battle. There is one difficult detail: at that time Jerusalem did not yet belong to Israel, since David conquered it years later. Some think the author names the place as it would be known later, or that the head was taken there afterward. It is not known for certain.

For today: David did not boast about his victory, but kept the trophy simply. When God gives you a triumph, thank him and do not fill up with pride.
exp.16:56:
This verse tells how David, after defeating Goliath, came back carrying the Philistine's head in his hand. Abner, the commander of the army, took him and brought him before King Saul.

The narrator of the book now speaks. Saul asks whose son David is, even though David had earlier played the harp for him (1 Samuel 16). Scholars explain this in several ways: perhaps Saul did not remember David well, or perhaps he was asking about the family that would receive the promised reward. The reason cannot be known for certain.

For today: God can use the one the world overlooks. David came to the palace without fame, but with faith. Be faithful in what God places in front of you, even when no one yet knows who you are.
exp.16:57:
Saul asks David: "Whose son are you, young man?" And David answers respectfully: "I am the son of your servant Jesse, from Bethlehem."

David has just defeated Goliath and is still holding the Philistine's head in his hand. Abner, the commander of the army, brings him before Saul. It is striking that Saul asks this question, since David had earlier played the harp for him (1 Samuel 16). Some think Saul did not remember David well, or wanted to know about his family because of the promised reward. The Bible does not explain this with certainty.

After a great victory, David does not boast. He answers simply and mentions his humble origin. Today we can learn to receive success with humility, remembering who we are and where God has brought us from.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that, when David had finished speaking with Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David. Jonathan loved him as his own soul.

Here there is no character speaking; it is the narrator of the book. David had just spoken with Saul after defeating Goliath. Jonathan, the king's son, listened and felt a deep bond with him. Afterward they made a covenant, that is, a pact of loyalty. The text does not explain all the reasons, but it shows a sincere friendship.

For today: value and care for loyal friendships. A good friendship shows itself in affection, faithfulness, and support, even when there is envy or difficulty around.
exp.17:2:
It says that Jonathan and David made a covenant, that is, a serious promise of loyalty between the two of them. The reason is that Jonathan loved him as his own soul, that is, as his own life. In today's language this would be: he cared for him as much as he cared for himself.

It does not speak of one particular person; it is the narrator of the book. David had just spoken with King Saul after defeating Goliath. Jonathan, Saul's son, felt joined to him from the heart. The following verses show that he gave him his robe, his sword, and his bow, a gesture that expresses respect and devotion. Scholars discuss the exact scope of that gesture, but it clearly shows a deep friendship.

For today: value and care for loyal friendships. Be a friend who gives, protects, and keeps his word, without envy or rivalry, even when the other person seems to stand out more than you do.
exp.17:3:
Jonathan took off his robe and gave it to David. He also gave him other pieces of his clothing and his equipment: his sword, his bow, and his belt.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had just defeated Goliath, and Saul had taken him to live with him. Jonathan, the king's son and the natural heir to the throne, made a covenant with David because he loved him very much. Giving him his clothing and his weapons was a sign of friendship and loyalty. Some think he also recognized David as someone chosen by God, but the text does not state this clearly.

Today we can learn to give generously and without envy. Jonathan had much to lose, but he valued friendship and what God was doing in another person more highly. Ask yourself whom you can truly encourage and support.
exp.17:4:
This verse tells us that David carried out every assignment Saul gave him, and he did it with wisdom and good judgment. Saul's appointment of David as commander over the men of war came because David conducted himself with intelligence and care. The people and Saul's servants approved of him and received him well.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. It comes after David defeated Goliath and became a close friend of Jonathan. The text shows that David's success came not only from his courage but also from his conduct. What follows, the song of the women, will stir up Saul's jealousy.

For today: do well whatever you are given to do, even when it is small, and do it with wisdom and honesty. That builds a good reputation. And if others praise you, keep a humble heart.
exp.17:5:
This verse tells that, when David was returning after defeating Goliath, the women from all the towns of Israel came out to meet King Saul and the army. They did it with singing, dancing, and joy.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. It was customary to celebrate victories this way in Israel. David was already very beloved by the people and by Saul's servants. However, what seems like a festival soon becomes a cause of jealousy in Saul's heart, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: when others receive praise or success, we can choose to rejoice with them instead of comparing ourselves. If we feel envy, it is better to acknowledge it before God and ask Him for a grateful heart, before it grows and harms us.
exp.17:7:
This verse says that Saul became very angry. The women's song bothered him, and he said, "They have credited David with ten thousands, and to me they have credited only thousands; what more can he have but the kingdom?" The phrase about the saying displeasing him means that it upset him deeply.

Saul, the king of Israel, is the one speaking. David had just defeated the Philistine Goliath, and the women came out to celebrate with songs and music. Saul felt that he was being compared with David and that David was outshining him. His anger came from pride and from fear of losing the throne. According to the text that follows, from that day on he looked at David with suspicion.

For today: when we see that someone receives praise or success, we can choose to rejoice instead of comparing ourselves. If we feel envy, it is wise to bring it to God in prayer soon, before it grows and leads us to do harm.
exp.17:9:
The verse tells us that the next day an evil spirit, sent or allowed by God, came upon Saul. Inside his house he acted as if in a trance, prophesying and behaving in an agitated, wild manner. Meanwhile David played the harp as usual, and Saul had a spear in his hand.

The narrator relates this after the women sang that David had defeated his tens of thousands and Saul his thousands. Saul was filled with jealousy and anger. Scholars explain in several ways how an evil spirit could come from God; the text does not make this clear, but it shows that God had already withdrawn his favor from Saul.

Unchecked jealousy can become something that dominates us and leads us to harm others. When we feel envy at another's success, let us bring it to God in prayer and celebrate what he is doing in others before it grows.
exp.17:10:
He says that Saul threw his spear at David, thinking to himself that he would pin him to the wall. But David stepped aside, and this happened twice. The verse's word for the spear hitting its mark is not used here; the spear is simply thrown.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was playing the harp to soothe Saul, who was tormented by a harmful spirit that came from God. Scholars explain this phrase in several ways, and the text gives no further detail. Saul was already jealous of David because the people praised him. Then the account says that Saul was afraid of him, because God was with David.

For today: unaddressed jealousy can grow until it turns into violence. If you feel envy, bring it to God quickly in prayer and rejoice in the success of others, before it harms you and those around you.
exp.17:18:
This verse tells us that when the time came to give Merab, Saul's eldest daughter, to David, the king did not keep his word. Instead, he gave her as a wife to Adriel, from the town of Mehola. The sentences that explained the old wording have been removed, since the phrases they discussed do not appear in the verse you are reading.

The narrator is describing what happened after Saul's promise. The text suggests that Saul offered his daughter with a hidden purpose: he hoped the Philistines would kill David in battle. When that did not happen, Saul broke his word. The passage does not explain all his motives in detail, but it shows his jealousy and his duplicity.

Today it reminds us that not everyone keeps what they promise, and that David did not need to manipulate anything to move forward. We can trust that God watches over our path even when someone fails or deceives us. It also invites us to be people of our word, without hidden intentions.
exp.17:21:
Saul orders his servants to speak with David in private. They are to tell him that the king is pleased with him, that everyone at court thinks well of him, and that he should accept becoming the king's son-in-law. Saul's officials are his servants, and when the verse says they hold David in affection, it means they regard him kindly.

Saul speaks, but he has a hidden purpose. The previous passage says he wanted to give his daughter Michal to David as a snare, that is, as a trap, so that the Philistines would kill him. That is why he uses messengers and flattery instead of speaking frankly himself.

For today: not all praise is sincere. We can be grateful for kind words, but it is wise to examine motives with prayer and discernment. And let us seek to speak honestly, without using pleasant words to manipulate others.
exp.17:24:
Saul instructs his servants to tell David that the king does not want money as a bride price for marrying his daughter. Instead, he asks for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, as proof that David has avenged the king of his enemies. The bride price was the payment given for a bride, and the foreskins were the flesh removed in circumcision. The text makes the real plan clear: Saul hoped the Philistines would kill David.

Saul, the king, speaks through his servants. He feels envy and fear toward David, because the people admire him for his victories. He appears to honor David with an offer of marriage, but he is hiding a trap. The Philistines were enemies of Israel, and this mission was very dangerous.

For today: let us be wary of kind appearances when bad intentions lie behind them, and let us not act that way toward others. We can trust that God cares for those who are faithful to him, even when someone plans to harm them.
exp.17:26:
