This verse says that David went out with his men, defeated two hundred Philistines, and brought the king proof of his victory: the foreskins, that is, the skin cut away in circumcision. These were the bride price that Saul had asked for. He handed over the full count, even double what had been asked, and so Saul gave him his daughter Michal as wife.

Saul had asked for a hundred foreskins, but his real plan was for the Philistines to kill David. He wanted to be rid of him without getting his own hands dirty. David, unaware of that trap, gladly accepted the chance to become the king's son-in-law. The text that follows shows that the plan failed: God was with David, and Saul feared him all the more.

For today: faithfully do what is your responsibility, even when others have evil intentions against you. Do your part with integrity and trust that God can care for you and turn into good what others planned for harm.
exp.17:29:
Here it says that whenever the leaders of the Philistines went out to fight, David acted with more wisdom and success than all of Saul's other officers. For this reason his name was very respected and well known. The phrase about acting with good judgment and success is simply about David's conduct and results. The word about being highly honored and recognized is simply about how well regarded he was.

This is the closing part of chapter 18, and it is told by the narrator. Saul already felt jealousy and fear, because he saw that God was with David. Even so, David kept carrying out his military duties with good results. The text shows that his reputation grew because of how he conducted himself, and that Saul's envy had no just reason behind it.

For today: do your work and your responsibilities well, even when someone envies you or treats you badly. Consistent good conduct, with God's help, speaks for itself. You do not need to defend yourself with pride; serve with honesty and trust that God watches over your path.
exp.18:0:
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants that they should kill David. Jonathan, although he was Saul's son, loved David very much.

The narrator tells us that Saul's jealousy of David had grown, because David was successful and the people admired him. Now Saul stops hiding it and gives an open order to kill him. Jonathan is caught in the middle: he is the king's son, but he is also David's faithful friend. So he warns David of the danger and promises to speak with his father.

When a friendship or a loyalty places us between two people in conflict, we can choose what is right, even when it costs us. Jonathan did not keep silent or go along with the crowd. He protected an innocent man with courage, and he also tried to speak respectfully to his father. Let us ask God for wisdom to defend what is just without losing humility.
exp.18:1:
Jonathan warns David that his father, King Saul, is looking for a way to kill him. He advises David to take heed to himself until the morning, that is, to stay alert until the next day, and to hide in a remote place.

Jonathan speaks, the son of Saul and a very close friend of David. Saul had just ordered that David be killed, because he was jealous of him. Jonathan finds himself between loyalty to his father and love for his friend, and he decides to protect David's life. Soon afterward he promises to speak well of David before Saul.

For today: true friendship acts with courage on behalf of the other, even when it costs. Ask yourself whom you can care for, defend, or warn of danger, and do it with wisdom and love, without ceasing to seek peace.
exp.18:2:
Jonathan tells David that he will go out and stand beside his father Saul, in the field where David is hiding. There he will speak well of David in front of Saul. Afterward he will tell David whatever he manages to see or hear.

Jonathan, Saul's son, is the one speaking. Saul had ordered David killed out of jealousy, but Jonathan loved David as a loyal friend. That is why he warns him of the danger and proposes a plan: to find out the king's intentions and to plead for David. What happened next is seen in the verses that follow.

Today we can learn from Jonathan's brave loyalty. He risked his relationship with his father to defend an innocent man. When someone is treated unjustly, we can speak up for them with respect and sincerity, and help them with prudence, without gossip or violence.
exp.18:5:
Saul listened to the words of his son Jonathan and made a solemn oath. He swore "as the Lord lives" that he would not kill David. In today's English: "As surely as God lives, David will not die."

Jonathan, David's faithful friend, spoke with his father the king. Saul was jealous of David and had wanted to kill him. Jonathan reminded him that David had done him no wrong, that he had risked his life against the Philistine (Goliath), and that God had given Israel a great victory. Saul was moved and promised not to harm him. Later on, however, his jealousy returned, so his change of heart did not last.

Today we can learn to be peacemakers: speaking well of someone who is unjustly attacked and defending the truth with respect. But we must also guard the heart, because good intentions without a true change can fade away.
exp.18:7:
It says that war broke out again with the Philistines, and that David went out to fight against them. He defeated them with a great slaughter, and the enemies fled before him. The phrase about war starting again simply means that the fighting began once more.

This account comes from the narrator of 1 Samuel. It follows directly after Jonathan succeeded in reconciling his father Saul with David. Saul had sworn not to kill him. David went back to serving him and kept bringing victories to Israel. But the next verse shows that jealousy and an evil spirit took hold of Saul again, so the peace did not last long.

For today: do your work well even when someone looks at you with envy or distrust. David stayed faithful and useful, without seeking revenge. That does not always prevent problems, but it keeps your conscience clear and leaves the outcome in God's hands.
exp.18:8:
It says that an evil spirit, sent or allowed by God, came upon Saul. He was sitting in his house with a spear in his hand, while David was playing the harp.

Here it is not a character speaking, but the narrator of the book. Saul had already disobeyed God and had lost his favor. Now he was dominated by jealousy toward David, who had just defeated the Philistines. Interpreters explain in different ways how God allowed that spirit, but the text shows that God still rules even in dark times.

Unchecked jealousy can turn into violence. If you feel envy at another person's success, bring it to God in prayer soon and ask for a humble heart, before it grows and takes control of you.
exp.18:9:
This verse tells how Saul tried to pin David to the wall with his spear. But David stepped aside, and the spear struck the wall. Then David fled and escaped that night.

The narrator describes how Saul, full of jealousy because David was winning battles and was admired, was taken over by an evil spirit from the LORD. People understand this phrase in different ways: some see it as God's permission as a judgment, others as a tormenting spiritual distress. David would play music to calm him, but Saul answered with violence.

For today: when someone treats us with hatred without reason, we do not have to answer with the same evil. We can step away with wisdom, seek protection, and trust that God cares for us.
exp.18:10:
Saul sent messengers to David's house to keep watch over it through the night and to kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, found out and warned him: if he did not escape that very night, the next day he would be dead. Saul's men were set to watch, so that David would not get away.

It is a narrated scene, not a speech. Saul, filled with jealousy and fear, had already tried to pin David to the wall with his spear. Michal is Saul's daughter, yet she protects her husband. The text says that an evil spirit from the Lord was upon Saul, and scholars explain that phrase in several ways. What is clear is that Saul was acting with great violence.

For today: when God gives you a warning through someone sensible, do not put it off. Listen with humility and act with prudence, without neglecting your trust in God.
exp.18:13:
This verse tells how Saul sent his messengers to arrest David, but Michal, David's wife, answered them that he was sick. She said this to buy time.

Michal is Saul's daughter and David's wife. Saul wanted to kill David out of jealousy. She had helped him escape through a window and put a statue in the bed to deceive the soldiers. That lie gave David an advantage to flee. The Bible only tells what happened; it does not say whether God approved of the deception. Some readers see courage here, others a questionable method.

For today: when loving and protecting someone costs us something, God calls us to have courage. But let us always seek to act with wisdom and truth, trusting that He cares for his own.
exp.18:17:
This verse tells us that David managed to flee from Saul and came to Samuel at Ramah. There he told him everything Saul had done to him. Afterward, David and Samuel went to stay in Naioth.

The narrator describes what happened after Michal, David's wife, helped him get away and tricked Saul's messengers with a statue in the bed. David sought out Samuel, the prophet who had anointed him as the future king. Naioth was probably a place where prophets gathered, though it is not known exactly what it was like.

When everything becomes unjust or dangerous, it is wise to seek out someone of mature faith to share what we are going through. David did not carry his pain alone. Talking with a wise counselor and praying together gives us clarity and protection.
exp.18:21:
Saul, tired of sending messengers who never come back, goes himself to Ramah. He arrives at the great well that is in Sechu, and asks where Samuel and David are. Someone tells him they are at Naioth, in Ramah.

The narrator is the author of the book, not a character in the story. Saul wants to catch David, who had fled to Samuel. Three groups of messengers were touched by the Spirit of God and ended up prophesying. Now Saul himself goes, and he too will be stopped by God. Some think God is protecting David in this way.

When someone insists on going against God's purpose, they can be stopped in surprising ways. Today we can ask God to make us let go of plans driven by pride or resentment, and trust that He cares for His own.
exp.19:4:
It says that the next day was the start of the new moon, a festival at which David would usually sit down to eat with King Saul. David asks Jonathan to let him hide in the field until the evening of the third day.

David speaks with his friend Jonathan, Saul's son. David knows that Saul wants to kill him and is in danger. Jonathan offers to help him, and David proposes a test: his absence from the king's table will show how Saul reacts. In this way they will know for certain whether there is real danger.

For today: when you face a difficult situation, seek the help of faithful friends and act with prudence. Trusting God does not mean acting without thinking, but asking for wisdom and relying on people you can trust.
exp.19:5:
Here David explains to Jonathan what to say if Saul asks about his absence. He is to say that David asked permission to hurry to Bethlehem, his city, because his family was holding its yearly sacrifice there.

David speaks with Jonathan, Saul's son and his faithful friend. Saul was looking for him in order to kill him, and David wanted to test the king's intentions without exposing himself. So he proposes a believable family excuse. The Bible does not say in detail what that yearly sacrifice was like, but it shows that David used an explanation Saul could accept. It is a test, not a direct confrontation.

For today: when you face a conflict or a threat, seek the counsel of someone you trust and act with prudence. If you depend on God, you do not have to react impulsively. Ask for wisdom, lean on faithful friends, and move forward with patience.
exp.19:7:
Here David asks Jonathan to deal faithfully with him. He calls for kindness and loyalty, and he reminds Jonathan that the two of them have made a covenant before the Lord. If there is any wrongdoing in him, he asks Jonathan to kill him himself, and not to hand him over to Jonathan's father, King Saul.

David speaks with Jonathan, the son of King Saul. David suspects that Saul wants to kill him, but Jonathan does not yet believe it. David proposes a test during the New Moon feast: if Saul becomes angry because of David's absence, they will know Saul's true intentions. David shows himself to be sincere and is willing to be judged if he is guilty.

For today: when a friendship or a commitment is based on truth and on God, we can speak with sincerity, even in difficult moments. Let us strive to be honest people, faithful to what we have promised.
exp.19:14:
Jonathan asks David never to stop showing kindness and loyalty to his family. That promise was meant to hold even when God destroyed every one of David's enemies. The second sentence is difficult and is translated in several different ways. It seems to be a solemn formula: if David failed to keep this promise, Jonathan would be cut off from David's house.

Jonathan, the son of King Saul, is speaking. Saul wanted to kill David, but Jonathan was his faithful friend. He sensed that David would be the future king, and so he asks for protection for his descendants. In this way they make a covenant of friendship before God.

For today: keep your promises, especially the ones you make to those you love. Show steady kindness, not only when it suits you, and think also about the well-being of your friends' children and family.
exp.19:17:
Jonathan tells David that tomorrow is the feast of the new moon, and that his absence will be noticed, because his place at the table will be empty. "Missed" means that someone will notice that a person is gone. "Seat" refers to the place David used to occupy at the king's table.

Jonathan, the son of King Saul, is speaking. David is fleeing because Saul wants to kill him. Jonathan, who loves him as himself, makes a plan to learn his father's true intentions. David's absence at the feast will be the signal. Scholars give no further detail about how that celebration was held, but it was an important gathering where the king's close companions were expected to be present.

For today: a true friend notices when someone is missing and cares about them. Think about who has stopped coming to your church, your family, or your group, and reach out to them with kindness this week.
exp.19:19:
Jonathan explains a secret plan. He says that he will shoot three arrows to one side, as though he were shooting at a target. In reality, it will be a signal. The word "target" here is the mark that is aimed at.

Jonathan is speaking to David. Saul, the king, seeks to kill David, and Jonathan, his son, is David's loyal friend. He wants to find out his father's intentions without putting them both in danger. David will hide near the stone of Ezel, and the warning will come through the servant and the place where the arrows fall. The following verses explain each signal.

For today: true friendship is loyal and sometimes requires prudence and courage. Ask yourself whom you can protect or encourage this week, and do it wisely, without seeking your own advantage.
exp.19:21:
It says that Jonathan will use a signal with arrows. If he calls out to the young man, "The arrows are beyond you," it will mean that David must leave, because the Lord is sending him away. The word "arrows" refers to the weapons shot from a bow, and "young man" means a young servant. "Beyond" means farther away, ahead.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, is speaking to his friend David. Saul wanted to kill David, and Jonathan had promised to find out his father's intentions. Since they could not speak openly, they agreed on a secret signal during the feast of the new moon. Jonathan recognizes that, if David must flee, that escape is under God's direction.

For today: sometimes God calls us to leave a place that is no longer safe, even when it hurts. We can accept such changes in faith, trusting that He cares for us, and lean on faithful friends who tell us the truth with love.
exp.19:24:
This verse describes how the king's table was arranged at the feast of the new moon. Saul sits in his usual place, next to the wall. Jonathan gets up, Abner sits at Saul's side, and David's place is left empty. The words for the places at the table here refer only to their seats at the table.

Here the narrator speaks. David had hidden himself, in line with the plan he made with Jonathan to find out whether Saul wanted to kill him. David's absence from the table is the proof. Saul says nothing that day, since he assumes David is ceremonially unclean. But his reaction the next day will show his true intentions.

For today: absences and silences say a great deal. Let us learn to notice who is missing from our table, whether at home, in our family, or in our church, and to approach them with love, without resentment or suspicion.
exp.19:33:
This verse says that Jonathan got up from the table in great anger and ate no food on the second day of the new moon feast. He was grieved for David and hurt because his father had shamed him.

Here the narrator is speaking, not a character. Jonathan had just defended David before his father Saul, and Saul responded by hurling a spear at him. So Jonathan understood that Saul was determined to kill David. His anger comes from the injustice, and his grief from his friendship with David.

For today: when you see injustice done to someone innocent, do not ignore it. Let it hurt you, but seek to act with wisdom and loyalty, as Jonathan did, and not with revenge.
exp.19:34:
This verse says that the next morning Jonathan went out into the field at the time he had agreed with David. A small boy, his servant, was with him. Where it explains the wording: the word for the boy means a young servant who attends someone, and the word for the time means the moment that had been set beforehand.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jonathan has just seen that his father, King Saul, wanted to kill David, and he left the table in great anger and sorrow. Now he carries out the plan he made with David: going out to shoot arrows, and by the way he would signal the boy, David would know whether he could return or had to flee. The boy does not know the real reason.

For today: when a painful truth shakes us, we can act faithfully to our word and to those we love, even when it costs us. Jonathan kept what he had promised despite the conflict with his own family.
exp.19:35:
He tells his young attendant (servant boy, helper) to run and find the arrows (darts) that he is about to shoot. While the boy runs, Jonathan shoots an arrow that falls farther than the boy, that is, it goes past him.

Jonathan speaks with his helper. He has just confirmed that his father, King Saul, intends to kill David. Jonathan and David had agreed on a signal: the words Jonathan called out to the boy would be the secret message for David, who was hiding nearby. The young man did not understand anything; he was only gathering arrows.

For today: sometimes we have to deliver bad news or make painful decisions. Jonathan loved his friend and was loyal to him even when it cost him his relationship with his father. Let us ask God for courage and wisdom to be faithful to what is right, caring for the people we love.
exp.19:37:
Jonathan called out again to his young helper, telling him to hurry, not to delay, and to make haste. The boy gathered up the arrows and came back to his master.

Jonathan was speaking with a signal agreed on beforehand with David, who was hiding because Saul wanted to kill him. If Jonathan said the arrows were beyond the boy, it meant David had to flee. The boy did not understand anything; he only obeyed. The shouts seemed like an ordinary command, but they were a secret message.

For today: sometimes truly loving someone means acting with prudence and faithfulness, even when others do not understand what we are doing. Jonathan risked his own position for his friend. Ask yourself today whom you can protect or support with loyalty, without seeking recognition.
exp.19:38:
He says that the young man who was helping Jonathan did not understand anything of what was happening. Only Jonathan and David knew the true meaning of what was done. The young servant is simply the boy, and the arrow is the arrow the boy was sent to find, and the matter means the business or the situation at hand.

Jonathan had agreed with David on a secret signal: he would shoot arrows, and by what he called out to the boy, David would know whether Saul meant to kill him or not. Jonathan's words seemed like an ordinary instruction, but they were a message of danger for David, who was hiding nearby. In this way Jonathan protected his friend without betraying him.

There are truths and difficult decisions that sometimes only those who live through them understand. Let us ask for wisdom to care for those we love, being prudent and loyal, while still acting with honesty before God.
exp.20:1:
Here David speaks with the priest Ahimelech at Nob. He tells him that King Saul had given him a secret task and that no one was to know what it was about. He also says that he had already told his servants, that is, his young helpers, where to meet him.

David is fleeing from Saul, who wants to kill him. He arrives alone, hungry and without weapons, and Ahimelech is alarmed to see him in that state. David then gives an explanation that is not true: Saul had not sent him. The Bible only reports what he said, without approving it. Later there were serious consequences (1 Samuel 22).

For today: fear can lead us to bend the truth, even when we are believers. Instead of trusting in a lie to save ourselves, we can pray and ask God for wisdom and courage to act honestly.
exp.20:5:
It says that the priest Ahimelech gave David the holy bread, because he had no other. It was the bread set out before God in the sanctuary. That day the old bread had been taken away to make room for hot bread, that is, freshly baked bread.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. David was fleeing from King Saul, he was hungry, and he came to Nob, where the priest was. David said he was on a mission from the king, and that was not entirely true. The priest set one condition: that the young men be ceremonially clean. Jesus mentioned this episode in Matthew 12, to teach that mercy weighs more than ritual.

For today: God's law seeks the good of people. When someone is hungry or in need, help them generously, without hiding behind rules.
exp.20:6:
This verse introduces a new man into the scene: Doeg, an Edomite who served Saul as chief of his herdsmen. He was held back before the Lord that day, that is, kept or set apart at the sanctuary. The text does not say with certainty why. Some think he was fulfilling a vow, a purification, or some matter of religious duty.

The narrator speaks here, not David. He interrupts the scene between David and the priest Ahimelech to tell us that someone saw them. David was fleeing from Saul and had asked for bread and a sword. What follows, in chapter 22, shows that Doeg reported to Saul, and this brought terrible consequences upon the priests.

For today: even when we believe no one sees us, our words and decisions have witnesses and consequences. Let us act with wisdom and truth, and trust that God cares for us.
exp.20:7:
Here David asks the priest Ahimelech whether there is a spear or a sword on hand. He explains that he left without his sword or his other weapons, because the king's business required haste, a matter that allowed no time for anything.

David is fleeing from Saul, who wants to kill him. He speaks with Ahimelech, the priest at Nob, and gives him an excuse to hide the fact that he is running away. That explanation was not entirely true, and later Doeg, who was present, reported it to Saul, with terrible consequences for the priests. The Bible records what David said, but it does not approve of his deception for that reason.

For today: when you are afraid, it is tempting to hide the truth to protect yourself. Remember that God can care for you without your having to lie, and that your words can affect other people.
exp.20:8:
Here the priest Ahimelech tells David that the only sword available is that of Goliath, the Philistine giant whom David defeated in the valley of the terebinth (or of Elah). It was kept wrapped in a cloth, behind the ephod, which was a priestly garment. David replies that there is none like it and asks that it be given to him.

David was fleeing from Saul, who wanted to kill him. He arrived without weapons and told Ahimelech that he was on an urgent mission for the king, which was not true. Nearby was Doeg, a servant of Saul, and his presence signals that this will have serious consequences for the priests.

For today: when you are in trouble, remember how God helped you before. That sword reminded David of the victory God had given him. Even so, his fear led him to lie, and that teaches us to trust God without resorting to deception.
exp.20:9:
This verse says that David got up that same day and fled from Saul. He came as far as Achish, king of Gath, a Philistine city. The word "fled" in the verse means he went away and kept his distance from the place where Saul could reach him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David was running away because Saul wanted to kill him. He had just passed through Nob, where the priest Ahimelech gave him bread and the sword of Goliath. Then he went to Gath, land of the Philistines, the same city Goliath came from. The text does not explain why he went there, so one can think he was looking for shelter, although his decision proved risky, as the fear he felt afterward shows.

For today: when fear presses on us, we can make decisions without consulting God. Before we run, let us ask God for direction in prayer.
exp.20:11:
It says that David kept in his mind what Achish's servants had said about him, and he was greatly afraid of the king of Gath. The phrase about keeping these words in his heart means that he took them seriously and thought them over.

Here the book's narrator is speaking. David was fleeing from Saul and came to Gath, a Philistine city, perhaps thinking he would go unnoticed there. But the servants recognized him as the hero who had defeated the Philistines, and David found himself in danger. That is why, in the verses that follow, he pretended to be insane in order to save himself.

For today: sometimes fear leads us to look for ways out on our own. David was afraid, and this reminds us that feeling fear is not sin. What matters is what we do with it. We can bring it to God in prayer, as David later wrote in Psalm 34, which tradition connects with this episode.
exp.21:1:
This verse tells us that everyone who was in trouble gathered around David: those who were distressed, those who were in debt, and those who were bitter of soul. David became their leader, and about four hundred men followed him.

David was fleeing from King Saul, who wanted to kill him, and he hid in the cave of Adullam. The text is a narrative; it is not David speaking. It shows that David, though still without a throne and pursued, drew in people who had no one to turn to. The Bible does not detail why each one came, or what their lives had been like before.

Today we can remember that God often builds community among wounded and needy people. If you are going through a difficult time, do not isolate yourself: seek healthy companionship. And if you are standing firm, open your heart to accompany someone who is suffering.
exp.21:2:
David left the cave of Adullam and went to Mizpeh of Moab. There he asked the king of Moab to let his father and mother come forth and be with them, that is, under his care, until he knew what God would do for him.

David spoke because he was fleeing from King Saul, who wanted to kill him. He already had about four hundred men with him, and his family was in danger. Moab may have seemed like a safe place to him, and the Bible also connects David to Moab through his great-grandmother Ruth, although the text does not say that this was the reason. Later, the prophet Gad tells him to return to Judah.

For today: when you do not know what is coming, care lovingly for your family and take the wise steps within your reach. Then say to God, with humility: "I will wait on you and see what you will do."
exp.21:4:
This verse says that the prophet Gad told David to leave the stronghold and go back to the land of Judah. David obeyed and went into the forest of Hareth.

Here Gad speaks, a prophet who was with David while he was fleeing from King Saul. David had left his parents with the king of Moab and was hiding in a stronghold, probably a place of concealment. It is not known with certainty which one it was. Gad's message led him out of a safe refuge into a more exposed place, within his own people. Later Saul learned where David was.

For today: sometimes God asks us to leave a comfortable and secure place in order to follow his way. Listening to wise counsel and obeying, even when it costs us, is a sign of trust in him.
exp.21:5:
When Saul learned that David had been seen, along with the men who were with him, Saul was sitting under a tree in Ramah with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing around him. The narrator describes what happens right after the prophet Gad advised David to return to Judah. Saul hears about it and gathers his men. The spear shows his power, but also his suspicion. In the verses that follow, he accuses his servants of conspiring against him, even though he has no proof.

For today: when fear and jealousy take hold of us, we begin to see enemies where there are none. Instead of clinging to control, we can pray, trust God, and listen to sincere advice.
exp.21:8:
Doeg, an Edomite who was placed over Saul's servants, speaks up. He says he saw David come to Nob, to the priest Ahimelech son of Ahitub.

Saul is furious and suspicious. He believes everyone is plotting against him, and he complains that no one tells him what his son Jonathan is doing with David. Doeg seizes that moment and speaks. What he says is true, but he tells it without mentioning that Ahimelech did not know David was fleeing from the king. That missing information will lead to tragedy.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself why you are saying it. A truth spoken without love, out of ambition, or in order to harm can cause great damage. Let us speak to help, not to destroy.
exp.21:12:
Saul accuses the priest Ahimelech of having joined forces with David against him. He charges that Ahimelech gave David bread and a sword, and that he inquired of God on David's behalf. To "conspire" means to make secret plans against someone. To "lie in wait" means to hide and wait in order to attack. Saul believes David is lying in wait to harm him.

King Saul speaks here, full of jealousy and distrust toward David. Ahimelech, in Nob, had helped David without knowing that David was fleeing from Saul (1 Samuel 21). The accusation had no evidence behind it, and Ahimelech's answer in the next passage shows that he acted in good faith.

Jealousy and fear can make us see enemies where there are none. Before accusing someone, it is wise to stop, ask questions with humility, and look for the facts. Let us ask God for a heart free from unjust suspicion.
exp.21:13:
Ahimelech, the priest, answers King Saul with courage. He asks who among all the king's servants is as faithful as David. He reminds Saul that David is the king's son-in-law, that he carries out his orders, and that he is highly respected in the king's house. Honourable here means worthy of respect and good standing.

Saul accuses Ahimelech of conspiring with David, who is fleeing from him. Ahimelech did help David with bread and a sword, but he did so without knowing that David was being hunted. To him, David was a loyal servant of the king. His defense is sincere, though Saul, ruled by jealousy and suspicion, does not accept it.

For today: Ahimelech told the truth even while afraid. We can speak with honesty and respect when something is unjust, and trust God, even when others do not believe us.
exp.21:16:
Here King Saul gives a terrible order to his guard: "Surround and kill the priests of the Lord." He accuses them of being on David's side, because they knew he was fleeing and did not tell him. But the king's servants refused to raise their hand against the priests of the Lord.

Saul speaks full of jealousy and fear, convinced that everyone is plotting against him. Ahimelech had just defended himself by saying he knew nothing of the conflict. Saul did not listen to him and pronounced an unjust sentence.

For today: when fear and pride govern, we can harm the innocent. Let us learn from those servants: obeying an authority does not oblige us to do wrong. Let us obey God first.
exp.21:19:
Of all those who died at Nob, this verse says that only one of the sons of the priest Ahimelech survived. His name was Abiathar. He escaped the massacre and went to find David.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. King Saul, consumed by jealousy and suspicion, had ordered the priests killed because Ahimelech had helped David. Doeg the Edomite carried out that terrible command. Abiathar was left as the only survivor of that family, and he sought refuge with David, whom Saul was pursuing.

Even in the midst of the greatest injustice and grief, God can preserve someone. When everything seems lost, we can seek refuge with those who follow God, and we do not have to carry our sorrow alone.
exp.21:20:
Here the text says that Abiathar, the only son of the priest Ahimelech who survived, told David that Saul had killed the Lord's priests.

The account is told by the narrator of Samuel. Saul, full of suspicion and jealousy, believed that the priests of Nob were helping David. Doeg the Edomite accused them, and Saul ordered the slaughter. Abiathar fled to David, who was hiding, and brought him the terrible news. David acknowledged that he bore part of the blame for having been there that day.

For today: when our actions, even without bad intent, bring pain to others, the best thing is to acknowledge it honestly and care for the one who suffered. David did not justify himself, but protected Abiathar and gave him a safe place at his side.
exp.21:21:
Here David tells Abiathar that he knew, on that day, that Doeg the Edomite was present and would surely tell Saul. The reference to Edom is clear in the verse itself, so no separate comment is needed. David acknowledges that he was the occasion, that is, the cause or reason, for the death of all the people of his father's house, the priests of Nob.

David is speaking while fleeing from Saul. He had passed through Nob and received help from the priest Ahimelech, and Doeg saw him. Saul ordered the priests killed, and only Abiathar escaped. David, on hearing of it, feels grief and takes his share of responsibility, although Saul and Doeg were the ones who carried out the slaughter.

For today: when our decisions, even without bad intent, have contributed to harm, we can acknowledge it with humility, without excuses. Then, like David, let us care for those who were wounded, offering them companionship and protection, and trust God with what we cannot repair.
exp.22:0:
This verse tells that someone brought word to David that the Philistines were attacking the city of Keilah and robbing the threshingfloors. A threshingfloor was a flat place where wheat and barley were beaten to separate the grain from the straw. To rob the threshingfloors was to take away people's harvest, their food for the whole year.

The verse does not say who brought the news, only that they told David. David was running from King Saul and living with a small band of followers. Keilah was a town in Judah, and its people could not defend themselves alone. The news reaches David as a plea for help, and he responds by first asking God what to do.

For today: when you learn of a need, do not act only on impulse or fear. First pray and ask God for direction; then obey, even when others doubt.
exp.22:5:
This verse tells how Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech, escaped and came to David at Keilah. He brought with him the ephod, a sacred garment of the priest, used to seek God's guidance.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. Abiathar was the only priest who survived when Saul ordered the priests of Nob to be killed (chapter 22). By joining David, he gave David a way to ask God what to do. That is why, in the verses that follow, David can inquire of the Lord before he acts, while Saul only relies on his own fortune.

For today: God knows how to give us help just when we need it. Before deciding something important, let us seek his direction in prayer and in his Word, and let us value the people who walk beside us in faith during difficult times.
exp.22:8:
This verse says that David realized Saul was planning to harm him. So he asked the priest Abiathar to bring the ephod. The ephod was a sacred garment of the priest, and it was used to seek God's guidance and receive his answer.

David had rescued the city of Keilah from the Philistines. Saul, believing that God had handed David over to him, gathered the army to surround the city. David, who was being pursued without cause, did not act on impulse. Before deciding, he wanted to ask God what he should do, and in the verses that follow God answers him.

For today: when we feel threatened or under pressure, the best thing is to stop and seek God before acting. We can pray, open his Word, and ask for wise counsel, instead of being carried along by fear or haste.
exp.22:11:
Here David asks the Lord whether the citizens of Keilah would surrender him and his men to King Saul. The Lord answers plainly: they will. The verse's note about the divine name and the word for neighbors is not needed here, since those terms do not appear in the verse you are reading.

David speaks in prayer, using the guidance God provided through the priest and the ephod. He had rescued Keilah from the Philistines, but Saul was pursuing him and planned to attack the city. David wanted to know whether the people of Keilah, whom he had helped, would be loyal to him. God warns him that they would not, and so David leaves with his six hundred men. The Bible does not say why the people of Keilah would act this way; it could have been fear of Saul.

For today: God can give us wisdom when we ask him sincerely. Sometimes his answer is not what we expect, but it protects us. Before deciding something important, pray, seek wise counsel, and do not trust only that others will repay your kindness.
exp.22:13:
David stayed hidden in the wilderness, in strongholds and rocky places, and lived on a mountain in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul searched for him every day, but God did not let him be caught.

The narrator of the book is speaking here. David was running away because Saul, out of jealousy, wanted to kill him. Shortly before this, David had left Keilah because God warned him that its people would hand him over. With about six hundred men, he kept moving from one place to another. Later, Jonathan would come to encourage him in God.

For today: even when you go through times of pressure or danger, God keeps caring for you, often in ways you cannot see. Do what you can with wisdom, listen to his guidance, and trust that he sustains your life.
exp.22:19:
The people of Ziph tell Saul to come down as soon as possible, to do everything his heart desires. They promise that they themselves will hand David over into the king's hands. The word for "come down" refers to going down from Gibeah toward the region of Ziph, which was higher and more desert-like terrain.

The speakers are some men of Ziph, from the tribe of Judah, who had already revealed David's hiding place. David, unjustly pursued, had just made a covenant with Jonathan before God. The men of Ziph seek to win Saul's favor, and he blesses them without seeing that he is pursuing an innocent man. The Bible does not fully explain why they acted this way.

For today: before joining in with what a powerful person wants, let us ask whether it is just. Pleasing others is worth no more than obeying God and protecting the innocent.
exp.22:23:
The verse says that the men of Ziph went up to their town ahead of Saul, to keep watch on David. Meanwhile, David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the plain to the south of the desert.

The men of Ziph had betrayed David to Saul. Saul praised them and asked them to find out for certain where David was hiding, because he considered him very cunning. They went to investigate, and David was nearby, pursued although he had done nothing wrong.

For today: even when we sometimes feel cornered or wrongly judged, we can keep trusting that God sees our situation. And like David, we can act with prudence, without seeking revenge, trusting that God will care for us.
exp.22:24:
Saul went out with his men to look for David, but someone warned David. So he went down into the rock and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. When Saul heard this, he pursued David into that wilderness.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Saul, the king, was chasing David out of jealousy and fear, even though David had done him no harm. The people of Ziph had offered to help Saul find him. David, for his part, kept moving from one place to another to save his life. Shortly afterward, a message about the Philistines interrupts the pursuit.

When we feel hunted or in danger, God can use warnings, people, or circumstances to care for us. It is wise to act with prudence, without despairing, and to trust that God continues to work even in times of uncertainty.
exp.22:25:
This verse describes a very tense chase. Saul went along one side of the mountain and David with his men along the other. David hurried to escape from Saul. But Saul and his men were closing in around him, surrounding David and his men to catch them.

It is part of the narrative, not a speech. Saul, the king, was pursuing David out of jealousy, even though David had done him no wrong. David was in the wilderness of Maon, fleeing. Just when it seemed there was no way out, a messenger arrived with news of a Philistine attack, and Saul had to leave.

For today: sometimes we feel surrounded, with no way out. This passage reminds us that God can act in unexpected ways, at just the right moment. We can keep doing what is right and trust that He cares for us, even when we cannot see how.
exp.23:0:
He says that David left where he was and settled in hard-to-reach places, at En-gedi. Strongholds are places protected by nature, such as caves, cliffs, or natural fortresses. En-gedi lies by the Dead Sea, in a desert area with rocks and springs.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator who tells the story. David was fleeing from King Saul, who pursued him out of jealousy and fear of losing the throne, even though David had already been anointed as the future king. Shortly before, David had spared Saul's life on another occasion, and now he had to look for refuge again. The verses that follow show that Saul came after him with three thousand men.

For today: in times of pressure or injustice, seeking a safe place is not a lack of faith. We can protect ourselves with prudence, rest in God, and keep trusting that He keeps His promises, without responding with revenge.
exp.23:1:
This verse tells that Saul had just returned from fighting the Philistines. As soon as he came back, someone told him that David was in the wilderness of En-gedi. The phrase about being told is simply the news being given to him. En-gedi was a desert area near the Dead Sea, with caves and rocky cliffs.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Saul, the king, was pursuing David because he felt jealousy and fear of losing the throne. David kept hiding in strong places, that is, places that were hard to reach. As soon as Saul finished a war against an enemy of the people, he spent his strength again against David, whom God had chosen.

For today: Saul had a real enemy outside, but his greatest problem was inside, in his heart full of envy. Let us ask God to help us recognize these feelings and surrender them to him before they take control of us and harm others.
exp.23:7:
This verse says that David calmed his men with firm words and did not let them attack Saul. Here, the idea is that he held them back and stopped them, like someone who grips another person firmly. Afterward, Saul left the cave and went on his way, without knowing what had happened.

Saul was chasing David to kill him. Without knowing it, he entered a cave where David and his men were hiding. His men saw there an opportunity to finish off their enemy. David only cut off a piece of Saul's robe, and even that weighed on his conscience. He respected Saul as the anointed of God, that is, the king chosen by Him.

When we have the chance to take revenge, we can choose the opposite: let God be the judge. And if others urge us to do wrong, we need courage to tell them no.
exp.23:9:
David asks Saul why he listens to those who tell him that David wants to harm him. It is a direct and respectful question.

David is speaking to King Saul, who had been pursuing him in order to kill him. He had just had the chance to finish off Saul in the cave, and his men urged him to do it. But David held back, cut off only a piece of the robe, and now comes out to show Saul that he is not his enemy. His question points to the rumors that had poisoned Saul's heart.

Today we can learn not to believe everything we are told about others, and not to let gossip fill us with anger. When people accuse us unfairly, we can answer with calm, with respect, and with facts, without repaying evil for evil.
exp.23:12:
David tells Saul that God should be the judge between the two of them. He asks God to judge his case and to decide between them. David will not take revenge on his own: he places his cause in God's hands and declares that his hand will not be raised against the king.

David is speaking from the mouth of a cave, where Saul had gone in without knowing that David was inside. His men urged him to kill Saul, but David only cut off a corner of Saul's robe. Now he shows it to Saul as proof that he could have killed him and did not, even though Saul was pursuing him unjustly.

For today: when someone treats you unfairly, do not repay evil with evil. Place your cause in God's hands, do what is right, and trust that He is a just judge. Waiting on Him requires patience, but it protects your heart from bitterness.
exp.23:13:
David tells Saul there is an old saying: wickedness comes from wicked people. By this he means that if he were a wicked man, he would already have harmed Saul. Since he is not, he will not raise his hand against him.

David speaks in a cave, after Saul, who was pursuing him to kill him, entered there without knowing David was inside. David cut off only the edge of Saul's robe and did him no harm. Now he shows it to Saul as proof that he is not his enemy, and he leaves God to be the judge between the two of them.

For today: when someone treats us unfairly, we do not have to answer with the same wickedness. We can act with integrity, speak the truth with respect, and trust that God will do justice in his time.
exp.23:15:
David says that God will be the judge between him and Saul. He asks God to look at the case, defend his cause, and free him from Saul's power.

David is speaking, after having been hunted by King Saul. In the cave he could have killed him, but he only cut off a piece of Saul's robe and did him no harm. Now, from a distance, he tells Saul that he will not take revenge with his own hand and leaves the matter in God's hands. In many Bibles this passage appears as verse 15.

When people treat you unjustly, you do not have to repay evil with evil. You can bring your case before God, act with uprightness, and trust that he judges with justice.
exp.23:19:
Saul asks who, upon finding his enemy, would let him go unharmed. It is a question that shows his amazement. Saul then asks that the LORD reward David with good for having spared his life.

The king Saul, who was pursuing David in order to kill him, is speaking. David had the chance to finish him off in a cave, but he only cut off a piece of his robe and spared his life. Saul acknowledges his wrong, although the Bible shows that this repentance did not last forever.

For today: when someone has wronged us and we have the opportunity to take revenge, we can choose to do good and leave the matter in God's hands. Responding with kindness can show others our faith.
exp.23:21:
Saul asks David to swear to him by God that he will not destroy his descendants or wipe out his name from the family. David promises that he will do so. Then Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to a stronghold.

Saul speaks after David spared his life in the cave of En-gedi, although he could have killed him. Saul acknowledges that David will be king. In those times, a new king sometimes wiped out the family of the previous one, and that is why Saul asks for protection. David keeps his word, and later he cares for Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson (2 Samuel 9). That David stays in the stronghold shows that he does not fully trust Saul, and the Bible does not explain his reasons.

For today: keep what you promise, even to someone who has wronged you. But also be wise: forgiving and acting with wisdom can go together.
exp.24:3:
This verse says that David, while he was in the wilderness, learned that Nabal was shearing his sheep. "Shear" means cutting the wool off the sheep. It was important work and, in that time, also a season of feasting and abundance.

The narrator tells this after introducing Nabal, a very wealthy man, but harsh and wicked in his deeds. David was living on the run from Saul, and his band stayed in those lands. Upon learning that it was shearing time, he sends messengers to ask for help respectfully. The text does not explain all his reasons, but that season was usually one of generosity.

For today: before asking for something or making a decision, pay attention to the moment and to the person. Ask with respect and humility, and do not assume that others owe you something. Even so, be ready to respond calmly if they treat you badly.
exp.24:15:
They were like a wall around Nabal's shepherds, protecting them day and night while they tended the sheep in the field.

The one speaking is a servant of Nabal, who tells Abigail what happened. David had sent greetings to Nabal and asked him for some provisions, but Nabal treated them with scorn. The servant defends David's men and warns of the danger, because he knows the situation could end very badly. Abigail is seen as a wise woman who can act.

For today: it is worth recognizing and thanking those who have looked after us without asking for anything, and not repaying their kindness with contempt. Also, when we see danger, it is wise to warn honestly the person who can help resolve it.
exp.24:18:
She tells her servants to go on ahead with the gifts, and she will follow after them. The servants are the household's attendants. The verse says she did not tell her husband Nabal anything.

The narrator describes what Abigail did. Nabal had insulted David's men, and David was coming with armed men to take revenge. One of the young men warned Abigail about the danger. She acted quickly, without asking her husband's permission. Some think she did this because Nabal was very harsh and would not have listened to her. The Bible does not explain her reasons any further.

When a situation is urgent and dangerous, sometimes we must act with courage and wisdom to seek peace. Ask God for discernment, and act with humility and respect, not with pride or rebellion.
exp.24:22:
This verse tells how Abigail, when she saw David, quickly got down from her donkey and bowed low to the ground with her face toward the earth. The phrase about getting down quickly means she dismounted right away from her animal. The actions of falling forward and bowing down show a gesture of deep respect and humility.

David was coming in anger with his men to kill Nabal, because Nabal had refused him help and had treated him with contempt, even though David had protected Nabal's shepherds. Abigail, Nabal's wife, learned what had happened from a servant and went out in great haste with provisions to stop the disaster. Here the narrative shows her acting with wisdom and courage.

For today: when a conflict is about to break out, humility and quickness to seek peace can prevent a great deal of harm. Sometimes it is wise to set aside pride and speak calmly before anger makes the decision for us.
exp.24:23:
Abigail throws herself at David's feet and says, "My lord, may the blame be on me alone, but please let your servant speak to you; hear the words of your servant." She is asking David to let her speak and to listen closely to what she has to say.

Abigail is the wife of Nabal, a rich and foolish man. Nabal had insulted David's men and refused them help. David, furious, was on his way with four hundred men to take revenge. Abigail goes out to meet him to stop the violence. By offering to take the blame on herself, she tries to calm David and win his attention.

For today: when there is a conflict, humility and wise words can stop greater harm. Sometimes it is worth taking the first step toward reconciliation, even if the mistake was not ours, and asking God for wisdom before reacting in anger.
exp.24:29:
Abigail tells David that when God fulfills all the good things He promised him, and appoints him ruler over Israel, something is going to happen. The sentence is left open and continues in the next verse.

Abigail speaks with David, who was coming with his men to kill Nabal, her husband, because Nabal had treated them with contempt. She goes out to meet him and asks him not to act out of revenge. She reminds him that God will call him to be king, and that it is not good for him to carry the guilt of bloodshed without need.

For today: when you feel that you have been wronged, think about what God wants to do with you over the long run. Do not let the anger of a moment rob you of peace or damage your future. Trust that God can bring about justice better than you can.
exp.24:33:
In this passage David swears by the name of God that, if Abigail had not hurried to come out and meet him, he would have killed every male in Nabal's household before morning light. Since the verse does not appear in the reader's wording in those terms, the verse of the old phrasing is simply rendered as plain speech: David says that no one in Nabal's house who urinates against a wall would have been left alive by morning. He acknowledges that God held him back from doing harm.

David goes out with his men, angry, because Nabal, a rich man, rudely refused to give them food even though they had protected his flocks. Abigail, Nabal's wife, acted quickly and wisely, and brought provisions to David. Here David speaks with gratitude and recognizes that she stopped him.

Today we can learn to pause before acting in anger. If someone offends us, it is wise to listen to a wise voice and leave revenge in God's hands. Giving thanks for those who correct us in time spares us from mistakes we would later regret.
exp.24:36:
It says that the next morning, when Nabal was already sober (the wine had gone out of him), his wife Abigail told him what had happened. Then his heart died within him, meaning he was struck down and lost his strength, and he became as a stone. Many think it may have been a stroke or a heart attack, though the text gives no further details.

Context: the narrator explains that Abigail had saved her household from David's anger, since David was coming to take revenge because Nabal had insulted him. She waited until Nabal was sober before speaking to him. Ten days later, the text says the LORD struck Nabal and he died.

For today: there are right moments and right ways to speak hard truths. Abigail acted with prudence, and her hope was in God, not in revenge. Before we react with anger, let us ask for wisdom to act with calm and to trust in the justice of God.
exp.24:37:
This verse says that ten days after that night, God struck Nabal and he died. "Struck" here means that God hit him or punished him. The Bible does not explain how it happened; it only states that God was the one who acted.

The narrator tells of the end of Nabal, a rich and foolish man who scorned David and his men when they asked for help. David was going to take revenge with violence, but Abigail, Nabal's wife, stopped him with wisdom. Then, when he learned what had happened, Nabal's heart failed within him. Some think it may have been a stroke or a heart attack, but the text does not specify.

For today: we do not need to take revenge on someone who wrongs us. David recognized that God brought about justice without him having to stain his hands. We can entrust our hurts to God, do what is right, and trust that He judges with justice.
exp.24:39:
This verse says that David's servants went to Abigail, who was at Carmel, and delivered their master's message: David wanted to marry her. The word for the servants here means the servants or messengers. The phrase about taking her as his wife means asking her to marry him.

Abigail had been the wife of Nabal, a foolish man who insulted David and treated him with contempt. She stepped in with wisdom and kept David from shedding blood. Now Nabal has died, and David, who recognizes that God brought about justice, proposes marriage to her. In that period it was common for leaders to have several wives; the Bible records this, but does not necessarily approve of it.

For today: God sees those who act with prudence and humility in the midst of unjust situations. Trust that He cares for you and can open new doors, even after difficult times.
exp.24:40:
Abigail receives David's marriage proposal. She rises, bows down to the ground, and offers herself with humility. She says she is willing to be a servant who washes the feet of David's servants.

After Nabal died, David praised God and sent messengers to Abigail. She had acted with wisdom and courage to prevent bloodshed. Her response shows respect and humility before David. The text tells us that she then married him, although it does not explain her innermost feelings.

For today: true greatness is shown in humble service. We can serve others without seeking applause, with a willing and grateful heart before God.
exp.24:41:
Abigail did not waste any time. She got up right away, mounted a donkey, and went off with David's messengers, accompanied by five young women who served her. When she arrived, she married David and became his wife.

The narrator is telling the end of a story that began when Nabal, Abigail's foolish husband, insulted David and died shortly afterward. Abigail had acted with wisdom and humility to prevent a tragedy. Now David takes her as his wife. In that time it was common for a man to have more than one wife, and the Bible reports this here without approving or explaining it. The passage then mentions Ahinoam and Michal, which shows that David's life was complicated.

For today: Abigail responded promptly and humbly when a new chapter opened. When God opens a door, we can act with simplicity and without delay, trusting Him even when the future is not entirely clear.
exp.24:43:
This verse tells how Saul gave his daughter Michal, David's wife, to another man named Phalti, son of Laish, who was from a place called Gallim. The word "wife" in the verse is the one that reflects David's wife, so the reader can see her as David's wife directly.

The author of the book is the one telling this, not a character in the story. He makes this point right after mentioning David's other marriages. Saul, angry and jealous of David, had taken Michal away from him. Later, in 2 Samuel 3, David gets her back. So we see how the king's decisions affected the lives of others.

For today: when someone with power acts out of jealousy or resentment, others end up suffering. Let us ask God for a humble heart, so that we do not use our influence to harm others, and so that we care with respect for the people He places in our charge.
exp.25:0:
This verse tells how some people from Ziph went to Saul at Gibeah and let him know where David was hiding. The old form of their name, which the verse mentions, is simply the people of Ziph, and the reader can take it as the Ziphites named in the verse. The word meaning hill or ridge is the hill of Hachilah, and the phrase meaning in front of the wilderness refers to the hill lying before the desert area, or in view of it.

The Ziphites were people from the land of Judah, and they spoke to King Saul. Saul had been pursuing David for some time out of jealousy and fear. Earlier, in 1 Samuel 23, the Ziphites had given him similar information. Here they betray David again, and this leads Saul to set out with three thousand men to search for him.

For today: we should be careful about what we say about others. A word spoken out of convenience or fear can put an innocent person in danger. Let us ask God for the courage to speak the truth and not feed injustice.
exp.25:1:
This verse says that King Saul rose up and went to the wilderness of Ziph. He took three thousand of the best soldiers of Israel with one purpose: to seek David. The verse says Saul went down from Gibeah toward that desert region.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The Ziphites, who lived in that area, had just told Saul where David was. Saul had pursued David before, and this shows that his jealousy was still alive. Meanwhile, David trusted that God was watching over him, even though he was living as a fugitive.

For today: when someone pursues us or treats us unjustly, we can respond with calm and trust in God, without letting resentment carry us away. And we ourselves should examine our hearts, so that envy does not lead us to harm others.
exp.25:2:
This verse says that Saul set up his camp on the hill of Hachilah, facing the wilderness, beside the road. Meanwhile, David was in the wilderness and realized that Saul was coming after him.

The narrator tells us that the Ziphites, people who lived in the area, informed Saul where David was hiding. Saul went out with three thousand chosen men to search for him. David had been running from Saul for some time, since Saul was pursuing him out of jealousy. This moment sets up a scene in which David will have the chance to harm Saul, but he will not take it.

For today: when someone pursues us or treats us unjustly, we should first be alert and trust God, rather than acting in haste or seeking revenge. We can ask him for wisdom to respond with integrity, as David did.
exp.25:3:
This verse tells how David sent out men to watch Saul's movements in secret. The "spies" are scouts sent out to gather information. They came back with the news, and David knew for certain that Saul had really arrived with his army.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not David speaking. Saul had brought three thousand men to capture David, who was hiding in the wilderness of Ziph. David had already heard rumors that Saul was following him, but he was not satisfied with that. He wanted to confirm it before acting, and what he did afterward, sparing Saul's life, grew out of that preparation.

For today: before making an important decision, look for clear information and confirm the facts. Trusting God does not remove the duty to be wise. We can pray and, at the same time, investigate calmly so that we act with understanding.
exp.25:4:
David got up and went to the place where Saul had camped. From there he looked at where Saul and Abner, son of Ner, the commander of the army, were lying. Saul was sleeping inside the camp's defensive ring, which was probably the circle of wagons or baggage that surrounded the camp. The army's people were sleeping all around him.

Here the narrator is speaking. Saul was pursuing David in the wilderness, and David, who was fleeing for his life, learned from his spies where Saul was. This is the second time David has the chance to harm Saul.

When someone has treated us unjustly, we may have the chance to get even. Before acting, it is wise to stop, observe calmly, and ask God to guide us, so that we respond with justice and respect rather than revenge.
exp.25:6:
So David and Abishai went to the camp at night. They found the king asleep inside the trench, which was probably the ring of chariots or baggage that surrounded the camp. His spear was stuck in the ground beside his head. Abner, his commander, and all the soldiers were sleeping around him.

Saul had been chasing David for a long time, trying to kill him, even though David had done him no wrong. Here the narrator describes the scene to show how close David was to Saul and how easy revenge seemed. In the verses that follow, Abishai sees an opportunity that God seems to be giving them, but David refuses to kill the Lord's anointed.

For today: not every chance to take revenge is a door that God opens. When someone wounds us, we can trust that God will do justice and choose to act with respect and self-control.
exp.25:7:
Abishai tells David that God has handed his enemy over to him. For that reason he offers to kill Saul with one blow of the spear, pinning him to the ground.

Abishai, David's nephew and a loyal soldier, speaks in the middle of the night. Saul had been pursuing David to kill him for a long time, and now he is sleeping in his camp, with no one keeping proper watch. Abishai reads the opportunity as a sign from God. David, in the next verse, will reject that plan.

For today: a favorable opportunity is not always a sign from God to do what we want. Before acting, it is wise to ask ourselves whether what we are about to do honors God and respects his principles, even when someone has wronged us.
exp.25:8:
Here David tells Abishai not to kill Saul. He asks firmly: "who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed, and be guiltless?" That is, no one who does that will go free from blame.

David speaks at night, inside Saul's camp, the camp of the man who had been pursuing him to kill him. Everyone is asleep, and Abishai sees an opportunity that seems sent by God. David, however, honors Saul because God had placed him as king. He prefers to wait for God to judge and act in his own time.

For today: an opportunity for revenge is not the same as God's permission to take it. When someone has done us harm, we can choose not to repay evil with evil, to trust God's justice, and to act with integrity even when no one sees us.
exp.25:11:
This verse tells that David took the spear and the jug of water that were beside Saul's head, and went away with Abishai. No one saw them or noticed, and no one woke up, because they were all asleep. The text says that God himself sent a very deep sleep upon them.

Saul was pursuing David in order to kill him. That night David entered the camp and found Saul asleep. Abishai wanted to kill him, but David refused, because Saul was the anointed one of the Lord, the king chosen by God. David took the spear and the jug as proof that he could have killed him and did not.

For today: when you have the chance to take revenge or gain at someone else's expense, remember that justice belongs to God. You can act with respect and leave the outcome in his hands, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.25:18:
Here David asks Saul to listen. He sets out two possibilities: if the Lord himself has stirred Saul up against him, then let Saul offer a sacrifice to seek peace with God. But if it is men who have provoked him, then let them be cursed, because they have driven David out from living in the Lord's inheritance, that is, the land of Israel. "Other gods" are foreign, false gods.

David speaks from the wilderness, after sparing Saul's life while Saul was sleeping. Saul was pursuing him unjustly, perhaps influenced by accusations from others. David suffers from being far from the land and from worshiping God. Interpreters debate how to understand "if the Lord has stirred you up"; David seems to leave the possibility open without affirming it.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, speak with respect and truth, without seeking revenge. Leave your cause in God's hands, and value being close to him more than any advantage.
exp.25:21:
David answers Saul and shows him that the king's spear is there, in his possession. He asks that one of his servants (his helpers or attendants) be sent to cross over and pick it up. It is a way of returning it without Saul having to come near him.

David speaks from the other side of the valley, after he entered Saul's camp at night while everyone was sleeping. He could have killed the king, but he did not, because Saul was the anointed one of the LORD, that is, the one chosen by God. He took the spear as proof that he had respected him. Saul acknowledges his wrong, although the Bible shows that his change did not last.

When you have the chance to take revenge, trust that God is just. Do what is right, even if others do not do so toward you, and leave it to God to judge and to defend.
exp.26:2:
David went to live with Achish, king of Gath, one of the Philistine rulers. He did not go alone: he took his men, each one with his household, and also his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, Nabal's widow, from Carmel.

The narrator is describing what happened after David came to believe that Saul would eventually kill him. That is why he chose to take refuge in Philistine territory, where Saul would stop pursuing him. Some see here a prudent decision, and others a lack of trust in God. The text does not make this clear.

When fear presses on us, it is easy to look for quick ways out. We can ask God for wisdom before we decide, and remember that He also cares for our families in uncertain times.
exp.26:7:
David and his men would go out on raids, meaning surprise attacks, against the Geshurites, the Gezrites, and the Amalekites. These peoples had lived for a long time in the area stretching from Shur to Egypt, south of Canaan.

The narrator tells what David was doing while he lived in Ziklag, the town that the Philistine king Achish had given him. The Amalekites were enemies of Israel and had been condemned by God before. But the account that follows shows that David was deceiving Achish about whom he was attacking. The text describes these events, and it does not say that everything David did was right.

Today we can learn that God can carry out his plans even in the midst of our weaknesses, but that does not justify deception. Let us strive to live with truthfulness and without a double life, trusting that God cares for us without our having to pretend.
exp.26:10:
He says that David would leave alive no man or woman who could reach Gath, so that no one would tell what he was really doing. This was his custom for as long as he lived among the Philistines.

The narrator tells how David, fleeing from Saul, lived in Ziklag under King Achish of Gath. David raided enemy peoples of the south, but he led Achish to believe he was attacking Judah. The text only reports what happened; it does not approve of either the violence or the deception. No direction from God about these actions is mentioned here.

For today: fear and pressure can lead us to lie, and to cover our steps with more lies. David was a man of faith, but here we see his frailty. We can ask God for the courage to live in truth, without depending on deception to protect ourselves.
exp.27:0:
These verses tell how the Philistines gathered their armies to attack Israel. Achish, the Philistine king, tells David that he must go out with him to war, along with his men.

Here the one speaking is Achish, king of Gath, where David had taken refuge while fleeing from Saul. Achish trusted David and believed that David was hated by his own people. David finds himself in a difficult bind: appearing loyal to the Philistines could lead him to fight against Israel. The Bible does not resolve this tension right away; David's response is ambiguous.

For today: when our past decisions lead us into difficult situations, it is wise to stop and ask God for wisdom and a way out, instead of pressing on without thinking. God can guide us even in our tangles.
exp.27:2:
This verse reminds us that Samuel, the prophet and judge of Israel, had already died. All the people mourned him, and they buried him in Ramah, his city. It also says that Saul had driven out of the land those who called up the dead, and those who claimed to know the future by forbidden means.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Before he tells us that Saul, frightened by the Philistine army, would seek out a woman who consults spirits, he makes two things clear: Samuel was no longer there to guide him, and Saul himself had banned these practices, which God's law condemned. This shows a contradiction in his heart.

For today: when fear comes, it is easy to set aside what we say we believe. Let us seek God in prayer and in his Word, and not take shortcuts that he has forbidden.
exp.27:5:
It says that Saul, very frightened, asked God what to do before the Philistine army, but God did not answer him. The three ways God used to answer were: dreams, the Urim (a sacred object that the priests used to learn God's will; it is not known exactly how it worked), and prophets. None of them worked.

The narrator tells that Saul, the first king of Israel, faced an enormous battle and was afraid. He had earlier disobeyed God repeatedly, and God's silence appears in the story as part of that distance. In despair, he sought out a medium, something God's law forbade.

When we feel afraid, it is good to draw near to God with sincerity and repentance before the crisis arrives, and not to look for forbidden shortcuts when we feel that He is silent.
exp.27:8:
Here the woman of Endor speaks to the man in disguise, who is Saul, though she does not yet know it. She reminds him that the king has cut off from the land those who have familiar spirits, that is, people who claimed to have a spirit through which they could communicate with the dead, and the wizards. She is afraid and asks why he is laying a trap for her that could cost her her life.

Saul had forbidden these practices, which the law of God condemned (Leviticus 19:31). Now, with no answer from God and filled with fear before the Philistines, he himself breaks his own law. The woman is suspicious because she believes it is a trap. Saul swears to her by the LORD that no harm will come to her, which is a sad irony.

For today: when we feel afraid and God seems silent, it is tempting to look for answers in forbidden places. It is better to wait on God, to be consistent with what we say we believe, and to seek his Word with humility.
exp.27:13:
Saul asks the woman what form the figure has that she is seeing. She describes an old man coming up, covered with a robe. Saul concludes that it is Samuel and bows down with his face to the ground.

Saul speaks with a medium at Endor. He is desperate because the Philistines are attacking him and God no longer answers him. He had banned divination, but now he seeks it out. Notice that Saul works out who it is from the description, since he himself sees nothing. Some believe it was truly Samuel; others, that it was a deception. The text does not fully settle the question.

When we are distressed, it is easy to look for answers in places God does not approve. It is better to return to him with humility and sincerity, and not look for shortcuts.
exp.27:14:
Samuel asks Saul why he has troubled him by bringing him up. Saul answers that he is in great distress: the Philistines are attacking him, God has departed from him, and he no longer answers him, neither by prophets nor by dreams. That is why he called Samuel, so that he could tell him what to do.

Saul, the first king of Israel, had disobeyed God, and now he faced a war without divine guidance. In his desperation, he sought out a medium, something the Law forbade. The text presents the appearance as Samuel, though scholars debate how it should be understood. What is clear is that Samuel's answer confirms the judgment already announced.

When we are distressed, it is better to return to God with humility and repentance than to seek answers by forbidden or desperate means. He continues to listen to those who come to him sincerely.
exp.27:15:
Here Samuel answers Saul with a hard question: if the Lord has already departed from you and become your enemy, why do you come to me?

Saul is desperate because the Philistines are attacking and God is not answering him. For this reason he turns to a medium at Endor, something the law forbade. The text says that Samuel appears, though commentators explain this in different ways. What is clear is that the message agrees with what God had already said: Saul lost the kingdom because of his disobedience.

For today: let us not seek answers in ways God forbids when we are in distress. If we feel that God is far away, let us return to Him with humility and repentance, before fear pushes us into wrong decisions.
exp.27:19:
This verse says that Saul fell suddenly to the ground, stretched out full length on his body. He was filled with fear because of what Samuel had told him, and he was left without strength. Moreover, he had eaten nothing all day or all night.

Saul, the king of Israel, was desperate because the Philistines were coming to attack him and God no longer answered him. So he sought out a woman who consulted the dead, something God's law forbade. What appeared to him announced his defeat and his death. Scholars debate how to understand this scene, but the message is clear: Saul had disobeyed God.

For today: when we are in trouble, let us seek God with humility and obedience, not forbidden shortcuts. And let us remember that fear, fasting and exhaustion weaken us; caring for the body matters too.
exp.27:21:
In this verse the woman asks Saul to listen to her, just as he listened to her. She offers him a little bread to eat, so that he may regain his strength and be able to continue on his way.

The speaker is the woman of Endor, to whom Saul had gone to consult Samuel. Saul had just received a dreadful message of judgment, and he was so distressed that he fell to the ground. Moreover, he had not eaten all day or all night. She, who had risked her life in helping him, now shows compassion and care for him. At first he refused, but then he accepted.

For today: when someone is exhausted or downcast, a simple gesture of care, such as sharing a meal, can be a real act of kindness. God calls us to notice the practical needs of others.
exp.27:23:
The woman of Endor had a fattened calf at home, and she killed it right away. She also took flour, kneaded the dough, and baked unleavened bread, that is, bread that is prepared quickly because it does not need to wait for the dough to rise.

The narrator tells what happened after Samuel, who had been called by the woman, announced to Saul his defeat and his death.
