Saul was left without strength, for he had not eaten all day or the night before. The woman, who had seen his distress, urged him to eat, and his servants encouraged him too. She took a great risk in helping Saul.

For today: the woman generously cared for someone weak, expecting nothing in return. We can imitate that gesture by serving someone who is suffering with something concrete, such as a meal.
exp.28:4:
The Philistine lords remind their king Achish of a famous song among the Israelites. The women sang it while dancing in rounds, which were groups or circle dances. The song said that Saul had defeated his thousands, but David his ten thousands. The lords use it as proof that David is a warrior greatly feared.

The Philistine princes speak, distrustful. Achish trusted David, but they thought that, in the middle of a battle against Israel, David could win Saul's favor by handing over Philistine heads. For this reason they demand that he leave. Without knowing it, they spare David from having to fight against his own people.

For today: sometimes God closes a door for us through people who reject us, and later we see that it was a protection. We can trust that He watches over our path, even when we do not understand it.
exp.28:5:
Here Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, calls David and speaks to him honestly. He swears by the Lord that David has been upright, that he is pleased with David's conduct in coming and going, and that he has found no wrong in him. But he adds that the rulers, the leaders of the Philistines, do not approve of him.

The Philistines are preparing to fight against Israel. Their leaders distrust David and fear that in the middle of the battle he will turn against them. Achish, who did trust him, explains that David must go back. We do not know for certain what David would have done in the battle; the text does not make it clear. What we see is that God delivers him from a very difficult situation.

For today: sometimes someone recognizes our good conduct and yet others reject us. Let us not depend on everyone's approval; let us live with integrity and trust that God cares for our way.
exp.28:9:
Here Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, tells David to rise up early in the morning, together with his men, and go. The men of David are described as servants of Achish's lord, meaning they were regarded as serving Achish. The verse's command to get going is clear: leave as soon as it is light in the morning.

Achish speaks this way because the Philistine lords distrusted David and did not want him to fight alongside them against Israel. Although Achish trusted him, he had to send him away. Some think this protected David from having to fight against his own people, though the text does not directly explain it that way.

For today: sometimes a door closes without our understanding why. We can obey calmly and trust that God watches over our path, even when He saves us from situations we did not know were dangerous.
exp.28:10:
This verse tells us that David got up early, together with his men, to return to the land of the Philistines, that is, to Ziklag, the city that Achish had given him. Meanwhile, the Philistines went up to Jezreel to prepare for war against Israel. "Early in the morning" means very early, and "his men" are David's men.

King Achish explained to David that the Philistine lords did not trust him and did not want him to fight at their side. Achish respected him, but he had to send him away. So David was spared from fighting against his own people, although the text does not say what David was thinking at that moment. Many see in this the care of God, who protected him without his planning it.

For today: sometimes a door closes and it hurts us, like a rejection or a plan that falls through. We can obey calmly, without fighting, and trust that God may be caring for us in something we cannot yet see.
exp.29:0:
This verse tells that David and his men returned to Ziklag after three days of travel. They found that the Amalekites had invaded the south and burned the city with fire.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had been living in Ziklag, a city that the Philistine king Achish had given him while he was fleeing from Saul. David's men had gone off with the Philistine army, and the city was left without defense. The following verses explain that the women and children were taken captive, and that no one was killed.

For today: sometimes we come home and find that we have lost everything all at once. In those moments we are not alone. The chapter shows that David, though deeply distressed, ended up seeking strength in God. When loss comes, bring it to Him before deciding what to do.
exp.29:2:
It says that David and his men returned to Ziklag and found the city burned down. Their wives, their sons and their daughters were gone: they had been taken captive.

This is the narrator of the book speaking. David was living among the Philistines, and while he and his men were away, the Amalekites attacked Ziklag. The text makes clear that they killed no one, but carried off the people. David arrived on the third day and found this total loss, at a moment that was already very hard for him.

For today: when a loss seems total, it is natural to weep and to feel the blow. But one should not remain alone in the grief. In verse 6 of this same chapter, David strengthens himself in the Lord. He seeks God before deciding what to do.
exp.29:3:
This verse tells how David and all his men wept aloud, without holding back, until they were worn out. They no longer had the strength to keep weeping. The phrase about raising their voice means they wept loudly, and the word for the men refers to his soldiers.

No one speaks here; the narrator describes the scene. David and his men returned to Ziklag and found it burned. The Amalekites had taken captive their wives, sons, and daughters. They did not know whether they were still alive. The grief was enormous, and soon it turned into tension, because the men spoke of stoning David. Even so, the text says that David strengthened himself in the Lord his God.

Weeping is not a lack of faith. The Bible shows that even a man of faith can be left without strength in the face of a loss. First we can unburden ourselves honestly before God, and then seek encouragement in Him to take the next step.
exp.29:10:
Some of David's men found an Egyptian out in the field and brought him to David. They gave him food to eat and water to drink.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book. David and his men were chasing the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off their families. Tired and hungry, this young man was a servant of an Amalekite, and his master had left him behind when he became sick. Later, he will guide David to the enemy camp. The Bible does not explain everything, but it shows that God works even in an unexpected encounter.

For today: even in the midst of your own urgency, do not walk past a person in need. A simple act of kindness, like giving food or water, can open doors you never imagined.
exp.29:12:
Here David asks the young Egyptian he and his men found nearly dead from hunger two questions: whose are you, and where are you from? The young man explains that he is a servant of an Amalekite, and that his master left him behind because he became sick three days ago.

David and his men return to Ziklag and find it burned, with their families taken captive by the Amalekites. They pursue the raiders, and along the way they find this abandoned servant. David first takes care of him and then asks him questions. This young man will be the one who leads them to the enemy camp.

For today: God can use people who have been forgotten and discarded to open a way forward. If we treat someone who is suffering with kindness, no matter who they are, we may discover that God is also helping us through that person.
exp.29:15:
The passage tells how the Egyptian servant led David to the camp of the Amalekites. They were spread out over the whole area, eating, drinking and celebrating, because they had taken a great deal of plunder from the land of the Philistines and from Judah.

Earlier, the Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the families of David and his men. David found an abandoned servant, helped him, and the servant promised to guide him if David did not kill him or hand him back to his master. The narrator shows that the enemies were confident and careless.

For today: pleasures gained through injustice may seem secure, but they do not last. And when we feel we have lost everything, God can open unexpected paths. Trust in Him, act with prudence, and seek his direction before taking the next step.
exp.29:16:
This verse tells that David and his men attacked the Amalekites from dawn until the evening of the next day. No one escaped, except four hundred young men who fled riding on camels.

This is part of the story, not a speech. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and taken the families of David and his men. An Egyptian servant, sick and left behind by them, guided David to their camp. They found them celebrating the plunder, confident and unprepared. Some scholars also see here the judgment on a people who had long been an enemy of Israel.

For today: when you feel you have lost everything, first seek God and then act with courage and perseverance. David did not stay weeping; he moved forward, and God sustained him until he recovered what was his.
exp.29:20:
David came back to the brook Besor, where two hundred men had been left behind, too exhausted to continue the pursuit. They went out to meet David and the people who were with him. David drew near and greeted them with peace; that is, he asked how they were and treated them with kindness.

The narrator tells what happened after David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken at Ziklag. The two hundred had stayed behind to guard the baggage (v. 24). This kind greeting sets up the scene that follows, where some selfish men want to keep the two hundred out of the spoils, and David stops them.

For today: let us not measure people's worth only by what they manage to accomplish. Whoever is tired or limited also deserves respect and care. Let us receive the weak with peace and generosity.
exp.29:22:
Here David corrects his men. He tells them they must not act that way with what God has given them. He acknowledges that it was the Lord who protected them and delivered into their hands the band that had attacked their camp at Ziklag, a group of raiders.

David speaks after recovering everything the Amalekites had taken. Two hundred men stayed behind because they were exhausted. Some of those who did fight, described as wicked and worthless men, wanted to deny them their share of the spoil. David prevents this and establishes that the division be equal, both for the one who fights and for the one who guards the baggage.

For today: what we have is a gift from God, not only the result of our own merit. This invites us to share generously and to value those who serve quietly, even when they are not at the front.
exp.29:24:
This verse says that what David decided that day became a permanent rule in Israel. The text uses a phrase meaning an official norm that had to be followed, and it also shows that the writer saw this practice still in force in his own time.

David had just rescued the families and possessions that the Amalekites had taken from Ziklag. Two hundred of his men, who were very tired, had stayed behind to guard the baggage. Some of the men who had fought wanted to deny them a share of the spoils. David answered that the victory came from the LORD, and that those who guarded the supplies should receive the same share as those who went into battle.

Today we can remember that everything we have is a gift from God. That leads us to value and acknowledge the work of those who serve quietly, without being noticed, in the church, in the family, or at work.
exp.29:27:
This verse is part of a list of places. David sends gifts from the plunder to the people who lived in Aroer, in Siphmoth, and in Eshtemoa. Plunder means goods taken in war. "Siphmoth" and "Eshtemoa" are old names of towns in the south of Judah. Today they would be written Siphmoth and Eshtemoa.

The narrator of the book speaks here, telling what David did. He had recovered everything the Amalekites had taken at Ziklag. Instead of keeping the riches for himself, he shared them with the leaders of Judah who had supported or helped him while he was fleeing from Saul. Some details about these places are uncertain, since not all of them are known for sure.

For today: David saw the victory as a blessing from God, not only as something of his own. We can ask ourselves whom I can bless with what God has given me, and give thanks to those who have supported us in difficult times.
exp.30:3:
Saul, wounded and surrounded by the enemy, asks his armor-bearer, the soldier who carried his weapons, to kill him with his sword. He fears that the Philistines, whom he calls "uncircumcised" (people who did not belong to Israel's covenant), will kill him and mock him. The armor-bearer refused out of great fear, so Saul himself fell upon the sword.

Saul, the first king of Israel, speaks in his last battle on Mount Gilboa. His sons had already died, and the archers had struck him. His life ended in despair, after years of turning away from God. The Bible only records the event and does not present it as an example to follow.

When everything seems lost, do not face your distress alone or let fear or pride decide for you. Seek God and people you trust. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, ask for help today.
exp.30:4:
This verse tells how Saul's armourbearer, the soldier who carried his weapons, saw that the king was already dead. Then he too threw himself on his own sword and died beside Saul.

The armourbearer was the warrior's helper, the one who carried his weapons.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel was losing the battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa. Saul, wounded and afraid of being abused by the enemy, took his own life. The text only tells what happened; it does not approve or recommend these deaths.

For today: in the middle of fear and defeat, it is easy to lose hope. If you are weighed down, do not carry that burden alone. Talk with someone you trust, with a pastor or a professional, and seek help. God cares for you and receives you in your distress.
exp.30:5:
It says that Saul, the first king of Israel, died that same day in the battle against the Philistines. With him died his three sons, his armourbearer (the young man who carried his weapons) and his men. It was the end of his reign and of his family's place on the throne.

The narrator tells how the battle of Mount Gilboa ended. Saul, wounded and fearing that the Philistines, the uncircumcised, would mock him, took his own life. His armourbearer followed his example. Years before, Saul had disobeyed God, and his story ended in tragedy. Some scholars debate how to understand his death, and the Bible only records it without approving it.

For today: a life can end badly when it drifts away from God, but today we can return to Him with humility. Our decisions also affect those who follow us, so it is wise to walk in obedience and ask for His guidance.
exp.30:6:
This verse says that the Israelites who lived on the other side of the valley (probably the Valley of Jezreel) and on the other side of the Jordan learned that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons had died. So they abandoned their cities and ran away. The Philistines came and settled in those cities.

No one is speaking here; it is the narrator of the book, who recounts the consequences of the defeat on Mount Gilboa. The king's death left the people without protection or direction, and the Philistines gained territory. The text does not explain more; it only shows how serious the fall was.

For today: when firm guidance is missing, fear can make us let go of what God had entrusted to us. Let us seek strength in God and live united, so that we do not flee at the first defeat.
exp.30:7:
This verse says that on the day after the battle, the Philistines went out to the field to take the valuable things from the dead soldiers. There they found the bodies of Saul and his three sons lying on mount Gilboa. Stripping the fallen means taking their weapons, clothing and belongings, and the bodies lying there means they had been left on the ground.

It is part of the account of the end of Saul's reign, the first king of Israel. The narrator tells with simplicity how the defeat ended. Earlier, Saul had turned away from God, and here we see the sad end of his life. At the same time, the story prepares the way for David to become king.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and power or reputation do not last forever. Today you can choose to obey God and trust in Him, instead of relying only on your position or your own strength.
exp.30:8:
This verse tells what the Philistines did with Saul after his death. They cut off his head and took his armor. Then they sent messengers throughout their territory to announce the news in the temples of their idols and among the people.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the events without commenting on them. Israel had just lost the battle on Mount Gilboa, and Saul and his sons had died. The Philistines wanted to celebrate their victory and credit it to their gods. The verses that follow show that the armor was placed in the temple of Ashtoreth and that the body was hung on a wall.

For today: when the world celebrates a defeat or mocks something we love, let us remember that the story does not end there. God is still at work, and it is better to live faithfully than to meet an end like Saul's.
exp.30:9:
The Philistines put Saul's weapons in the temple of Ashtaroth, a goddess they worshiped. They also hung the king's body on the wall of Beth-shan, a nearby town. The word "hung" simply means they displayed it publicly, as a sign of victory and mockery.

The narrator of the book tells this without speaking in the first person. He describes the tragic end of Saul, who died on Mount Gilboa. The Philistines believed their victory came from their gods, and that is why they displayed the spoils. Afterward, the men of Jabesh-gilead rescued the bodies, grateful for what Saul had done for them earlier.

For today: Saul's life reminds us that disobedience to God has painful consequences. Today we can ask him for a humble and obedient heart. We can also honor with gratitude those who have helped us, as the people of Jabesh did.
exp.30:10:
This verse says that the people of Jabesh-gilead heard about what the Philistines had done to Saul: they cut off his head, put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan. The sentence is left open, and the next verse shows what they did.

Context: the one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts the tragic end of Saul on Mount Gilboa. Jabesh-gilead was a city that Saul had rescued at the beginning of his reign (1 Samuel 11). For this reason, many understand that their brave response was a gesture of gratitude and loyalty.

For today: gratitude and loyalty do not stay in words alone. Think of someone who helped you in a difficult moment, and look for a concrete way today to honor them, even if it is with a phone call, a visit, or an act of service.
exp.20:14:
King Achish speaks here with anger and sarcasm. He asks whether he is so short of madmen that his servants had to bring him one more. Rave is the word he uses for David's behavior, and he rejects the idea that this man should come into his house.

David was fleeing from King Saul and arrived at Gath, a Philistine city, where people recognized him as the famous warrior from Israel. Fearing for his life, he pretended to be mad. Achish, convinced, rebukes his servants and sends David away. Psalm 34 is connected to this episode according to its title, and there David gives thanks to God for rescuing him.

For today: God can take care of us even when we act out of fear and with very human means. We do not have to depend on our own cleverness. We can ask him for help with sincerity, thank him for his deliverance, and keep trusting that he sustains us.
exp.2:6:
This verse explains why Samuel did not recognize the voice calling him. "Did not yet know the LORD" does not mean that he did not believe in God, but that he had not yet had a personal experience of God speaking to him. "Because the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him" means that God had not yet made his message known to him.

The narrator is the author of the book. Samuel was a boy who served Eli at the sanctuary in Shiloh. It was a time when the word of God was scarce. The narrator makes clear that Samuel mistook God's voice for Eli's, and that this moment was new to him.

For today: knowing about God and knowing him personally are different things. We can grow in faith by listening with humility, asking help from mature believers, and praying: "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening."
exp.29:14:
David asks the young Egyptian whether he will lead him to the band of raiders that burned Ziklag. The young man agrees, but he asks David to swear by God that he will not kill him or hand him over to his master. The phrase "young man" here refers to the servant, and "master" is the owner whom he had served as a slave.

David had just returned to Ziklag and found it burned, with his people carried off captive. The young man was an abandoned slave, sick and left behind by the Amalekites. David had found him and given him food. Now the young man, knowing his life was worth nothing to his master, seeks protection. David accepts the arrangement, and the young man leads him to the enemy camp.

For today: God can use people who seem insignificant or cast aside to show us the way. Treat everyone with kindness and respect, even those you do not see as important. Your compassion may open a door you did not expect.
exp.23:10:
Here David tells Saul that God gave him the chance to take his life in the cave. Some of David's men urged him to kill Saul, but David chose to spare him. The word "anointed" refers to someone chosen and set apart by God to be king. David respected that position and did not want to raise his hand against him.

It is David speaking, who was fleeing from Saul because the king wanted to kill him. Saul had gone into the cave without knowing that David and his men were inside. David only cut off the edge of Saul's robe, and afterward came out to show him that he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm.

When someone treats us unjustly, we may have the chance to take revenge, but David teaches us not to do so. We can speak the truth with respect, act with integrity, and let God be the judge.
exp.19:31:
Jonathan answers his father Saul with two questions: "Why must he be put to death? What has he done?" These are words of defense. Jonathan asks Saul for a just reason to kill David.

Jonathan speaks at a new moon meal, at the king's table. David was absent, and Jonathan had to find out whether Saul meant to kill him. Saul grew angry, insulted his son, and ordered that David be brought. Jonathan, even knowing his father was furious, defended an innocent friend. Afterward Saul hurled a spear at him, and so Jonathan understood the truth.

Today we can learn to defend with respect someone who is treated unjustly. Sometimes it costs dearly, but speaking the truth and asking "What has he done?" helps to halt accusations that have no basis.
exp.24:0:
This verse tells us that Samuel died. All of Israel gathered together to mourn him, and they buried him at his home in Ramah, his hometown. After that, David set out and went down to the Wilderness of Paran.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Samuel had been a prophet and a judge, and he was the one who anointed David as the future king. His death marks the end of an era. David was still running from King Saul, which is why he sought refuge in the wilderness. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact location of Paran, but it was an arid region in the south.

For today: when someone who guided us dies, it is natural to grieve. But life goes on and God keeps working. We can honor that person and, even in sadness, take the next step with faith.
exp.22:9:
David prays to God and tells him what he has heard: that Saul intends to go to Keilah and destroy the city because of David. "Has heard" here means David has learned this news. "Intends" means Saul is planning it. "Your servant" is the humble way David refers to himself before God.

David speaks with God after asking the priest Abiathar for the ephod, the priestly garment used to seek God's guidance. Saul was pursuing him, and David had just rescued Keilah from the Philistines. Now he fears that the city will suffer for protecting him, and he wants to know what to do before he acts.

Before making a difficult decision, we can bring God our concerns honestly and in detail. David did not act on fear alone or on what he himself thought. He asked first. Today we too can pray, seek wise counsel, and wait for direction before we move.
exp.14:19:
Saul answers Samuel that he did obey God. He says he went on the mission the LORD gave him, that he brought back Agag, king of Amalek, and that he devoted the Amalekites to destruction.

Samuel has just rebuked Saul for not obeying fully. God had commanded him to wipe out Amalek, but Saul let King Agag live, and the people kept the best of the livestock. Here Saul defends himself and presents his obedience as complete, even though Samuel had already pointed out the opposite. The verses that follow show that he blames the people.

For today: when God or his Word correct us, it is easy to justify ourselves by saying "I did almost everything right." Let us pray for a humble heart that acknowledges its failures and obeys completely, without excuses.
exp.29:25:
It says that when David arrived in Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to his friends, the elders of Judah. He sent the gift with these words: "Here is a gift for you," taken from what had been seized from the enemies of the LORD. "Plunder" means goods taken in war. "Gift" is the word the verse uses to describe what he sent.

David had defeated the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the families. After recovering everything, he decided that the plunder should be shared equally between those who fought and those who stayed to guard the supplies. Then he also sent gifts to several towns of Judah, probably in gratitude for their support while he was fleeing from Saul. The text presents the victory as one given by the LORD.

For today: what God gives us is not only for ourselves. We can share with generosity and gratitude, remembering those who supported us in difficult times.
exp.30:2:
This verse says the battle grew more intense against King Saul. The archers, that is, the Philistine soldiers who shot bows, caught up with him and wounded him critically. Seeing himself in that state, Saul was overcome with fear. The verse shows the situation becoming harder and more dangerous for him.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, who tells of the end of Saul's reign. The Philistines had already killed his sons, among them Jonathan. Earlier, Saul had turned away from God and disobeyed, and God no longer answered him (1 Samuel 28:6). Some interpreters see in this the result of that path. The Bible tells of his death without hiding his grief.

Today, this passage invites us not to put off turning back to God. If we walk alone, fear takes control when troubles come. Let us seek God with humility today, and He will sustain us.
exp.14:2:
Here God, through the prophet Samuel, tells Saul to attack the Amalekites and destroy everything that belongs to them, sparing no one: people and animals alike. Words like "attack" mean to strike against an enemy; "spare" means to hold back from harming; and the words about children and infants refer to the youngest, who are still very small.

Samuel speaks in God's name. The reason given is that Amalek attacked Israel when it came out of Egypt, a tired and defenseless people (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). It is a very harsh text. Scholars understand it in several ways: as God's judgment on a hostile people, or as exaggerated language typical of ancient warfare. Even so, it remains difficult, and it is fair to acknowledge that.

For today: do not use this passage to justify violence. Instead, learn to obey God fully, without leaving things half done, and trust that He is just even when we do not understand everything.
exp.19:18:
Jonathan tells David to stay hidden for three days. After that, David must hurry down and return to the place where he hid on the day this trouble began, and wait there beside the stone Ezel. Hurrying down means leaving his hiding place. Some scholars debate exactly what the day this trouble began refers to, so it is wise to read this phrase with caution.

Jonathan speaks with David, whom he loves as his own soul. Saul, Jonathan's father, seeks to kill David. The feast of the new moon is near, and Jonathan will watch how his father reacts. For this reason he arranges a secret signal with arrows to warn David if there is danger.

For today: when you face an uncertain situation, do not act on impulse. Seek counsel from someone faithful, make a careful plan, and wait patiently, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.13:23:
This verse tells us that the soldiers of Israel were worn out and in distress that day. Saul had placed the troops under an oath, declaring that anyone who ate any food before evening, before he had taken vengeance on his enemies, would be cursed. Saul's command meant that no one could eat even a little before evening, and so none of the troops ate anything.

Here the narrator is speaking, and he reports Saul's order in the middle of the pursuit of the Philistines. God had just given Israel the victory. Saul probably wanted speed and wanted to waste no time, but his order left the people weak. Some think it was sincere zeal, others that it was pride or rashness. The text does not fully make this clear, though it shows that it was an unnecessary burden.

For today: before demanding something with great force, it is wise to think about whether it truly helps others. Religious zeal without wisdom can do harm. Let us ask God for prudence and compassion.
exp.17:22:
Saul's servants passed along to David what the king had told them to say. David answered with a question: did they think it a small thing to become the king's son-in-law, when he was a poor man and lightly esteemed? A son-in-law is the husband of one's daughter, and being "lightly esteemed" means that others did not think much of him.

Saul was speaking in secret through his servants. He pretended to show affection, but his plan was for the Philistines to kill David. David, not knowing this, answered with humility: he did not consider himself worthy to become related to the royal family.

Today we can learn from David's humility. When we receive honor or an opportunity, we need not boast or demand. It is also wise to ask God for wisdom, because not every compliment comes from good intentions.
exp.14:15:
What it says: Samuel cuts off Saul's excuses and asks him to stop so that he can tell him what the LORD said to him last night. Saul answers, "Tell me," and agrees to listen.

Context: Samuel, the prophet, confronts Saul, the king. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites, but Saul and the people kept the best of the livestock. Saul says it was to offer as a sacrifice. Samuel stops him because before responding to the excuse, he wants Saul to hear what God actually said.

For today: Before justifying our decisions, it is wise to be quiet and listen to what God says in His Word. A humble attitude, like Saul's willingness to say, "Tell me," helps us see our mistakes in time and correct our course.
exp.1:19:
Eli, the priest, blessed Elkanah and his wife Hannah. He prayed that the Lord would give them children by this woman in place of the son she had dedicated to the Lord. Samuel was that son. Hannah had asked God for him, and then she gave him back to the Lord's service. After the blessing, the couple went home.

The verse is a blessing spoken by Eli, and it is also a glimpse into the family's yearly life. Each year Elkanah and Hannah went up to the sanctuary to worship and offer sacrifice, and they visited Samuel, who served there. Eli's words show his gratitude for their gift and his desire for good things to come to them. The verses that follow describe how the Lord did bless Hannah with three more sons and two daughters.

For today: when we give something to God sincerely, we can trust that He cares for us. We can also bless others with our words, especially those who serve at a cost to themselves, by encouraging them and praying for them.
exp.14:30:
It says that Samuel went back with Saul, and that Saul worshiped the LORD. Here "worshiped" means that he fell prostrate as a sign of reverence. The phrase "went back with" means that Samuel returned and walked alongside him.

Samuel, the prophet, had just told Saul that God had rejected him as king for disobeying the command to destroy the Amalekites. Saul acknowledged his sin, but asked to be honored before the people. Samuel agreed to go back with him. There are different opinions on whether Saul's worship was sincere or whether he was more concerned with protecting his image. The text does not make this clear.

For today: worshiping God is good, but it does not replace obedience and heartfelt repentance. Before we worry about what others think of us, let us ask God for a humble heart willing to obey him.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that the people of Israel sent men to Shiloh and brought back the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Hosts, who is described as sitting enthroned between the cherubim (figures of angels on the lid of the ark). The two sons of the priest Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark. "LORD" is the name of God, and "of Hosts" speaks of his power over all things.

The narrator tells what happened after Israel lost to the Philistines. The elders wondered why God had struck them, but they did not seek to repent. They thought the ark would save them like a charm. The sons of Eli were corrupt priests, according to chapter 2, so their presence already signals trouble.

For today: let us not treat religious objects as if they were a guarantee of God's help. When something goes wrong, let us first draw near to Him with humility and sincerity, not only with symbols or customs.
exp.24:30:
Abigail tells David that, when God makes him king, he will have no remorse or guilt of conscience. A "stumbling block" is something that makes a person fall, and "trouble of heart" is an inner unrest. She asks him not to shed needless blood or take revenge with his own hand. "Take heed" means "be careful." In the end, she asks him to remember her when God blesses him.

Abigail, the wife of Nabal, speaks. Nabal was a foolish man who treated David and his men badly. David was armed and set out to kill Nabal and his household. Abigail goes out to meet him with provisions and stops him with humility, trusting that God will care for David and bring about justice.

When someone wrongs us, anger pushes us to respond at once. This passage invites us to pause, listen to wise counsel, and leave justice in God's hands, so that we do not carry regret afterward.
exp.13:5:
Jonathan says to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men." By "uncircumcised" he means the Philistines, who did not have the sign of God's covenant.

He adds, "Perhaps the Lord will work on our behalf. Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few."

Jonathan speaks in the middle of the war against the Philistines. Israel was at a disadvantage and had few people. Jonathan does not take the outcome for granted: he says "perhaps," acknowledging that God acts as He chooses. But he trusts that nothing can stop God from saving, and that God does not depend on the size of the army.

For today: when you feel small or short on resources, take the step you can with faith and humility. Trust God, without demanding results, because He can work even with very little.
exp.22:1:
This verse tells how David asked the Lord whether he should go to attack the Philistines who were threatening Keilah. The Lord answered plainly: go, attack them, and save that town.

The phrase "inquired of the LORD" in this verse means David sought direction from God, and "attack" here means to strike against and defeat. The threshing floors mentioned in the wider passage were the places where grain was separated from the straw.

David was running from King Saul, and yet he learned that Keilah, a town in Judah, was being plundered. Before acting, he did not rely only on his own courage; he asked God. Later, when his men became afraid, he asked again and received the same answer along with a promise of victory.

For today: before making important decisions, even good ones, pray and seek God's guidance. When doubts or fears arise, ask him again for direction with humility, and look for confirmation in his Word and in wise counsel.
exp.5:2:
The Philistine priests and diviners advise that, if they send back the ark of the God of Israel, they must not send it away empty. They should return it with a guilt offering. Here "guilt offering" means a payment for the wrong done, and "being healed" refers to being freed from the plague. In this way they would understand why His hand had not been lifted from them.

The ark had been among the Philistines for seven months, and with it came plagues and suffering. Their own religious leaders speak, without knowing the God of Israel well, but they recognize that the punishment could come from Him. Their advice resembles the customs of their culture, and the Bible records only what they said.

For today: when we recognize that we have done wrong, feeling sorry is not enough. It is good to humble ourselves before God and make amends for the harm with sincerity. Today we know that Christ paid for our sin, so we come to Him with confidence.
exp.9:17:
Samuel speaks to the Israelites on behalf of God. He reminds them that the LORD, the God of Israel, brought Israel up out of Egypt and rescued them from the hands of the Egyptians and from all the kingdoms that oppressed them.

Samuel, the prophet and judge, gathers the people at Mizpah. They want a king like the other nations, and Samuel first reminds them of what God had already done for them. Afterward he will tell them that, in asking for a king, they are rejecting God as their protector. Meanwhile, Saul has not yet told anyone what Samuel said to him about the kingdom.

For today: before looking for human solutions to our fears or problems, it is good to remember how God has cared for us in the past. That remembrance strengthens trust. You can write down three moments when God helped you and give thanks for them.
exp.12:13:
Samuel tells Saul that his kingdom will not endure. The LORD has already sought out a man after His own heart, meaning someone who seeks Him and remains faithful to Him, and has appointed him ruler over His people. The reason is that Saul did not keep the command of the LORD. The word "But" at the start of this verse links this statement to what came before, and "will not endure" means that his family line would not go on ruling.

Samuel speaks in Gilgal. Saul, frightened by the Philistines and seeing that Samuel was delayed, offered the burnt offering himself, something that was not his place to do. Samuel rebukes him for acting out of fear and not obeying. Many believe this refers to David, although the verse does not name him here.

For today: when we feel pressure or fear, it is tempting to take shortcuts and justify ourselves. God values an obedient and trusting heart more than hurried solutions. We can wait on Him and obey Him even when it costs us.
exp.22:17:
So the two of them made a binding promise before the LORD. Each man committed himself to the other, with God as witness. Then they parted ways: David remained at Horesh, while Jonathan went home.

The narrator tells this moment while Saul is hunting David in order to kill him. Jonathan, Saul's son, risks his own safety to encourage his friend. He tells David that God will protect him and that he will be king. This was the last meeting between the two men recorded in the Bible. Right after this, the people of Ziph betray David to Saul.

For today: a faithful friendship encourages the other person to trust God, even when everything seems difficult. Look for someone who is going through a hard time, encourage them with sincere words, and remind them that God is still with them. And keep the promises you make.
exp.8:8:
In earlier times in Israel, a person going to ask God a question would say, "Come, let us go to the seer." Over time, the one who was called a seer came to be called a prophet. A seer is someone to whom God gave the ability to see or know things that others could not.

The narrator of the book explains this change in wording for readers of his own time. Saul and his servant are searching for some lost donkeys. When they cannot find them, the servant suggests they go to the man of God so that he can give them direction. That man is Samuel. Scholars do not know for certain when this note was written, but it shows that the language changed over the years.

For today: when we do not know which way to take, let us seek God in prayer and also the counsel of wise and faithful people. Asking for direction is not weakness; it is humility.
exp.0:22:
Elkanah tells Hannah to do what she thinks is best and to stay home until she has weaned the child. He adds, "Only may the LORD confirm His word." To wean means to stop nursing the baby. Hannah stays and raises her son Samuel until that time.

Elkanah, Hannah's husband, is the one speaking. She had promised to dedicate the son she was given to God, and he respects that decision. The verse does not make clear which word he means; it could be God's promise or Hannah's vow. In that time weaning usually took place around two or three years of age, although the Bible does not give the exact age here.

Today we can respectfully support the promises others make to God, and keep our own promises with patience. Waiting for the right moment is also a form of faithfulness.
exp.11:5:
Samuel reminds the people that the Lord is the one who appointed Moses and Aaron as leaders, and that He brought their ancestors out of Egypt. The verse points to God as the true source of Israel's leaders and deliverance.

Samuel speaks at a national gathering, when Israel was asking for a king. He had just shown that he had been an honest leader. Now he wants to turn the people's attention from human leaders to God. He is going to review how God has rescued and guided them throughout their history.

For today: before seeking security in leaders, money, or plans, let us remember the times God has sustained us. Remembering His faithfulness strengthens trust and helps us put God first.
exp.1:31:
God announces to Eli that trouble will come to his family. The word "adversary" means a rival or opponent, and some readers take it to mean a trouble or affliction in God's house, since the Hebrew is hard to pin down. Even when God blesses Israel, Eli's house will not share in that blessing. No one in his family will live to old age.

A man of God speaks to Eli, the priest. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing their office, and Eli did not correct them firmly. God had promised that this family would serve before him, but the promise did not protect them from the consequences of despising him. He honors those who honor him.

For today: serving God is not a title but an obedient life. If you have authority in your home, your work, or your church, correct with love and with truth, without looking the other way.
exp.29:30:
This verse finishes a list of places. After defeating the Amalekites, David sent part of the plunder to those in Hebron and in all the places where he and his men had roamed.

The narrator of the book speaks here. David had returned to Ziklag and found it burned, but God gave him the victory and he recovered everything that had been taken. Then he distributed gifts to the elders of Judah, who had surely helped him or welcomed him while he was fleeing from Saul. The text does not detail how each town helped, so it is not wise to invent that.

For today: do not forget those who have supported you in difficult times. When God gives you a blessing, share it with gratitude. A phone call, a visit, or a concrete act of help can be your way of saying thank you.
exp.24:7:
Nabal can ask his own servants, and they will tell him that David and his men behaved well. So David asks that his young men be received kindly. The Berean wording says they have come on the day of a feast, which is why David describes it as a good day. He asks Nabal to give whatever he can spare, meaning whatever he has available. David also calls himself Nabal's son as a sign of respect.

David speaks through his young messengers. He and his men had been living in the wilderness, and they had protected Nabal's shepherds. Now it was time for sheep-shearing, a season of plenty, and David asked for a sign of gratitude. Nabal answers with contempt, as will soon be seen.

For today: when you have done good, ask with respect and without demanding. And when someone asks you humbly, remember what you have received and respond with gratitude and generosity, not with pride.
exp.11:20:
They say we should not go after worthless things, meaning empty, false, or useless things such as idols. These things cannot profit you, which means they serve no real purpose and bring no benefit, and they cannot deliver you, which means they cannot rescue anyone in a moment of danger. The reason is simple: they are empty, and they have no real power.

Samuel, the prophet and judge of Israel, is speaking. The people had just asked for a king, and they acknowledged that this was a mistake. Samuel does not frighten them but encourages them not to turn away from God. He reminds them that God does not abandon his people, and that he himself will continue to pray for them and teach them the good way.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust: money, success, the approval of others. Those things may help a little, but they do not sustain us in a crisis. Even after failing, we can return to God with our whole heart.
exp.20:0:
David came to Nob, where the priest Ahimelech was. The priest was startled and worried to see him, and asked him why he was alone, with no one with him. "Trembled" describes a visible sign of fear or agitation.

David was running away from King Saul, who wanted to kill him. Nob was the place where the sanctuary stood, and Ahimelech served as priest there. Ahimelech asks the question because a man as important as David, the king's son-in-law and military commander, would normally travel with an escort. Later David tells him he is on a mission for the king, but that was not true. The Bible reports the event without approving his deception, and the consequences were painful.

When we are in trouble, it is tempting to bend the truth to get out of a difficulty. This passage invites us to seek God sincerely, trusting that his care is better than any lie that might seem useful to us.
exp.12:17:
The text tells us that the Philistines sent out three groups of soldiers to make a raid, that is, a sudden attack to seize plunder. One group went toward Beth-horon, another went down the border road overlooking the Valley of Zeboim facing the wilderness, and the third is the group the verse describes next.

The narrator describes how the Philistines were closing in on Israel. Saul and Jonathan were at Gibeah with only a few men, and the people were afraid. The Philistines were moving out in several directions to take control of the land. It is not known with certainty where the Valley of Zeboim was.

For today: sometimes problems seem to come from every direction. Instead of despairing, we can bring each worry honestly before God and ask him for wisdom to take the next step.
exp.23:18:
Saul tells David that today he has shown that he did him good. David could have killed him, because God himself had put him into his hands, but he chose not to do it. The name "LORD" refers to God, and the phrase "delivered you into my hand" means "allowed me to overcome him."

It is King Saul speaking, the man who was hunting David to kill him. Saul had entered a cave without knowing David was hiding there. David cut off a piece of his robe, but he spared his life and then showed it to him. Seeing this, Saul wept and admitted that David was more righteous than he was. Some see here a sincere repentance, although afterward Saul went back to pursuing David.

Today we can answer evil with good. When someone wounds us and we have the chance to take revenge, we can choose to forgive and trust that God will do justice. That path can also move the heart of the person who wronged us.
exp.29:23:
Here David says that no one will agree with those who want to take the spoils away from the tired soldiers. He says the share should be the same for the one who went to battle and for the one who stayed behind to guard the supplies. And he gives the order: "They will share alike," meaning that everything is to be divided equally.

David speaks after recovering what the Amalekites had taken from Ziklag. Two hundred men, very exhausted, had stayed behind to guard the supplies. Some of those who did fight, described as wicked and worthless, did not want to share with them. David reminds them that the victory was a gift from the LORD, not their own achievement. Later this became a rule in Israel.

For today: value those who serve in places that go unseen. If God has given you success, remember that it is a gift, and share it with generosity and justice.
exp.27:6:
Saul, desperate, orders his servants to find him a woman who is a medium, someone who claimed to speak with the dead, so that he can go and consult her. His servants tell him that there is such a woman at En-dor.

Saul speaks this way because he is very afraid of the Philistine army. God had not answered him by dreams, by the Urim (a sacred means of learning God's will), or through prophets. Moreover, Saul himself had driven the mediums and fortune-tellers out of the land, because God's law forbade them. Now he breaks what he himself had commanded.

When we feel that God is silent, it is tempting to look for answers in forbidden places. It is better to examine our hearts, return to God with sincerity, and wait on Him, even when the answer is slow in coming.
exp.14:8:
This verse says that Saul and his troops spared Agag, the king of the Amalekites, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, and the best of everything else. They were unwilling to devote these to destruction. What they did destroy was everything that was despised and worthless. The word "spared" here means they let these things live.

The text is narrated; no character is speaking. Earlier, God had commanded through Samuel that the Amalekites be destroyed (1 Samuel 15:3). Saul won, but he obeyed only in part. Afterward, God says that he regrets having made Saul king, because Saul did not carry out his instructions. Some readers see here a problem of greed; others, of pride. The text clearly shows selective disobedience.

For today: it is easy to obey God only in what suits us and to keep "the best" for ourselves. Today you can ask yourself in what area you are obeying halfway, and ask God for help in surrendering it completely.
exp.21:6:
Saul speaks to his servants who are standing around him, and he calls them "men of Benjamin", that is, men of his own tribe. He asks them with irony whether the son of Jesse is giving all of them fields and vineyards, and making them commanders of thousands or of hundreds.

Saul is in Gibeah, with his spear in his hand, surrounded by his people. He feels betrayed because David has fled and has followers. He suspects that everyone is conspiring against him. For this reason he appeals to self-interest and to tribal loyalty. He does not even say David's name, only "the son of Jesse", as a sign of contempt. Afterward Doeg the Edomite will accuse him before everyone.

For today: when fear and jealousy dominate us, we begin to see enemies where there are none. Let us ask God for humility and a trusting heart, so that we may listen calmly before we accuse.
exp.19:2:
Here David again swears to Jonathan that he is in real danger. He tells him that Saul, Jonathan's father, knows very well that Jonathan cares for David, and for that reason Saul will not tell him his plans, so as not to grieve him. "Grieved" means feeling sorrow or pain. "As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live" is a solemn way of swearing. "There is but a step between me and death" means that death is very close.

David speaks with his friend Jonathan after fleeing from Naioth, in Ramah. Jonathan does not believe that his father Saul wants to kill David, because Saul usually tells him everything. David insists with an oath, since he knows that Saul is looking for him to take his life.

When someone close to us tells us that they are suffering or in danger, it is good to listen with humility, even when it is hard for us to believe. Listening patiently and helping in concrete ways, as Jonathan will do, is a way of truly loving.
exp.13:10:
This verse tells how Jonathan and his armor-bearer revealed themselves to the Philistine outpost. The Philistine guards saw them and called out in mockery, asking whether the Hebrews were coming out of the holes where they had been hiding. An "outpost" is a small group of soldiers posted to watch over a place. The "armor-bearer" was the young man who carried a warrior's weapons.

Here the narrator speaks first, and then the Philistines. Jonathan had proposed a sign: if the enemy called out for them to come up, it would show that God was giving them the victory. The Philistines, confident and proud, did not realize they were walking into that very sign.

For today: sometimes others look down on us or underestimate us. Instead of being discouraged, we can take steps of faith and obedience, trusting that God can act even when we seem few or weak.
exp.19:1:
Jonathan answers David: "Far from it! You will not die." He says that his father, Saul, does nothing, great or small, without telling him. So why would he hide this matter from him? Jonathan believes this cannot be true.

David has just fled from Naioth, in Ramah, because Saul is searching for him to kill him. He comes before his friend Jonathan and asks what wrong he has done. Jonathan speaks from what he knows of his father, but he is mistaken: Saul was in fact keeping his plan from him, as will be seen later.

For today: even when we trust someone deeply, we sometimes do not see everything that is going on. Listening humbly to someone who warns us, and not dismissing their fears at once, can save us from mistakes and help us care for those who are suffering.
exp.0:7:
Elkanah notices that his wife Hannah is crying and will not eat. He asks her four questions: why she is crying, why she won't eat, why her heart is so grieved, and whether he himself is not better to her than ten sons. Hannah could not have children, and the other wife, Peninnah, was the one who had them.

The speaker is Elkanah, Hannah's husband, during the yearly trip to Shiloh to worship. Peninnah, who did have children, provoked Hannah and made her suffer. Elkanah wants to comfort her with love, though he does not fully grasp the depth of her pain. His question shows affection, but also its limits.

For today: when someone suffers, listening patiently is worth more than giving quick answers. And if you are in pain, as Hannah was, you can bring your honest distress to God, who understands what others cannot see.
exp.21:10:
Then the king sent messengers to summon Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and his father's whole family, who were priests at Nob. All of them came to the king.

After Doeg the Edomite made his accusation, Saul acted. Doeg reported that Ahimelech had given David bread, had given him the sword of Goliath, and had inquired of God on his behalf. Saul, filled with suspicion, believed that David and the priests were conspiring against him. The priests came without suspecting the danger, probably because they did not know what they were being accused of.

For today: before reacting to a rumor or an accusation, it is wise to listen calmly and seek the truth. Jealousy and fear cloud judgment and can lead us to harm innocent people.
exp.24:24:
Here Abigail asks David not to pay attention to her husband, Nabal. The phrase "this scoundrel" describes a wicked or worthless person. "Nabal" means "fool," and she admits that his name fits him. She also makes clear that she did not see the young men David sent. The "servants" in this passage are the young men who worked for someone.

Abigail speaks with David, who was coming with four hundred men intent on taking revenge. Nabal had refused his request for help and had insulted him. Abigail goes out to meet him with provisions, humbles herself, and seeks to prevent bloodshed. Some think she blames herself to calm David.

When someone offends us, we do not always have to respond with anger. We can pause, listen with humility, and seek peace before we act. A calm word can prevent harm that we would later regret.
exp.13:39:
Saul divides the people into two groups: all Israel on one side, and he with his son Jonathan on the other. The troops reply, "Do what seems good to you," which means "Do whatever you think is best."

Saul speaks as king in the middle of the war against the Philistines. God had not answered his inquiry, and Saul thought someone had committed a sin. He had made a rash oath, and Jonathan, without knowing it, had broken it. Saul is about to find the guilty person by lot, and he includes himself and his son. Commentators see this as a gesture of justice, though also of a reckless oath.

Today we can learn to be honest when examining our faults, without protecting our loved ones or ourselves. We should also think carefully before making solemn promises.
exp.10:14:
The verse says that all the people went to Gilgal and there confirmed Saul as king in the presence of the LORD. Here, confirming him means they publicly affirmed him in his position as king. Then they offered peace offerings before the LORD, sacrifices of fellowship and thanksgiving to God, and Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.

The passage describes what happened after Saul rescued the city of Jabesh-gilead. Saul gave the credit for the victory to God, not to himself, and he showed mercy to those who had earlier doubted him. Samuel, the prophet, called the people to gather at Gilgal and publicly affirm Saul as king. Scholars debate whether this was a first coronation or a ratification, but the text stresses that everything was done in the presence of the LORD.

When God gives us a victory, it is fitting to pause, give thanks, and celebrate with others. We can also recognize those who lead with humility, setting aside pride and the desire for revenge.
exp.14:29:
Saul admits that he has sinned, but right away he asks Samuel to honor him before the elders of his people and before all Israel. He also asks Samuel to come back with him so that he may worship the LORD his God. The request to "honor" him uses the verse's own wording, and "worship" carries the same idea of showing reverence to God.

Saul speaks after Samuel has announced that God is taking the kingdom from him because he disobeyed in the war against the Amalekites. Saul says, "I have sinned," but his main concern seems to be his public standing. Some readers see in this an incomplete repentance; others see a real fear mixed with pride. The text does not explain his heart in detail. Samuel does return with him, and Saul worships.

Today we might ask ourselves whether, when we fail, we grieve more over offending God or over losing our reputation. Sincere repentance seeks first the truth and the forgiveness of God, and trusts that he cares for our name.
exp.13:45:
This verse tells us that Saul gave up his pursuit of the Philistines, and that they returned to their own land. The word "pursuit" here means chasing them. The battle that day ended without Israel completely destroying them.

The narrator is the author of the book, and he writes right after a serious conflict. Saul had made a rash oath, and because of it he wanted to kill his son Jonathan, who had broken it without knowing. The people defended Jonathan, since God had given the victory through him. After that episode, Saul calls off the pursuit. The text does not fully explain his reasons, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

For today: impulsive decisions and inner conflicts can halt what God is doing. Before speaking or promising something in haste, it is wise to pray, think calmly, and listen to wise people.
exp.30:12:
The men of Jabesh gathered the bones of Saul and his sons, buried them under a tamarisk tree, and went without eating for seven days. "They buried them" is the same as "they buried them." The reading of the verse here is that they spent those days without eating, as a sign of mourning.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after Saul died in battle. The Philistines had dishonored his body. The brave men of Jabesh risked their lives to recover it. Many think they did this out of gratitude, since Saul had rescued them years earlier (1 Samuel 11), although the text does not state this directly.

For today: gratitude and respect are shown through deeds. Think of someone who helped you in the past, even if they are no longer at their best, and look for a concrete way today to honor or accompany them.
exp.12:20:
This verse says that when the Israelites needed to repair or sharpen their tools, they had to go down to the Philistines. The Berean Standard Bible speaks of a "pim" as the charge for sharpening a plowshare or mattock, and of a third of a shekel for sharpening a pitchfork or axe, and a third of a shekel for repointing an oxgoad. In other words, even the simplest parts of daily work depended on the enemy.

The narrator describes Israel's situation under Saul. The Philistines controlled the working of iron so that the Israelites could not make weapons. In this way they kept them weak and dependent. That is why, on the day of battle, almost no one had a sword or a spear.

For today: when we depend completely on something that dominates us, we lose our freedom. It is wise to ask God for wisdom so that we are not tied to anything that weakens us, and to remember that He can work even when we lack resources.
exp.22:15:
Jonathan, the son of King Saul, rose and went to find David at Horesh, and there he strengthened David's hand in God. The phrase "strengthened his hand in God" is an older way of saying that Jonathan encouraged David and helped him to trust in God.

David was on the run because Saul was hunting him in order to kill him. He was worn out and living in fear. Jonathan, his faithful friend, risked his own safety to visit him. He reminded David that God had a plan for him and that Saul would not reach him. Afterward, the two of them made a covenant before the Lord.

Today we can be like Jonathan: seek out someone who is discouraged and encourage them, not only with kind words but by pointing them to God and his promises. And if you are exhausted, let a believing friend strengthen you.
exp.16:24:
The Israelite soldiers are talking among themselves about Goliath, who comes out every day to challenge the army. "Defy" here means to insult and dare. They say that King Saul will give great riches to whoever kills him, and will give his daughter in marriage, and will exempt that man's father's house from taxation in Israel. The text gives no further details about how the exemption would work.

The Israelites speak, and David listens. Everyone was afraid and fled from Goliath. That is why the king was offering rewards, hoping someone would dare. David, who had come to bring supplies to his brothers, begins to ask what is happening.

For today: when everyone looks at the size of the problem, we can look to God. David did not fix his attention on the prize, but on the fact that someone was defying the living God.
exp.17:28:
Saul was even more afraid of David, and from then on he regarded him as his enemy for as long as he lived. The word the verse uses for "afraid" simply means he was afraid. The phrase "from then on" means that this hostility did not end but remained steady.

No one speaks in this passage; the narrator is explaining what was going on in Saul's heart. Saul had hoped the Philistines would kill David, but David returned successful and married Michal, the king's daughter. Saul saw that the Lord was with David and that his daughter loved him. That did not lead him to peace, but to more fear and jealousy.

When fear and envy rule the heart, we see as a threat the one whom God is blessing. Today we can ask God to deliver us from envy and teach us to rejoice in the good of others.
exp.29:9:
This verse tells us that David continued the pursuit of the Amalekites with four hundred men. Two hundred stayed behind because they were too exhausted to cross the brook Besor. The phrase that says David and his men "continued in pursuit" means they kept up the chase. A brook like this one carries a great deal of water at certain seasons.

It is part of the account in chapter 30. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the families of David and his men as captives. David asked God whether he should pursue them, and God promised that he would overtake them and recover everything. The narrator only reports that two hundred men could go no further. He does not say they were cowards, but that they were exhausted.

For today: God calls us to keep moving forward, but he also recognizes our limits. We can advance with confidence in his promise, and we can treat those who are tired with compassion, without looking down on them.
exp.29:21:
Some of the men who had gone with David, the verse calls them "wicked and worthless," were unwilling to share the plunder with the two hundred companions who stayed behind. They would give back only the wives and children, so that those could be taken away and the men could leave. The "plunder" is the spoil taken in battle.

The men speaking had recovered everything the Amalekites had taken from them at Ziklag. Two hundred of their companions had been left at the brook Besor because they were too exhausted to go on. The selfish men reasoned that, since these had not fought, they did not deserve any of the plunder.

For today: what we receive comes from God's grace, not only from our own effort. For that reason we should value and treat generously those who support quietly or cannot give more.
exp.16:9:
This verse says that the Philistine Goliath adds another provocation: he declares that he is defying the ranks of Israel this very day, and he demands that someone come out to fight him, one man against one man. "Defied" means that he challenged them openly, like someone hurling a taunt to provoke a fight.

The one speaking is Goliath, the Philistine champion. The two armies were facing each other, and he proposes to settle the war with a single combat. His challenge does not only threaten the soldiers; it attacks the confidence of the whole people. That is why, in the next verse, Saul and all the Israelites are filled with fear.

For today: when a big problem shouts at us every day, it can paralyze us. We should remember that fear often grows when we look only at the giant. Today we can pause, pray, and ask God to help us see our situation with faith.
exp.11:21:
This verse says that God will not abandon his people. The reason is not that the people deserve it, but for the sake of his "great name" and because he himself chose to make them his own. "Will not abandon" means to leave someone alone or cut them off. "Was pleased to make you His own" means that he chose them of his own will.

Samuel, the prophet and judge, speaks here in his old age. Israel had just asked for a king, showing little trust in God. The people were frightened and recognized their mistake. Samuel reassures them: they sinned, but God does not reject them. He asks them to keep serving him wholeheartedly and not to chase after empty idols.

For today: when you fail, do not pull away from God out of shame. His faithfulness does not depend on your perfection, but on his character and his love. Return to him sincerely, trusting that he has not let go of you.
exp.17:20:
Saul says he will give his daughter Michal to David, but with a bad purpose: that she will be a "snare," that is, a trap, and that the Philistines will attack him. A "son-in-law" is the husband of one's daughter. Saul's words "For a second time now you can be my son-in-law" are understood as a second chance, since the first daughter, Merab, had already been given to another man.

The king Saul speaks. He was jealous of David because of his success and feared losing the throne. Since Michal loved David, Saul saw an opportunity: to use that marriage to expose David to death in battle, without getting his own hands dirty.

For today: jealousy can lead us to disguise as favor what is really harm. Let us ask God to heal our hearts from envy, and sincerely rejoice in the success of others, instead of seeing them as a threat.
exp.1:34:
God promises to raise up for himself a faithful priest, someone who will do whatever is in his heart and mind, that is, whatever God desires and wills. He will build for this priest an enduring house, meaning a lasting line of descendants, and the priest will walk before God's anointed one for all time.

A man of God speaks to the priest Eli. Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing their priestly role, and Eli did not correct them. Because of this, God announces judgment on Eli's house. Many believe the faithful priest points first to Samuel or to Zadok, though some also see in him a shadow of Christ. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: even when others fail, God still looks for faithful people. Ask him to give you a heart that seeks to please him more than to gain something for yourself.
exp.10:2:
The elders of Jabesh ask Nahash, king of the Ammonites, for seven days. During that time they want to send messengers throughout Israel. If no one comes to defend them, they will surrender to him. The word "throughout" in this verse refers to the whole nation of Israel.

The leaders of Jabesh in Gilead are speaking, from a city under siege. Nahash had set a cruel condition: to gouge out the right eye of every one of them, to humiliate Israel. The elders ask for time, perhaps to seek help from their fellow Israelites. We do not know for certain whether Nahash accepted out of confidence or out of pride, but the text shows that he granted them the time.

For today: when you face a situation that overwhelms you, do not remain silent or alone. Ask for help in time from your family, your church, or trusted people, and at the same time trust that God can use others to come to your aid.
exp.13:41:
Saul asks that the lot be cast between him and his son Jonathan, and the lot selects Jonathan. "Cast the lot" refers to a means by which God would reveal who was guilty. "Was selected" means he was singled out as the one at fault.

Saul had made a hasty vow: no one was to eat until evening while they fought against the Philistines. Jonathan had not heard of the vow and tasted a little honey. Since God was not answering Saul, he sought to find out who had broken the vow. We do not know exactly how the lot worked; it is understood as a way of seeking God's answer.

Today we learn that words spoken in haste can hurt those we love. Before making a serious promise, it is wise to pray, think, and ask God for wisdom.
exp.0:3:
This verse tells us that whenever the day came for Elkanah to present his sacrifice at Shiloh, he would give portions of the meal to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters. The idea of "presenting" the sacrifice means he brought the offering before God, and each "portion" was the share of the sacrificial meal given to each person.

Here the narrator describes the household customs of Elkanah's family. Notice that Hannah is not named in this list, and the next verse explains why: she received a special portion, because Elkanah loved her. This sets the scene for Hannah's sorrow, since she had no children and was mistreated by Peninnah.

For today: in family gatherings and at church, there are people who carry quiet sorrows. Let us think of someone who sits beside us with sadness, and offer them attention and sincere comfort.
exp.23:16:
This verse tells us that David finished speaking to Saul. Then Saul asked him, "Is this your voice, my son David?" and he began to weep out loud. The word "happened" in the verse means "came about," and "lifted up his voice" means that he wept openly.

David had Saul in his power inside a cave and did him no harm; he only cut off a piece of his robe. Then he went out and spoke to him from a distance, showing him that he was not his enemy. Saul had been pursuing him out of jealousy. Here Saul calls him "my son," and his weeping shows that, at least for a moment, he recognized his wrong. The Bible does not say whether that change lasted.

For today: when someone treats you badly, responding with kindness and truth can touch a hardened heart. You will not always succeed in changing them, but you will keep your conscience clear before God.
exp.9:10:
Those who had known Saul for a long time saw him prophesying with a group of prophets, and they were astonished. They asked one another, "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" "Prophesying" here seems to describe a Spirit-filled expression, like praise or inspired speech. The phrase "for a long time" means the same as "always."

The speakers are Saul's acquaintances and neighbors. God had just changed his heart, and Samuel had announced this sign to him after anointing him as the future king. People did not expect that change in an ordinary young man from a simple family. The saying became a popular proverb. Scholars understand it in several ways: as astonishment, as mockery, or as doubt.

For today: God can work in people whom others have already "filed away" and labeled. Let us avoid pigeonholing anyone, and if God calls us, let us not depend on what others think of us.
exp.24:13:
Here a servant of Nabal tells Abigail, the wife of his master, that David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet Nabal, and that Nabal screamed at them. The word "screamed" in this verse means he shouted angrily at the messengers.

The one speaking is a young servant of Nabal. We already know that David asked for provisions respectfully, because his men had protected Nabal's flocks. Nabal answered with scorn, and David armed himself with four hundred men. The servant knows there is danger and goes to Abigail, because she has good sense, and Nabal listens to no one.

For today: when you see that a situation may end badly because of someone's pride, do not stay silent. Speak in time and with respect to the wise person who can help calm things down.
exp.2:15:
Samuel had just received a very hard message from God: Eli's house would be judged. Samuel was young and afraid to tell his teacher. Eli, already old and a priest, calls him kindly, though afterward he will firmly ask him to tell him everything. His gentle manner opens the way for Samuel to speak with confidence.

Today, when you have to say a difficult truth, do it with respect and without hiding what is essential. And if someone corrects you or listens to you, answer with the same readiness as Samuel: "Here I am."
exp.19:11:
Jonathan makes a solemn vow before God. He promises that he will find out what his father thinks by this time tomorrow or the next day, and that if Saul is favorable toward David, he will send for David and tell him.

David fears that Saul wants to kill him and asks who will warn him if the king answers harshly. Jonathan, Saul's son and David's loyal friend, takes him out into the field so they can speak in private. There he calls on the LORD, the God of Israel, as witness to his commitment. His loyalty to David is great, even though he is the king's son.

For today: when you promise something to someone, keep your word sincerely and openly, even when it is difficult. True friendship tells the truth and protects the other person, even when it costs something.
exp.1:30:
God says that days are coming when he will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house. Strength here stands for power, influence and protection. Taking it away means taking away the family's standing and ability to lead. The phrase "so that no one in it will reach old age" means that no one in his family would live to be old; many would die young.

A prophet, called a "man of God," speaks on behalf of the LORD to the priest Eli. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, abused the offerings, and Eli did not correct them firmly. God had promised that his family would serve as priests, but that promise depended on their truly honoring him.

For today: God looks at the heart, not just the office or the tradition. Honoring him means obeying him, even when it costs us to correct those we love.
exp.18:6:
Jonathan summoned David and told him all these things. Then Jonathan brought David to Saul, and David was with Saul as before. "Summoned" means he called him to come, and "brought" means that he took him there in person.

Saul had wanted to kill David out of jealousy. Jonathan, Saul's son and David's loyal friend, spoke up for David before his father and reminded him that David had risked his life against the Philistine. Saul promised with an oath that he would not kill him. This verse shows the result of that mediation. As we see later, the peace did not last, and Saul again tried to harm him.

Today we can learn from Jonathan to be peacemakers. When there is conflict between people, God sometimes calls us to speak with truth and respect, without taking sides out of resentment. Even so, we do not control the hearts of others, so we do what is right and trust God.
exp.9:11:
A man who lived there replied with a question of his own: "And who is their father?" That is why people began repeating the saying: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" A "proverb" here is a popular saying that people passed along.

Saul had just been anointed by Samuel, and the Spirit of God came upon him. Those who knew him were astonished to see him prophesying. The man's words are hard to interpret. Perhaps he meant that the gift of prophecy does not depend on family, neither on the fathers of the prophets nor on Saul's. Others understand it as mockery or amazement. The text does not make it clear.

God does not work according to appearances or people's background. Avoid pigeonholing others by their past or their family. And if God calls you, do not let other people's opinions hold you back.
exp.25:15:
