David rebukes Abner, the commander of Saul's army, for failing to protect the king. He tells him that what they did is not good, and that all of them deserve to die, meaning they have earned death because of that failure. To protect someone means to watch over and defend them, and a water jug is a container for water. David gives them the proof: the king's spear and water jug, which he took while everyone slept.

David speaks from a distant hill, after slipping into Saul's camp at night. Saul was hunting him in order to kill him. David could have killed Saul, but he did not want to harm the LORD's anointed, the king chosen by God. He uses these proofs to show that he is not a traitor.

For today: trusting God frees us from taking revenge. When someone treats us unjustly, we can act with integrity and respect, leaving God to be the judge.
exp.26:11:
This verse says that Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, trusted David. He thought David had made himself a stench to his own people, Israel, and so David would serve him forever. "Trusted" here means believed and relied on. "Stench" is a strong word for something hateful and offensive, and it shows how Achish understood David's reputation among his people.

The narrator tells how David deceived Achish. David was fleeing from Saul and living in Philistine territory. He told Achish that he was raiding towns of Judah, when in fact he was attacking other enemies of Israel. So that no one would report him, he left no survivors. The text does not approve of everything David did; it only describes what happened.

For today: a lie may bring security for a while, but it is not a healthy path. When you are in trouble, seek God and act with truth, because trust gained through deception is fragile.
exp.3:20:
Here the wife of Phinehas, already dying after giving birth, names the boy Ichabod. She says, "The glory has departed from Israel." The reason she gives is that the ark of God was captured by the Philistines, and that her father-in-law and her husband had been killed.

She speaks in the midst of enormous grief. Israel had lost a battle, and the bad news reached her at the very moment of childbirth. The name Ichabod is commonly understood to mean "where is the glory?" For her, the capture of the ark meant that the presence of God was departing.

For today: the presence of God is not reduced to objects or rituals. Let us seek God with a sincere heart, and not only with religious customs, and remember that He remains faithful even in our darkest hours.
exp.8:10:
This verse tells how Saul and his servant were climbing the hill toward the city when they met some young women coming out to draw water. They asked them whether the seer was there. "Young women" means young girls, and "seer" was an older word for the prophet, someone who received messages from God.

It is Saul and his servant who speak. They were searching for his father's lost donkeys, and the servant suggested consulting the man of God to learn which way to go. The young women answered promptly and gave them directions. Without knowing it, Saul was on his way to meet Samuel, who would anoint him as king.

For today: when you need direction, do not hesitate to ask and to seek wise counsel. God can use an ordinary search, such as one for lost donkeys, to lead you to an important encounter.
exp.23:4:
David's men tell him that this is the day God had promised: Saul, his enemy, is in his hands, and he can do to him whatever he wishes. David gets up and, without making a sound, cuts off the corner of Saul's robe. The word for "quietly" means in silence. The corner is the hem or lower edge of the garment.

Saul was pursuing David with three thousand soldiers in order to kill him. He entered a cave alone to relieve himself, and David and his men were hidden at the back. His men read the situation as an opportunity given by God. The Bible does not record that God said those exact words; they apply them in their own way.

A favorable opportunity is not always a sign that God wants us to act. Before taking advantage of it, it is wise to ask ourselves whether it is right before God. David, even under pressure from his own men, stopped and sought to act with respect and a clear conscience.
exp.8:22:
Samuel asks the cook to bring the portion of meat that he had given him and told him to set aside. The cook was the one who prepared the food for the feast. The verse says "the portion I gave you" and "to set aside."

Samuel is speaking at a feast at the high place, with about thirty guests. Saul had just said that he came from the smallest tribe. Samuel receives him with honor and gives him the best place. That separate portion shows that God had already prepared Saul for that day. Some believe the portion had a special value, but the text does not explain its meaning in detail.

God sees and prepares things for us long before we notice. When you feel small or unimportant, remember that God knows you and can have a place prepared for you. Trust in Him with humility.
exp.19:30:
Saul tells his son Jonathan that as long as David is alive, neither Jonathan nor Jonathan's kingdom will be secure. Then Saul orders his men to send for David and bring him, because David must surely die. "Established" here means settled and secure.

Saul speaks in fury against Jonathan, because David did not come to the king's table and Jonathan defended him. Saul already knew that God had taken his kingdom away from him, and out of jealousy and fear he wants to kill David. The text only shows that Saul is not thinking clearly.

For today: jealousy and fear can make us unjust and cruel. When you feel envy toward someone, stop, pray, and ask God for a humble heart. Like Jonathan, choose to do what is right, even when it costs you.
exp.16:21:
He says that David set down the supplies he had brought and left them in the care of the quartermaster at the camp. Then he ran to the battle line. When he arrived, he asked his brothers how they were doing. The word "supplies" is used in the verse above, and "battle line" describes where the soldiers stood ready to fight, so the verse keeps to those words.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, and he does so with simple detail. Jesse, David's father, had sent him with food for his older brothers, who were in Saul's army. David carries out the errand with care and haste, just before Goliath appears. The text does not say that he knew what was about to happen.

For today: God often prepares important moments in the middle of small tasks. David was only carrying out a family errand, and there he met his great opportunity. Be faithful in doing what is at hand today.
exp.24:17:
Abigail acts quickly and gathers a generous gift of food: two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five butchered sheep, five seahs of roasted grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs. She loads everything onto donkeys. "Butchered" means the sheep have been killed and prepared, ready to be eaten. The raisins are given as clusters of raisins.

This is the narrator's account. A servant had warned Abigail that Nabal, her husband, had insulted David's men, and that David was coming with his men to harm him. She acts at once to calm the situation and provide what her husband had refused, without telling him.

When we see a problem that could grow, it is wise to act early, with humility and with concrete deeds. A generous and wise gesture at the right time can prevent much pain and open the way to peace.
exp.27:17:
Saul is living with the consequences of not obeying God. The judgment God ordered against the Amalekites is what this verse refers to. Saul did not carry out that command fully, and for this reason God allows what is now happening.

Samuel, or someone presenting himself as Samuel, speaks to Saul. Saul, distressed by the Philistine army and without an answer from God, had sought a medium in Endor. Many understand that God allowed Samuel to appear; others think it was something else. The text does not fully clarify this. The message repeats what Samuel had already said earlier about the kingdom.

For today: partial obedience is not obedience. If we know what God asks of us, we should do it honestly and without excuses. And when we fail, it is wise to return to Him soon with humility, rather than looking for ways out through other paths.
exp.27:3:
The Philistines gathered together and camped at Shunem. Saul also gathered all Israel and camped at Gilboa. The phrases "camped" and "gathered" mean that they set up their military camp, and that he assembled his army.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel is about to enter a serious war. Samuel had already died, and Saul had driven out the mediums and fortune-tellers. Even so, in the next verse Saul feels an enormous fear, seeks God, and receives no answer. The text does not explain here all the reasons for God's silence, but the earlier story shows Saul's disobedience.

When pressure comes, what is in our heart becomes visible. Do not wait until you are afraid to seek God. Draw near to Him every day with sincerity and obedience, so that in times of crisis your trust is already firm.
exp.1:11:
The verse says that the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were wicked men. To be wicked here means they lived with no regard for God. The phrase "they had no regard for the LORD" does not mean they had never heard of Him, but that they did not honor Him or take Him seriously in how they lived.

This is the narrator of the book speaking. It comes right after Hannah's prayer, and the author sets Samuel, who serves the Lord, against these corrupt priests. The verses that follow show how they abused their role and took for themselves the best portions of the people's sacrifices.

For today: we can know a great deal about religion and even serve in the church, but that is not the same as honoring God. Let us ask Him for a sincere heart that respects Him, and that our service never becomes an excuse for taking advantage of others.
exp.15:20:
David came to where King Saul was and entered his service, that is, he put himself at the king's disposal. Saul came to love him very much, and David became his armor-bearer. "Armor-bearer" refers to the attendant who carried the weapons and shield of the king or of a soldier. "Loved him very much" means that Saul grew very fond of him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul was tormented by an evil spirit, and his servants suggested that he seek someone who could play the harp. David, a young shepherd from Bethlehem, was recommended. God had already chosen him in secret as the future king, but he began by serving with humility.

For today: serve faithfully in small things and in unseen places, without rushing your future. God can use your simple gifts to open doors for you and to help others.
exp.18:19:
Saul sent messengers to seize David. When they arrived and saw a group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel leading them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers, and Saul's men also began to prophesy. "Leading them" means that he was in charge of the group. "Prophesying" here refers to speaking or praising under the influence of God, although the text does not describe in detail how this happened.

This is a narrative. David fled from Saul, who wanted to kill him, and took refuge with Samuel in Naioth, near Ramah. Saul insists on capturing him, but God protects David in an unexpected way: the soldiers cannot carry out the king's order. The text does not explain everything, but it shows that God is acting upon them.

When someone seems to have all the power to do harm, God remains greater. We can seek refuge in Him and in people of faith, and trust that He cares for his own, even when we do not see how.
exp.26:0:
David thought to himself: "One of these days Saul is going to sweep me away. The best thing I can do is escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will stop searching for me all over Israel, and I will slip out of his hand." In this way David planned to get free of Saul's pursuit.

David is the one speaking, but he is speaking only to himself. Saul, the king, was hunting him out of jealousy, even though God had already chosen David to be king. Worn down by the chase, David takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath, a Philistine ruler and an enemy of Israel. The Bible does not say here that God told him to do this, and he did not seek the Lord's counsel first. Some see wisdom in his decision; others see a lack of faith.

When fear and weariness weigh on us, we can reach conclusions without praying. Before making a major decision, stop and ask God. Remember also his promises, even when the road is long.
exp.16:51:
Here the verse says that, after seeing Goliath fall, the soldiers of Israel and Judah charged forward with a shout and chased the Philistines. They pursued them as far as the entrance to Gath and the gates of Ekron. Many Philistine bodies were left strewn along the road to Shaaraim, all the way to Gath and Ekron. "Shout" means crying out loudly, and "strewn" here refers to men who were killed or badly struck down.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. For forty days Israel had been paralyzed with fear before Goliath. When David defeated him by trusting in God, the army regained its courage and advanced. Israel and Judah are mentioned separately, perhaps because the kingdom was already divided into two groups, though scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: the courage of one person can encourage many. When you face your fear by trusting in God, your faith can give strength to others. And when God gives you a victory, do not stand still: move forward with gratitude and courage.
exp.24:12:
David said to his men, "Strap on your swords!" So David and all his men strapped on their swords, and about four hundred men followed David, while two hundred stayed with the supplies. The supplies are the provisions and belongings of the group.

David, who was hiding from Saul in the wilderness, spoke these words. His men had protected Nabal's flocks, and David had politely asked for some food. Nabal insulted him and treated him with contempt. David responded in anger and decided to take revenge through violence. The account does not approve of that decision; Abigail soon appears and will intervene to stop him.

For today: when someone offends us, let us not act in the heat of the moment. Before we respond, let us stop, pray, and listen to wise counsel. A hasty reaction can cause harm that we cannot later repair.
exp.26:3:
When Saul learned that David had fled to Gath, he no longer searched for him. The word "learned" means he received the report, and "fled" means David had gone away to escape.

The narrator describes what happened after David, with his six hundred men and their families, went to live with Achish, a Philistine king of Gath. David had already had to flee from Saul many times. Earlier, he had said that one day he might die at the hands of Saul. The Bible does not say that going to Gath was a command from God, so some see it as a fearful human decision and others as a wise way out. What we do see is that Saul gave up the search.

For today: when you feel great pressure, ask God for wisdom before you decide. He can take care of you even when your decisions are not perfect.
exp.28:3:
The Philistine commanders were angry with Achish and insisted that he send David back to the town he had given him, Ziklag. They did not want David to go with them into battle, because in the middle of the fight he might turn against them. They said that the only way David could win back his master Saul's favor would be by handing over the heads of the Philistine soldiers. "Commanders" here means military leaders.

The Philistine leaders speak with distrust of David and his men, who had come to Achish for refuge while fleeing from Saul. Achish trusted David, but the others saw the danger. Without knowing it, they kept David from having to fight against his own people. The Bible does not say that David planned this; it shows that God was at work in that situation.

For today: sometimes a door closes, and it hurts or seems unfair. Even so, God may be protecting us from a worse path. Trust Him, and thank Him for the closed doors too.
exp.18:15:
It says that when Saul's messengers entered the house to take David, they found the idol in the bed. It had goat hair on its head, so that it looked like a person lying down. The word "idol" refers to a household idol (in Hebrew, "teraphim"); scholars are not sure of its exact form, but it was large enough to appear to be a body.

Saul wanted to kill David out of jealousy. Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, helped him escape through a window and set up this deception to buy him time. The narrator tells what the messengers saw.

For today: when we face a threat, God often works through wisdom and the help of people close to us. We can act wisely and ask for help, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.16:8:
Goliath proposes a duel between two men. If Israel's champion is able to fight him and kill him, then the Philistines will be servants to Israel. But if Goliath prevails and kills the Israelite, then the Israelites will be servants to the Philistines. The phrase "if he is able to fight me and kill me" sets out the terms: the outcome depends on whether the other man can overcome Goliath in battle. Servants are people who serve another, like slaves or subjects.

Goliath, the Philistine champion, speaks before the army of Israel. It was an old custom for a single warrior to represent a whole people in order to avoid a large battle. Goliath uses this challenge to humiliate Israel, and the text that follows says that Saul and all the Israelites were filled with fear.

For today: our fears often speak with a loud voice and make us feel that losing is unavoidable. Before you let yourself be paralyzed, remember that God can work in ways we do not expect. Place your trust in Him and take the next step with faith.
exp.1:6:
God is the one who directs the changes in life. The words "poverty" and "wealth" speak of losing or gaining possessions. "Humbles" means to bring down, and "exalts" means to raise up or give honor. The verse shows that God has the final say over wealth, position, and the future of people.

Hannah speaks in a prayer of thanksgiving. She was childless and suffered mockery, but God gave her Samuel. Her song celebrates that God changes the circumstances of the weak and humbles the pride of the powerful. Scholars see in her prayer an announcement of the kingdom that would come in Israel.

For today: if you are in a time of need or humiliation, you can entrust your situation to God with hope. And if things are going well for you, do not become proud, because you receive everything from Him. Be humble and generous.
exp.12:16:
The verse tells that the Philistines sent three groups of raiders out of their camp at Michmash to attack the territory of Israel. "Raiders" means a quick attack to steal and cause harm. A "division" is a group of fighters. The first group headed toward Ophrah, in the land of Shual. The other two are mentioned in the next verse.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel was weak: Saul had only about six hundred men, and the Philistines dominated the area, even controlling the weapons. No one knows exactly where each place was, but the account shows that the people lived under constant threat.

For today: when you feel surrounded by pressure and short on resources, do not just stare at your weakness. Bring your situation to God in prayer, ask for his guidance, and take the next step with faith and patience, trusting that he works even when everything seems to be against you.
exp.20:4:
David tells the priest Ahimelech that his men have kept away from women for these past three days. The bodies of the young men are holy even on an ordinary errand, which is to say a mission that is not set apart for worship. He adds that the bread they take will be replaced today by other bread.

David speaks while fleeing from King Saul, who wants to kill him. He arrives at Nob hungry and asks the priest for bread, but the priest has only the bread of the Presence, which is reserved for the sanctuary. David does not tell him the whole truth about his mission, and some interpreters see deception here. Jesus later mentioned this episode (Matthew 12:3-4).

Today we learn that God values mercy and human need above the cold letter of the rules. Even so, we should live with integrity and without deceit, because God cares for those who are hungry.
exp.9:20:
Here Samuel narrows down the selection of Israel's first king. First the tribe of Benjamin was brought forward by its clans, then the clan of Matri was selected, and finally Saul son of Kish was selected. "Selected" means that he was singled out, probably by casting lots. But when they looked for him, they could not find him.

Samuel speaks before the whole people gathered at Mizpah. Israel had asked for a king like the other nations, and Samuel reminds them that by this they were rejecting God as their protector. God grants them a king, but He is the one who makes the choice. According to the next verse, Saul was hidden among the baggage. The Bible does not explain why; many think it was out of fear or humility, though this is an interpretation.

For today: when God calls you to a responsibility, do not run away out of fear. Pray, ask for strength, and trust that He sustains the one He calls.
exp.25:16:
Saul recognizes David's voice in the darkness and asks him, "Is that your voice, David my son?" David answers with respect: "It is my voice, my lord and king."

David has just entered Saul's camp at night, while everyone was sleeping, and he could have killed him, but he did not. He took the spear and the water jug as proof and, from a distance, rebuked Abner for failing to guard the king. Saul was pursuing him unjustly, and yet David still calls him "my lord and king." Saul calls him "my son," though it is not certain how sincere he was.

Today, even when someone treats us badly, we can speak with respect and without revenge, leaving justice in God's hands. A calm answer can open doors to reconciliation.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that Samuel summoned all the people of Israel to gather before the LORD at Mizpah. "Summoned" means that he called them together and invited them to an assembly. "Before the LORD" shows that this was not an ordinary gathering, but a meeting in the presence of God.

Samuel was a prophet and judge of Israel. He had already anointed Saul in private, but had not yet presented him to the people. Now he gathers them to announce God's message: the people had asked for a king and, in doing so, had stopped trusting God as their protector. Mizpah had already been a place of assembly and prayer for Israel before.

For today: before making important decisions, it is good to pause and come before God with sincerity. Let us ask ourselves whether we are trusting in Him or seeking security in other things.
exp.16:38:
David fastened Saul's sword over the tunic the king had lent him and tried to walk, but he could not, because he was not accustomed to them. He told Saul honestly, "I cannot walk in these," and took everything off. The words "tried to walk" mean that he attempted to move in that gear, and "not accustomed to them" means that he had never worn such equipment before.

David speaks with King Saul. Israel was facing the Philistine giant Goliath, and Saul, with good intentions, wanted to protect David by dressing him like a soldier. But David trusted that God, who had delivered him from the lion and the bear, would deliver him now as well.

For today: God uses us with the gifts and experience He has already given us. We do not need to imitate others in order to serve with faith. Trust God and be yourself, with humility.
exp.24:16:
A servant tells Abigail that serious trouble is coming. He asks her to think carefully and decide what she must do, because disaster is already looming over Nabal and all his household. The phrase "disaster looms over our master" means that the trouble has effectively been set in motion and is on its way. And "nobody can speak to him" means that Nabal is so scornful and so hard to deal with that no one can reason with him.

It is one of Nabal's young servants who speaks. Nabal had insulted David's men, who earlier had protected his flocks. David, angry, was coming with armed men. The servant does not dare to speak to Nabal, so he goes to Abigail, known for her good judgment.

For today: when you see a serious problem, do not stay silent or wait for it to change on its own. Humbly seek out the wise person who can act with calm, and do what is within your power to prevent the harm.
exp.6:4:
Samuel asks that all the people gather at Mizpah, and he promises to pray to God for them.

Samuel is a prophet and judge of Israel. The people had spent years suffering under the Philistines and worshiping idols such as the Baals and Ashtaroth. Samuel called them to turn back to God with all their heart, and they removed their idols. Now he summons them to a time of prayer and repentance, where they acknowledge: "We have sinned against the Lord."

Turning back to God is not only leaving what is wrong; it also means coming near to Him with humility. It is also a great help to have brothers and sisters who pray for us and with us. Today you can ask someone you trust to pray for you and pray for others.
exp.24:32:
Here David tells Abigail that her wisdom is good and that she is blessed, because she kept him from bloodshed and from taking revenge by his own hand. "Discernment" means sound thinking, the wise way of reasoning. "Kept" means held back or stopped.

David speaks after Nabal, a rich and foolish man, treated him with contempt and refused food to his men. David, angry, set out with armed men to kill the males of Nabal's household. Abigail, Nabal's wife, went out to meet him with provisions and spoke to him humbly, reminding him not to burden his conscience with a needless revenge. David acknowledges that God sent her.

When we are angry, it is wise to listen to someone who speaks to us with wisdom. Before we take revenge, let us pause and allow God to guide the situation.
exp.27:4:
This verse tells us that Saul looked at the camp of the Philistines and was very afraid. The word "trembled" in the verse above conveys that he was shaken, filled with anxiety and restlessness. The word "violently" means exceedingly much. His heart, that is, his whole inner self, was shaken by fear.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samuel had already died, and Saul, king of Israel, faced an enemy army at Shunem. He had turned away from God through his disobedience, and that is why his fear was so great. Because God was not answering him, Saul ended up seeking a medium, something God's law forbade.

For today: when fear overwhelms you, do not rush to forbidden or doubtful sources looking for security. Come to God sincerely, acknowledge your failures, and trust that he listens to those who approach him with humility.
exp.19:3:
Jonathan asks David what he truly wants or needs. In this verse, the phrase "Whatever you desire" simply means "What do you want me to do?" Jonathan offers to help without attaching any conditions.

David is running away from King Saul, who wants to kill him. Jonathan, Saul's son, does not believe his father is as determined as David fears, but he sees David's fear and hears how serious his words are. Because of their friendship, Jonathan decides to listen to him and act.

Today we can imitate Jonathan: before offering quick advice, we can kindly ask what the other person needs. Really listening and offering concrete help is a practical way of showing love.
exp.0:11:
This verse tells us that Hannah was praying at length before God, and that the priest Eli was watching her. The phrase "watched her mouth" means that Eli was paying attention to how her lips were moving. The words "as Hannah kept on praying" tell us that she went on praying without hurry, for quite a while.

The narrator of the book places us at the sanctuary in Shiloh. Hannah had no children and was deeply distressed. She had just made a vow: if God gave her a son, she would dedicate him to God. Eli, who was observing closely, saw her lips moving without hearing any voice, and so he mistakenly thought she was drunk.

For today: God hears sincere prayers, even silent ones that others do not understand. Speak with Him honestly about your pain. And when you see someone weeping or acting strangely, do not rush to judge them; ask gently and listen first.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that the Philistines were defeated and overcome. Because of this, they stopped invading the territory of Israel. The phrase "the hand of the LORD" speaks of God's power acting against them while Samuel lived and led the people.

It is the narrator of the book who sums up what happened. Israel had returned to the LORD at Mizpah, with repentance and prayer, and God helped them to win. Samuel set up the stone Ebenezer as a memorial that the LORD had helped them. This verse shows the result: a time of protection and relief.

For today: when God helps us, it is good to return to Him wholeheartedly and to remember His faithfulness. We can keep memorial stones of our own, such as a prayer journal, to give thanks and to trust Him when new difficulties come.
exp.24:42:
David had also married Ahinoam, a woman from Jezreel. "Had married" tells us she became his wife, and "she and Abigail were both his wives" means the two of them were his wives at the same time. So Abigail and Ahinoam were both David's wives.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. David was fleeing from Saul, who was pursuing him, and he had just married Abigail. The next verse tells that Saul had given Michal, David's wife, to another man. Although the Bible reports that David had several wives, that does not mean it approves of that practice. Several passages show the problems it brought.

For today: it is not enough for something to be common in our culture. It is wise to measure our decisions by what God teaches throughout the whole Bible, and to trust Him, especially in uncertain times.
exp.3:18:
This verse tells of the wife of Phinehas, daughter-in-law of Eli, who was pregnant and about to give birth. When she heard the news that God's ark had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she collapsed and went into labor, for her labor pains came upon her.

The speaker is the narrator of the book. Israel had lost the battle against the Philistines, and the ark, the sign of God's presence among the people, had been taken. She died shortly afterward. Her son was named Ichabod, a name usually understood to mean "the glory has departed," because she felt that Israel's glory had gone.

For today: when you feel that everything is falling apart, remember that God does not depend on objects or places. Seek him sincerely, with humility and repentance, and trust that he is still at work even in dark times.
exp.0:26:
Hannah tells the priest Eli that this boy is the answer to her prayer. She prayed for him, and the LORD granted what she asked.

Hannah, a woman who could not have children, speaks. Years earlier, at the sanctuary in Shiloh, she had prayed with tears and promised to dedicate her son to God. Eli had seen her praying and at first thought she was drunk. Now she returns with Samuel, already weaned, to keep her promise and remind Eli of that moment.

When God answers a prayer, it is worth remembering it and giving thanks. Hannah did not only receive; she also gave back, with gratitude, what God had given her. We may ask ourselves: how can I use what God has given me to serve Him and others?
exp.16:30:
This verse says that David's words were overheard and reported to King Saul, and then Saul sent for David. The word "reported" means that what David said was carried back to the king by people who had heard it, and "sent for him" means that Saul called for David to be brought before him.

David had come to the camp to bring food to his brothers. There he heard how the giant Goliath was challenging the army of Israel, and he boldly asked what would be done for the man who defeated him. His brother Eliab became angry with him, but David kept speaking. His words reached the king, who needed someone with faith to face the fear of everyone.

For today: do not keep quiet about your faith even when others mock you or correct you harshly. God can use simple, brave words to open doors you never imagined.
exp.6:7:
The Israelites ask Samuel to keep praying to the LORD for them, so that He will rescue them from the power of the Philistines. "Do not stop crying out" means "keep asking earnestly without giving up," and the word "save" in the verse means "protect" or "rescue."

The people have gathered at Mizpah. They have just confessed their sin through fasting and by pouring out water before the LORD (its exact meaning is not explained in the text). When they learned that the Philistines were coming to attack them, they were afraid and turned to Samuel as their intercessor. God then answered with a thunder that threw the enemy into confusion.

For today: when you are afraid, begin by returning to God with humility and sincerity. Ask Him for help, and also let other believers pray with you and for you.
exp.19:40:
When the young man had gone, David got up from the south side of the stone, where he had been hiding. He fell facedown and bowed three times to the ground, as a sign of respect and gratitude. Then he and Jonathan kissed each other and wept together, though David wept more.

The phrase "the south side of the stone" refers to where David was waiting, and kissing was a common expression of affection between close friends in that culture.

This is part of the account in 1 Samuel. Jonathan, son of King Saul, had just confirmed with a signal of arrows that his father meant to kill David. The young man understood nothing, since it was a secret message. Now the friends say goodbye, knowing that David will have to flee and live far away.

For today: do not hide your pain in the face of a farewell or a loss. Weeping with a faithful friend is a way of caring for the friendship. If someone is suffering, stay with them without rushing; your presence can comfort more than many words.
exp.23:17:
King Saul speaks. For a long time he had been pursuing David in order to kill him. In a cave, David had the chance to kill him, but he only cut off a piece of his robe and spared his life. When David shows it to him and speaks to him with respect, Saul weeps and admits his wrong. Even so, the Bible later shows that his heart did not change completely.

Today we can learn to respond well when someone treats us badly, leaving God to be the judge. It also invites us to humbly acknowledge our faults, without excuses, and to seek a true change, not just words or tears of the moment.
exp.19:9:
Here David asks Jonathan: "Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?" The word "harshly" means with anger and in a bad manner. David fears that there is no sure way to find out what King Saul is thinking.

David speaks with his friend Jonathan, Saul's son. David suspects that Saul wants to kill him, but Jonathan does not yet believe it. They had already made a covenant before the LORD. David asks for help, and Jonathan promises to warn him. So they immediately go out into the field to talk in private and make a plan.

For today: when you are afraid or in an uncertain situation, do not hide it. Speak with a faithful friend, ask for help with humility, and seek together a sensible plan, trusting that God cares for you in the midst of uncertainty.
exp.19:28:
Here Jonathan repeats to Saul the excuse that David had asked him to use: that David had to go to Bethlehem for his clan's yearly sacrifice, and that his brother had ordered him to be there. The verse says "our clan is holding a sacrifice in the city" and asks, "please let me go and see my brothers." The phrase about finding favor in someone's eyes is a polite way of saying "if you think well of me," and it shows how humbly David wanted his request to sound.

Jonathan is speaking and quoting David. Saul had noticed that David was absent from the table at the New Moon feast. David and Jonathan had agreed on this explanation in order to test whether Saul wanted to kill David. Some think the excuse was partly true and others that it was a cover story; the text does not make this clear. Saul's furious reaction confirms his intentions.

For today: when the truth is dangerous, it is not enough to look after our own safety; we must also look after our integrity. Let us ask God for wisdom to be honest and to protect the innocent, while continuing to trust Him.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that the mighty warriors lose their strength: their bows, which were their main weapon, are broken. In contrast, the weak are equipped with power. The phrase that the weak are "equipped with strength" means that they are provided with power, much as a soldier is fitted out with what he needs before going into battle.

The one speaking is Hannah, in a prayer of thanksgiving. She had been barren and suffered mockery, but God gave her Samuel. She sees in her own case an example of how God works: he humbles the proud and lifts up the one who depends on him.

For today: if you feel weak or without resources, do not lose heart. Bring your need to God with humility. And if you feel strong, remember that your strength is not your own. Trusting in God, and not in our own weapons, is the safest course.
exp.23:3:
The passage tells us that Saul, while pursuing David, came to a sheepfold beside the road where there was a cave. He went into that cave to relieve himself. David and his men were hidden deep inside the same cave, off to the sides, and Saul had no idea they were there.

This is part of the account given by the narrator of 1 Samuel. Saul, king of Israel, was seeking to kill David with three thousand chosen soldiers. David, already anointed as the future king, was fleeing through the wilderness of Engedi. Without realizing it, Saul found himself defenseless, alone, and close to David.

Look at what David's men said to him in this moment. They reminded him that the Lord had promised to deliver his enemy into his hand, so that David could do with Saul as he wished. Saul was now completely at David's mercy, and David's men saw this as the fulfillment of God's word. Yet David did not strike. Instead, he crept up and quietly cut off a corner of Saul's robe.

For today: sometimes God allows us the chance to take revenge or to gain something at someone else's expense. Before seizing it, it is worth stopping to ask whether doing so honors God. What looks like an open door may be a test of character.
exp.25:10:
David says he will not raise a hand against Saul, because Saul is the one "the LORD's anointed," that is, the king whom God himself set apart for that office. Instead, he tells Abishai to take the spear and the water jug that are by Saul's head, and then the two of them should leave.

David speaks with Abishai, his companion, during the night, in Saul's camp. Saul was pursuing him to kill him, and Abishai saw the perfect opportunity to end the matter. David refuses: he prefers to wait for God to settle the matter in his own way and in his own time. Taking the spear and the jug would serve as proof that he could have harmed Saul and did not.

For today: when someone treats us unjustly and the opportunity for revenge presents itself, we can choose to trust God and not take justice into our own hands.
exp.16:0:
The Philistines gathered their forces for war. They came together at Socoh, a town in Judah, and camped between Socoh and Azekah, in a place called Ephes-dammim. The phrase "camped" simply means they set up their military camp there.

Here the narrator speaks, setting the scene before the famous story of David and Goliath. The Philistines were an enemy people of Israel, and they had moved into the territory of Judah. The next verse shows that Saul and his army went out to face them, and that the two sides ended up facing each other, separated by a valley.

For today: big problems sometimes arrive all at once and settle in close to us. Before we look at the size of the conflict, we can remember that God remains faithful and can give us courage to face it, as he will do with David.
exp.26:1:
It says that David set out with his six hundred men and went to live with Achish, the son of Maoch, king of Gath, a Philistine city. Gath was the city of Goliath, the giant whom David had defeated.

The narrator tells us what David decided after thinking in his heart that Saul would one day kill him. He had been pursued many times and was tired of running. Escaping among Israel's enemies seemed to him the way out. The Bible does not say here that God had commanded him to do this, and many readers see in this a moment of fear rather than of faith.

When fear weighs heavily on us, we may make decisions only to get out of the problem. Before acting, it is wise to pray, to seek counsel, and to remember God's promises, since He had already anointed David as the future king.
exp.10:6:
Saul takes a pair of oxen, cuts them into pieces, and sends the pieces by messengers throughout the land of Israel. The message is clear: whoever does not march behind Saul and Samuel, the same will be done to his oxen. The verse of "cut them into pieces" and "sent them" is simply what the verse says: he took the oxen, cut them up, and sent the pieces out. Then the terror of the LORD fell upon the people: a strong fear, sent by God, and everyone came out together as one man.

Saul speaks after hearing that Jabesh-gilead was threatened and that the people were weeping. The Spirit of God came upon him, and he burned with anger at the injustice. He uses a harsh sign, which in that culture was understood as an urgent call and a warning. The oxen were valuable working tools.

Today, when someone suffers an injustice, do not look the other way. Ask God for courage and seek to unite others to help, in concrete ways and with humility.
exp.19:25:
This verse says that Saul said nothing on the first day of the feast, when he saw that David's place was empty. He thought that something had happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean, and so he could not take part in the meal. The Berean wording makes this clear: "Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean—surely he is unclean."

Here the narrator tells us what Saul was thinking. David and Jonathan had planned this new moon feast to see whether Saul wanted to kill David. Saul kept silent that day because he believed there was a religious reason for the absence. The law mentioned impurities that kept a person from taking part in certain sacred meals (Leviticus 7:20-21). His reaction would change the next day.

For today: we often explain the behavior of others according to what we believe, and we get it wrong. Before drawing conclusions, it is wise to ask, to listen, and to wait. And when tension lives in the heart, let us ask God to free us from suspicion and resentment.
exp.0:8:
This verse tells us that Hannah stood up after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh. Meanwhile, the priest Eli was sitting on a chair beside the doorpost of the temple of the LORD. The temple here is the sanctuary where worship took place in Shiloh.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts what happened. Hannah came from a family that went up to worship every year. Her rival wounded her with words, and she wept and would not eat. Although her husband comforted her, her pain continued. So, when she stood up, she went to pray. The verse sets the scene for her sincere prayer.

For today: when your sorrow weighs on you, do not keep it silent. Hannah brought her sadness to God with honesty. You can do the same, even if you do not have beautiful words, and trust that he listens.
exp.18:23:
The verse tells that Saul took off his robes, prophesied in front of Samuel, and collapsed and lay without clothing all that day and all that night. "Prophesy" here means speaking or acting under a strong spiritual influence, not necessarily foretelling the future. That is why people repeated the saying: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" The phrase "stripped off his robes" probably indicates that he removed his royal robes, or part of them.

Saul was pursuing David to kill him. David had taken refuge with Samuel in Naioth. Three groups of Saul's messengers arrived and prophesied; then Saul himself went. God stopped his plan to kill David and humbled him.

For today: no one can stop what God decides to protect. When you feel that someone or something rises against your good plans, trust that God cares for his own and knows how to set limits on evil.
exp.22:21:
Saul asks the men of Ziph to go back and make further preparations. They are to find out exactly where David goes and who has seen him there. The word "prepare" here means getting ready and making sure everything is in order, and "cunning" describes someone very skilled at avoiding being caught. Saul says he has been told that David is extremely cunning.

King Saul, who pursues David out of jealousy and fear, is the one speaking. The Ziphites, people of that region of Judah, have just offered to hand David over to him. Saul blesses them in the name of the LORD, though he is seeking something unjust. He wants certainty before he acts, because he knows David has already slipped away from him.

Today we can notice how much effort is spent when the heart is full of envy. Saul calls on God, yet he pursues his own desire. It is worth asking ourselves whether what we do truly pleases God, or whether we only decorate it with pious words.
exp.13:17:
Saul tells the priest Ahijah to bring the ark of God. The verse adds that at that time the ark was with the Israelites. The ark is the sacred chest that represented God's presence.

Saul and his people notice great confusion in the Philistine camp and discover that Jonathan and his armor-bearer are missing. Saul wants to consult God through the priest. But the commotion grows so much that Saul says, "Withdraw your hand," and goes out to battle without waiting for an answer. Some scholars point out that, according to the Hebrew text, it could be the ephod and not the ark; this is debated.

Seeking God is good, but doing it halfway, in a hurry, or without waiting for his answer leaves us acting on our own. Before deciding, take the time to pray and listen, and do not leave it unfinished when the pressure comes.
exp.13:46:
This verse sums up Saul's military campaigns once his kingdom was secure. It says he fought against the enemies surrounding Israel: the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Edomites, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. The phrase "wherever he turned" means "wherever he went," and "he routed them" indicates that he was successful and drove them back.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After the episode in which the people rescued Jonathan, the text offers a summary of Saul's reign. It shows that Israel was surrounded by hostile peoples and that Saul had real achievements, before his fall is narrated.

For today: good results do not guarantee a faithful heart. Let us give thanks for successes, but let us guard our obedience to God each day.
exp.29:7:
David asks the LORD whether he should chase the raiders who carried off the families of his people. "Should I pursue" is a plain question about whether to go after them, and "overtake" means catching up with them to fight. God answers directly: pursue them, because you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives.

David speaks after the Amalekites burned Ziklag and carried off the women and children as captives. His men, filled with grief, were talking about stoning him. He strengthened himself in the LORD and asked the priest Abiathar for the ephod, which was a means of seeking God's guidance.

When you are distressed or under pressure, do not act on impulse alone. Seek God first in prayer and in His Word, and then take the steps He shows you with confidence.
exp.15:15:
Saul's servants offer him a practical solution: that the king command them to look for someone who can skillfully play the harp. Then, whenever the spirit of distress from God comes upon him, that person will play, and Saul will find relief.

The ones speaking are Saul's attendants. God had already withdrawn his Spirit from Saul because of his disobedience, and the king was suffering torment. How to understand the "spirit of distress from God" is debated: some see a spiritual being that God allowed, others an inner torment. The Bible does not explain it in more detail. This advice prepares the way for David's arrival.

For today: when someone is suffering, God can use simple means, such as music, companionship or good advice. Receive the help of others with humility, and offer yours with kindness.
exp.6:10:
Then the men of Israel charged out of Mizpah and chased the Philistines, striking them down all the way to an area below Beth-car. The wording here shows that Israel was not just pushing the enemy back but pressing the attack, defeating them again and again as they ran.

The book describes what led up to this moment. Israel had gathered at Mizpah to turn back to God. The Philistines came to attack them, but God answered with a great thunder that threw the enemy into confusion. Only then did Israel go out to pursue them. Where Beth-car was located is not known for certain, and scholars have not agreed on its exact position.

For today: God acts when his people return to him with humility. Even so, we must take the step that we are able to take. Israel did not win alone, but neither did it stay still. Trust in God and act with courage.
exp.15:8:
Jesse brings his son Shammah before Samuel, but Samuel says that the Lord has not chosen this one either.

Samuel had been sent by God to the house of Jesse in Bethlehem to anoint a new king, since Saul had been rejected. Jesse presents his sons one by one. Earlier, God had told Samuel not to look at appearance or height, because He looks at the heart. Shammah is the third son whom God does not choose.

Often we judge people, and even ourselves, by what can be seen on the outside. Today we can ask God to help us value sincerity, humility, and love, and to trust that He sees what no one else sees.
exp.19:27:
Jonathan answers his father Saul that David urgently asked his permission to go to Bethlehem. "Urgently" means with great insistence, with all his eagerness. Jonathan repeats the excuse that he and David had agreed on to explain David's absence from the king's table.

Saul noticed that David's place was empty at the feast of the new moon. Jonathan speaks to protect his friend, while he finds out whether Saul really intends to kill David. His answer provokes Saul's anger, and so Jonathan confirms that the danger is real. Some think his answer is only an agreed-upon excuse, not a malicious lie; the text does not judge this directly.

For today: loyalty to a friend sometimes costs dearly. Jonathan risked his relationship with his father to do what was right. Let us ask God for wisdom and courage to defend others with truth and love, even when it brings us discomfort.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that this went on year after year. Whenever Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, her rival Peninnah, Elkanah's other wife, would taunt her until she wept and would not eat. The verse shows that the pain was repeated again and again, on every yearly trip to Shiloh.

The narrator describes Hannah's suffering, since she could not have children. Peninnah, her rival, cut at her precisely on the journey to worship. It is striking that the place of worship was where the hurt cut deepest. Elkanah loved her, but he could not take away that sorrow. The text does not say that God was punishing her; it only states that the LORD had closed her womb, and it does not explain his reasons.

When someone wounds us, it is natural to weep and to feel drained of strength. Hannah teaches us not to stay alone with that pain. In the verses that follow she brings her anguish to God. We can do the same: pray honestly and seek support.
exp.1:10:
Elkanah returns to his home in Ramah and leaves his young son, Samuel, behind in Shiloh. "Began ministering" means that Samuel started to serve, helping with the work of worship. He did this "before Eli the priest," that is, under his supervision.

Hannah, the mother, had just prayed with gratitude, and Elkanah had been with her. She had promised to give to God the son she was given, and here that promise is being fulfilled. The verse works as a bridge: after Hannah's song, which speaks of a God who cares for his own, we see a child beginning to serve, and immediately it is set in contrast with the sons of Eli, who were corrupt.

For today: serving God does not require being great or perfect. Samuel was a child in an environment with bad examples, and yet he began to serve. We can do the same with whatever simple things we have at hand, even when others around us do not give a good witness.
exp.24:19:
Abigail came riding her donkey into a mountain ravine, and she saw David and his men coming down toward her. She went out to meet them. A mountain ravine is a narrow valley cut between the hills. To meet them means she went to them on purpose to greet and receive them.

The narrator describes this moment. Nabal, Abigail's husband, had scorned David and his men, even though they had protected his flocks. David, angered, was coming with armed men to take revenge. Abigail, without telling her husband, brought food to calm the situation and prevent a tragedy.

For today: when you see that a conflict could end in harm, do not wait for others to fix it. Act with wisdom, humility, and courage, seeking peace. Sometimes a generous gesture, offered at the right time, prevents a greater evil.
exp.19:16:
Jonathan had David reaffirm his vow, and he did so out of love for him. The verse says that Jonathan loved David as he loved himself, which describes a deep and sincere affection.

David was fleeing from King Saul, Jonathan's father, who wanted to kill him. Jonathan, although he was the king's son, recognized that God was with David. For that reason he made a covenant with him, asking for kindness toward his family in the future. The narrator makes clear that the oath arose from love, not from self-interest. It is a faithful friendship in the midst of danger.

For today: true friendship is shown through loyalty and sacrifice, above all when it is costly. Ask yourself whom you can accompany or protect this week, even if it costs you something, and do it with a sincere love.
exp.29:29:
This verse is part of a list of places. It says that David sent gifts to the people of Hormah, of Bor-ashan and of Athach. These were towns in the south of Judah.

After defeating the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the families, David recovered everything. With the spoils he had won, he wanted to share gifts among the leaders and the towns that had helped him or welcomed him during his time of flight from Saul. The narrator tells this to show David's generosity. The exact location of some of these places is not known.

God blesses us and also invites us to remember those who helped us in difficult times. Today you can show your gratitude with a message, a visit, or a concrete gesture to someone who supported you when you needed it most.
exp.5:6:
It says that the Philistines were to build a new cart and hitch to it two milk cows that had never worn a yoke. The calves would be taken away from the cows and penned up at home.

The speakers are the Philistine priests and diviners. They had taken the ark of God, and a plague had fallen on them. They wanted to send it back and to know whether the punishment came from the God of Israel or was mere chance. The cows, which would naturally want to return to their calves, would serve as a test: if they went toward Beth-shemesh, it would be a sign that God was guiding them.

For today: when we recognize that we have done wrong, fear alone is not enough. It is good to humble ourselves, make right what we did, and seek God sincerely, without hardening our hearts.
exp.10:8:
This verse tells how the men of Israel answered the messengers from Jabesh-gilead by saying that deliverance would come for them tomorrow, by the time the sun was hot. "By the time the sun is hot" means when the sun was already strong, around mid-morning. The men of Jabesh rejoiced when they heard the news.

The ones speaking are the Israelites gathered by Saul and Samuel. Jabesh was surrounded by the Ammonites, and its people had asked for help urgently. Saul had called the people to join together, and the fear of the LORD moved them to set out united. This answer brings hope to a distressed city.

For today: when someone is in trouble, a word of encouragement and a real commitment to help can restore their joy. We can be people who stand with others, keep an honest promise, and then act together with courage.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that the ark of the Lord, the sacred chest that represented God's presence among Israel, remained for seven months in Philistine territory. The phrase "had been" shows that it had stayed there for that length of time. The Philistines had captured it in battle.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. During those months, the ark brought trouble and sickness to the Philistine cities where it was kept. That is why, in the verses that follow, their priests and diviners look for a way to return it. They suggest sending it back with a guilt offering, to acknowledge that they had wronged the God of Israel.

For today: God cannot be treated as an object that we control or use as it suits us. The Philistines learned by force that he had to be acknowledged. We can do this willingly: come near to God with humility and admit our wrongs, before the consequences force us to.
exp.27:16:
It says that God carried out what he had already announced through Samuel. The kingdom was no longer in Saul's hands, because the LORD had torn it away and given it to David, whom the verse calls Saul's neighbor. Here, "neighbor" points to someone close to Saul, a fellow member of his community. The image of the kingdom being torn out of his hand means it was taken from him completely and for good.

Samuel speaks to Saul, or an apparition presenting itself as Samuel does. Saul, desperate before the Philistines and without any answer from God, sought out a medium in Endor. Some believe that Samuel truly appeared with God's permission; others think it was something else. The text presents the message as a word of judgment for Saul's disobedience.

For today: do not wait until you are in crisis to turn back to God. Obeying him in good time and with sincerity is better than seeking answers by mistaken paths when it is already too late.
exp.15:13:
What it says: The Spirit of the LORD left Saul, that is, He no longer guided him or gave him strength to reign. In his place, a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him. The word "torment" here means that it troubled him and took away his peace. That it came "from the LORD" indicates that God allowed it or used it as judgment; the text does not explain how, and scholars understand it in several ways.

Context: The narrator of the book recounts this right after Samuel anointed David. Saul had disobeyed God before, and for that reason he lost God's favor. While the Spirit passes to David, Saul is troubled. His servants notice and suggest he seek a musician who can play the harp to soothe him.

For today: Obeying God guards the heart. If we have failed, let us not harden our soul; let us seek God's forgiveness and guidance quickly. And, like Saul's servants, let us help with love those who are suffering.
exp.14:7:
It says that Saul captured Agag, the king of Amalek, alive, but put all the others to death with the sword. "Captured alive" means that he did not kill the king. "Devoted to destruction" means the people were set apart to be completely destroyed.

The narrator tells of the war against Amalek. God, through Samuel, had commanded Saul to destroy this people completely (1 Samuel 15:1-3). Earlier, Saul had spared the Kenites, who had been kind to Israel. But here the disobedience begins: Saul lets the king live. The verses that follow show that the best of the livestock was also kept. This command of total destruction is hard, and Christians understand it in various ways.

Obeying God halfway is a form of disobedience. We can ask ourselves: in what area am I leaving alive something that God has asked me to let go of? Let us ask him for help to obey him sincerely and completely.
exp.6:15:
It says that Samuel went around each year to three places: Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. In each one he took care of the people's cases and gave them justice. The phrase "went around" here means that he made a circuit, and "judged" means that he governed and settled disputes, not only that he handed down verdicts.

The one telling this is the narrator of the book, not Samuel. After the victory over the Philistines and a time of peace, it shows how Samuel led the people. The three places were in the part of Israel where he could reach many people. Then he would return to Ramah, his home, where he also judged and built an altar to the LORD.

For today: good leadership draws near to people. Samuel went to where the people were, with steadiness and service. We can ask ourselves whom we need to draw near to in order to help, listen, or act justly, and do it with faithfulness and humility.
exp.12:14:
Samuel set out from Gilgal and went up to Gibeah in Benjamin. There Saul counted the troops who were still with him, about six hundred men. Here "troops" means soldiers.

This is the narrator's account. Samuel had just rebuked Saul for offering the sacrifice without waiting, which disobeyed God's command. Samuel goes away, and Saul is left with a very small army facing the Philistines. Earlier he had about three thousand men (13:2), so many had left. The text does not explain all the reasons, but the fear and weakness are evident.

For today: obedience to God matters more than the results we can see or the pressure of the moment. Saul counted his soldiers, but he did not stop to correct his heart. When we fail, it is good to acknowledge it with humility and to trust God again, not only our own resources.
exp.22:14:
David saw that Saul had come out to take his life. That is why David was hiding in Horesh, in the Wilderness of Ziph. The verse places him in a specific place, so readers can picture the rough, hilly country where he was staying out of sight.

This is part of the story, not a speech. David was running from Saul, who was chasing him out of jealousy and fear of losing the throne. David had just left Keilah with about six hundred men. Although Saul searched for him every day, the text makes clear that God did not hand David over into Saul's hands.

For today: when you feel persecuted, pressured, or afraid, you are not alone. David was afraid and went into hiding, but he kept trusting God. God can also use people like Jonathan, who comes right after this, to encourage you. Seek that support and rest in God's care.
exp.15:9:
Here the account tells how Jesse brought seven of his sons before Samuel, one after another. After looking at each of them, Samuel told him that the Lord had not chosen any of these. The wording is easy to follow: "made to pass" means Jesse had his sons walk in front of the prophet one at a time, and "chosen" means picked out for a task.

Samuel had gone to Bethlehem on God's command to anoint a new king over Israel, because Saul had been rejected. Jesse was the head of the family, and Samuel was looking for the man whom God would point out. The older sons seemed like good candidates, but God was looking at something different. David, the youngest, was still missing; he was out caring for the sheep.

For today: let us not judge people, or ourselves, only by appearance or by the place they hold. God sees the heart and can call the one no one expected.
exp.24:14:
This verse says that David's men were very good to Nabal's shepherds. They did them no harm, and nothing of theirs went missing while they stayed near them in the field. The phrase here translated as "lived among" describes the time the men spent close to them.

The one speaking is a servant of Nabal, one of his shepherds. He tells this to Abigail, Nabal's wife, because Nabal had insulted David's messengers, and David was coming with four hundred armed men. The servant wants her to act before a tragedy happens. His testimony shows that David's complaint had a real basis: David's men had looked after them.

For today: when someone has done us good, let us not forget it or repay it with contempt. And if we see a conflict approaching, let us speak truthfully and in time, as this servant did, to seek peace.
exp.21:17:
This verse tells that King Saul ordered Doeg, a man from Edom, to attack the priests. Doeg obeyed, and that same day he struck down eighty-five men who wore a linen ephod, a simple garment that priests wore while serving. The phrase "strike down" means to attack with force until someone falls.

Saul acts out of jealousy and fear toward David. He had accused the priests of helping his enemy, even though Ahimelech had helped David without knowing there was any treachery. Saul's own guards refused to kill the priests of the Lord, but Doeg, a foreigner, carried out the killing.

For today: when fear and pride rule the heart, they can lead a person to commit terrible injustices. Let us ask God for a humble heart, and have the courage to refuse to obey an unjust order, as those guards did.
exp.0:16:
Eli tells Hannah to go in peace, and he prays that the God of Israel will grant the petition she has asked of Him. The word "grant" here means to give or allow something to happen, and it is the word this explanation is pointing to.

The speaker is Eli, the priest. A moment before, he had thought Hannah was drunk, because she was praying silently and only her lips were moving. Hannah explained to him that she was suffering greatly and was pouring out her heart before the Lord. Eli then changes his attitude and blesses her. The text does not say that Eli knew what her request was, only that he wishes God would grant it.

For today: when you are weighed down by pain, pray sincerely, as Hannah did, without pretending to be strong. And when someone tells you of their sorrow, listen before you judge, and bless them. Notice that Hannah left that place in peace, even before she saw the answer.
exp.30:0:
This verse tells us that the Philistines attacked Israel. The Israelites fled before them, and many were killed on Mount Gilboa. "Fought against Israel" simply means they went to war with them. "Slain" means they were killed in the fighting.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book, who recounts the last battle of Saul's reign. It comes after Saul had turned away from God and God had stopped answering him (1 Samuel 28). The verses that follow show that Saul and his sons also died. It is a sad ending, and the Bible tells it plainly, without embellishment.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and listening to God in time matters. If today you have drifted away from Him, you can return and ask for His help with humility, before things get worse.
exp.1:15:
When someone answered the servant, "The fat must be burned first, and then you may take whatever you want," the servant replied, "No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!" The fat is the fat of the animal, and the servant's threat is plain: he would take it by force.

This happens at Shiloh, where the sons of the priest Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing their position. The servant and the worshiper are the ones speaking. The law required that the fat be burned for God before the meat was shared out. The servants demanded their share first and by force, and in this way they despised the offering to the Lord, as the text says afterward.

For today: God should hold first place, not our own interests. Anyone who has authority in the church, at work, or at home should serve with humility, without taking advantage of others.
exp.0:0:
This verse introduces a man named Elkanah, who was from Ramathaim-zophim, in the hill country of Ephraim. His family line is traced: he was the son of Jeroham, and before him came Elihu, Tohu and Zuph.

The word "man" here simply means a man, and "Ephraimite" indicates that his family belonged to the tribe of Ephraim (there is debate about whether it refers to this or to Bethlehem).

Here the narrator of the book speaks, beginning the story of Samuel. We do not know for certain who wrote the book. First he introduces Elkanah's family, because Samuel, an important prophet for Israel, will be born from it. The verses that follow speak of Hannah, her sorrow and her faith.

For today: God begins great works with ordinary people and simple families. Your daily life, though it may seem small, can be the place where God does something important.
exp.27:10:
Here the woman asks Saul whom he wants her to bring up. Saul tells her to bring up Samuel, the prophet who had already died. "Bring up" means "call him up for me."

Saul, in disguise, and a woman who consulted the dead at Endor are speaking. Saul was frightened by the Philistine army, and God was no longer answering him. He himself had driven out the mediums, yet now he was doing exactly what he had forbidden. The Bible does not fully explain what happened next, and interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: when you feel fear and see no answer, do not look for forbidden shortcuts. Return to God with humility, even when you are in silence, because He remains the only safe refuge.
exp.27:24:
She served the food to Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then, that same night, they got up and left.

The narrator describes the end of a very dark night. Saul, king of Israel, was afraid of the Philistines, and God did not answer him. So he sought out a medium, something God's law forbade. She told him of his defeat, and Saul collapsed, weak and without having eaten all day. The woman served him a meal with kindness, and then he set out toward his fate.

When we turn away from God, we can end up looking for answers in the wrong places, and those answers do not bring peace. Today we can come to God with sincerity, in prayer and in his Word, before the night of despair arrives.
exp.9:12:
He says that Saul stopped prophesying and then went up to the high place, a raised site where people often worshiped and offered sacrifices. Prophesying here means speaking or praising under the influence of God's Spirit, not only foretelling future events.

The narrator tells what happened after Samuel had already anointed Saul as the future king. God gave him a sign: the Spirit came upon him and he joined a group of prophets. The people were amazed, and the saying "Is Saul also among the prophets?" arose. Some think it was an expression of surprise, others that it was mockery; the text does not make this clear. Then Saul went up to the high place, and his uncle asked him what had happened.

For today: a strong spiritual experience is not enough; what counts is steady obedience. Let us ask God to make us faithful in daily life as well.
exp.17:15:
It says that all the people, both Israel (the northern tribes) and Judah (David's own tribe), loved David. The reason given is that he was leading them out to battle and back. This describes David guiding the people through their conflicts and bringing them home again, a sign of the care and courage he showed them. "Loved" is simply the ordinary word for love.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier it was said that God was with David and that Saul, the king, feared him. This verse shows the contrast: while Saul felt fear and envy, the people held David in high regard. Afterward Saul will try to use the Philistines to get rid of him.

For today: true leadership is earned through constant service and faithfulness, not through appearances. If you have some responsibility, make it a point to be present, to fulfill your duties, and to care for others, trusting that God sees and sustains your effort.
exp.30:11:
This verse says that the men of valor from Jabesh-gilead set out and walked all night to Beth-shan. There they retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall, where the Philistines had hung them. Then they carried them to Jabesh and burned them there. "Retrieved" means they took the bodies down from the wall, and "burned" describes what they did with them at Jabesh.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Saul had died in battle, and the Philistines displayed his body to humiliate him. Years earlier, Saul had rescued Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11), and for that reason they showed him gratitude and loyalty. Some wonder why they burned the bodies, since this was not the common practice in Israel. The Bible does not explain it, and perhaps it was done to protect them from further insult.

Today we can remember with gratitude those who helped us, even when they can no longer repay us. A brave act of respect and care, done at a cost to oneself, honors God and comforts others.
exp.12:18:
It says that throughout all the land of Israel no blacksmith could be found, that is, no one who worked iron. The Philistines had arranged it this way, reasoning that the Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.

It is the narrator of the book who explains the situation. Israel lived under Philistine rule, and Saul was king. The Philistines controlled the iron to keep the people weak and to prevent rebellions. For this reason the Israelites depended on them even to sharpen their farming tools. The verses that follow show how humiliating and costly this was.

For today: when you feel without resources or at a disadvantage, remember that God does not depend on the weapons of the world. In chapter 14, He gave the victory with very little. Do with faith what you have at hand, and trust Him.
exp.5:10:
This verse tells how the Philistines placed the ark of the Lord on the cart. They also put a chest containing gold rats and gold figures in the shape of the tumors that had afflicted them. The "tumors" here are the painful sores that had plagued them, and the "chest" is a small container.

The Philistines had captured the ark, but a plague fell upon them. Their priests and diviners advised them to return it with an offering. To test whether the suffering came from God or was mere chance, they let two milk cows that had calves pull the cart. If the cows went toward Beth-shemesh, that would be a sign that God was acting.

When we face difficult situations, it is wise to recognize God rather than look for explanations that let us carry on as if nothing had happened. Humbling ourselves before Him opens the way to restoration.
exp.22:3:
David did not stop after one answer. He asked the LORD again whether he should go to Keilah, and the LORD confirmed it. He was told to go at once, because God was going to hand the Philistines over to him. "Inquired" here means asking God for direction and seeking his guidance.

David was being hunted by Saul and was living with about six hundred men. Keilah was under attack by the Philistines, who were taking its grain. David's men were afraid, so he asked God once more for assurance. God answered with a clear promise of victory.

When we face hard decisions or fears, we can pray with humility and look for confirmation in Scripture, in the counsel of wise people, and in the peace God gives. Obeying, even with fear, is a step of faith.
exp.2:12:
God says He will judge Eli's family forever, because of the wrong Eli knew about: Eli was aware of his sons' sin. In the Berean Standard Bible, the sin is described as blasphemy against God. The sons blasphemed God, and Eli did not restrain them. To restrain them would mean to stop them or correct them.

The speaker is the LORD, and He says this to the young Samuel during the night, in the sanctuary at Shiloh. Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests and misused their position (1 Samuel 2:12-17, 22). Eli spoke to them about it, but he did not remove them from service. God holds this failure to act against Eli as a responsibility he left unfulfilled.

For today: if we have authority or influence, whether as parents, leaders, or teachers, God calls us to correct with love and firmness, without looking away out of comfort or fear of conflict.
exp.13:27:
A soldier from the army tells Jonathan that his father, King Saul, had bound the troops with a solemn oath, saying that anyone who ate food that day would be cursed. Being "bound with a solemn oath" means being made to swear under the threat of punishment. "Food" means anything a person eats. "Faint" means worn out and without strength.

The soldier speaks after Jonathan, who did not know about the oath, had tasted some honey and felt refreshed. Israel was chasing the Philistines in the middle of the battle. Saul perhaps wanted to keep the army focused on victory, but his order left the troops weak. Jonathan himself says it was a harmful decision.

For today: before demanding something very firmly, it is wise to ask ourselves whether it truly helps or only looks very spiritual. Seeking God's help is good, but the rules we set should care for people, not burden them further.
exp.15:3:
Samuel does what the LORD told him and goes to Bethlehem. When he arrives, the elders of the town come out to meet him, trembling with fear, and they ask, "Do you come in peace?" Their question means whether his visit is for good or for something bad.

God had rejected Saul as king, and he sent Samuel to anoint another man in secret. Samuel feared that Saul would kill him. The elders probably knew that Samuel was a prophet of great weight and that he sometimes arrived with messages of judgment. That is why they were frightened.

For today: obeying God does not always remove fear or tension, but He gives the next step. Do what God shows you, even when you feel afraid, and trust that He will guide you.
exp.24:31:
In this verse, David praises God after listening to Abigail. He says, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel," because God sent her to meet him this very day. The word "blessed" here means praised or thankful. David recognizes that God was behind that meeting.

David was coming with his men, armed to kill Nabal and his household, because Nabal had insulted them and refused to help them. Abigail, Nabal's wife, went out with food and wise words, and asked him not to stain his conscience with blood shed without cause. David listens to her and sees the hand of God in her.

For today: when you are about to react in anger, stop. God sometimes uses a wise person and a timely word to hold you back. Listen to the advice and give thanks.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that when the ark of the covenant of the LORD entered the camp, the Israelites raised such a loud shout that the ground shook. The word "shout" simply means a loud cry. The people were overjoyed, and their noise was so enormous that it seemed to shake the earth.
