Israel had just lost a battle against the Philistines. The elders thought that if they brought the ark from Shiloh, God would save them. But they did not ask God what to do. The text also notes that Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, were coming with the ark. Later in the chapter, Israel loses again, so their trust was placed in an object rather than in a relationship with God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in. Religious things, such as a cross, a song, or a custom, can help us, but they do not replace obeying God and seeking him sincerely. Before celebrating, it is wise to pray and to listen.
exp.21:22:
Here David tells Abiathar to stay with him and not to be afraid. The wording is simple: the first phrase means "stay," and the safety he offers is the same protection the verse promises. David explains that the one who wants to kill him also wants to kill Abiathar, so together they will be safer.

David is speaking while he flees from King Saul. He has just learned that Saul ordered the priests of Nob to be killed, and only Abiathar escaped. David feels guilty, because he knew that Doeg the Edomite could report to Saul. With these words he offers shelter and company to a man who has lost everything.

For today: when someone is hurt or frightened, you do not need great answers. Sometimes it is enough to open the door, stay with them, and say, "You are not alone." Think about who needs your company and sincere support today.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that Samuel would return to Ramah, his home, after traveling to other places. There he judged Israel, settling the people's disputes, and he built an altar to the LORD.

This passage is the narrator of the book speaking. It describes what Samuel's life was like after Israel turned back to God and defeated the Philistines. Samuel made a yearly circuit through Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah to guide the people, and then he returned to his house. It is noteworthy that, even in his own home, he kept worship of God going.

For today: make your home a place where God is honored. Even if you work or serve away from home, set aside time each day in your household to pray, read the Bible and give thanks to him.
exp.17:8:
From that day forward, the verse says, Saul began to watch David with suspicion and jealousy, after the women sang that song. The phrase "kept a jealous eye on David" describes a wary, resentful gaze, not a friendly or trusting one.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Saul had just come back from a battle, and the women were celebrating the victories with a song that put David above him. Saul, already turned away from God, felt threatened, and his anger turned into a watchful stare. The verses that follow show where that leads: he tries to kill David.

For today: jealousy usually starts small, with a look or a thought. If someone else receives praise and that bothers you, bring it to God early and rejoice with that person before resentment grows.
exp.15:17:
A servant of Saul recommends a young man, the son of Jesse from Bethlehem. He says that David knows how to play the harp, that he is a mighty man of valor and a warrior, that he is eloquent and handsome, and that "the LORD is with him," meaning God accompanies him.

Saul is troubled by an evil spirit sent from God, a phrase that has been understood in several ways and that the Bible does not fully explain. His servants look for music that will bring him relief. One of them speaks of David without yet naming him. Shortly after, Saul sends for him, and David arrives with a gift from his father.

For today: God often forms his people in simple places, such as caring for the sheep. Be faithful and honest in small things, and develop your character along with your skills. Others may notice when the opportunity comes.
exp.19:39:
Jonathan hands his equipment (his bow, his arrows, and whatever else he was carrying) to his young attendant. He tells the boy to go and take it back to the city. The word "boy" here means a young servant, and the equipment is his archery gear.

Jonathan and David had agreed on a signal with the arrows to learn whether Saul meant to kill David. Jonathan had already given that signal, and only the two of them understood its meaning. He sends the boy away so that he can say farewell to his friend in private, without witnesses. What follows is a very emotional farewell, with tears and a covenant made before God.

There are moments when love and loyalty call for privacy and courage. Jonathan cared for his friend with prudence: he protected the secret and gave him time to truly say goodbye. Today we can do the same: guard the trust of someone who is suffering, and be present in difficult moments.
exp.26:6:
This verse says that David lived in Philistine territory for a year and four months. It is a brief note about time. The word "lived" means that he made his home there, and the wording here is plain.

The narrator is the one speaking, not David. He tells how long that period lasted. David was fleeing from King Saul, who wanted to kill him, and he took refuge with Achish, a Philistine king of Gath. Achish gave him Ziklag, a small town where he could live apart with his people. The texts that follow show that David carried out raids and deceived Achish about them. The Bible only reports these events here and does not approve or condemn them.

For today: difficult times have a limit, even though we sometimes cannot see it. If you are in an uncomfortable season, ask God for wisdom so that you do not take doubtful shortcuts. Trust that He sustains you and knows when it will end.
exp.21:0:
David left Gath, where he had taken refuge, and hid in the cave of Adullam. The verse says he "took refuge" there, meaning he went into hiding to protect his life. When his brothers and the rest of his father's household heard about it, they went down to him there, meaning they went to be with him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David was fleeing from King Saul, who was pursuing him out of jealousy and wanted to kill him. Although he had been anointed as the future king, he was living as a fugitive. His family was also in danger because of their relation to him, though the text does not explain this in detail. Adullam was in the lowland area of Judah, and caves were known to be found there.

For today: in our darkest moments, God often uses family and friends as support. We can seek trustworthy companionship, and we can also be a refuge for others who are suffering.
exp.21:14:
Ahimelec, the priest, defends himself before Saul. With the question "Was that day the first time I inquired of God for him?" he means that this was not the first time he had helped David, and that he did it as something ordinary, with no conspiracy behind it. "Far be it from me!" means "I would never think of it." To "accuse" is what he asks the king not to do. He declares that he knew nothing of the whole affair, not in part or in whole.

Ahimelec speaks before a jealous and furious king. Earlier, David had come to Nob saying he was on a mission for the king, and the priest believed him. So Ahimelec acted in good faith, but Saul did not believe him and sentenced him to death.

For today: you can act with honesty and still be misunderstood or unjustly accused. Even so, tell the truth calmly and trust God, who sees the heart.
exp.12:9:
Saul had just finished offering the burnt offering, a sacrifice that was burned completely on the altar, when Samuel arrived. Saul went out to greet him. Here the phrase "went out to greet him" simply means that Saul went to welcome Samuel.

The narrator describes the moment with irony and tension. Saul had waited seven days, just as Samuel had instructed, but the people were scattering out of fear of the Philistines. Saul decided to offer the sacrifice himself, something that was not his task, since that duty belonged to the priest or the prophet. Samuel arrived just after.

When pressure mounts, it is tempting to take shortcuts and justify ourselves. God values obedience and trust more than quick results. Waiting on Him, even when it is hard, is an act of faith.
exp.9:26:
These verses tell of certain worthless men who looked down on Saul and asked how this man could save them. Their contempt showed that they held him in low regard. They did not bring him a gift, the kind that was customarily offered to a king as a sign of honor. Saul remained silent about it and did not answer them.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul had just been presented as king before Israel. While many followed him, with hearts that God had moved, others rejected him. Some understand his silence as a sign of wisdom or humility; others think he did not yet have firm authority.

For today: not every criticism deserves an immediate reply. When someone despises us, we can remain calm, trust God, and act wisely, without letting the offense carry us away.
exp.17:12:
This verse says that Saul sent David away from his court and gave him command of a thousand soldiers. The phrase "sent David away" means "moved him away," and "command of a thousand men" refers to leading a unit of a thousand soldiers. The statement that "David led the troops out to battle and back" describes David leading the people in their daily work and in war, in full view of everyone.

The narrator is the author of the book, not Saul. Saul had already thrown his spear at David and was afraid of him, because he saw that God was with David and had turned away from Saul. Many think this promotion was a way of moving him away from the palace, and perhaps of putting him in danger. The text does not say this clearly.

For today: sometimes others treat us badly or push us away out of envy. Even so, God can use that place to shape us. Serve faithfully where you are, and trust that God cares for you.
exp.1:4:
It says that things are turned around. Those who were well fed now have to work for wages to get food. In contrast, those who were starving no longer go hungry. The woman who could not have children ends up having seven, and the one who had many sons is left pining away. The number seven speaks of completeness.

It is part of Hannah's prayer, a woman who could not have children before and now has Samuel. She gives thanks to God and praises how he changes circumstances, bringing down the proud and lifting up the humble. She speaks with gratitude, but also with a warning to the arrogant.

For today: if you are going through a difficult season, do not lose hope, because God can change your situation. And if things are going well for you, do not boast, but be humble and thankful, for everything comes from him.
exp.26:5:
That same day, King Achish gave David the city of Ziklag. The verse adds that from then on the city has belonged to the kings of Judah, and that this is still true at the time of writing. That closing remark was added by someone telling the story long after it happened.

David had fled from Saul and sought refuge among the Philistines, Israel's enemies. He asked Achish for a place of his own to live, rather than staying in the royal city, where he would be watched. In this way he kept some distance, although the Bible does not explain all of his reasons, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God can care for us even in confusing or difficult times. Even when we do not understand the whole path, we can ask him for wisdom to decide well and trust that he is still at work.
exp.2:1:
This verse tells us that at that time Eli was lying in his room. His eyesight had already grown weak, and he could hardly see. The word "room" describes the place where he rested, and "grown so dim" means he was losing his sight gradually.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier it was said that the word of the LORD was rare and that visions were not frequent. Eli was the aging priest, and the young Samuel served him. His failing sight may also reflect the spiritual dullness of those times, though the text does not state this directly. In this way the scene is set for God's call to Samuel.

For today: when everything seems dim or confused, God can still speak and act. Stay attentive to his voice, especially in his Word, and serve him faithfully even when others seem not to see.
exp.5:19:
The people of Beth-shemesh, frightened by the death of so many men, ask two questions. The first: "Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God?" That is, who can come near so pure a God without being punished? The second: "To whom should the ark go up from here?" In other words, to whom should we send it so that the ark will leave here?

The people of Beth-shemesh are the ones speaking. The Philistines had returned the ark, and the inhabitants received it with joy, but some looked into it with irreverence and God struck them down. The number of those who died is much debated: some scholars think the original text or its copy may have varied in the number. For that reason the people, in mourning and fear, decide to send the ark to Kiriath-jearim.

God is holy, and drawing near to Him calls for respect, not carelessness. Today we can approach Him with confidence thanks to Christ, but always with humility and sincere reverence.
exp.22:2:
David's men said they were already afraid here in Judah, so they were far more afraid of going to Keilah to face the Philistine army. The phrase "driven their livestock ahead of them" describes how they moved their herds along in front of them, and the threshing floors are the places where grain was beaten out.

Here the speakers are David's followers, who were fleeing from King Saul and living as fugitives. God had already told David to go and rescue Keilah. Even so, his men hesitated, because they felt weak and vulnerable. David consulted God again, and God confirmed the command and promised victory.

For today: being afraid is normal, and it is not sin. When we are afraid, we can do what David did: pray again, seek God's direction once more, and move forward with confidence in his promise, even when the task seems larger than our strength.
exp.24:26:
Abigail tells David that she brings him a gift, a "blessing," and asks that it be shared among the young men who follow him. The phrase "your servant" refers to herself, speaking with humility. "My lord" is David, whom she addresses with respect.

Abigail speaks with David when he is coming out armed to kill Nabal and his household, because Nabal had insulted him and refused him food. She goes out to meet him with bread, wine, and other provisions to calm David's anger and prevent bloodshed. Her gift comes with wise and humble words.

For today: when there is tension or anger, a generous and humble gesture can disarm a conflict. Before reacting with vengeance, we can look for ways to bring peace, and ask God to guide our hearts.
exp.7:18:
This verse says that the people of Israel refused to listen to Samuel. "Nevertheless" means "but," and "to listen to" means to pay attention to what is said. They answered firmly, "No! We must have a king over us." They rejected the warning without giving it much thought.

Samuel had just warned them, on God's behalf, what it would cost to have a king: the king would take their sons, their fields, and their flocks. The leaders had asked for a king so that they could be like all the other nations, and so that he would lead them in war. Samuel was distressed, and God told him that the people were rejecting Him as their King. Some see here a desire for political security; others, a lack of trust in God.

Today, before deciding something important, it is wise to listen to wise counsel, even when we do not like it. And we should ask ourselves whether we are looking for security in God or only in copying what others do.
exp.25:5:
David asks for a volunteer to go with him into Saul's camp. He speaks directly to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai, son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab. In the verse, David asks, "Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?" Abishai answers right away: "I will go with you."

David makes this request because Saul was hunting him with three thousand soldiers, intending to kill him. David already knew from his scouts where Saul was camped, and he wanted to enter the camp while the men were asleep. Only Abishai offers himself, and the text does not say that Ahimelech responded. Later, Abishai will want to kill Saul, but David will refuse.

For today: when we face risky or confusing situations, it is wise not to go alone and to seek companions who are willing. But we must also test their advice by the Word of God, because a loyal friend may propose a mistaken path.
exp.10:4:
This verse tells how Saul was coming back from the field, behind his oxen, when he noticed that the people were weeping. He asked what was troubling them, and they passed along the message from the men of Jabesh. "Behind his oxen" means that he had been working with his animals.

The men of Jabesh in Gilead were threatened by Nahash, king of the Ammonites, and they asked for seven days to seek help in Israel. The messengers arrived at Gibeah, where Saul lived, and the people wept. Saul did not yet act as king in any visible way; he was still going about his daily work. What follows shows that the Spirit of God moved him to act.

For today: God can call us to act in the midst of everyday life. It is good to listen to the pain of others, to ask, and not to ignore it. When someone suffers, we can offer concrete help, with humility and depending on God.
exp.14:14:
Saul explains to Samuel why animals can be heard. He says the troops brought them from the Amalekites, and that they spared the best sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD their God. According to him, everything else was destroyed.

The Lord had commanded Saul to destroy the Amalekites completely. Samuel, the prophet, discovers that Saul did not obey fully, since Saul had just said he had carried out the word of the LORD. Notice that Saul says "the troops" and "your God," as if he were stepping away from responsibility. His excuse sounds religious, but it does not change the fact that he disobeyed.

For today: do not use good religious intentions to justify what God has already asked of you clearly. Obeying from the heart is worth more than any offering. And when you fail, admit it without blaming others.
exp.11:18:
Here the people of Israel come to Samuel in fear and ask him to pray to the LORD their God for them so that they will not die. They recognize that, on top of their earlier sins, they have done something else wrong: asking for a king.

The phrase "pray to the LORD your God" shows that they were asking Samuel to stand between them and God, and it suggests that they felt a certain distance from Him.

Samuel had warned them, and as a sign, God sent thunder and rain during the wheat harvest, which was unusual. Seeing this, the people were frightened and understood that their request for a king showed distrust in God, who was their true King. Samuel, as prophet and judge, interceded for them.

For today: when you recognize a mistake, do not stay only in fear. Confess honestly, turn to God, and keep serving Him wholeheartedly. He receives those who return to Him with humility.
exp.25:22:
In this verse David says that the LORD is the one who repays each person according to their righteousness (doing what is right) and their faithfulness (being loyal). He points out that the LORD delivered Saul into his hands that day, yet he refused to harm him. "The LORD's anointed" refers to the king, whom the LORD himself had set apart for that role.

David speaks to Saul after slipping into his camp at night and taking his spear while everyone was asleep. Saul had been pursuing David to kill him. David could have taken revenge, but he chose to respect the king and leave it to the LORD to be the judge. Saul, for his part, admits that he has done wrong.

For today: when someone has treated us unfairly and we have the chance to get even, we can choose to trust that the LORD will bring about justice. Acting with integrity, even when no one sees us, is a way of honoring God.
exp.24:9:
Nabal answers David's messengers with contempt. He pretends not to know who David is and asks, "Who is this son of Jesse?" as if David were a man of no importance. Then he suggests that David is a rebellious servant who runs away from his master. Here "servants" refers to the men who serve a master, and "break away" means to run off and escape.

Nabal was a rich man, the owner of many sheep, and he was at the time of the sheep-shearing, a season of feasting and plenty. David, who was fleeing from Saul, had protected Nabal's shepherds, and now he respectfully asked for some food. Nabal, whose name means "fool," answered with pride and stinginess. The Bible does not say that David was a runaway servant of Nabal; it is a mockery.

Today we can learn to respond with gratitude and humility to those who have done us good. Pride and contempt, even in words, can bring serious consequences.
exp.29:5:
David was in deep trouble. His men, grieving over their sons and daughters who had been taken captive, spoke of stoning him. The words "greatly distressed" mean he was in great difficulty. The reason the people were so angry is that their hearts were full of sorrow and anger over their loss. The verse says that David found strength in the LORD his God.

The verse is part of a longer account, and there is no speaker here, only the story itself. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the families while David and his men were away. David also lost his two wives, and now his people, in despair, were looking for someone to blame, namely their leader.

For today: when everything falls apart and even those close to us blame us, we can do what David did: stop and seek God before we react. Praying, asking for direction, and remembering who God is give us strength we cannot find in ourselves.
exp.23:8:
David came out of the cave after Saul and called out to him from behind: "My lord the king!" When Saul turned around, David bowed with his face to the ground and showed him respect, a gesture of honor and humility. Calling out means that he spoke in a loud voice.

David was hiding from Saul, who was chasing him to kill him. Saul had gone into the cave without knowing that David and his men were inside. David could have killed him, but he did not want to, because Saul was the anointed of the LORD, the king set in place by God. Now he speaks to him with respect to show him that he is not his enemy.

For today: even when someone treats us unjustly, we can respond with respect and self-control, without seeking revenge. Leaving justice in God's hands keeps us from acting out of bitterness.
exp.1:24:
When one person wrongs another, God can intercede on that person's behalf. But if someone sins directly against the LORD, who can plead for him? Elí's sons would not listen to their father's warning, and the verse says that the LORD intended to put them to death. The word "intercede" here means to plead on behalf of another.

Elí, an elderly priest, is rebuking his sons Hofni and Finehas. They abused their position at the sanctuary and led the people into sin. The closing words of the verse do not say that God took away their freedom; they show that, because of their persistent stubbornness, judgment was already coming. Some scholars see it as hardening that came from their own folly.

For today: do not take sin lightly or the calls to correct you. If someone warns you with love, listen to them, and come before God today with humility.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the young assistants at the sanctuary were committing a very serious sin in the sight of the LORD. The young helpers of the priests are the ones described here. The verse says they were treating the LORD's offering with contempt, showing no respect for what the people brought to worship God.

The narrator explains the conduct of Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, and of their servants. According to the law, the fat was burned for God first. They demanded the meat before that and took it by force, turning worship into abuse. By contrast, the account goes on to the young Samuel, who served faithfully.

For today: God notices how we treat what is holy and how we treat those who come to worship. If we serve in the church, let us examine whether we seek to honor God or to take advantage of our position.
exp.21:9:
This verse is part of Doeg the Edomite's report to Saul. It says that Ahimelech inquired of the LORD for David, gave him provisions, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine. The word "provisions" means food for the journey. "Inquired" means that he asked God.

Doeg speaks as Saul's chief servant. Saul was full of suspicion and believed that everyone was plotting against him. Doeg took the chance to accuse the priest. His account leaves out details found in chapter 21, where Ahimelech helped David without knowing that he was fleeing from the king. That is why his report is partial and malicious.

Today we can learn not to repeat half-told reports, especially when they can harm others. It is also good to help someone in need in good faith, even when others misunderstand him. Before we speak, let us ask whether what we are saying is complete, true, and necessary.
exp.27:12:
The woman of Endor is frightened here because she sees something she did not expect. She realizes that her client is King Saul, and she protests to him. Saul reassures her and asks what she sees. She answers that she sees a god coming up out of the earth. The Hebrew word behind "god" can mean a spiritual being or someone of great importance.

Saul had gone in disguise at night, since he himself had forbidden consulting the dead. He was desperate: the Philistines were attacking him, and God no longer answered him. Scholars disagree about whether Samuel truly appeared or something else took place, but the text says that Samuel spoke.

Today, when we feel that God is silent, let us not look for answers in forbidden places. Instead, let us return to Him with humility and sincerity, and wait with patience.
exp.19:23:
So David hid in the field, just as he and Jonathan had agreed. When the New Moon had come, which was a monthly festival, King Saul sat down to eat. The word "hid" is the plain form used in the Berean Standard Bible, and "New Moon" refers to the beginning of the month, a time of celebration. To "eat" here means to take a meal, a feast.

This is part of the account in which Saul seeks to kill David. Jonathan, Saul's son and David's faithful friend, had made a plan to discover his father's intentions. David was to be absent from the king's table, and Jonathan would watch Saul's reaction. The narrator describes the scene before the empty seat is noticed.

For today: when we face threats or injustice, we can act with prudence, seek the counsel of loyal friends, and trust in God, as David and Jonathan did, without seeking revenge or acting in haste.
exp.17:16:
Saul offers David the chance to marry Merab, his older daughter, on one condition: that David be valiant and fight the LORD's battles. But Saul privately plans something else. He does not want to kill David with his own hand. He wants the Philistines to be the ones who strike him down.

Here the king Saul is speaking. David had become very popular and successful, and Saul felt fear and jealousy. His offer looks like an honor, but it is really a trap, a way to get rid of David by using the enemy. Later, Merab was given to another man, and the Bible does not explain in detail why.

For today: be wary of praise or favors that hide wrong intentions, and do not act out of envy. Like David, serve with humility and trust that God cares for you, even when others want to harm you.
exp.9:8:
As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul's heart, and all the signs came to pass that same day. The phrase "turned his shoulder" in the old wording simply means he turned around to head off on his way, so the change is tied to the moment he set out.

Samuel had just anointed Saul as the first king of Israel, and he had given him several signs to confirm that God was with him. Saul doubted himself, so God was preparing him for his new task. This change of heart can be understood as a new readiness to lead, though the Bible does not spell out exactly what it consisted of.

For today: when God calls you to something that seems bigger than you, you do not depend on your own strength alone. Ask Him to give you the courage, wisdom and attitude you need, and trust that He keeps what He promises.
exp.16:48:
David reached into his bag, took out a stone, and slung it, striking the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground. This verse describes the exact moment of the blow. David took a stone from his shepherd's bag and hurled it with the sling. The stone struck Goliath on the forehead and sank into it, and the giant fell facedown to the ground.

The narrator then tells what happens after David declared that the battle belongs to the LORD, not to sword or spear. Goliath advanced toward him, and David ran to meet him. David wanted everyone to see that the victory came from God and not from weapons. The text does not explain how the stone sank so deeply; it simply reports it as a fact.

For today: God can use what little you have, like a simple stone, when you trust in Him. Do not wait until you have the best resources; act with courage and entrust the outcome to the Lord.
exp.26:4:
David asks King Achish to give him his own place to live, in one of the outlying towns. He speaks politely: "If I have found favor in your eyes" means "If you think well of me" or "If I have pleased you." He asks why his servant should have to live in the royal city alongside the king.

David is speaking while he is running away from Saul, who was hunting him to kill him. He was already in Philistine territory with his men and their families. When Saul learned that David had gone to Gath, he stopped searching for him. The Bible does not explain all of David's reasons; some think he wanted more freedom and less supervision, and others think he wanted to avoid tension with the Philistines.

For today: sometimes the Lord places us in difficult situations, and we should ask with humility and think with wisdom, remembering that God cares for his people even in confusing times.
exp.25:13:
Here David shouts from a distance, from the top of a hill, to all of Saul's army and especially to Abner, their commander. He calls out to him: "Will you not answer me, Abner?" Abner replies with another question: "Who are you who calls to the king?"

David has just entered the camp at night and taken Saul's spear and water jug while Saul was sleeping. Everyone was in a deep sleep sent by God. David stands at a safe distance and calls out to Abner to show that he could have killed the king but did not. He wants to prove his innocence and rebuke Abner for neglecting his duty.

For today: when someone accuses us or pursues us, we can respond with respect and truth, without seeking revenge. David had the chance to do harm and chose to trust God. Today too we can let God do justice.
exp.17:25:
When Saul's servants reported the king's terms to David, he was pleased with the idea of becoming the king's son-in-law. The payment the king asked for was a hundred Philistine foreskins, proof that David had killed a hundred Philistines.

Saul's servants were speaking on the king's orders. Saul was jealous of David and hoped the Philistines would kill him in the attempt. David did not know about this trap, or at least the text does not say so. He saw an opportunity to serve Israel and to become related to the king.

For today: sometimes the people around us have hidden motives, even when they speak to us kindly. It is wise to act with simplicity and integrity, and to trust that God cares for us, as he cared for David, even when we cannot see the whole picture.
exp.13:14:
The verse tells us that panic struck the whole Philistine camp: the military camp itself, the open countryside, and everyone among the people. Even the men stationed at the outposts and those sent out on raids trembled. The verse says the earth quaked, meaning the ground seemed to shake, or that everything fell into confusion. The Berean wording adds that the panic spread from God, so the fear was not just a matter of nerves but something that came from him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonathan and his armor-bearer had just attacked a Philistine outpost alone and killed about twenty men. Then the fear spread. The text presents this as something God allowed, and some understand the trembling as literal while others understand it as only panic.

For today: God can use a small and courageous act of faith to open the way to something much greater. Take the faithful step in front of you today.
exp.19:12:
Jonathan makes a solemn vow before God. He says that if his father intends to bring harm on David, he will tell him and send him away safely. The vow is strong: if Jonathan does not keep his word, he calls for the Lord to punish him severely. Here "tell" means to warn or make known. Jonathan also prays that the Lord would be with David, just as the Lord has been with Jonathan's father.

Jonathan, the son of King Saul, speaks with his friend David in the field. Saul was jealous of David and perhaps wanted to kill him. Jonathan, although he was the rightful heir, respects what God is planning and protects David with loyalty.

For today: true friendship shows itself in loyalty when there is risk. Seek to be someone who keeps your word, protects others, and trusts God's plans, even when that costs you something personally.
exp.24:21:
David makes a very strong oath: he asks that God punish him, and even more severely, if he lets any male of Nabal's household live until morning. The verse says "May God punish David," though the wording is a roundabout way of putting a curse on himself, and many understand the phrase this way because he does not want to speak the curse directly against his own name.

David speaks in anger. Nabal, a rich man, refused to give him provisions and insulted him, even though David and his men had protected his flocks. Because of this, David sets out with four hundred men to take revenge. Abigail, Nabal's wife, goes to meet him to stop him.

Today: when you are hurt or angry, do not make decisions or impulsive promises. Stop, seek wise counsel, and listen to the person God puts in your path, as David listened to Abigail. In this way you will avoid harm that you would later regret.
exp.13:3:
This verse describes the place where Jonathan planned to cross over toward the Philistine outpost. On both sides of the pass there were cliffs. They were called Bozez and Seneh. The word "outpost" refers to a military station with soldiers. "Intended" means he was planning and looking for a way to do it.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator's account. Jonathan, the son of King Saul, went out in secret, and neither his father nor the people knew about it. Saul had only about six hundred men. The author describes the terrain to show how difficult and risky the plan was. Shortly afterward, Jonathan says that God can save by many or by few.

For today: sometimes the path God sets before us is narrow and seems dangerous. Jonathan did not wait to have the advantage; he took a step of faith, trusting that God could act. Let us ask God for wisdom and courage to obey Him, without depending only on our own strength.
exp.5:4:
The passage says the Philistines were to make golden figures of their tumors and of the rats that were ravaging their land. By doing this, they would give glory to the God of Israel. They said "perhaps," hoping that God would lift his hand from them, from their gods, and from their land.

The priests and diviners of the Philistines are speaking. They had captured the ark of God, and since then they had suffered a plague. They wanted to send it back with a guilt offering. We do not know for certain what the sores were exactly; some think of tumors or of a disease linked to the rats, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: when we recognize that God is greater than whatever we worship or trust in, the first step is to humble ourselves and honor him. We do not have to pay to be forgiven, but we can come to him with sincerity and not with pride.
exp.16:46:
What it says: David declares that everyone gathered there will see that the LORD does not save by sword or spear. He explains that the battle belongs to the LORD, meaning the outcome depends on God, not on weapons. Then he says God will give all of them into the hands of the Israelites.

Context: David, a young shepherd, speaks in front of Goliath, the Philistine giant who had for weeks been challenging the army of Israel. The Israelite soldiers were afraid. David does not trust in armor or military experience but in God, and he wants everyone, Israelites and Philistines alike, to recognize that God acts on behalf of his people.

For today: When a problem seems bigger than you are, do what is within your reach with honesty, but do not place your final trust in your own resources. Pray, ask for direction, and rest in the fact that God remains the one who sustains your life.
exp.24:34:
In this verse David accepts the gifts Abigail brought him. He tells her to go home in peace, because he has heeded what she said and granted her request. The phrase here, "I have heeded your voice and granted your request," is the one that carries the meaning of showing her respect and taking her seriously.

David speaks with Abigail, the wife of Nabal. Nabal had insulted David and refused to help him and his men. David, angry, was going out with armed men to kill the males of that household. Abigail went out to meet him with food and with humble and wise words. David acknowledges that she kept him from shedding blood and from avenging himself with his own hands.

For today: when we are very angry, we can stop and listen to someone prudent. A wise word at the right time can keep us from doing something we will regret for the rest of our lives.
exp.16:55:
Abner swears, "I do not know, as your soul lives, O king." Then Saul orders him to find out whose son the young man is. The phrase "as your soul lives" is an old way of swearing, like saying "as you live." "Young man" means a youth.

Saul and Abner have just watched David face Goliath. Saul asks about David's family, not necessarily about his name. Earlier David had played the harp for Saul, so many wonder why Saul does not recognize him. Several explanations have been proposed, such as Saul's troubled mind or his interest in the family of the victor because of the promised reward. The Bible does not make it clear.

For today: God can use people whom others do not notice or do not know well. Serve faithfully even when no one recognizes you yet.
exp.0:18:
This verse tells us that Elkanah and Hannah got up early the next morning to bow in worship before the LORD, then returned home to Ramah. There, Elkanah had relations with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her, meaning that he answered her prayer and acted on her behalf.

The narrator of the book recounts what happened after Hannah, deeply troubled, prayed at the sanctuary and the priest Eli blessed her. Hannah left in peace and went back to eating. Here we see that she placed her burden in God's hands, and that he responded in his own time.

For today: after praying, we can rest in God and carry on with our lives, worshiping him with confidence. He does not forget the one who cries out to him, even when the answer is delayed or comes in his own way.
exp.13:9:
Jonathan tells his young armor-bearer that if the Philistines say, "Come on up," then they will go up. They will take this as the sign that the LORD has handed the enemy into Israel's hands, meaning God will give them the victory.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, speaks with his young assistant in front of a Philistine outpost. Israel was at a disadvantage and afraid. Jonathan does not act recklessly: he asks for a clear sign before taking the step. He trusts that God can save by few or by many, as he says in the verse just before this passage.

For today: before making a difficult decision, pray and place your trust in God. Seek his direction humbly, and then take the step with courage when you see the door open.
exp.0:27:
Here, Hannah says she is giving her son Samuel to the LORD for as long as he lives. The words "I now dedicate the boy to the LORD" mark a clear, deliberate act: she is committing him fully to God's service and calling. The verse then says that for as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD, so her promise is not a short-term gesture but a commitment for his whole life. The verse closes by saying that they worshiped the LORD there, describing people bowing down and praising God in that place.

The speaker is Hannah, who could not have children before and asked God for a son at Shiloh, at the sanctuary. God gave her Samuel, and now she fulfills her promise by bringing him to the priest Eli. Some think the one who worshiped was Eli, others that it was Hannah or her family; the Hebrew text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: think about something valuable that God has given you, such as your family, your time, or your gifts. Present it to God with gratitude and ask him how to use it to serve him. Giving thanks and offering what we have is one way of worshiping.
exp.15:14:
What it says: King Saul's servants notice that something is wrong with him. They say that a spirit of distress from God is tormenting him. "Servants" are the attendants or staff of the king's household, and "tormenting" means it causes him great anguish and disturbance.

Context: Shortly before this, God had rejected Saul as king because of his disobedience, and the Spirit of the LORD had departed from him. Samuel had just anointed David. The servants speak out of concern and suggest that Saul seek a skilled harp player to bring him relief. Interpreters explain in different ways how God allowed or sent that spirit, and the text does not spell it out.

For today: When someone close to us suffers in their spirit, we should not ignore it. Like those servants, we can speak with respect, notice their pain, and offer concrete help, such as companionship, music, or pointing them toward appropriate support.
exp.11:22:
Samuel says it would be a sin against the LORD for him to stop praying for the people. "Far be it from me" means "I will never do that." The verse uses the word "ceasing," meaning stopping or giving up, to describe what he refuses to do with prayer. He also promises to keep teaching them the good and right way, that is, the correct and honest way of living before God.

Samuel speaks in his farewell address, when Israel already has a king. The people had asked for a king and admitted that this was a mistake. Samuel does not reject them or become bitter. He reminds them that God will not abandon them, and that he himself will continue serving them through prayer and teaching.

For today: praying for others is not optional. Even when someone has failed us or does not listen to us, we can keep praying for that person and teaching them with patience and good example.
exp.8:12:
As soon as you enter the city, you will find him before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not begin eating until he arrives, because he must bless the sacrifice. After that, the guests will eat. The high place is a raised place of worship, a seer is a prophet, and the guests are those who have been invited. They are told to go up at once, because this is the right moment.

Some young women who are going out to draw water are speaking. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys and wanted to consult the prophet. They give him precise and urgent information. The verses that follow show that God had already spoken to Samuel a day earlier, so this meeting was not chance.

God can guide our steps even in small and everyday matters. Today we can be attentive, act with diligence, and trust that God works behind circumstances, even when we do not notice it right away.
exp.4:6:
What it says: The people of Ashdod see what is happening and decide they cannot keep the ark of God. They say that "His hand is heavy" upon them and upon their god Dagon, meaning that God's power is pressing down hard on them and on their idol. The verse describes the suffering only in general terms as God's hand being heavy upon them. Some think it may have been a plague or tumors, but the text does not specify.

Context: The speakers are the Philistines of Ashdod. They had captured the ark of Israel and placed it in the temple of Dagon. Then came the fall of their idol and the trouble that followed. They admit the power of the God of Israel, but they do not turn to him in repentance; they only want the ark gone, and they send it to another city.

For today: We can recognize that God is powerful and still resist surrendering our lives to him. Instead of pushing God away from what troubles us, we can draw near with humility and let him correct our hearts.
exp.13:7:
Jonathan tells his young helper that they are going to cross over toward where the Philistines are and show themselves to them. "We will cross over toward these men" means they will go up close to the enemy. "Show ourselves to them" means they will let themselves be seen, without hiding.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, speaks with his armor-bearer, the young man who carried his weapons. Israel was in a difficult situation in the face of the Philistine garrison. Jonathan trusts that for the LORD it is no hard thing to save by many or by few. So he proposes a sign: if the enemies invite them to come up, he will take that as a sign that God will give them the victory.

For today: when you feel you are taking a step of faith, do not act recklessly, but with confidence and attention to God. Take the step that lies before you, ask for direction, and stay willing to accept his guidance, whether he opens the door or closes it.
exp.28:0:
The verse tells how the Philistines brought all their forces together at Aphek, a place where they were getting ready to fight. Meanwhile, Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel. Here "forces" refers to the fighting men themselves, and Jezreel is a well-known valley in the region.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The two peoples are preparing for a great battle, and Saul is the king of Israel. David is living among the Philistines, because he had been fleeing from Saul, and now he finds himself in a difficult situation: it seems he will have to march with the enemies of his own people. The verses that follow show how God delivers him from that conflict.

For today: at times we find ourselves in situations with no clear way out, through our own decisions or because of circumstances. We can trust that God cares for us and can open paths we never imagined. Let us pray for wisdom.
exp.19:10:
Jonathan says to David, "Come, let us go out to the field," and the two of them go out into the field together. The field is an open place outside the city. It is a simple act, but it marks a change: they are going to talk in private.

Jonathan, the son of King Saul, is the one speaking. David has just asked him who would warn him if Saul answered harshly. Jonathan wants to give him reassurance, but he needs a private place, far from curious ears, to make a covenant and plan how to find out his father's intentions. The Bible does not explain why he chose the field, but it fits the need for discretion.

For today: when someone is afraid or confused, sometimes the best thing is to step aside with them to a quiet place. Listening calmly, speaking the truth, and offering concrete support can be a real way of showing love.
exp.2:16:
Eli asks Samuel to tell him everything the Lord said to him during the night. "Do not hide it from me" is the request, and "May God punish you, and ever so severely, if you hide from me anything He said to you" is a serious oath, calling on God to bring judgment on anyone who does not keep their word. Eli wants Samuel to hold nothing back, not even one part of the message.

Eli speaks as the aged priest. Samuel was a young man serving in the sanctuary, and God had given him a hard message of judgment against the house of Eli. Samuel was afraid to tell it. Eli, with the authority of a father and teacher, insists that he tell the whole truth.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, it is wise to receive it in full, even when it is uncomfortable. And if we must speak a hard truth to someone, let us do it with respect, adding nothing and leaving nothing out.
exp.3:6:
The Philistines were frightened when they heard the shouting of the Israelites. "The gods have entered their camp!" they said. "Woe to us, for nothing like this has happened before." The phrase "woe to us" is a cry of distress, and "camp" means the military camp.

The speakers are the Philistines, enemies of Israel. Israel had lost a battle and brought the ark of the covenant into the camp, as if its presence would guarantee victory. The Philistines believed in many gods, which is why they speak of their gods in the plural. They knew, though in a vague way, the stories of the Exodus. Their fear was real, but the account will show that Israel trusted in an object rather than in a sincere relationship with God.

Today we can learn that God is not a charm we control. Having religious symbols or shouting with enthusiasm is not enough. What matters is drawing near to Him with obedience and a sincere heart, not using Him for our own purposes.
exp.22:20:
Saul responds to the people of Ziph with a blessing: "May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me."

Saul, the king of Israel, pursues David with the intention of killing him. The Ziphites inform him where David is hiding, and Saul thanks them. But there is a sad irony here: he calls on the name of the LORD while he chases an innocent man whom God had chosen. His "compassion" is in fact help for his own obsession.

Today we can learn to examine our motives. It is easy to use spiritual words to justify actions that do not please God. Before we say "God bless you" or look for support, let us ask whether what we are doing is truly aligned with his will and with justice.
exp.14:31:
Samuel orders that Agag, the king of the Amalekites, be brought to him. Saul had spared him. Agag comes cheerfully, and he thinks to himself: "Surely the bitterness of death is past." In other words, he believes the danger is over. Some readers take his words as a question or as a confident statement, and it is not entirely certain what the exact meaning is.

Samuel speaks as a prophet of God. God had commanded that the Amalekites be destroyed, but Saul spared the king and kept the best of the spoil. Samuel corrects that disobedience and does what Saul should have done. It is a hard passage, tied to a particular judgment in the history of Israel.

For today: do not feel secure when you think a problem is over, and do not leave unfinished what God asks of you. Partial obedience is a form of disobedience, and God invites us to obey him completely.
exp.11:8:
The verse says that the people of Israel forgot the LORD their God. Because of this, God gave them over to their enemies, allowing them to fall under the power of Sisera, the commander of the army of Hazor, the Philistines, and the king of Moab. These enemies fought against them.

Samuel, now an old man, is speaking at the ceremony where Saul is confirmed as king. He wants the people to remember the story: God was always faithful, but they kept turning away again and again. He shows them that their troubles did not come because God failed, but because they left him.

For today: when life becomes complicated, it is worth asking ourselves whether we have drifted away from God. If so, we can return as Israel did, with humility, because God is still willing to forgive and to rescue.
exp.17:19:
Michal, Saul's other daughter, loved David, and when this was reported to Saul, it pleased him. The phrase "it pleased him" means that Saul was glad to hear it, or that he approved of it.

Here the narrator tells us what was happening in the palace. Saul had earlier promised his older daughter Merab to David, but she was given to another man. The verses that follow show that Saul was not glad about Michal's love for David out of affection for him, but because he planned to use it as a trap so that the Philistines would kill him. It is worth noting that the Bible says Michal loved David, but it does not say that Saul acted with good intentions.

For today: not everything that looks like good news is good for everyone. Before we rejoice or make a decision, let us ask God for discernment to see the true motives, including our own.
exp.3:8:
The Philistines urge one another to be brave. "Take courage and be men" means to show courage and resolve. "Be men and fight" means to act bravely and get into the battle. "Otherwise, you will serve the Hebrews just as they served you" means they should not become slaves to the Hebrews, as the Hebrews had once been to them.

The speakers are Philistine leaders or soldiers. They had heard that the ark had come into the camp of Israel, and they felt terror, remembering the plagues of Egypt. Even with that fear, they decide to fight. The following text shows that they won, and the ark was taken. Israel had treated the ark as a good-luck charm, not in obedience to God.

For today: fear does not have to paralyze us, but we must not use what is sacred as an object of luck. Let us seek God with an obedient heart, and face challenges with courage and responsibility.
exp.25:17:
David asks King Saul why he keeps chasing him. He calls Saul "my lord" and calls himself "his servant," showing respect. His questions, "What have I done? What evil is in my hand?" mean: "What is my fault? What wrong did I commit?"

David speaks from a hill, at night, after entering Saul's camp while everyone was sleeping. He could have killed the king, but he took only his spear and his water jug as proof. Saul, jealous, was looking for him in order to kill him. David defends his innocence with humility and respect.

For today: when someone treats us unjustly, we can ask for explanations calmly and respectfully, without seeking revenge. We can leave our case in God's hands, for he sees everything and is just.
exp.13:40:
Saul asks God to reveal the truth, and the lot falls on him and his son Jonathan, while the people are set free. The request in this verse is put in a way that may be unfamiliar. Saul asks God to answer his question, and then to show whether the fault lies with himself and Jonathan or with the people. The Hebrew here is the key to understanding what Saul is really asking for: a clear and decisive answer from God.

Saul had made a hasty oath: no one was to eat anything that day, on pain of death. God did not answer him, and Saul wanted to discover who had failed. Jonathan, who had not heard about the oath, had tasted a little honey. Scholars debate exactly how this lot was carried out, and the text itself does not explain the procedure.

For today: before making promises or declaring strong decisions, let us think calmly. A vow spoken in haste can hurt those we love most.
exp.24:1:
This verse introduces a man from Maon whose business was in Carmel. He was very wealthy, with three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. "Business" here means his property and his livestock operation. "Shearing" means cutting the wool from the sheep, and at that very moment he was doing it.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator who introduces a new character. Samuel has just died, and David is running from Saul in the wilderness. This Carmel is a town in the south of Judah, not the mountain in the north. The next verse will reveal that this rich man is named Nabal. Sheep-shearing was usually a time of celebration and abundance.

For today: having wealth says nothing about a person's heart. What matters is how we use it. Let us ask God for a generous and humble heart, one that serves others instead of boasting.
exp.14:1:
Here God, called "the LORD of Hosts," says that he witnessed what the Amalekites did to the Israelites. The verse describes how they opposed Israel on their way up from Egypt toward the promised land.

Samuel speaks to Saul, the first king of Israel, and passes on an order from God. That attack by Amalek is recounted in Exodus 17, and Deuteronomy 25 recalls that it was against the weak who were lagging behind. The verses that follow command that Amalek be destroyed, which is hard to read. Scholars explain it in different ways, and it is wise to read it with humility.

For today: God sees and remembers the unjust treatment that his people suffer. We can trust that justice is in his hands, and so we do not need to take revenge. We are also called to listen to and obey his voice attentively.
exp.18:16:
Saul confronts his daughter Michal: "Why did you deceive me like this? You sent my enemy away, and he has escaped!" She answers that David told her, "Help me get away, or I will kill you!" The word "deceived" means that Saul felt tricked, and "enemy" is how he saw David.

Saul wanted to kill David, but Michal, David's wife and Saul's daughter, helped him escape and put a statue in the bed to buy time. Now, before her father, she gives an excuse. The Bible does not say whether that threat was real or whether Michal made it up to protect herself. Many believe it was an excuse, but this is not certain.

For today: When we must choose between obeying an unjust authority and protecting a life, let us ask God for wisdom and courage. And when we stand up for what is right, let us take care that our words are honest, for the truth honors God.
exp.8:14:
This verse says that the day before Saul arrived, the LORD had already made his plan known to Samuel. The phrase about God revealing something to Samuel means that God spoke to him clearly and directly, like someone sharing a secret. After this, God explains his plan to him.

The narrator tells a detail that Saul did not know. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys, and without knowing it he was being led toward Samuel. God had already prepared the meeting. He wanted to raise up a leader to deliver Israel from the Philistines, because he had heard the cry of his people.

For today: God may be at work in your life even when you do not notice it. What seems like coincidence or an ordinary problem, God can use to guide you. Trust that he hears your cry and move forward faithfully, one step at a time.
exp.15:22:
It says that whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would pick up his harp and play. Then Saul would find relief and feel better, and the spirit of distress would leave him. The verb for "play" here is the one used for making music on an instrument.

It is the narrator who tells this. Shortly before, the Spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul, and a troubling spirit distressed him. His servants suggested finding a skilled musician, and so David came to him, the one who would later become king. How this spirit could be described as coming "from God" is explained in several ways; the text gives no further detail.

For today: music and humble service can bring relief to someone who is suffering. Think of someone who is distressed and offer them your company, a song, or a simple prayer. Sometimes God uses small acts to bring rest.
exp.22:22:
Saul asks the men of Ziph to investigate carefully. They must find out all of David's hiding places, make sure of where he is, and come back with reliable information. "Certainty" means assurance, something confirmed. "Clans of Judah" refers to the family groups within the tribe of Judah. Saul promises to go with them and search for David throughout the whole land.

King Saul is speaking, pursuing David out of jealousy and fear of losing the throne. The Ziphites offered to help him, and Saul blesses them in the name of Jehovah, although his goal is unjust. Meanwhile, David remains protected and receives warning in time.

We can use religious words without our hearts being aligned with God. Saul speaks of blessing while he pursues an innocent man. Today it is worth asking ourselves whether our plans truly please God, or whether we merely cover them with spiritual language.
exp.9:3:
He tells Saul that when he meets three men going up to Bethel, they will greet him and give him two loaves of bread, which he will accept from their hands. "As soon as they greet you" means "as soon as they greet you." The loaves were part of the offering they were carrying to worship God.

The speaker is the prophet Samuel, who had just anointed Saul as the future king of Israel. He gives him a series of concrete signs to confirm that God was with him. It is interesting that Saul, being the chosen one, was to accept the bread with humility, and not ask for it or demand it. Scholars do not agree on the exact meaning of the gesture, but it is clear that God cared for every detail of the journey.

Today we can learn to accept with gratitude the help God sends us through other people, even in simple things like a loaf of bread, and to recognize his care in the small details of each day.
exp.17:1:
Saul kept David with him that same day and did not let him return to his father's house, Jesse's. The original wording is "took him into his service" and "did not allow him to go back."

The narrator describes what followed David's victory over Goliath and his conversation with Saul. Until then David had gone back and forth between the palace and home, where he tended the sheep. Now Saul brings him into his court on a lasting basis. The text does not say what exact position he gave him at this point; later he places him in charge of men of war. All of this happens while the friendship with Jonathan is taking root.

God sometimes takes us out of our daily routine and leads us to a new place of service. If you face a change like this, trust that God is with you. And while it unfolds, be faithful in small things, as David was with his sheep.
exp.11:0:
Samuel speaks to all the people of Israel. He reminds them that he listened to them and set over them the king they asked for. "I have listened to your voice" means "I listened to you." The words "I have set over you a king" show that Samuel did what they asked him to do, although the choice came from God.

Samuel was a prophet and judge of Israel. The people had asked for a king so they could be like the other nations, and this grieved Samuel. Now, with Saul already acknowledged as king, Samuel prepares to step away from leadership and to defend the integrity of his service, as the following verses show.

For today: when we serve others, let us strive to live so that we can look everyone in the eye, with clean and honest conduct. And when God gives us a path different from the one we expected, let us keep trusting in Him.
exp.24:28:
Abigail is saying that even though someone has come after David to take his life, God will keep David safe. The image of his life being "bound securely... in the bundle of the living" is like a precious thing wrapped up and tied tight, held carefully in a safe place. By contrast, God will fling the lives of David's enemies away, like stones hurled from a sling, sent far off and beyond their control.

Abigail is the speaker here, the wife of Nabal. David was coming in anger to kill every man in Nabal's household because of an insult. She goes out to meet him with food and supplies and pleads with him not to take revenge with his own hands. She reminds him that God is defending him, and that he should not stain his conscience with bloodshed that serves no real purpose. The one pursuing David at this point is Saul.

For today: when someone wrongs you or comes after you, do not take revenge. Entrust your life and your cause to God, who knows how to care for you and to bring justice in his time.
exp.25:14:
Here David speaks to Abner, the commander of Saul's army, with irony. He asks whether Abner is not a man of worth, the equal of anyone in Israel, and then why he did not protect his lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him. To "protect" the king means to guard him, and "one of the people" refers to an ordinary person who got into the camp.

David and Abishai had entered Saul's camp by night, while everyone was sleeping, and had taken the king's spear and water jar. David could have killed him, but he did not want to harm the one anointed by God. Now, from a distance, he exposes Abner's carelessness.

For today: when God entrusts us with a responsibility, we should take care of it seriously and not neglect it. We also learn from David to correct others without taking revenge, respecting people even when we have the opportunity to harm them.
exp.23:14:
Here David asks Saul some questions to make him think: whom is the king of Israel chasing? He compares himself to a dead dog and to a flea, something of no worth and no danger. The phrase about whom he has come out after is rendered as "whom he is chasing."

David speaks from a distance, after he was able to kill Saul in the cave and did not do it. Saul, the king, was pursuing him with soldiers because he saw him as an enemy. David humbles himself to show that he is no threat, and he trusts that God will be the judge between the two of them.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not take revenge with your own hands. Speak with truth, with humility and respect, and leave your cause in the hands of God, who judges with justice.
exp.27:1:
Here David answers Achish, the Philistine king, with ambiguous words: "Then you will come to know what your servant can do." Achish takes this to mean that David will fight on his side, and he replies, "Very well. I will make you my bodyguard for life."

David was living among the Philistines because he was fleeing from King Saul. Achish trusted him, and now the Philistines were preparing to attack Israel, David's own people. David does not say clearly whether he will fight against Israel. His answer is shrewd, and the Bible does not explain what he actually intended to do.

For today: when we find ourselves in a difficult situation because of past decisions, we should seek God honestly. Doubtful answers can confuse others and ourselves as well. It is better to ask God for wisdom so that we act with integrity.
exp.22:28:
The text of verse 29 seems to have come through empty. The verse reads: "And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En-gedi."

It says David left that place and went to live in the strongholds of En-gedi, an area of caves and rocks, with springs, beside the Dead Sea. "Strongholds" refers to places that are hard to attack, like natural fortresses.

The narrator tells what happened after David escaped from Saul, thanks to the Philistines distracting Saul. David was still on the run, for Saul was pursuing him unjustly. En-gedi gave him shelter and time to catch his breath. There the episode will later take place in which David spares Saul's life.

For today: when a lull comes in the middle of a trial, do not waste it. Rest, seek refuge in God, and prepare for what comes next. He often gives us safe places along the way.
exp.2:14:
Samuel spent the rest of the night lying down, without sleeping, as it is understood. In the morning he did what he always did: he opened the doors of the house of the LORD, that is, of the sanctuary at Shiloh. He was afraid to tell Eli the vision, meaning what God had shown him and said to him.

The narrator tells us that Samuel was a young man who served alongside Eli. God had just spoken to him about a harsh judgment against Eli's house, because his sons were doing wrong and he did not restrain them. Samuel feared the message and the respect he owed to his teacher.

Today, telling the truth can sometimes frighten us, especially when it is said to people we love or respect. This verse encourages us to keep carrying out our tasks faithfully, to ask God for courage, and to speak with humility, without harshness, but without hiding what is true.
exp.21:11:
Saul calls the priest Ahimelech and tells him to listen. "Listen now" is a direct command from a king to his subject. "Son of Ahitub" is the way of naming Ahimelech by his father. He answers, "Here I am, my lord," which means "I am here, at your service." It is a response of respect and readiness.

Saul is furious because Ahimelech helped David, who was fleeing from the king. He summoned all the priests of Nob and accuses them of conspiring. Ahimelech answers calmly and without fear, since he did not know that David was being pursued. Here an unjust trial begins, and the Bible does not present it as right.

Today we can learn from Ahimelech: when someone accuses us unjustly, it is wise to respond with truth and calm. We should also be careful not to let jealousy or fear lead us to judge and hurt the innocent.
exp.25:9:
David says that God himself will decide Saul's fate. The verse's phrase "as surely as the Lord lives" is an oath, the way of swearing by the living God. David names three possibilities: that the Lord will strike Saul down, that Saul's day will come and he will die, or that he will go into battle and perish. In every case the decision rests in God's hands, not David's.

David speaks with his nephew Abishai in Saul's camp at night. Saul had been pursuing David to kill him, and Abishai saw an opportunity to end the threat. David refused, because Saul was the Lord's anointed, the king chosen by God, and David would not take justice into his own hands.

When someone wounds us or treats us unjustly, we can resist the temptation to take revenge. Trusting that God is the righteous judge frees us to act with integrity and to wait on him.
exp.11:24:
It says that if the people keep on doing wrong, both they and their king will face ruin. The word "persist" in the verse shows that this is about continuing in wrongdoing. This is a serious warning, given plainly.

The prophet Samuel speaks in his farewell address as judge of Israel. The people had asked for a king, though God was already their King, and Samuel reminds them that God had cared for them. He shows them that, with a king or without one, what matters most is obeying God. This follows the line of the blessings and warnings of the law of Moses.

For today: no one is so high up or so secure that they can ignore God. Today you can examine whether there is something wrong that you keep repeating, and ask God for help to change and to serve him wholeheartedly.
exp.19:26:
On the second day after the new moon, David's place at the table was still empty. Saul asks his son Jonathan why the son of Jesse has not come to the meal, either yesterday or today.

The word "unclean" in the verse refers to a ritual impurity that would have kept David from taking part, but that detail is not in this verse, so it is left out here.

Here Saul, the king, speaks with Jonathan. David had fled because Saul wanted to kill him, and Jonathan and David had agreed on this test to learn the king's intentions. Notice that Saul says "the son of Jesse" and not "David," a disdainful tone that shows his contempt and anger.

Today we can pay attention to how we speak about people. When resentment grows in the heart, even another person's name becomes uncomfortable to say. Let us ask God to heal what hardens us, so that we can speak with respect even about those who make us uneasy.
exp.22:27:
This verse tells how Saul gave up his pursuit of David and went to meet the Philistines. Because of this, the place was called Sela-hammahlekoth. That name is usually translated as "Rock of Separation" or "Rock of Division," although some understand it in another way.

The one who narrates is the author of the book. Saul had David nearly surrounded in the wilderness of Maon, but a messenger called him away because the Philistines were raiding the land. David was saved just in time. The text does not say that David planned this; the reader understands that God watched over him in the midst of danger.

For today: when you feel there is no way out, remember that God can act at exactly the right moment and by unexpected means. Trust Him, faithfully do what is yours to do, and thank Him when He delivers you.
exp.1:26:
A prophet, whom the Bible calls a "man of God," comes to the priest Eli with a message from the Lord. God reminds Eli that he clearly revealed himself to his family line when they were in Egypt under Pharaoh. The question "Did I not clearly reveal Myself?" points to a past act of God that had made his presence unmistakable to them.

Eli was both priest and judge over Israel, but his sons, Hophni and Phinehas, abused their office and treated the offerings with contempt. Eli did not correct them firmly. Through this messenger, God begins by recalling his past kindness, to show that the sin of that family was even more serious, since they had received so much.

For today: God has given us much, beginning with rescuing us and calling us. Before asking him for anything, let us remember what he has already done for us. This helps us live with gratitude and not put anything, not even our family, above him.
exp.7:3:
This verse tells us that all the leaders of the people of Israel, called "elders," came together and went to find Samuel at Ramah, which was their town. The words "gathered together" and "came" are older forms that we would today say as "assembled" and "arrived." It is the beginning of an important conversation.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samuel was already old, and his sons Joel and Abijah, whom he had appointed as judges, were accepting bribes and bending justice. The elders come to Samuel with a real complaint and with a request that, as the account goes on, displeased Samuel and ended up leading him to pray.

For today: when we see injustice or problems in our church, family, or community, we can speak with those who have responsibility. But before asking for a solution, it is wise to pray and to ask ourselves whether what we are asking pleases God, not only whether it seems practical to us.
exp.16:15:
This verse says that the Philistine, Goliath, came forward toward the battlefield every morning and every evening. He did this for forty days in a row. The phrase "came forward to take his stand" means that he stepped out in front of Israel's army to challenge them.

The narrator describes how things stood before David arrived. Israel's soldiers lived under constant threat. Meanwhile, David was going back and forth between his father's sheep and the camp. The text does not say what each soldier was thinking, but it does show that fear became a habit over so many days.

For today: the voices that frighten us often repeat themselves every day and can wear us down. Don't let them set your mood. Begin and end your day listening to God's Word and speaking with Him in prayer.
exp.6:1:
It says the ark of the Lord stayed at Kiriath-jearim for a long time, twenty years in all. During that time, all Israel mournfully sought the LORD, that is, they felt sorrow and longing for God and looked for him with grief over being separated from him.

The narrator tells what happened after the Philistines returned the ark. It was kept in the house of Abinadab, and Israel remained far from God, though with pain. The text does not say exactly what they were doing during those years. Then Samuel calls them to turn to the LORD with all their heart and to put away their idols.

When we feel emptiness or sorrow over being far from God, that pain can be a first step toward him. But sorrow alone is not enough: we must act, remove whatever has taken his place in our heart, and serve him again with sincerity.
exp.13:6:
Here the young man who carried Jonathan's weapons responds with complete loyalty. He tells him to do what his heart has already decided, to go forward, and that he is with him heart and soul. An armor-bearer was the assistant who carried a warrior's weapons and stayed close to him in battle. Saying "I am with you heart and soul" means he is willing to follow him in whatever he decides, as if his heart were one with Jonathan's.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, proposes to attack alone with his assistant a garrison of the Philistines, whom he calls "uncircumcised", that is, outsiders to God's covenant. Israel was at a disadvantage, and Jonathan trusts that for the LORD to save does not depend on whether there are many or few. The assistant supports his faith with courage.

Today we can learn the value of faithfully accompanying someone who walks with sincere faith in God. We can also be that kind of support: someone who encourages, without leaving alone the one who takes a brave and good step.
exp.3:19:
This verse tells of the last moments of Phinehas's wife. As she was dying after giving birth, the women attending her said, "Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son!" But she did not respond, and she paid no heed to their words, giving them no importance.

The women who helped with the birth speak to her and try to comfort her with news that would normally bring great joy. But she had just learned that the Philistines had captured the ark of God and that her father-in-law Eli and her husband had died. Her grief over the loss of the ark weighed more heavily on her than the news of the son. That is why she named him Ichabod, a name explained in the following verse.

Today, we sometimes offer comfort with good intentions, but without understanding the person's deeper pain. Let us learn to accompany others with patience, by listening and simply being present. And let us remember that the most valuable thing in life is the presence of God.
exp.13:25:
This verse says that Israel's army entered a forest where honey was flowing on the ground, yet not one of them lifted a hand to their mouth to eat it. "Put the hand to the mouth" means to eat. They were hungry and the food was right there, but they respected Saul's oath. "Feared the oath" means they took the curse seriously.

The narrator tells us that Israel was fighting against the Philistines. Saul, without anyone asking him to, had forbidden eating until evening. Many understand that it was a hasty order, one that left the people weak and exhausted. The Bible does not say that God asked for it.

Today we can learn to take care with our words and promises. A commitment made in haste or pride can burden others unnecessarily. Before demanding something from others, it is wise to pray and to think about whether it truly serves God and helps people.
exp.13:16:
Saul tells his men to call the roll and find out who has left the camp. In the Berean Standard Bible, "call the roll" means checking who is present. The "armor-bearer" was the young man who carried a soldier's weapons. When they checked, they saw that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there.

Saul speaks as king and commander of the army. The Philistines were in great confusion and panic, and Saul's watchmen noticed the disorder in the enemy camp. Saul wanted to understand what was happening, and in this way he realized that Jonathan had attacked on his own. Afterward, Saul asks for the ark and speaks with the priest, but then he stops him, because the commotion was growing.
