For today: when something strange happens, it is good to pause and calmly find out what took place, but without forgetting to seek God before acting. Many times He works through ordinary, faithful people who take a step of faith.
exp.14:28:
The verse says that God, called here "the Glory of Israel," does not lie or change his mind the way a person does. "Change His mind" here means to back away from a decision. God is firm and faithful to what he says.

Samuel speaks with King Saul, who had disobeyed a clear command from God. Samuel tells him that the kingdom will be taken from him. Saul tears Samuel's robe, and Samuel uses this as a sign that the kingdom would also be torn away. Some note that God does indeed change his mind about having made Saul king (vv. 11, 35), but here the point is that his judgment is not arbitrary and does not change because of human pressure.

For today: you can trust that God keeps his word, both in his promises and in his warnings. That invites you to obey him with seriousness and to rest in his faithfulness.
exp.29:26:
This verse is part of a list of places to which David sent gifts. It names the people who lived in Bethel, in Ramoth Negev, and in Jattir. These were towns in the territory of Judah.

The narrator tells that David, after defeating the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag, shared part of the spoil among the elders of Judah, who were his friends. He called them a gift from the enemies of the Lord. He probably wanted to thank those who had supported him while he was fleeing from Saul, though the text does not give the details. It is not certain that this Bethel in the south is the same famous one in Benjamin.

For today: David did not keep everything for himself, but recognized those who had helped him. Think about who has supported you and express your gratitude with a concrete gesture, acknowledging that what you have comes from God.
exp.22:26:
A messenger came to Saul with urgent news: the Philistines had raided the land. The phrase "Come quickly" means "come right away." A raid is a sudden, violent attack that comes by surprise.

Saul and his men had almost surrounded David in the wilderness of Maon. Just as they were about to catch him, this warning arrived, and Saul had to abandon the pursuit to defend his people. The messenger speaks out of the urgency of war. The place was called "Sela-hammah-lecoth," which is usually understood as "the rock of divisions" or "of escapes."

For today: when everything seems lost, God can change the situation in unexpected ways. Trust that He cares for you, even when you cannot see how the way out will come.
exp.14:27:
Samuel tells Saul that the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel away from him, as one tears a piece of cloth. "Torn" here means ripped off forcefully. "Your neighbor" means another person close by, someone from his own people. That person is described as "better than you," meaning more faithful to God. The text does not give his name here.

Samuel, the prophet, speaks after Saul disobeyed a clear command from God. Saul grabbed Samuel's robe to stop him, and it tore. Samuel uses that moment as a sign: in this way Saul's kingdom is broken. Many understand that he is referring to David, although this verse does not say so.

For today: obedience to God matters more than titles or appearances. If God corrects us, it is best to respond with humble and sincere repentance, not with excuses.
exp.4:7:
This verse tells how the Philistine rulers came together to decide what to do with the ark of God. The phrase "called together all the rulers" means they summoned everyone who held power. The "rulers" were the leaders of the five Philistine cities. They decided to move the ark to Gath, another Philistine city.

The Philistines had taken the ark in battle. In Ashdod, the people suffered a plague, and their god Dagon fell before the ark. The leaders speak with fear, but they do not repent. They only move the ark from place to place, as if the problem were a matter of location. The following text shows that the plague followed them.

For today: when God confronts us, it is tempting to change our place or our excuse instead of surrendering our heart. God does not evade us; let us ask him for humility to listen to him and obey him.
exp.14:17:
God sent Saul on a mission with a clear command: to devote to destruction the sinful Amalekites and to fight against them until they were wiped out. The verse's own words make the instruction plain, so no explanation of older language is needed here.

Samuel speaks in God's name and reminds Saul of exactly what he was commanded. Before that, he reminds him that God made him king when he felt small. Later Saul did not fully obey: he spared Agag and the best of the plunder. This passage is difficult, and many Christians understand it as God's judgment on a nation with a long history of wickedness, not as a model for us.

For today: partial obedience is not obedience. If God shows us something clearly, such as leaving a bad habit or forgiving someone, we should do it with humility and without excuses.
exp.2:13:
Here God says he has made a solemn promise about Eli's family: the sin of that house will never be atoned for through sacrifice or offering. "Atoned for" means covered over or set right through a payment or sacrifice. "Sacrifice or offering" refers to the gifts brought to God. "Iniquity" means wickedness or sin.

God speaks at night to the young Samuel. Eli's sons, who were priests, treated the holy things with contempt, and Eli, although he knew it, did not correct them firmly. Some scholars point out that this judgment refers to an attitude of persistent rebellion without repentance, and not to God rejecting everyone who repents. The Bible does not explain this in more detail.

For today: it is not enough to carry out religious rituals if the heart keeps disobeying. If you have responsibility over others, as a parent, leader, or teacher, correct them with love and truth, without looking the other way.
exp.8:25:
They got up early in the morning, and just before dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof. He said, "Get ready, and I will send you on your way!" So Saul got ready, and the two of them went outside together onto the street. Samuel is the prophet and judge of Israel. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys, and God had already told Samuel that this young man would be the first king. Samuel had hosted him, given him a place of honor at the meal, and talked with him. Now he wakes him early to take him aside and give him a message from God, as the next verse shows.

God often speaks to those who rise ready to listen. If we give the first hours of the day to prayer and to the Word, our hearts will be more attentive to hear his direction.
exp.5:3:
Here the Philistines ask what offering they should send back with the ark to make up for their wrong. A "guilt offering" is an offering made to set things right. The priests and diviners answer that they should send five gold tumors and five gold rats, one for each Philistine ruler. The tumors likely refer to the growths or sores of the plague, though the exact nature of them is not entirely clear. They explain that the same plague has struck both the people and their rulers.

The speakers are the Philistine priests and diviners. The ark of God had been in their land, and plagues had come upon them. They wanted to return it to Israel without further offending the God of Israel. The gold figures represented what was afflicting them, and they were a way of acknowledging his power.

For today: when we recognize that we have failed before God, it is not enough to feel fear or to look only for relief. We can humble ourselves, acknowledge his authority, and come to him sincerely, trusting in the grace he offers us in Christ.
exp.19:41:
Jonathan sends David away with the words "Go in peace." He reminds him that the two of them swore an oath in the name of the LORD, asking that the LORD would be a witness between them and between their descendants forever. David got up and left, and Jonathan went back into the city.

Jonathan speaks after warning David, by a sign with arrows, that his father, King Saul, wanted to kill him. It was a farewell full of tears. They had already made a covenant of friendship and loyalty, and now David had to flee. Jonathan trusted that God would uphold that commitment.

For today: when you have to part from someone you love, or when a promise is hard to keep, place God at the center of the relationship. Keep your word faithfully, pray for that person, and trust that God cares for them even when you are not near.
exp.11:11:
The verse says that when the people saw Nahash, king of the Ammonites, moving against them, they came to Samuel and said, "No, we must have a king to rule over us." Yet the LORD their God was already their king.

Samuel, now old, speaks in his farewell address as judge. He reminds them that God had rescued them many times, even when they had turned away from Him. Samuel shows them that asking for a king out of fear was doubting God's care. Even so, he makes it clear that God could still guide them if they obeyed.

Today, when something frightens us, it is easy to look for security in people, money or plans, and to forget God. Before deciding, we can pray and ask ourselves: am I trusting God, or only reacting to fear?
exp.22:4:
He says that David went with his men to Keilah and fought against the Philistines. "Carried off their livestock" means that he took the Philistines' animals, and "striking them with a mighty blow" means that he defeated them badly. So David saved the people of Keilah.

The narrator tells what happened after God gave David his command. David's men were afraid, but he asked God again, and God promised him the victory. Keilah was being attacked by the Philistines, who were stealing its grain. David obeyed, though he was in danger, since Saul was pursuing him.

When God shows us clearly what to do, we can obey even when we feel afraid. It is good to seek his direction more than once, as David did, and then to act with courage to help someone in need.
exp.1:20:
The verse says that the LORD attended to Hannah, meaning he showed her kindness and granted her desire to be a mother. She then conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. Meanwhile, the boy Samuel, whom she had dedicated to God, grew up in the presence of the LORD, that is, under his care and in the sanctuary.

The narrator tells this after Eli blessed Elkanah and Hannah for having given Samuel over. Hannah had made a request and a vow to God. Now it is shown that God answers with generosity. The account contrasts Samuel, who grows faithfully, with the sons of Eli, who behave badly, as becomes clear soon after.

For today: God cares for what we entrust to him in faith. We can dedicate to him our children, our time, and our plans, and trust that he is faithful, even though he does not always respond in the same way.
exp.16:2:
This verse describes how the two armies were positioned. The Philistines occupied one hill, Israel occupied another, and a valley lay between them. The phrase "on one hill" and "on another" in the verse shows which army stood where.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the events without giving an opinion. The Philistines, enemies of Israel, had gathered to fight, and Saul with his men went out to face them. The verse sets the scene where Goliath will appear. The valley separates the two sides and shows that the battle has come to a standstill, with both armies looking at each other.

For today: sometimes we feel stuck in front of a "valley" of fear or waiting, looking at a large problem. While the solution has not yet come, we can ask God for calm and trust, instead of letting ourselves be paralyzed by what we see.
exp.1:28:
God asks Eli a pointed question: why do you kick at my sacrifice and offering, the ones I commanded for my dwelling place? Eli has honored his sons more than he has honored me. They are growing fat on the best of the offerings brought by my people Israel. The "offering" here refers to the gifts brought to God, and "honored" means giving something the first place.

A "man of God" speaks, a prophet whose name is not given, sent to Eli the priest. God reminds him that his family was chosen to serve. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing the offerings (1 Samuel 2:12-17), and Eli did not restrain them firmly. That is why judgment is coming.

For today: examine whom you give first place. Sometimes, out of affection or to avoid conflict, we let pass what offends God. Truly loving someone includes correcting them gently and putting God first.
exp.14:9:
This verse says that God spoke to Samuel. Your verse reads "Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel, saying," which means the same thing: the LORD gave Samuel a message. It is a short phrase, but it introduces a very serious message.

God speaks just after Saul and the people did not fully obey. They had been told to destroy the Amalekites and all that belonged to them, but they spared King Agag and the best of the livestock. Samuel was the prophet, and God shares with him what he thinks of Saul. What follows shows that God grieves over Saul's disobedience, and Samuel is deeply saddened.

For today: God speaks to us, above all through his Word, and he expects us to obey completely, not only in what is convenient for us. We might ask ourselves: is there something God has asked of me that I am only doing halfway?
exp.5:7:
This verse says that the Philistines were to set the ark of the Lord on a new cart. In a chest beside it they would put the gold objects, given as a guilt offering, which is a payment to make up for the wrong done. Then they were to send the ark on its way.

The Philistine priests and diviners are the ones speaking here. The ark had been among them for seven months and had brought them plagues. They wanted to return it and find out whether those troubles came from God or were just chance. The cows, which had never worn a yoke and had calves, would go against their nature if they went toward Israel. It was a pagan test, not a method that God had commanded.

Today we can learn that when we recognize we have offended God, gifts or rituals are not enough. God looks for a humble heart that surrenders and obeys, not an attempt to fix things on our own.
exp.17:14:
This verse says that Saul saw how successfully David was doing, and for that reason he was afraid of him. The word "successful" describes someone whose efforts are bringing good results, and it reflects David's good judgment and steady work.

The narrator tells us that Saul had appointed David as commander of a thousand soldiers. David carried out his duties well, and the text says that the Lord was with him. Saul already knew that the Lord had departed from him, so David's good conduct troubled him instead of gladdening him. His fear would lead him to plot against David.

For today: when you see that someone else is doing well, do not let envy or fear take control of you. Ask God for a thankful and humble heart, and seek to live with wisdom and honesty in whatever task is yours.
exp.14:6:
This verse tells us that Saul defeated the Amalekites over a very wide area. The word "struck down" means that he beat them in battle. The campaign went all the way from Havilah to Shur, which is east of Egypt. Scholars are not sure exactly where Havilah was, but the text marks out a large territory.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not a character. God, through the prophet Samuel, had commanded Saul to destroy the Amalekites for attacking Israel when they came out of Egypt. Saul warned the Kenites to move away, since they had shown kindness to Israel. This victory seems complete, but the verses that follow show that Saul obeyed only in part.

For today: a good start is not enough if we do not finish by obeying fully. We can ask ourselves whether we are doing what God asks with a whole heart, or only what suits us.
exp.3:16:
Here the messenger gives Eli four pieces of news in a row: Israel has fled before the Philistines, many of the people have died, his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are both dead, and the ark of God has been captured. The word for the great loss of life means a great slaughter. The phrase about the ark simply means it was captured.

The speaker is a man who escaped from the battle and arrives at Shiloh with terrible news. Eli, an old man who is nearly blind, is waiting to learn what happened. The messenger saves the most painful news for last: the ark, the symbol of God's presence. For Eli, that was the gravest loss. His sons had acted wickedly as priests, and the people had treated the ark almost like a good-luck charm.

For today: let us not use what is sacred as a talisman, and let us not allow religion to become only a custom. God cannot be manipulated. Let us seek him with a sincere and obedient heart, and not merely with symbols or rituals.
exp.12:11:
Saul explains why he offered the sacrifice. He thought the Philistines would attack him at Gilgal before he had sought the favor of the Lord. Seeking the Lord's favor means asking God for help through prayer. A burnt offering was an offering burned up completely. "Felt compelled" means he felt pressed to do it, as if he had no real choice.

He is speaking to Samuel, the first king of Israel. Samuel had told him to wait seven days, and Saul, afraid and seeing the people scattering, offered the sacrifice himself, something that was not his place to do. His excuse sounds pious, but Samuel calls it foolishness.

For today: pressure can lead us to justify disobedience with religious words. When you feel you must act right now, stop and ask yourself whether you are trusting God or only calming your fear. Waiting on God is also obeying him.
exp.9:19:
He says that Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, and that the tribe of Benjamin was the one selected. "Come forward" means to step up or gather in front of others. "Selected" means it was singled out, probably by a lot cast before God. The Bible does not describe the exact method here.

Samuel speaks at Mizpah before all the people. First he reminds them that God had brought them out of Egypt and that, even so, they asked for a human king. Now Samuel begins the process of presenting the first king. God guides the choice step by step: first the tribe, then the family, and then the person, Saul.

For today: God can guide our decisions, but first He wants us to examine our hearts. Before we ask Him for something, let us ask ourselves whether we trust that He cares for us and that He is enough.
exp.4:5:
This verse says that God acted with force against the city of Ashdod. Speaking of "the hand of the LORD" is a way of speaking about God's power. The phrase about his hand being heavy means that his hand pressed down on them with great weight. The verse describes the affliction as tumors, which were painful sores; the exact nature of the illness is not known for certain.

The narrator recounts what happened when the Philistines captured the ark of God and placed it in the temple of their god Dagon. Dagon was found fallen and broken before the ark. Then this affliction came. The people of Ashdod understood that the ark could not remain with them, although they still did not fully acknowledge God.

For today: nothing and no one can take the place of God. We can examine the things in which we place our trust and surrender them to Him with humility, before they fall apart.
exp.16:54:
As Saul watched David go out to meet the Philistine, Goliath, he turned to Abner, the commander of his army, and asked, "Abner, whose son is this young man?" Abner answered, "As surely as you live, O king, I do not know." The word translated "young man" refers to a young person, someone still in his youth.

It seems strange that Saul would ask this question, since David had already played the harp for him before (1 Samuel 16). Scholars offer several explanations. Perhaps Saul did not remember David well. Perhaps he was deeply troubled and his mind was elsewhere. Or perhaps he was asking about David's family, since he had promised a great reward to whoever defeated the giant. The Bible does not say clearly which of these is true.

God can use people whom others overlook or do not know. David was an unknown young man, but he trusted God and was faithful in whatever task was placed before him. Today, you do not need fame or recognition to be useful. Do faithfully what God places in your hands, and trust Him with the rest.
exp.15:5:
Samuel arrives in Bethlehem, sees Eliab, the oldest son of Jesse, and thinks he is the chosen one. He says, "Surely here before the LORD is His anointed," meaning "surely this is the one God has chosen."

The speaker is the prophet Samuel. God sent him to the house of Jesse to anoint a new king, because Saul had already been rejected. Samuel looks at what can be seen on the outside, and that is why he is mistaken. In the verses that follow, God corrects him: He does not look at appearance or height, but at the heart.

For today: before judging a person by their appearance, their success, or the way they speak, let us ask God to help us see with more care. And let us cultivate a sincere heart before Him.
exp.5:15:
This verse says that the five rulers of the Philistines saw what happened at Beth-shemesh: the cart carrying the ark, the sacrifice of the cows, and the offering. After they saw it, they returned to Ekron that same day. "Rulers" refers to the leaders or chiefs of the Philistine cities. A "whole burnt offering" was an offering burned completely as a gift to God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had captured the ark and suffered plagues, so they decided to send it back with an offering of gold. The rulers followed the cart to Beth-shemesh to see what would happen. The text does not explain what they thought when they went back, so it is best not to invent their motives. It does show that they witnessed the ark arrive at its place.

For today: when we recognize that we have acted wrongly toward God or toward others, feeling fear or unease is not enough. It is good to take concrete steps to make things right, to return what is owed, and to approach God with reverence.
exp.1:29:
God says he had promised that Eli's family would serve before him as priests forever. But now he withdraws that promise, declaring, "Far be it from Me!" The principle is clear: God honors those who honor him, and those who despise him will be disdained.

A prophet, sent by God, speaks to Eli the priest. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing the offerings, and Eli did not correct them firmly. So God announces judgment on his house. The promise was real, but it depended on faithfulness.

For today: honoring God is not only saying so, but obeying him in everyday life. We can ask ourselves whether in some things we are putting people, or our own comfort, above him.
exp.14:13:
Samuel asks Saul a question that sounds simple: what is this noise of sheep and cattle that I can hear? The "bleating" is the sound sheep make, and the "lowing" is the deep sound cattle make. A monument is a memorial that Saul set up to his own glory.

Samuel speaks with Saul after the war against the Amalekites. God had commanded that everything be destroyed, but Saul said, "I have carried out the word of the LORD." The living animals showed the opposite. Samuel does not accuse him right away; he lets the evidence speak and lets Saul explain himself.

For today: saying "I already obeyed" is easy, but the facts show the truth. Let us ask God to make us honest enough to recognize where we have obeyed only halfway, without excuses or cover-ups.
exp.3:14:
Now Eli was ninety-eight years old, and he could no longer see anything. The phrase "his gaze was fixed" describes an old man whose eyes had grown unable to see, so that he sat staring at nothing. He was a blind old man, sitting by the side of the road.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. It explains why Eli could not see the messenger and had to hear everything. Eli was waiting for news of the battle against the Philistines, and his heart trembled for the ark of God. Soon he would be told that his sons had died and that the ark had been captured.

For today: even though we cannot see what is coming, we can care more about what belongs to God than about what belongs to us. And while we wait, it is good to ask God for strength to receive bad news with faith and not only with fear.
exp.29:17:
This verse says that David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail.

The verse itself says that David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives. The word "including" in the verse tells us that the wives were part of what was taken, and David's recovery covered them along with everything else.

The narrator then tells what happened at Ziklag. The Amalekites burned the city and carried off the families of David and his men. David was deeply distressed, since his own men were talking about stoning him. Even so, he strengthened himself in the Lord, asked God what to do, and set out after the enemy. God assured him that he would recover everything.

For today: when everything seems lost, do not freeze or give in to despair. Seek God first in prayer, ask for direction, and then take the steps He shows you. He can restore what seemed to be lost.
exp.8:3:
This verse tells of the journey of Saul and his servant searching for his father's lost female donkeys. They went through the hill country of Ephraim, through the land of Shalishah, through the region of Shaalim, and through the land of Benjamin, and they did not find the donkeys. The phrase "female donkeys" refers to she-donkeys, and "find" means to come upon or locate. It was a long and tiring search that brought no result.

Context: the account is narrated by the author of the book, not by a character. Kish, Saul's father, had sent his son to look for the lost animals. Kingship is not yet mentioned here. Later, in this same search, Saul will meet the prophet Samuel. The exact locations are not known with certainty, but all of them lie in the central region of Israel.

For today: sometimes our efforts do not bear fruit, and we feel discouraged. This passage reminds us that God can use ordinary tasks, even those that seem like failures, to lead us to what He has prepared. Keep faithfully doing what is your responsibility and trust in God.
exp.13:38:
Saúl makes a solemn oath in God's name. The phrase "As surely as the LORD lives" is an oath, meaning "as surely as God lives." He promises that whoever has sinned must die, even if it is his own son, Jonathan. "He must die" means "he will certainly die, without exception." No one among the troops said anything, because they all knew what had happened, or at least they feared to speak.

King Saúl is speaking. God had not answered him when he asked whether he should pursue the Philistines, and Saúl concluded that someone had sinned. He did not know that Jonathan, without knowing the order, had tasted honey. Earlier, Saúl had forbidden anyone to eat that day. Many see in this a hasty oath, although the text does not fully explain it.

Before demanding justice from others, it is wise to think carefully about what we promise and to listen to God with humility. Let us be just, but also prudent and merciful, beginning with our own household.
exp.20:13:
Here Achish, king of Gath, speaks to his servants and says they can see that the man is insane. He asks them why they have brought him to him. "Insane" means that he is not in his right mind, that he has lost his grip on reality.

David was fleeing from King Saul and came to Gath, a Philistine city, looking for refuge. His servants recognized him, and Achish had him in his hands. David felt great fear and pretended to be insane: he scribbled on the doors and let saliva run down his beard. So Achish, the one speaking here, dismissed him as harmless and let him go. Some think this episode inspired Psalm 34, although that is interpreted in different ways.

For today: David was afraid and did not hide it. When you are afraid, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Be honest with God, ask him for wisdom, and trust that he can take care of you even in difficult situations.
exp.15:12:
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed David in the presence of his brothers. Anointing means pouring oil over someone to set them apart for a task. From that day on, the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David and remained with him. Then Samuel set out and went back to his home in Ramah.

God had rejected Saul as king, and he sent Samuel to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, to choose another. David, the youngest, was tending the sheep, and no one took him into account. The text presents this as a contrast with Saul, from whom the Spirit had departed. How that departure happened, the text does not explain further.

God often calls people whom others overlook, and he shapes their character over time. If today you feel small or ignored, remember that God looks at the heart. Be faithful in the simple things, as David was with the sheep.
exp.3:10:
This verse records two terrible blows to Israel on the same day: the Philistines captured the ark of God, and Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died. "Was captured" means that the enemy seized it. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among his people.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts the events plainly. Earlier, the Philistines gathered courage to fight hard and defeated Israel. The Israelites had brought the ark into battle as if it were a charm for victory, but they had not turned back to God. Eli's sons, moreover, were corrupt priests.

For today: we cannot treat sacred things as if they were a talisman to obtain what we want. God asks for a sincere heart, one that repents and obeys him, rather than symbols or rituals.
exp.9:25:
Samuel sent the people away, and each one went back to his home. Saul also went to his home in Gibeah, his town. The men of valor whose hearts God had touched went with him. The word here most likely refers not to a formal army but to people who were strong and faithful.

The narrator tells what happened after Samuel presented Saul as king at Mizpah and explained the rules of the kingdom. God moves some to support him, but soon others look down on him. So we see that Saul's authority began with both support and opposition.

For today: if God gives you a task, do not depend only on everyone's approval. Thank those whom God moves to help you, serve with humility, and do not despair over criticism. Ask God to touch your heart and the hearts of others to do his will.
exp.7:19:
Here the people of Israel insist on having a king. They say they want to be "like all the other nations," that is, like the other peoples around them. They expect the king to rule over them, go out before them, and fight their battles. The phrase "all the other nations" here refers to the peoples or nations around them.

The people speak, through their leaders, before the prophet Samuel. He had just warned them what it would cost to have a king: he would take their sons, their lands, and their goods. Even so, they would not listen. God had already shown them that he himself was their King and their defender, so asking for a king like the other peoples showed a lack of trust. Even so, God grants them what they ask.

For today: it is easy to want to live like everyone else and to seek security in something visible. Before deciding, ask yourself whether you are trusting in God or merely copying others.
exp.13:33:
Saul tells the troops to spread out among the people and give this order: each man must bring his ox or his sheep to be slaughtered right there, and then they may eat. In this way they can eat without sinning against the LORD, that is, without eating meat with the blood still in it. The words that need explaining are "scatter," which means "spread out," and "slaughter," which means "kill the animal." That night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there.

Saul, king of Israel, speaks after a battle against the Philistines. The people were worn out and hungry, and they killed animals on the ground and ate the meat with the blood. The law of Moses forbade eating blood (Leviticus 17:10-14). Saul uses a large stone to kill the animals in the proper way, and then he builds an altar.

God cares about how we obey, even in simple things, and not only about what we do. When we notice that we have gone astray, let us correct ourselves with humility and not ignore the mistake.
exp.11:13:
He says that if the people and their king fear the Lord, serve him, obey his voice, and do not rebel against his command, then all will be well as they follow the Lord their God. "Fear" here means to respect and honor God with reverence. "Rebel" refers to those who refuse to obey. The closing words can be understood as "you will follow the Lord your God" or as "all will be well"; the verse is brief and can be read both ways.

Samuel speaks, now an old man, at an assembly in Gilgal, when Saul has just been confirmed as king. Israel had asked for a king, partly out of fear of Nahash the Ammonite. Samuel reminds them that their true King is still God and that the new king must also obey him.

For today: it does not matter who leads us or how secure we feel; what is essential is to keep a heart attentive to God. Today you can read his Word and ask him for help to obey it in a concrete decision.
exp.26:9:
This verse tells how King Achish asked David, "What have you raided today?" David answered that they had raided the Negev of Judah, the Negev of Jerahmeel, or the Negev of the Kenites. Here "raided" means carried out armed attacks, and "Negev" is the southern region of the land.

David was living among the Philistines, fleeing from Saul. Achish had given him the city of Ziklag. In reality, David was attacking peoples who were enemies of Israel, but he led Achish to believe that he was attacking his own people. So Achish trusted him. The text recounts this without approving or condemning the deception; the reader should notice it carefully.

For today: the Bible sometimes shows the failings of its heroes. Let us be honest and seek God with integrity, rather than holding onto the truth with half-measures or deceit.
exp.19:29:
Saul was filled with rage against his son Jonathan. His anger flared up, and he lashed out with a harsh insult, calling Jonathan a son of a perverse and rebellious woman. That insult also reflected badly on Jonathan's mother. Saul told him that by taking David's side, he was bringing shame on himself and on the mother who bore him.

Saul spoke at the new moon feast. David had not come to the king's table, and Jonathan had given an explanation for his absence. Saul, driven by jealousy and fear of losing the throne, already saw David as an enemy. That is why he erupts against his son.

For today: sometimes the pressure comes from someone in authority, even from within your own family. Jonathan did not answer with insults but kept defending what was right. Ask God for calm and courage to remain loyal to what is right.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that Elkanah gave Hannah a double portion of the offering, because he loved her. But Hannah could not have children: the text states that the Lord had closed her womb. The Hebrew behind this wording is debated, and some scholars read it as a special portion of honor rather than a literal double share.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who presents a family that goes up every year to Shiloh to worship. He wants to show Elkanah's affection and, at the same time, Hannah's deep pain, which sets up what follows in the story.

For today: a gift or a kind gesture helps, but it does not take away the pain of the one who is suffering. Accompany others with patience and listen to someone who is going through grief. And if the pain is yours, bring it to God honestly, as Hannah will do.
exp.18:20:
This verse tells that Saul learned what had happened to his first messengers and sent others, and they also began to prophesy. Then he tried again and sent a third group, and the same thing happened to them. The phrase "was reported to Saul" is the wording of the verse above, and "prophesy" here means praising or speaking under the influence of God's Spirit.

This is part of the story of when Saul pursued David out of jealousy. David had taken refuge with Samuel in Naioth, in Ramah. Saul wanted to capture him, but God acted upon his men and prevented it. Scholars understand this episode as God's protection over David.

For today: human plans against God's purpose do not always prevail. If you are in the middle of an injustice, trust that God can care for you in unexpected ways. And examine your own heart: do not keep insisting on something that God is clearly closing to you.
exp.16:5:
This verse describes more of Goliath's battle gear. He wore bronze armor on his legs to protect his shins. He also carried a javelin of bronze slung over his shoulder, a weapon he could throw or keep ready for close fighting.

The narrator of the book describes Goliath, the Philistine champion, just before he challenges Israel. He wants the reader to notice how imposing he was: his size, his armor and his weapons. This helps us understand why the whole army of Israel was afraid to face him.

Today, we sometimes face problems that seem enormous and well armed. This passage reminds us not to measure everything by appearances. David, later on, trusted in God and not in visible strength. When you feel fear, pray and remember that God is greater than your giant.
exp.13:26:
He says that Jonathan had not heard that his father, King Saul, had bound the army with an oath. So he reached out the tip of the staff in his hand, dipped it into a honeycomb, and brought his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened, meaning he regained strength and his tiredness left him. The word "however" in the verse, and the phrase "bound... with the oath," show that the people had sworn under a solemn vow.

This is the account of a battle against the Philistines. Saul, without thinking it through carefully, forbade eating until evening, and the people were exhausted. Jonathan, who was not present when the order was given, ate without knowing it. Afterward he himself judges that his father's order was harmful.

For today: before imposing strict rules or vows, let us consider how they will affect other people. Religious zeal without wisdom can wear people out instead of helping them.
exp.0:20:
Elkanah, Hannah's husband, went up with his whole household to Shiloh to offer the sacrifice to the LORD that they made every year. He also set out to keep his vow, that is, a promise he had made to God. The verse does not say more about who this man was beyond the fact that he was Hannah's husband and the head of the household.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who describes how family life continued after Samuel was born. Hannah stayed at home with the small child, because she wanted to take him to the sanctuary once he was weaned. Elkanah respected her decision. We do not know for certain what Elkanah's vow was; the text does not explain it.

For today: God values constant faithfulness, even in everyday life. Keeping what we have promised, and respecting with love the decisions of those we care about, strengthens faith and family.
exp.18:14:
When Saul learned that David was supposedly ill, he sent the messengers back with a harsher order: bring David to him in his bed so that Saul could kill him. The bed was likely a couch, so David would have been carried in on it. Saul no longer cared about David's condition. His desire to kill him was stronger than any excuse.

The speaker is King Saul, full of jealousy and resentment toward David. Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, had put an idol in the bed to give David time to escape. Saul insists on the order, not knowing he has been deceived.

For today: jealousy and resentment, if not surrendered to God, grow and make us hard and blind. Ask God to heal your heart before envy decides for you.
exp.24:25:
Here Abigail tells David that the LORD himself has held him back from bloodshed and from avenging himself with his own hand. She swears by the living LORD and by David's own life. And she wishes that David's enemies end up like Nabal, that is, under the judgment of God. "Has held you back" means stopped you, and "those who seek harm for my lord" means people who are trying to do him harm.

Abigail is the wife of Nabal, a foolish man who insulted David and refused him food. David was going out with his armed men to kill Nabal's household. Abigail goes out to meet them with provisions, humbles herself, and tries to prevent a tragedy. She sees the hand of God in that meeting.

When someone wrongs us, it is better not to take revenge with our own hands. We can stop, listen to wise counsel, and let God bring justice in his own time.
exp.14:24:
Saul asks Samuel to come back with him so that he can worship the LORD. The word "worship" here means that Saul wants to give honor to God. His request, "return with me," is a plea that Samuel not leave him and that he come along.

The speaker is Saul, the first king of Israel. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but he did not fully obey and excused himself by saying he feared the people. Samuel has just told him that God has rejected him as king. Saul admits his sin, but he seems more concerned about looking good before the people than about a change of heart. Interpreters debate how sincere his repentance was.

For today: worshiping God does not replace obedience. Before seeking ceremonies or appearances, it is wise to honestly acknowledge our failures and turn to God with our whole heart.
exp.12:2:
Jonathan, Saul's son, attacked the Philistine outpost at Geba and defeated the enemy troops stationed there to guard the place. The Philistines heard about it, and Saul blew the ram's horn throughout the land, calling the Hebrews, that is, the Israelites, to hear.

The narrator tells how a war against the Philistines began, the people who held power over Israel. Saul was the first king, and here he calls the people together. The following verses show that Saul received the credit, though Jonathan was the one who struck the blow. Afterward the Philistines gathered a huge army, and the people were filled with fear.

For today: taking a brave step can bring a bigger reaction than expected. Before acting, let us pray, ask God for direction, and trust that He sustains the one who obeys Him, even when the path becomes hard.
exp.6:11:
Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen. He named it Ebenezer, which means "stone of help." He said, "Thus far the LORD has helped us."

The narrator tells what Samuel did. Samuel was the prophet and judge of Israel. The people had turned away from their idols and gathered at Mizpah. When the Philistines attacked, God thundered and confused them, and Israel won. Samuel raised the stone as a reminder that the victory came from God, not from Israel's weapons.

For today: make your own "stone of help." Write down or remember the times God has helped you. Looking back with gratitude strengthens confidence to face what comes next.
exp.29:6:
Here David asks the priest Abiathar to bring him the ephod. The verse simply has David making the request, with no word that carries the sense of "please." The ephod was a sacred garment of the priest, and it was used to seek God's answer. Abiathar brought it to him.

David is speaking in a very hard moment. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the women and children of the families. His own men, full of grief, were talking about stoning him. But David strengthened himself in the Lord and, before acting, wanted to ask him what to do. Scholars believe the ephod was used to receive God's answer, though it is not known with certainty how it worked.

When you are under pressure or afraid, do not act first on impulse. Seek God in prayer and in his Word, and ask him for direction before taking the next step.
exp.2:9:
It says that God came and stood there and called Samuel by name twice, as He had before. The word "stood" in the verse matches the idea of standing still and present in the verse. This time Samuel answered as Eli had taught him: "Speak, for Your servant is listening." That is, he was ready to hear and obey.

Samuel was a boy who served in the sanctuary under the priest Eli. In those days, the word of God was rare. Samuel did not yet know the voice of the Lord, so Eli, already old, understood that it was God and gave him the right instruction. Later God would give him a hard message about Eli's house.

For today: before asking God for anything, learn to be quiet and to listen. Open the Bible with a willing heart and say: "Speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening."
exp.2:11:
God says he will carry out against Eli everything he has spoken about his family, from beginning to end. "Carry out" means to set in motion and make it happen. The phrase "from beginning to end" means that God will both start and finish: he will not leave his word half done.

The LORD speaks, calling the young Samuel at night in the sanctuary at Shiloh. Earlier, a man of God had already warned Eli (1 Samuel 2:27-36). Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, abused their priestly office, and Eli did not correct them firmly. Now God confirms the judgment through Samuel.

For today: God takes correction and responsibility seriously, especially for those who lead others. If something in your home, church, or work needs to be corrected, do not put it off. And if God speaks to you through his Word, respond with Samuel's attitude: "Speak, for your servant is listening."
exp.2:10:
God tells Samuel that he is about to do something in Israel that will make the ears of everyone who hears it tingle. To tingle means to ring or sound sharply, the way shocking news can leave people stunned. The phrase points to something that will shake everyone who hears about it.

The Lord speaks just after calling Samuel, a young man serving in the house of the Lord alongside the priest Eli. Samuel answers with readiness: "Speak, for your servant is listening." What God tells him next is a judgment on Eli's house, because Eli's sons were sinning gravely and he did not restrain them.

For today: God speaks clearly, and sometimes his message is uncomfortable. Let us ask for a heart willing to listen to him, even when he confronts us, and act in time on what we need to correct, especially in our own family.
exp.13:13:
This verse tells of the first assault against the Philistines. Jonathan and his armor-bearer, just the two of them, struck down about twenty men. This happened on a small piece of ground, roughly half an acre, a field-sized area that the older text described by how much land a yoke of oxen could plow in a day.

The narrator then describes what followed Jonathan's climb up to the Philistine outpost. He had said that the LORD was giving them into Israel's hands. Israel was at a disadvantage, short of weapons, and Jonathan acted in faith, without telling his father Saul. This first attack set off the panic described next.

For today: sometimes God uses a small, brave step to open the way to something much greater. We do not need to have every resource; we need to trust God and take the step within our reach, with humility and good counsel.
exp.29:1:
The passage says that the Amalekites had taken the women and everyone else in Ziklag captive, both young and old. They did not kill anyone; they carried them off as they went on their way. "Captive" means taken as prisoners, and the verse simply tells us that the raiders left with the people they had seized.

No one is speaking here; it is the narrator of the book who tells what happened. David and his men returned home after being away and found the city burned and their families gone. It was a terrible blow, and the Bible says they wept until they had no strength left. The text does not explain why God allowed this, and it is not right to invent a reason.

For today: when a loss leaves you without strength, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Weeping is honest. But do not stay there: the story goes on, and David ended up seeking strength in God. Bring your pain to Him in prayer.
exp.9:4:
He says that Saul would come to Gibeah of God, where the Philistines had an outpost, meaning a military post of the enemy. As Saul approached the city, he would meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place, with harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres going before them, and they would be prophesying, that is, speaking and praising under the influence of God.

Samuel speaks to Saul after anointing him as the first king of Israel. He gives him concrete signs, one after another, to confirm that God had really chosen him. This is the third sign. Scholars do not agree on every detail of how that group prophesying worked, but here it is shown as something connected with music and worship.

God knows that we doubt, and sometimes he gives us confirmations so that we can move forward with confidence. If he has called you to something, walk step by step, attentive to his guidance, and do not expect to have everything clear from the beginning.
exp.1:25:
And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man.

This verse says that Samuel, while still a boy or young man, kept growing both in size and in character. The phrase "continued to grow" means that he kept advancing, improving, and making progress. He did so in a way that pleased both God and the people around him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He sets Samuel in contrast with the sons of the priest Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, who abused their position and led the people into sin. Eli rebuked them, but they did not listen. Afterward, a messenger of God arrives with a judgment against Eli's house.

For today: growing is not only a matter of getting older. We can ask God to help us advance in honesty, humility, and service, so that our lives are good before Him and also before others.
exp.7:20:
Samuel listened to all the words of the people and repeated them in the hearing of the LORD. That is, he brought their words to God directly, in prayer. Here the wording is "in the hearing of the LORD," and it means that Samuel placed their request before God himself.

Before this moment, Samuel had warned the people how a king would act, but they would not listen. They wanted a king so that they could be like all the nations around them. Samuel was hurt, for he felt that they were rejecting him, but he did not argue any further; he brought the matter to God. Afterward, God gave him an answer.

For today: when something hurts you or worries you, especially if others do not listen to you, tell it first to God with complete sincerity. He listens, and praying before you react helps you act with more calm and wisdom.
exp.8:19:
Samuel tells Saul not to worry anymore about the donkeys that were lost, because they have been found. Then he asks him a question: who is it that all of Israel desires? And he answers: it is you, and all your father's family. "Do not worry" means the same as "do not be concerned," and "three days ago" refers to the three days just past.

Saul was looking for the lost donkeys and came to Samuel, the seer, or prophet. God had already told Samuel that Saul would be the first king. That is why Samuel speaks this way. Some understand "all the desire of Israel" to mean the people's longing to have a king. Saul, surprised, answers with humility.

God can use ordinary things, even a search for lost animals, to lead us toward his purpose. Perhaps today something small worries you, or you feel that you are not worth much. Trust that God sees further than you do, and is attentive to your path.
exp.22:12:
This verse tells that David left Keilah together with his men, about six hundred of them. They kept moving from place to place, never staying fixed in any one spot. When Saul heard that David had escaped, he declined to go out after him to Keilah. The message that reached Saul is what the story calls the news, and the statement that he declined to go forth means that he called off his journey.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book. Before this, David had asked God whether Saul would come and whether the people of Keilah would hand him over, even though he had rescued them from the Philistines. God told him yes. David obeyed that warning and left in time.

For today: when God warns us of a danger, whether through his Word, through prayer, or through good counsel, it is wise to act with prudence and not simply wait for things to resolve on their own.
exp.29:4:
This verse says that David's two wives had also been taken prisoner. One was Ahinoam of Jezreel, and the other was Abigail, who had been the widow of Nabal of Carmel. The word "captive" means that they were seized and carried away by force.

The narrator tells what happened in Ziklag, the town where David and his men lived. While they were away, the Amalekites burned it and carried off all the families. David lost his wives and his loved ones too, and his own men, overcome with grief, spoke of stoning him.

When everything seems lost, we do not have to pretend to be strong. David wept until he had no strength left, but afterward he sought God and found strength in Him. We can weep honestly and then turn to God in prayer, asking Him for direction.
exp.2:5:
God calls Samuel a second time. The boy gets up, goes to Eli, and says, "Here I am, for you have called me." Eli replies, "My son, I did not call. Go back and lie down."

Samuel was a young man who served Eli, the priest, at the sanctuary in Shiloh. Eli was already old. Samuel thought the voice was Eli's, because, as the text says, he did not yet know the Lord personally or had not yet received his word. So he runs to obey his teacher.

For today: Samuel responded quickly and willingly, even though he did not understand what was happening. Sometimes God speaks to us in ways we do not recognize right away. We can cultivate an attentive and willing heart, and ask for help from people with more experience in the faith, as Samuel did with Eli.
exp.15:19:
Here the account tells us that Jesse, David's father, prepared a gift: a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat. He sent it all to Saul with his son David. The phrase "sent them to Saul" describes what Jesse did, and the words "with his son David" mean that David carried the gift himself.

The account describes what happened after Saul asked for David to be brought to him, because a servant had recommended him as a brave and prudent musician. It was customary to bring a gift when appearing before a king. Jesse acts with respect and humility. The text does not explain his motives any further.

For today: God often begins great things with simple gestures. David came before the king with bread, wine, and a young goat, not with pride. Serve with humility in small things, and let God open the doors.
exp.10:11:
The passage tells us that, after the victory, the people came to Samuel with a demand. They remembered the men who had earlier questioned Saul's right to be king, and they asked, "Who said that Saul should not reign over us?" Now they wanted those men brought to them so they could be killed.

The speakers are the Israelites, filled with excitement because Saul had just rescued Jabesh from the Ammonites. Earlier, some had looked down on Saul (1 Samuel 10:27). The people wanted to punish those critics, but Saul stopped them and said that day belonged to the salvation God had given.

For today: when God gives us a victory, the temptation can be to settle accounts with those who doubted us. Saul shows us another way: give God the glory, forgive, and seek peace instead of revenge.
exp.0:25:
Hannah approaches the priest Eli and reminds him who she is. The phrase "as surely as you live" was a way of speaking with respect, something like "I assure you by your life." She says that she is the woman who years earlier stood there beside him, praying to the LORD. The words "my lord" are a courteous form of address.

It is Hannah speaking, who for a long time was unable to have children. At Shiloh she had prayed with great sorrow and promised to dedicate to God the son she was given. Now Samuel has already been weaned, and she comes to fulfill her promise. Eli had seen her pray, but he probably did not remember her well, so she introduces herself.

For today: God hears our prayers, and it is good to remember and give thanks for what he has given us. If we have promised something to God, let us seek to keep it with sincerity and gratitude.
exp.5:5:
This verse is a question that serves as a warning. The speakers are telling the Philistine people: do not be stubborn like the Egyptians and Pharaoh. "Harden the heart" means refusing to obey or to acknowledge God. When God afflicted them, the Egyptians in the end sent the Israelites out so they could go on their way.

The speakers are the Philistine priests and diviners. They had captured the ark of the LORD, and since then they had suffered plagues. Now they advise returning it with an offering, so as not to repeat Egypt's stubbornness. Interpreters debate whether they truly believed or only acted out of fear, but they knew the story of the exodus.

For today: when God corrects us, it is better to listen quickly and change course than to resist until we suffer more. A humble heart saves much pain.
exp.15:21:
Here Saul sends word to Jesse, David's father. He asks that David be allowed to remain in his service. He says, "I am pleased with him," meaning that he likes David and holds him in high regard. The phrase "sent word to Jesse" simply means that he sent a message.

Here King Saul is speaking. His spirit was tormented by an evil spirit, and his servants had recommended David to play the harp. David arrived with a gift from his father, and Saul valued him greatly. It is striking that God had already anointed David in secret, and now he enters the palace through a humble door: serving.

For today: God often prepares people in small places and through service. Do with a good attitude what is at hand today, for there God may be shaping your character.
exp.12:10:
"What have you done?" Samuel asks. Saul gives three reasons for his action: the troops were deserting him, Samuel did not arrive at the appointed time, and the Philistines were gathering at Michmash. The phrase "the troops were deserting me" means that the soldiers were leaving him. The "appointed time" refers to the seven days that had been agreed upon.

Samuel had told Saul to wait seven days at Gilgal so that Samuel himself could offer the sacrifices (1 Samuel 10:8). Saul, pressed by fear, offered the burnt offering without waiting. Samuel arrived just afterward and confronted him. Saul does not confess his mistake; he makes excuses.

For today: when waiting becomes hard and the pressure grows, it is tempting to act on our own. Obeying God, even when it seems that everything is falling apart, is worth more than any quick solution. And when we fail, it is better to admit it sincerely than to justify ourselves.
exp.8:6:
Saul agrees with his servant's idea of going to see the man of God, but something practical worries him: they have nothing to bring him. The bread in their bags is gone, and there is no gift to take. Saul asks, "What do we have?"

Saul and his servant have been looking for their father Kish's lost donkeys for days. They no longer know where else to search. It was customary to bring a gift to the one you consulted, as a sign of respect. The servant suggests going to the man of God, who is Samuel, and finds a solution: he has a little silver.

For today: when we seek direction, it is good to acknowledge our need and ask for help from someone wise. And sometimes God uses ordinary people, like this servant, to give us a good idea.
exp.3:15:
This verse shows the moment a man runs in to bring news to Eli. He says he has just come from the battle and has barely managed to get away. Eli, already old and nearly blind, asks him gently: "What happened, my son?"

The man who speaks is a messenger from the tribe of Benjamin, who had come from the battlefield against the Philistines. Eli was waiting in anguish, because the ark of God had been taken into the battle. Eli was ninety-eight years old and could not see, so he depended on what others told him. Soon he would receive the worst news of his life.

For today: when someone is waiting for difficult news, they need patience and closeness. We can be people who listen with calm and compassion, and also learn to hand our fears over to God before we know what is coming.
exp.24:5:
Ask yourself how you greet someone before making a request. David's messengers are told to open with a wish for good things: "Long life to you, and peace to you and to your house and to all that belongs to you." That is much like saying, "May you have life, health, and well-being." Peace here means far more than the absence of quarrels. It means complete well-being, and the wish reaches Nabal, his household, and everything he owns.

David is on the run from Saul and living in the wilderness with his men. Meanwhile, those men have protected Nabal's flocks, and Nabal is a wealthy man. It is now sheep-shearing time, a season of feasting and plenty. David sends ten young men to ask Nabal for help, and they make the request courteously. With this greeting, David opens his request in a respectful way. Later in the story, we see that Nabal answers with contempt.

For today: before asking for something or raising a difficult matter, begin by sincerely wishing the other person well. A kind approach does not guarantee a good answer, as we see here, but it helps us act with dignity and peace.
exp.7:6:
God tells Samuel to listen to what the people say and give them what they ask for. But he makes clear that it is not Samuel they have rejected; they have rejected God himself as their king.

The Lord speaks with Samuel, the prophet and judge. Samuel was already old, and his sons did not follow God's ways. Israel's leaders asked for a king like all the other nations. Samuel was hurt by this, and he prayed. God answers him that the root problem was a lack of trust in him, something that had been building for a long time.

For today: sometimes we want to copy what everyone else does, instead of trusting God's guidance. Before asking for something, it is wise to ask ourselves whether, deep down, we are turning away from trusting him.
exp.14:23:
Saul admits that he sinned. He says that he transgressed the Lord's commandment and Samuel's instructions. He explains that he was afraid of the people and gave in to their voice. Then he asks for forgiveness. The phrase "I have transgressed the LORD's commandment" means he did not carry out what God had commanded, and "I obeyed their voice" means he gave in to what the people were asking for.

Samuel has just rebuked Saul. God had told him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but Saul and the people kept the best of the spoil. Saul had made excuses before. Now he acknowledges his wrong, although in the verses that follow he seems more concerned with how he looks before the people than with any real change. Some think his repentance was only partly sincere; the text does not make this entirely clear.

Obeying God can cost us the approval of others. If you feel pressure from your group today, ask God for the courage to obey him first, and when you fail, admit it honestly, without excuses.
exp.13:32:
Here someone reports to Saul that the troops are sinning against the Lord by eating meat with the blood still in it. The phrase "broken faith" in the verse means they went against a known law they were bound to keep. Saul orders a large stone to be rolled over to him at once, so that it can later be used as the place where the animals are slaughtered.

The Israelite soldiers were exhausted after chasing the Philistines. They threw themselves on the spoil and killed animals on the ground, without letting the blood drain out. The law of Moses forbade eating blood (Leviticus 17:10-14), because the life is in it. Those speaking are one of the people, who reports, and Saul, who reacts and corrects. Interpreters do not agree on how much genuine zeal there was in Saul.

For today: even in the middle of tiredness or haste, let us not allow need to make us neglect what God says. And when someone points out a mistake to us, let us correct it promptly.
exp.14:3:
Saul summoned the troops and counted them at Telaim. The word "counted" here means that he reviewed them and took stock of their numbers. There were 200,000 foot soldiers, and 10,000 men of Judah, numbered separately.

Samuel had passed on to Saul a command from God against the Amalekites, because they had opposed Israel. It is a hard passage, which must be understood within that time and that special commandment. Telaim was probably in the south, but its exact location is uncertain. Saul gathers the army to carry out what God asked.

Having resources and organization is good, but what matters most is obeying God completely. Before we trust in our numbers, plans, or strength, let us ask ourselves whether we are truly listening and sincerely following what He is actually telling us.
exp.4:3:
The next morning the Philistines got up early and found Dagon, their god, fallen face down on the ground in front of the ark of the LORD. This time the idol was broken: its head and both of its hands had been broken off and were lying on the threshold, and only the torso was left. The threshold is the entrance of the doorway.

The narrator tells what happened after the Philistines captured Israel's ark and placed it in the temple of Dagon, as a sign of victory over the God of Israel. Dagon was a god greatly honored by them. The text shows that the LORD is not just one god among others, and that he is not defeated even when his ark is in enemy hands.

Today we can remember that nothing and no one takes the place of God. If something in my life competes with Him, it is better to surrender it to Him, because only God stands firm.
exp.8:0:
This verse introduces Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin. He is described as "a powerful man," a phrase that can mean brave, but also influential or of good standing. His ancestors are traced back through Abiel, Zeror, Becorath and Aphiah, as was customary to show a person's family line.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. After the story of Samuel and the people's request for a king, the Bible begins to introduce the man who will become Israel's first king. It does not yet speak of Saul, but of his father and his family. This prepares the account that follows.

God often begins important things in humble places, within an ordinary family, without anyone noticing. Today we can remember that our home and our daily life also matter to God, even when they seem small.
exp.13:21:
This verse tells us that other Israelites, who had been hiding in the hill country of Ephraim out of fear of the Philistines, heard that the enemy was fleeing. Then they came out of their hiding places and joined the battle, pressing hard after the enemy as they ran.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonathan had bravely attacked the Philistine camp, and God caused confusion among them, so that they began to strike one another. Seeing this change, even the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines switched sides to join Israel. The text then says that it was the LORD who saved Israel that day.

For today: sometimes fear keeps us hidden, and we only move forward when we see that God is already at work. Let us ask him for the courage to take the step and join others in what he is already doing, without waiting for everything to be perfect.
exp.7:21:
God tells Samuel to listen to the people and appoint a king for them. "Listen to their voice" means "do what they ask." Then Samuel sends the men of Israel away and tells each one to go back to his own city.

The elders of Israel had asked for a king so that they could be like all the nations, that is, like the neighboring peoples. Samuel was troubled, but God explained to him that the people were rejecting Him as their King. God allows their request, although Samuel had earlier warned them what a human king would be like. Some see here a divine concession, not God's ideal plan.

Today, we sometimes want to copy what most people do instead of trusting God. Before asking for something, let us ask ourselves whether we really need it or only want to be like everyone else. God may allow what we ask for, but He also lets us live with its consequences.
exp.17:23:
This verse says that Saul's servants went back to the king and told him what David had said. The servants are the attendants or helpers of the king. In the words they brought back, David had answered that he was a poor man of little importance to be the king's son-in-law.

Saul was jealous of David and afraid of him. So he sent his servants to speak with David privately, as if they were doing it out of affection. In reality, Saul was looking for a plan that would lead the Philistines to kill David. The servants only carry the message back and forth.

For today: let us be careful with the words we carry from one person to another. We can be honest messengers and yet, without realizing it, help the plans of someone who wants to do harm. Before we repeat something, let us ask God for wisdom.
exp.29:19:
It says that David also took the sheep and the cattle, meaning the flocks and herds. His men would drive them out ahead of the other livestock, and they would call out, "This is David's plunder!" "Plunder" means what is taken from an enemy after a victory.

David and his men had just pursued the Amalekites, who had raided Ziklag and taken captive their families. God gave them the victory, and they recovered everything. This livestock seems to be extra plunder from the Amalekites. The text does not make clear who was calling out, but it was probably David's men, who acknowledged him as their leader. Right away a dispute arises over how to divide it.

For today: when God gives you a victory or a blessing, do not see it as yours alone. Recognize that it is a gift and share it generously, especially with those who could not help you.
exp.10:7:
Saul counted the army at Bezek. The verse says there were 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah. Some scholars take these numbers literally, while others think the word for "thousand" could have referred to smaller groups or military units. The exact meaning is not known for certain.

The story tells how Saul gathered the people to rescue Jabesh-gilead, a city threatened by Nahash the Ammonite. Saul sent out pieces of oxen as an urgent call to action. The people responded together, and the count shows that many came out in great numbers, including the men of Judah, the southern tribe.

For today: when someone suffers injustice or serious need, we should not simply stand by and watch. Let us ask God for courage and unity, and help one another together, each with what we have.
exp.29:18:
It says that David brought back every single thing the Amalekites had taken. Nothing was missing, whether young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder. The verse of "plunder" is the goods the raiders had seized, and "brought back" means that David got it all returned to his own people.

The narrator tells this after the Amalekites burned Ziklag and carried off the families of David and his men. David was distressed, since his people even spoke of stoning him. Even so, he strengthened himself in the Lord, asked him what to do, and God told him to pursue them with the assurance that he would recover everything (verse 8). This verse shows that the promise was fulfilled completely.

When everything seems lost, we can do what David did: seek God before we act. We will not always recover what was lost in the same way, but God remains faithful and knows how to guide us step by step. Ask him for direction today.
exp.13:37:
Saul calls the leaders of the troops to come forward. He asks them to investigate and find out how a sin occurred that day. The phrase "come here" in the verse above is a direct call for the leaders to step closer, and "the leaders of the troops" means those with the most authority over the army.

Saul speaks after God did not answer his inquiry about pursuing the Philistines. He takes that silence as a sign that there is a hidden sin. Without knowing it, Jonathan had eaten honey, breaking an oath that Saul had imposed on the army. Some think Saul acts with sincere zeal, but his hasty oath was also a mistake.

When God seems silent, it is worth examining our hearts with humility. But let us be careful not to rush to judge others, and let us first acknowledge our own hasty decisions.
exp.22:10:
David asks God two questions: will the people of Keilah hand him over to Saul, and will Saul really come down, as David has heard? He asks politely and humbly: "O LORD, God of Israel, please tell your servant." God gives a clear answer: "He will."

David speaks with God through the ephod, which the priest Abiathar carried in order to inquire of the Lord. Scholars do not agree on exactly how it worked. David had just saved Keilah from the Philistines, but Saul was pursuing him and wanted to catch him there. David needed to know what to do.

For today: before deciding something difficult, do not follow only your fears or assumptions. Bring your questions to God with honesty, seek his direction in prayer and in his Word, and act wisely when he shows you the way.
exp.24:11:
After being turned away by Nabal, David's men turned around and went back the way they had come. When they arrived, they relayed to David all the words Nabal had spoken. Their note has been removed here, since the wording about turning and the "young men" comes from the translation you read and is not part of the verse as you see it.

David and his men lived in the wilderness and had looked after Nabal's flocks without charging anything. David asked for some food during a feast day, but Nabal answered with scorn and mockery. The men simply carry out their task: they bring back the full message. What follows shows that David reacted with great anger.

For today: when someone offends us, we can pause before acting. David let anger take hold of him after hearing those words. Let us ask God for calm so that we may respond with wisdom and not with revenge.
exp.23:11:
David shows Saul a piece of his robe, the "edge," meaning the border or hem of the cloth. David cut it off when he could have killed Saul, but he did not harm him. "You are hunting my life" means that Saul is chasing David like prey in order to kill him. David asks Saul to recognize that there is no wrongdoing or betrayal in him.

David speaks with Saul, the king of Israel, who was pursuing him out of jealousy. David had hidden in a cave, and Saul went in without knowing he was there. His men kept urging him to kill Saul, but David respected Saul as the one anointed by the Lord, that is, chosen by God to be king.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not answer with revenge. Do what is right, speak the truth with respect, and leave the judging to the Lord.
exp.21:3:
This verse tells that David left his parents in the care of the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the whole time David was in the stronghold. The word "left" here matches the wording of the verse above. The stronghold was a protected place, probably a refuge in the mountains.

David was running from King Saul, who wanted to kill him. With four hundred distressed men around him, he looked for a safe place for his parents. Moab had some connection to his family, since Ruth, his great-grandmother, came from there. Soon after, the prophet Gad told him to return to Judah, and David obeyed.

For today: when hard times come, care for your family and seek counsel, but stay attentive to God's guidance. David said he hoped to know what God would do with him. A temporary refuge should not become a place where we stay if God tells us to move forward.
exp.16:32:
Saul tells David that he cannot go out to fight the Philistine Goliath. He gives two reasons: David is "just a boy," and Goliath "has been a warrior from his youth," a soldier who has been experienced in battle since he was young. The word "cannot" means "is not able."

King Saul is speaking. The whole army of Israel was afraid of Goliath, who challenged them every day. David offers to fight, and Saul calls him, but he hesitates, because by human measure the difference seems enormous. His concern is understandable. What Saul does not yet see is David's trust in God, which appears in the following verse.

For today: sometimes others will tell us that something is too big for us, and they may be right if they measure only our own strength. Before you give up, remember how God has sustained you before, and ask him for courage and wisdom for the challenge you face.
exp.23:6:
David told his men that God would keep him from harming Saul. He calls Saul "my lord" and "the anointed of the LORD," that is, the king whom God had set apart with oil to rule. To "stretch out my hand" means to attack or do violence to someone.

David and his men were hiding from Saul, who was chasing him to kill him. Saul went into a cave without knowing that David was inside. The men saw in this a sign from God, but David only cut off the edge of Saul's robe, and afterward his conscience troubled him. Even though Saul was his enemy, David respected the place God had given him.

For today: even when we have the chance to take revenge, we can choose to trust God and not repay evil with evil. Sometimes the right thing is not the easiest thing, nor what others advise us to do.
exp.24:38:
When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has upheld my cause against the insult of Nabal and has kept his servant from doing evil. The LORD has brought Nabal's wickedness down on his own head." Then David sent word to Abigail, asking her to become his wife.

David is the one speaking. Nabal, a rich and hard man, refused him help and humiliated him. David was going to take revenge with violence, but Abigail calmed him with good sense. Ten days later Nabal died, and David saw in it the hand of God. The text tells the details of his marriage plainly, without giving further explanation.

For today: when someone wrongs you, do not take revenge. Leave your hurt in God's hands, for he is just, and trust that he cares for you and keeps you from doing something you would regret.
exp.27:7:
Saul takes off his royal clothes and puts on different clothes so that no one will recognize him. He goes at night, with two of his men, to the house of a woman in Endor. He asks her to consult a spirit for him and to bring up the one he names, a dead man he wants to speak with.

The story tells us that Saul is desperate. The Philistines are gathering against him, and God no longer answers him. Ironically, Saul himself had driven the mediums and spirit consulters out of the land, because God's law forbade such practices. Now he breaks his own command.
