For today: when we feel that God is silent, it is tempting to seek answers by paths that He has forbidden. It is better to keep seeking Him with humility and repentance, and to trust what He has already told us in His Word.
exp.19:13:
Jonathan makes a request of David: "As long as I live, treat me with the LORD's loving devotion, that I may not die." The word translated "loving devotion" means loyal love, a goodness that stays faithful to a covenant. The phrase "that I may not die" points to the sense of "if I die." The request is left open and carries on into the following verse.

Jonathan speaks with David, his friend, whom his father, King Saul, wants to kill. Jonathan suspects that David will be the next king, and so he asks him to look after his family. They had already made a covenant of friendship before God.

For today: when we promise loyalty to someone, that promise should not depend on circumstances. We can care for the family of a friend who is no longer with us, or faithfully keep the commitments we have made, thereby reflecting the faithfulness with which God treats us.
exp.17:27:
This verse says that Saul watched closely what was happening and reached a conclusion: God was with David, and his daughter Michal loved David. The phrase "the LORD was with David" means that God was accompanying him and blessing him. "Realized" means coming to understand something clearly after thinking it over.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book. Saul had set a trap for David: he asked for a hundred foreskins of Philistines, hoping they would kill him. But David came back with twice that number. Saul could no longer deny that God backed David. What follows shows that this did not lead him to surrender to God, but to fear him more.

For today: one can clearly see the hand of God and still resist it. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that recognizes his work in others without envy and that responds with confidence, not fear.
exp.17:13:
This verse says that David continued to succeed in everything he did, and that the LORD was with him. The phrase "continued to prosper" means that his affairs kept going well and turned out favorably. "His ways" here means his actions, his tasks, and the way he carried out his responsibilities. "The LORD was with him" means that God accompanied him and supported him.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks. Saul, the king, was afraid of David because he saw that the LORD was with David and had departed from Saul. For that reason he moved him away from his side and made him commander over a thousand soldiers. Even so, David continued to prosper, and this increased Saul's fear, while the people loved him.

For today: do your work and your responsibilities with honesty and care, even when others treat you unjustly. Ask God for wisdom and trust that He is with you, without depending on the applause of people.
exp.28:1:
The verse describes how the Philistine leaders marched out with their troops, organized into units of a hundred and of a thousand men. David and his men marched behind them, alongside Achish, the Philistine king of Gath. The "leaders" were the rulers or chiefs of the Philistine cities.

The narrator describes how the Philistines were preparing to fight against Israel. David was living among them because he was fleeing from Saul, and Achish trusted him. The other chiefs did not trust him, and that is why the account goes on to their protest. The text does not explain what David was thinking at that moment, so it is not wise to assume it.

For today: sometimes we find ourselves in situations where we do not know how to get out without compromising what we believe. This passage reminds us that God can open a way out that we did not expect. In the meantime, it is good to pray, to act with prudence, and not to give up hope.
exp.13:18:
While Saul was still talking with the priest, the commotion in the Philistine camp kept getting louder. So Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand." That is, "stop what you are doing."

Saul had noticed that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing. He asked for the ark of God so that he could seek the Lord through the priest. But when he saw the enemy's chaos growing, he cut off the inquiry and went into battle. Scholars understand this in different ways: as a practical urgency, or as Saul's impatience. The text does not make it clear.

For today: seeking God should not be a formality that we drop when we are in a hurry. Pray calmly, listen, and act in obedience, without letting haste or fear pull you away from Him.
exp.23:5:
This verse shows David's conscience at work. Even after he had only cut off a corner of Saul's robe, he felt a deep sense of guilt. In the Berean Standard Bible he speaks plainly: "The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the LORD's anointed." David understood that Saul held his position by the Lord's appointment, and that harming him would be a serious wrong.

David and his men were hiding in a cave while Saul was pursuing him, trying to kill him. Then Saul walked into that same cave without knowing David was there. David's men urged him to seize the moment and finish off his enemy. David did not do that. He only cut off a piece of Saul's robe, yet even that small act weighed on him, because Saul was the Lord's anointed king. Right away he stopped his men and refused to let them harm Saul.

For today: let us not ignore the voice of conscience, even in faults that seem small. And when someone wrongs us, let us trust that the Lord will bring justice, rather than taking revenge with our own hands.
exp.30:1:
The verse tells us that the Philistines pursued Saul and his sons closely. They caught up with them and killed three of Saul's sons: Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua. The word "pursued" here means going after them hotly, chasing them down.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, who recounts the end of the battle of Mount Gilboa. Israel had already fled and many had fallen. This is the last day of Saul's reign. With the death of his sons, including Jonathan, the faithful friend of David, a painful chapter in the history of Israel comes to an end.

For today: our decisions can affect those we love. Saul turned away from God through his disobedience, and his family suffered the consequences as well. This invites us to live with humility and faithfulness, remembering that what we do influences others. And if you suffer a loss today, God remains faithful.
exp.18:3:
Jonathan speaks up for David in front of his father, King Saul. He tells the king that he should not sin against David, who is his servant, because David has done him no wrong. In fact, David's actions have been highly beneficial to the king. The phrase "spoke well of" means that he defended David with kind and well-chosen words.

Jonathan is Saul's son and David's loyal friend. Saul, consumed by jealousy, had decided to kill David. Jonathan warned David to hide and promised to plead for him. Here he keeps his word, reminding Saul of the victories God gave through David. Saul listened and swore that he would not kill David, although afterward his attitude changed.

We can defend with courage and kind words someone who is treated unjustly, even when doing so makes us uncomfortable. A true friendship does not stay silent in the face of wrong; it seeks truth and peace with respect.
exp.13:20:
This verse tells how some Hebrews who had been on the side of the Philistines, and who had gone up with them into the camp, switched sides. They went over to the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan. The phrase "previously" means they had already been with the Philistines for a good while.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not one of the characters. Jonathan had attacked a Philistine outpost, and God sent confusion into the enemy camp. When Saul arrived, the Philistines were fighting among themselves. These Hebrews, perhaps forced to serve the enemy (this is not stated with certainty), saw that the situation was turning and returned to their own people.

For today: when God is at work, He often encourages others to come back. We can pray and remain faithful even when we seem to be in the minority, because our steadfastness can help others return.
exp.23:20:
Saul says that he now understands, with complete clarity, that David is going to be king. He adds that the kingdom of Israel will be "firm and secure in your hand," that is, well established and safe under his rule. It is a statement that prepares the request in the next verse.

King Saul is speaking. David has just spared his life in a cave, when he could have killed him. Saul, moved, publicly acknowledges that God is with David. Since he knows David will reign, he asks him to promise by the LORD that he will not cut off his descendants or wipe out his name from his father's house. Some think his repentance was sincere but temporary, since he afterward continued pursuing David.

For today: when God shows you something clearly, do not stop at feeling it. Respond with steady obedience. And if someone admits their wrong, try to respond with the same peace and kindness David showed.
exp.18:12:
Michal took a household idol, laid it in the bed, placed some goat hair on its head, and covered it with a garment. In this way it appeared that David was sleeping. The Hebrew word here is usually "teraphim," household figures; it is not clear how large they were or how they were used. It is also not certain exactly what the goat hair was.

Michal is the daughter of Saul and the wife of David. Saul, jealous, had sent men to kill David early in the morning. Michal warned him and helped him escape through the window. She arranged this deception to give him time to flee.

For today: when we love someone, we sometimes have to act with courage and quickness to protect them. However, this passage tells what Michal did; it does not say that everything she did is an example to imitate. Let us ask for wisdom to help others with honesty and courage.
exp.0:14:
Hannah answers Eli the priest respectfully: "No, my lord." She explains to him that she is not drunk. She is a woman troubled in spirit, with a heavy and aching heart. She tells him that she has not had any wine or strong drink, but that she has poured out her soul before the LORD, opening her whole heart to God in prayer.

Hannah had no children and suffered greatly because of it. She had gone to pray at the sanctuary in Shiloh. She prayed silently, only moving her lips, and Eli, seeing her like that, thought she was drunk. She corrects the misunderstanding with humility and sincerity, without taking offense.

For today: God does not ask for perfect or well-arranged prayers. You can tell him your pain just as it is, even though others do not understand it or misjudge it. And if someone judges you wrongly, you can answer with calmness and gentleness, as Hannah did.
exp.7:14:
The passage says the king would take a tenth of the harvests and of the vineyards of the people to pay his officials and servants. Here "seed" refers to sown fields, which is to say the grain.

Samuel speaks to the people of Israel. They asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. Samuel was grieved, and God told him to warn them how a king would act. These words describe the cost of that decision: taxes, labor, and loss of freedom.

For today: before we insist on getting something, let us think about what it will cost. We often look for security in human persons or systems and forget that only God is our true King and protector. Let us ask Him for wisdom before we decide.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that the LORD called Samuel, a young man who was sleeping in the sanctuary, and that he answered at once: "Here I am." Note that Samuel believed it was Eli who was calling him, as the following verses show.

The narrator tells this moment at a time when Eli, the priest, was already old and nearly blind. Samuel served him in the sanctuary at Shiloh, near the ark. Later the text says that Samuel did not yet know the Lord's voice well. God calls him to give a message and to begin his work as a prophet.

For today: God can speak to us in ways we do not recognize at first. We can have a willing heart like Samuel's, read the Bible, pray, and ask advice from mature people in the faith, as Eli helped Samuel understand what was happening.
exp.20:2:
David asks the priest Ahimelech for something to eat: five loaves of bread, or whatever can be found. "What do you have on hand" means "what is within your reach," that is, whatever is available. The phrase "whatever can be found" means whatever may be available nearby.

David, who is fleeing from King Saul, speaks here. He arrives at Nob, where the priest was, alone and hungry. He tells Ahimelech that he comes on a secret mission from the king, but this was not true: David was hiding the fact that he was escaping from Saul. The text does not justify that lie, and later it brought serious consequences for the priests (1 Samuel 22).

For today: when we are in need, it is good to ask for help with humility and simplicity. But we do not need to resort to deceit to get it. God is the one who cares for us, and honesty also protects those who help us.
exp.19:22:
Jonathan reminds David of the agreement the two of them made. He says that the LORD himself is the witness to what they promised each other, and that he will be that witness forever. The phrase "as for the matter you and I have discussed" refers to the agreement itself, and the words "the LORD is a witness between you and me" mean that God stands as judge and guardian of their promise.

Jonathan speaks with David in the field. Saul, his father, wants to kill David. Jonathan promises to warn him with a signal of arrows if the king is angry with him. Since there could be danger for both of them, Jonathan calls God to witness their friendship and their loyalty, even in difficult times.

Today, when you make a promise, whether in friendship, in family, or at work, take it seriously, as if God were a witness. And when life becomes hard, keep your word faithfully, and not only when it suits you.
exp.16:29:
This verse says that David stopped speaking with his brother Eliab, turned toward other people, and asked them about the offer. The men answered him just as the first ones had. The phrase "turned from him" means he turned away from Eliab, and the people's reply is described as matching what they had said before.

Eliab had just accused David of pride and of being nosy. David did not get caught up in an argument. His question was about what would be given to the man who defeated Goliath and took away the disgrace from Israel. Those words reached the ears of Saul, and that opened the way for David to present himself before the king.

For today: when someone criticizes you unfairly, you do not have to defend yourself until you win the argument. Answer with calm, keep going with what God has placed in your heart, and keep doing what is right with patience.
exp.20:10:
The servants of Achish, king of Gath, recognize David and ask whether he is not the famous warrior of Israel. They call him "the king of the land," and they remember the song the women sang in their dances: Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands. The dances were performed by groups of people moving together.

David was fleeing from Saul and had come to Gath, the city of Goliath, the giant he himself had defeated. It is the Philistine officials who speak, and they see in David a dangerous enemy. They may call him "king" because of his fame, not because he already was one. This frightens David, as the next verse shows.

When fear leads us to look for a way out on our own, we can end up in dangerous places. David was strong, yet here he appears weak. This reminds us that we should bring our fears to God honestly. Later, Psalm 34 is traditionally connected with this episode and speaks of God who delivers the one who seeks him.
exp.13:43:
Saul responds with a very strong oath. The words "May God punish me, and ever so severely" were a way of saying: "May God punish me if I do not carry this out." And what he vows is that Jonathan will die without fail. "You, Jonathan, will surely die" means "you are certain to die."

Speaking is King Saul, in the middle of the war against the Philistines. Earlier he had made a hasty oath: no one was to eat until evening. Jonathan had not heard it and tasted a little honey. Saul, bound to his word, wants to keep it even though it means acting against his own son. The people step in and rescue him.

For today: let us think before we speak or make promises. Words spoken in haste or pride can wound those we love. Let us seek God's guidance and also the humility to correct ourselves.
exp.11:6:
Samuel asks the people to present themselves and wait before him. The Berean Standard Bible renders the phrase about making a case against them as "confront you before the LORD," which means he is going to set the matter out plainly in God's presence. The "righteous acts" are the good and faithful deeds the LORD has done, both for them and for their ancestors, meaning what He did to save and care for Israel.

Samuel is already an old man, and the people have asked for a king. He first defends his own honest conduct and then, as in a trial, goes over the history of God's faithfulness. He wants to show them that asking for a king was a way of distrusting the LORD, who had always rescued them.

For today: before we worry about the future, let us remember how God has sustained us in the past. Remembering His works strengthens trust and helps us not to seek security in other things.
exp.29:8:
David and his six hundred men set out at once to pursue the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off their families. They reached the Brook of Besor, a stream that can carry a great deal of water, and there some of the men stayed behind.

The narrator describes what happened just after David asked the Lord for guidance through the ephod, the priestly garment used to seek God's answer. David was in great distress, for even his own people were talking about stoning him. God promised him that he would overtake the enemies. The text does not say why some stayed behind, but the next verse makes clear that they were too exhausted.

For today: when God gives us clear guidance, it is good to act on it without delay. We should also show understanding toward those who, because of weariness, cannot keep the same pace.
exp.27:9:
Saul makes an oath to the woman. He invokes the name of the LORD, saying, "As surely as the LORD lives," a solemn form of swearing. He promises that no punishment will come upon her for practicing divination.

Saul is in disguise and speaks at night with a medium in Endor. He himself had driven the diviners out of the land, in keeping with God's law. The woman fears a trap that could cost her life. God no longer answered Saul, and in desperation he seeks what he had earlier forbidden. It is striking that he swears by God to ask for something God condemns.

For today: when we are desperate, it is easy to look for shortcuts and even to use holy words to justify them. Better to return to God with sincerity, for He receives the one who repents.
exp.4:11:
It says that in Ekron the plague kept striking the people. Those who did not die were left afflicted with tumors, a painful condition whose exact nature is not known. Also, the city's outcry rose to heaven, a sign of very great anguish.

The one who narrates is the author of Samuel. The Philistines had captured the ark of God and carried it from city to city. Wherever it arrived, punishment came with it. The people of Ekron became frightened and asked that it be sent back to Israel. They understood that they could not treat God as an object of war.

For today: God is not a piece we use for our own convenience. We can draw near to Him with respect and humility, without wanting to manage Him or ignore Him. If today we feel anguish, rather than hardening ourselves, let us cry out to Him with sincerity.
exp.13:36:
Saul asks God whether he should pursue the Philistines and whether God will give them into the hand of Israel. But God does not answer him that day. "Inquired of God" means that he sought direction, and "did not answer him" refers to the silence that followed.

Saul speaks after a great victory, when the army was hungry and exhausted. Earlier, he had made a hasty vow that no one should eat until evening. Jonathan, his son, did not know of it and ate some honey. The text suggests that God's silence led Saul to look for what had gone wrong. The passage does not explain everything in detail, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

When God is silent, it is wise to pause and examine our decisions, words, and promises with humility. Sometimes silence is an invitation to set something right, though we will not always know the reason.
exp.22:7:
Saul summoned all his troops to go to war at Keilah and surround David and his men, intending to trap them. To besiege a city means to encircle it with soldiers so that no one can get out or come in. The phrase "summoned all his troops" means that he gathered his army together.

Here the narrator speaks. David was in Keilah, a city he had just rescued from the Philistines. Saul, who was chasing David out of jealousy, believed that God had handed David over to him because the city had gates and bars. But Saul did not seek God's guidance; he simply reached a conclusion that suited him.

For today: be careful about saying "God has put him in my hands" when we only want to justify what we already desire to do. Before acting, it is wise to seek God with humility, as David did afterward, and to examine whether our heart is free of envy or resentment.
exp.0:17:
Hannah answers the priest Eli respectfully: "May your maidservant find favor with you" means "I hope you will look on me kindly and be pleased with me." Then she went on her way, began to eat, and "her face was no longer downcast."

Hannah had prayed in the sanctuary with great grief because she had no children. Eli had mistaken her for a drunken woman, but she explained her distress to him. He sent her off with a blessing: that God would grant what she had asked. Here Hannah responds to that blessing.

For today: after prayer, we can leave our burden in God's hands. The Bible does not say that her situation changed at that moment, but her spirit did. Praying sincerely can bring us rest, even before we see the answer.
exp.14:12:
When Samuel reaches him, Saul greets him with a blessing: "May the LORD bless you." Right away he declares with confidence: "I have carried out the LORD's instructions." That is, he says he fully did what God told him to do. The word "reached" here means arrived at that very place.

Saul speaks here, the first king of Israel. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but Saul and the people kept the best of the livestock and spared their king. Samuel already knew that Saul had failed, since Saul had spent the night crying out to God. Saul comes forward with a declaration of obedience, and the next verse contradicts it with the bleating of the sheep.

For today: it is easy to tell ourselves, or to tell others, that we obey God while we keep excuses or things He did not ask for. It is wise to ask Him to examine our hearts and to obey Him completely, not only in what is convenient for us.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that the Spirit of the LORD would rush upon Saul with power, that he would prophesy together with a group of prophets, and that he would be transformed into a different person. The phrase "rush upon" means to come on someone with force. "Prophesy" probably refers to praising or speaking under the inspiration of God. "Transformed" means changed.

Samuel is speaking to Saul after anointing him as the first king of Israel. He gives him several signs to confirm that God had chosen him. This is one of them. Saul was going to need an inner change to take on such a great responsibility, and God himself was promising it. It is not known exactly what that change was like, but the text shows that it came from God.

For today: when God calls us to something that feels bigger than us, it does not depend only on our own strength. We can ask him for his Spirit, who gives us courage, character, and direction to carry it out.
exp.7:9:
This verse says that Samuel told the people everything the Lord had commanded him to say. Here the name of God appears as "the LORD," and the phrase about the people who were asking him for a king refers to the people who were pressing Samuel for a king.

Samuel speaks as a prophet and judge of Israel. The people wanted a king like the other nations, and this grieved Samuel. God told him to listen to their request, but first to warn them clearly. God explains that they had rejected his guidance, as they had done before with other gods. For this reason, Samuel does not soften the message: he shows them what it would cost to have a king.

For today: before insisting on something, it is good to ask ourselves what it will cost and whether we are beginning to stop trusting God. He warns us out of love, even when he allows us to choose our own path.
exp.28:2:
The chiefs of the Philistines see David and his men among the army and ask in irritation, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Here "chiefs" refers to the rulers or leaders of the Philistine cities. Achish, the king of Gath, defends David. He says David has been with him all these days, even years, and that from the day David defected until today he has found no fault in him.

The Philistines were getting ready to fight against Israel. David had taken refuge with Achish while fleeing from Saul, and Achish trusted him. The other commanders distrusted him, fearing that David might turn against them in the middle of the battle. The Bible does not say that Achish knew of David's deceptions; it only shows what he believed.

For today: the way we live speaks about us. Even when others distrust us, honest and steady conduct can bear witness. But we must also take care that our alliances do not put us in difficult situations, and we should ask God for wisdom and direction.
exp.0:9:
This verse tells us that Hannah, in her bitter distress, prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears. The words "bitter distress" describe a deep grief inside her. The phrase "many tears" shows that she wept openly and did not hold back.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who shows us Hannah at Shiloh, beside the temple. She had no children and suffered because of it. Her husband Elkanah tried to comfort her, but her pain went deeper. So she stopped speaking to people and went to speak with God, and there she made her request.

For today: when pain weighs on you, you do not have to pretend or polish your words. You can bring your tears to God and tell him honestly what you feel. He does not tire of listening to you, and praying with honesty is a good first step.
exp.8:18:
Samuel tells Saul that he is the seer, the prophet Saul had been looking for. He invites him to go up to the high place and eat with him there. Samuel says Saul will eat with him today, and that when he sends him off in the morning, he will tell him everything in his heart.

Saul was looking for his father's donkeys that had gone missing, and he asked about the seer to seek guidance. Without Saul knowing it, God had already told Samuel that this young man would be the ruler of Israel. That is why Samuel receives him with confidence and promises him answers.

God often works behind the scenes, even in small and everyday matters. We can trust that he guides our steps, and seek his direction with humility, even when we are only busy with simple tasks.
exp.24:20:
This verse shows David's anger. He says it was for nothing that he protected all that belonged to this man in the wilderness, since nothing that belongs to Nabal went missing. And in return, Nabal has paid him back evil for good. The phrase "paid back evil for good" means that Nabal answered a kindness with an insult.

Here the narrator tells us what David had said before he met Abigail. David and his men had protected Nabal's flocks, and Nabal refused them help with contempt. For that reason David was on his way to take revenge with violence, and Abigail goes out to meet him without her husband knowing.

For today: when someone pays us back evil for a good we have done, the hurt is real, but we should not decide in the heat of anger. It is wise to stop, listen to wise counsel, and leave justice to God.
exp.2:4:
Samuel heard a voice in the night and thought it was the priest Eli. So he ran to him and said, "Here I am, for you have called me." Eli answered that he had not called him and told him to go back and lie down. Samuel obeyed.

Samuel was a boy who served Eli in the sanctuary. The one calling him was God, but the text makes clear that Samuel did not yet know the Lord or had received his word. That is why he did not recognize the voice. His willingness to get up and run shows a helpful heart.

God sometimes speaks to us in ways we do not know how to recognize at first. It is wise to stay alert, to be willing, and to seek the guidance of mature people of faith, like Eli, who help us discern.
exp.9:14:
Here Saul's uncle asks his nephew what Samuel said to him. The original wording is an old way of saying "Please, tell me," and the uncle is curious, because Saul and his servant had gone to see the prophet.

The uncle asks because he sees them come back after searching for some lost donkeys. Saul had just been secretly anointed by Samuel as the future king, and he had prophesied. That is why the people were amazed. In the next verse, Saul tells about the donkeys, but he keeps silent about the kingdom. Some see in this humility or prudence; others, fear. The text does not explain the reason.

For today: not everything God entrusts to us has to be told right away. Ask Him for wisdom to know when to speak and when to wait with humility.
exp.22:18:
The people of Ziph went up to Saul at Gibeah to betray David. They told him that David was hiding among them, in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah south of the desert of Jeshimon. The word "hill" here means a small hill or rise of land, and "south" is the direction they point to.

The Ziphites speak to Saul, who was pursuing David out of jealousy. Just before this, Jonathan had encouraged David, and the two of them had made a covenant before God. Now neighbors from the same tribe of Judah betray David, perhaps out of fear of Saul or to win his favor. The Bible does not explain their motives with certainty.

For today: when someone fails us or betrays us, let us remember that God remains faithful. Let us seek friends like Jonathan who strengthen us, and let us take care not to use our words to harm others.
exp.6:13:
This verse says that Israel got back the cities the Philistines had taken from them, from Ekron to Gath, along with the surrounding territory. "Restored" means given back. The Amorites were the peoples living in the region. There was also peace between Israel and them.

Here the narrator of the book summarizes what happened after the people put away their idols and turned back to God under Samuel's leadership. God gave them victory over the Philistines, and Samuel set up the stone Ebenezer, saying, "Thus far the LORD has helped us." This verse shows the result of that help.

For today: when we return to God with our whole heart, He can restore what was lost. It will not always be the same or immediate, but we can remember His past help and trust that He will remain with us.
exp.12:22:
A garrison, meaning a small military post of Philistine soldiers, had moved out to the pass at Michmash. A pass is a narrow road between mountains. The phrase "had gone out" tells us they had already moved into position, occupying or guarding that spot.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. Israel was at a disadvantage: it had almost no weapons, because the Philistines controlled the work of iron. This verse sets up the story that follows, where Jonathan, son of Saul, confronts that enemy post. What follows in the account (chapter 14) shows how he acted.

For today: sometimes we feel few and poorly equipped in the face of a great problem. This verse reminds us that God does not depend on our resources. We can take the next step with faith and trust that he can act even when everything seems against us.
exp.1:0:
Hannah begins her prayer with joy: her heart rejoices in the Lord. The picture of "my horn is exalted" is one of strength and dignity, like an animal that lifts its head with power. "My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies" means that she can now speak with confidence in the face of those who looked down on her.

The one speaking is Hannah, the wife of Elkanah. For years she had no children and suffered the taunts of Peninnah, the other wife. She prayed in pain at the sanctuary, and God granted her Samuel. After giving him over to serve the Lord, Hannah lifts up this prayer of thanksgiving. Her joy is centered on God, not only on the gift she received.

When God helps you through a difficulty, do not stop at relief. Take some time to thank Him aloud or in writing, and acknowledge that He was your strength and your refuge.
exp.1:2:
This verse asks us to stop boasting and speaking with pride. "Arrogance" refers to words full of self-importance. The reason is that the LORD is a God who knows, and it is by him that our actions are weighed, that is, evaluated and judged, both what we do and why we do it.

The one speaking is Hannah, who prays with thanksgiving after giving her son Samuel to serve God. Before this, she had suffered because she had no children and because of the mockery of her rival. Now she praises God and warns the proud, because he changes the fortune of the strong and the weak, as seen in the verses that follow.

Today we can guard our words: avoid bragging about our achievements or looking down on others. If we remember that God knows the heart, we will speak with more humility and gratitude.
exp.22:6:
When Saul was told that David had gone to Keilah, he believed God had handed David over to him, because David had trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars (the bars being the wooden beams that lock the gates).

The speaker is Saul, the king, who pursues David out of jealousy. David had just rescued Keilah from the Philistines. Saul reads the situation in his own favor and credits God with his own desire to do harm. But the account does not say that God did this; soon David, by asking God, discovers Saul's plan.

Today, we must be careful not to call something "God's will" when it only suits our desires. An open door or a good opportunity is not always a sign from God. It is wise to pray, to compare it with the Word of God, and to ask for a humble and clean heart.
exp.20:3:
Here the priest Ahimelech tells David that he has no ordinary bread on hand, but he does have some consecrated bread, the bread set apart for God. He is willing to give it to David, but on one condition: that the young men with him have kept themselves from women.

"Young men" refers to David's followers or attendants, and "common bread" is everyday bread.

David is fleeing from Saul and arrives at Nob, where the tabernacle stands. He is hungry and asks for food, though he does not tell the whole truth about his situation. Ahimelech protects the holiness of the bread, but he also sees human need. Scholars explain in various ways how this condition of purity is to be understood; what is clear is that the aim was respect for what is dedicated to God.

For today: God deserves our respect, but he also cares about people's needs. We can honor what is holy with reverence and, at the same time, help with compassion anyone who is hungry or in trouble.
exp.12:19:
This verse says that the Israelites had to go down to the Philistines to have their tools sharpened for work. Sharpening means putting an edge on a blade. The verse names four tools: plowshares, which are the blades of the plow that cut through the soil; mattocks, which are small hoes used for digging up the ground; axes, for chopping; and sickles, the curved blades used to cut the harvest.

It is the narrator of the book who describes Israel's situation under Saul. The Philistines dominated the country and did not allow there to be blacksmiths among the Hebrews. According to the text, they did this so that the Hebrews would not make swords or spears. In this way Israel depended on its enemies even for the most basic things, and it went into battle almost without weapons.

For today: when we depend entirely on what others control, we feel weak. This passage invites us to remember that our strength does not lie in having the best resources, but in trusting God, who would later give victory to Israel.
exp.21:15:
Here King Saul pronounces a sentence of death against Ahimelech, the priest, and against his whole family. The words "You will surely die" are a strong statement, meaning that he is certain to die. Ahimelech had already defended himself by saying that he knew nothing of the conflict between Saul and David.

Saul speaks out of jealousy and suspicion. David was fleeing from him, and Ahimelech had given him bread and the sword of Goliath, without knowing that David was escaping. Doeg, a servant of Saul, had accused him. Saul did not want to hear the priest's explanation.

For today: when fear and pride rule the heart, they shut our ears to the truth, and we can hurt innocent people. Let us ask God for humility to listen before we judge.
exp.21:18:
This verse tells that Nob, the city where the priests lived, was destroyed by the sword. Men and women, children and infants, along with oxen, donkeys and sheep, were all put to death. The phrase "put to the sword" means that they were killed with the sword, and the mention of infants refers to the youngest children, who were still being cared for at home.

The one who gives the order is King Saul, angry and filled with jealousy against David. He believed the priests had helped David escape. His own soldiers refused to kill the priests of the LORD, but Doeg the Edomite obeyed. Here the text narrates what happened without approving of it. This cruelty was not a command from God, but the fruit of Saul's heart.

For today: jealousy and pride, if they are not confronted, can lead us to do terrible harm. Let us ask God for a humble heart and the courage to refuse to obey what is unjust, as the soldiers did.
exp.16:7:
Goliath steps forward in front of Israel's army and shouts at them. He stands and calls out to the ranks of Israel, and the soldiers lined up before him are the ones he faces.

He mocks them. He asks why they have come out to array themselves for battle, and he reminds them that he is a Philistine while they are servants of Saul. Then he demands that they choose one of their men and send him down to fight against him.

The one speaking is Goliath, the Philistine champion, who stands in the valley of Elah, with Israel and the Philistines face to face. His proposal was to settle the war through a contest between two men. With his words he sought to intimidate and shame God's people, and he succeeded: later the text says that Saul and all of them were filled with fear.

For today: many times our problems shout at us that we are small and incapable. Before listening to those voices, let us remember who our God is. We can ask Him for courage and trust that He is with us.
exp.25:24:
Saul blesses David and tells him that he will surely accomplish great things and come out ahead. Then each of them goes his own way.

Saul was hunting David in order to kill him. David had the chance to strike Saul while he slept, but he refused to do it, because he respected the king whom God had anointed. Saul admits he has done wrong, though the account does not show any lasting change in him. David, for his part, does not go back to Saul, perhaps out of caution, since he had earlier regretted trusting Saul's promises.

We can act with integrity even when others treat us badly, leaving justice in God's hands. We also learn to be wise: forgiving someone does not always mean putting ourselves back in the same danger.
exp.17:11:
Saul was afraid of David. The reason given is that the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul. "Was afraid" means "felt fear." The verse says the LORD was with David, so this was not a fear of respect but of threat: Saul saw that David had something he no longer had.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Just before this, Saul tried to pin David to the wall with a spear while David was playing music. The text says that an evil spirit from God troubled him, something scholars explain in several ways. What is clear is that Saul's fear led him to violence, and David escaped by dodging the spear.

For today: when we see that others are doing well, let us not let envy or fear take control of us. Instead, let us seek God with humility and deal with whatever is in our hearts.
exp.10:13:
Samuel invites all the people to go to Gilgal. There he wants them to renew the kingship, that is, to publicly confirm or re-establish Saul as king. "Come" is the word the verse uses, and it means the same as "let us go," the invitation in the verse itself.

Samuel speaks after Saul defeated the Ammonites and rescued the city of Jabesh-gilead. Some had looked down on Saul earlier, and the people wanted to punish them. Saul pardoned them and gave the glory to God. Samuel uses that moment to unite the nation. Scholars debate whether this "renewal" was a second ceremony or a confirmation of the first, since the text does not make this clear.

For today: when God gives us a victory, it is a good time to let go of grudges, forgive, and come together with gratitude. Giving thanks together strengthens unity.
exp.5:12:
The people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. When they looked up and saw the ark of the LORD coming toward them, they were overjoyed at the sight.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had captured the ark, but they suffered plagues and decided to return it. They placed it on a cart pulled by two cows, and the cows went straight toward Beth-shemesh, an Israelite town. For the Israelites, the ark represented the presence of God, so seeing it returning was a cause for great joy.

For today: sometimes God surprises us in the middle of our daily work. These men were only harvesting when they saw something extraordinary. Let us live attentively, lifting our eyes to recognize the hand of God in the ordinary, and respond with joy and gratitude.
exp.16:6:
The shaft of Goliath's spear is described. Its shaft was like a weaver's beam, the thick wooden rod of a loom, so it was very thick. The iron point weighed six hundred shekels, about 7 kilograms according to common calculations. A shield bearer walked ahead of him, the assistant who carried his shield.

The narrator details the armor of the Philistine giant. He wants the reader to see how imposing he was, and why all Israel felt fear. Right after, Goliath challenges Israel's army to send one man to fight on behalf of them all.

Today, we sometimes face problems that seem enormous and well armed. This scene reminds us not to measure everything by its appearance. Before letting fear paralyze us, we can place the problem in God's hands and ask him for courage to act with faith.
exp.13:35:
Saul proposes to attack the Philistines during the night, plunder them until dawn, and leave no one alive. The troops reply, "Do what seems good to you," meaning they leave the decision to him. Then the priest says, "We must consult God here," which means: let us seek God's counsel before acting.

Saul speaks after a great day of battle. The people are exhausted, and they had eaten meat with the blood still in it, which the law forbade. Saul had the animals slaughtered properly and built an altar. The priest halts the plan and suggests seeking God's guidance. Then God does not answer that day, and Saul looks for the cause of the silence.

For today: before making important decisions, even when we are in a hurry or have the support of others, it is wise to stop and pray and seek God's direction.
exp.29:11:
This verse tells of a hungry young Egyptian who was given a piece of fig cake and two clusters of raisins. When he ate, he was revived, because he had gone three days and three nights without any food or water. The fig cake and the raisins were food for the weary, and eating them brought his strength back.

This is a narrative account. David was pursuing the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the families. On the way, his men found this servant abandoned because he was sick. David first cared for him, and afterward the servant helped them find the attackers.

For today: compassion is not a waste of time. Even in haste and grief, David stopped to help a needy stranger, and that kindness became a doorway to help. Let us care for those who suffer near us.
exp.14:32:
Samuel tells Agag, king of the Amalekites, that just as his sword has left many mothers without their children, so his own mother will be left without her son. Then Samuel puts him to death at Gilgal, before the LORD.

God had commanded Saul to destroy the Amalekites, but Saul spared Agag and kept the best of the plunder. Samuel, as a prophet, finishes what Saul failed to complete. The Amalekites had attacked Israel cruelly in the wilderness. It is a hard passage, and Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: half-hearted obedience is not obedience. We can ask God to help us fully carry out what He asks of us with sincerity, without keeping only what suits us. And let us remember that Christ taught us to love even our enemies.
exp.2:8:
Here is the verse Eli spoke to Samuel: "Go and lie down, and if He calls you, say, 'Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening.'" Samuel obeys and returns to his place.

Samuel was a boy serving in the sanctuary alongside the aged priest Eli. God had called him three times, and Samuel thought it was Eli calling him. At last Eli understood that it was God speaking, and he taught Samuel how to answer. Samuel did not yet know God from his own experience.

For today: God speaks to those who are ready to listen. Before you pray or speak in prayer, take a quiet moment and say sincerely, "Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening." It is also wise to learn from people with more experience in the faith, as Samuel did with Eli.
exp.11:3:
Here the people of Israel answer Samuel and say that he has never cheated them or treated them unjustly. The verse's wording "cheated" means taking advantage of someone or getting something from them dishonestly, "oppressed" means harming someone or treating them unfairly, and "nor have you taken anything from the hand of man" means that he never took what belonged to others or accepted a bribe.

Samuel is now an old man and hands over leadership to the new king, Saul. Before he steps aside, he asks the people to examine him before God. He wants it to be clear that he served with honesty. Later he will remind them of God's faithfulness.

For today: live with integrity in small things and in large ones, so that others can witness to our honesty. If you have any responsibility, at work, in the family, or in the church, carry it out with clean hands, knowing that God also sees.
exp.28:7:
David asks Achish what he has done wrong. He says that since he came to him, they have found no fault in him. So why won't they let him go to fight against the enemies of my lord the king? Here the word "found" means "discovered," and "servant" refers to someone who serves.

David was living among the Philistines, fleeing from King Saul. The Philistine leaders distrusted him, and Achish sent him back. Some think David was speaking sincerely; others think he used ambiguous words, since "my lord the king" could be understood in more than one way. The text does not make this clear.

When someone distrusts you without reason, you can answer with calm and with a clear conscience. And if a door closes, trust that God may be guiding your steps.
exp.16:17:
Jesse asks David to take ten portions of cheese to the commander of the unit where his brothers are serving. He also asks him to check on how his brothers are doing. The phrase "welfare of your brothers" refers to their well-being and health. To "bring back an assurance from them" means to return with some sign or proof that they are safe; some understand this as a personal token, others as a reliable report.

Jesse, David's father, is the one speaking. His three oldest sons were in Saul's army, and Goliath had been challenging Israel for forty days. Jesse did not know how things were going, so he sends his youngest son with food and the task of bringing back news. Without knowing it, that simple errand would put David face to face with Goliath.

For today: God often uses small, everyday assignments to prepare us for great things. Do faithfully and lovingly what is asked of you today in your family.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that God has control over life and death. "The LORD brings death and gives life" shows that everything depends on Him. "Sheol" is the place of the dead, the realm where people go when they die. "Raises up" means that He can restore, deliver, or give new life. Some understand it as rescue from deadly dangers, and others also see a foreshadowing of the hope of resurrection.

The one speaking is Hannah, in her prayer of thanksgiving. She was barren and humiliated, and God gave her a son, Samuel, whom she dedicated to the service of God. Her song celebrates that God changes situations: He brings down the proud and lifts up the humble.

For today: when you feel that your situation has no way out, remember that God still rules. Trust in Him with humility, pray with thankfulness, and wait for Him to be able to lift up what seems lost.
exp.28:6:
Here Achish tells David to turn back and go on his way in peace. "Turn back" means to return home, and "in peace" means without trouble or dispute. He asks David not to do anything that would displease the Philistine lords, that is, not to cause them offense or conflict.

Achish speaks as the Philistine king of Gath. David had lived under his protection and had traveled with him and his men, but the Philistine commanders distrusted David, remembering that he was Israel's hero. Achish personally trusted David, although he gave in to the pressure of the lords. Some understand that God used this situation to keep David from fighting against his own people, though the text does not say this in so many words.

For today: sometimes a door is closed to us even though we have done nothing wrong. We can respond with calm, without fighting, and trust that God can take care of us even when doors are shut.
exp.3:2:
What it says: After losing a battle to the Philistines, the troops returned to the camp. The elders, Israel's leaders, asked why the LORD had brought defeat on them. Then they proposed bringing the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh, hoping it would go with them and save them from their enemies. "Defeat" here means being beaten in battle.

Context: The elders of Israel speak, discouraged after about four thousand men had died. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence. They ask why, but they do not examine themselves or seek the LORD with repentance. The text does not say they consulted the LORD. Later, the story shows that treating the ark as a good luck charm did not bring them victory.

For today: When something goes wrong for us, it is not enough to ask for a quick fix or to rely on religious symbols. First let us seek God with humility, examine our hearts, and trust Him Himself, not objects or customs.
exp.0:21:
Hannah decides not to go up with her husband to Shiloh on that trip. She tells him she will wait until the child is weaned, that is, until he no longer nurses. Then she herself will take the boy and bring him to appear before the Lord, and he will stay there permanently. "But" here marks a change from the expected plan, and "I will take him" means she will bring him herself.

Hannah speaks with her husband Elkanah. Before she had children, she had prayed in deep distress and had promised God that if He gave her a son, she would give him back to Him. Now she wants to keep that promise at the right time. Elkanah supports her and lets her decide what seems best to her.

For today: keeping what we have promised to God, even when it costs us, and doing so with patience and good order. We can also entrust to God what we love most, trusting that He cares for it.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that the Philistines attacked and defeated Israel. The Israelites fled, each man back to his own tent. The verse describes this as a very great slaughter, with thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel falling. Some scholars believe this figure could be understood in another way, but the text presents it as a heavy loss.

The words quoted above were spoken by the Philistines, who were afraid because the ark had come into the Israelite camp. They encouraged one another to stand firm and fight like men. Israel had carried the ark as if it were a good luck charm, without turning to God with their whole heart. That is why the ark did not secure them the victory.

For today: it is not enough to use religious symbols or customs to have God on our side. What matters is a sincere relationship with Him, marked by obedience and humility.
exp.11:14:
It says that if the people will not obey God and rebel against his commands, God will act against them, just as he did with their ancestors. The phrase "if you will not obey the voice of the Lord" is the plain wording of your verse, and "the hand of the LORD" means his power and his judgment.

Samuel speaks in his farewell address as judge. Israel had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations, and Samuel saw this as a rejection of God's guidance over them. Even so, Samuel shows them that the king does not change what is essential: both the people and the king must continue to obey God. Then comes the sign of the storm during the wheat harvest.

For today: it is not enough to have good leaders, good structures, or good plans. What matters most is listening to God and obeying him sincerely. Today you can choose one word from the Bible and put it into practice.
exp.16:52:
This verse tells that the Israelites, after chasing the fleeing Philistines, came back and plundered their camps, carrying off the supplies, weapons and other goods they found there.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book who relates what happened. Goliath had just fallen at the hands of David, and the Philistine army had fled. Now Israel, which had trembled with fear before, gathers the fruits of a victory that began when a young man trusted in God. The account shows that the courage of one man encouraged the whole people.

For today: when someone takes a step of faith, they can encourage others to follow. And after a victory, it is good to remember that it was God who gave it, and to use what has been received with gratitude.
exp.0:5:
This verse tells us that Peninnah, Elkanah's other wife, treated Hannah cruelly. It says her rival would provoke her viciously, and this means she kept taunting and wounding her again and again. She did it to make Hannah miserable, and she used the fact that Hannah could not have children as her reason. The Bible says "the LORD had closed Hannah's womb," meaning that God had not allowed her to become pregnant.

Here the narrator of the book explains Hannah's pain. Elkanah had two wives, something the Bible shows happening in that time, although it is not presented as God's ideal. Peninnah had children and Hannah did not, and Elkanah loved Hannah and gave her a special portion. Peninnah, perhaps out of jealousy, took advantage of every trip to the house of the LORD to wound her.

Today we can learn not to mock anyone's pain. If you suffer from a wound like this, do as Hannah did: bring your sorrow to God with honesty.
exp.16:36:
What it says: David declares that the Lord, who rescued him earlier from the claws of the lion and the bear that attacked his sheep, will also rescue him from the hand of this Philistine. Saul agrees and sends him off: "Go, and may the Lord be with you." The "claws" are the wild beasts' attacks, and "the hand" here means the power of the Philistine.

Context: David is a young shepherd who offers to fight Goliath, when the whole army of Israel was afraid. He speaks to King Saul, who doubts that a boy could defeat a seasoned warrior. David does not trust in his own strength, but in what God had already done for him in private, while caring for the flock.

For today: When you face a big problem, remember how God helped you in earlier ones. That grateful memory strengthens your faith and gives you courage to take the next step, trusting that God remains faithful.
exp.11:4:
Explanation of what it says: Samuel tells the people that the LORD is a witness against them, and that his anointed is also a witness today, that they have not found anything in his hand. The one anointed is someone set apart by God for a task, marked with oil. The phrase "found anything in my hand" means they did not find him guilty of taking anything or wronging anyone. The people reply, "He is a witness."

Context: Samuel is now an old man. Israel asked for a king, and Saul has just been confirmed. Before stepping back from leadership, Samuel asks the people to declare whether he treated them unjustly. They confirm his honesty, and so he can remind them, with authority, of what God has done for them.

For today: Living with integrity gives us freedom and credibility. Try to act so that, if anyone examined your work, your money, and your dealings with others, there would be nothing to hide. And when you fail, admit it and repair the harm.
exp.12:15:
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the soldiers who were with them stayed in Geba, a place in the territory of Benjamin. Meanwhile, the Philistines, Israel's enemies, had camped at Michmash. The word "troops" here refers to the men gathered with them. There were two armies facing each other, not far from one another.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. Shortly before, Samuel had told Saul that his kingdom would not last, because he did not obey God. Samuel leaves, and Saul tells his people that only about six hundred men remain. The account shows a weakened king, with a small army and a huge threat in front of him.

For today: when you feel small before a big problem, do not act out of fear alone. Stop, pray, and seek to obey God in what you already know He has asked of you. His guidance is worth more than any hasty plan.
exp.25:12:
This verse tells that David crossed to the other side of the valley and climbed to the top of a mountain. He had gone far from Saul's camp, so there was a wide gulf between them, and he was safe.

The narrator describes what happened after David and Abishai entered the camp while everyone was asleep. David did not want to kill Saul, because he was the Lord's anointed, and he took only his spear and his water jug. Now David moves away so that he can speak to them without danger. He does this to show that he could have killed Saul and did not.

Today, David teaches us to act with wisdom and respect. We can defend the truth without seeking revenge, and keep a prudent distance when there is danger, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.18:4:
He says David took his life in his hands when he struck down the Philistine, that is, Goliath. The LORD used that to win a great victory for all Israel. "You saw it and rejoiced" means that Saul was glad about it. Jonathan asks him why he would now do wrong by killing an innocent man for no reason.

Jonathan, the son of Saul and friend of David, is the speaker. Saul had said he wanted to kill David out of jealousy. Jonathan defends him calmly, reminds Saul of the good David had done, and asks him not to act unjustly. His plan worked, and Saul swore that David would not die, at least for the time being.

For today: when someone is treated unjustly, we can speak up for them with truth and gentleness. Remembering the good we have received helps us overcome jealousy and resentment.
exp.2:20:
The verse says that the LORD continued to appear at Shiloh. "Continued" means that this was an ongoing pattern, not a single event. The verse adds that He revealed Himself to Samuel there by His word, meaning He made Himself known through a direct message. Earlier in the book, the word of the LORD was rare in those days (3:1), so this marks an important change.

The narrator closes chapter 3 here. Samuel was young and served alongside the priest Eli at Shiloh, where the tabernacle was. God called him, and from then on Samuel was recognized by all Israel as a faithful prophet. The verse does not describe the exact manner in which God appeared; it says only that He revealed Himself by His word.

God still seeks to communicate with those who listen to Him with humility. We can set aside a moment each day to read the Bible and say, as Samuel did: "Speak, for Your servant is listening." Listening willingly and being ready to obey opens the way for God to guide us.
exp.19:20:
Jonathan explains to David a secret signal. He will send a young servant to fetch the arrows. If he says to the boy, "Look, the arrows are on this side of you; bring them," David will know it is safe to come out of his hiding place, because there is no danger. The boy is a young servant, and the words "as surely as the LORD lives" form a solemn oath.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, speaks. David suspects that Saul wants to kill him, and Jonathan prepares a safe way to find out the truth and warn him without anyone else noticing. Their friendship is bound by a covenant made before God.

For today: true friendship shows itself in loyalty and care, even when it costs something. Think about who needs your discreet and faithful support this week, and help them sincerely, placing everything before God.
exp.19:15:
Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David. He asked that the LORD himself would hold David's enemies accountable if they failed to keep it. The wording "May the LORD hold David's enemies accountable" points to the idea that God would call them to answer for it and judge them.

Jonathan is the son of King Saul, who wants to kill David out of jealousy. Even so, Jonathan protects his friend. Since he knows David will be the future king, he asks for kindness toward his own family in case he dies. It is a solemn promise made in the presence of God. Some understand that Jonathan is speaking of the consequences that would fall on anyone who broke the covenant, including himself.

For today: when you pledge loyalty to someone, do it with seriousness and before God. Keep your word, especially when it costs you or when it would be convenient to stay silent. True friendship also thinks about the good of others.
exp.27:18:
This verse announces that Israel will lose the battle against the Philistines. Saul and his sons will die, and tomorrow they will be in the realm of the dead, which the text describes as being "with me," that is, in death. The verse says that the LORD will deliver Israel into the hand of the Philistines, meaning he will give them over to the enemy. Saying that they will be "with me" is a way of saying that they will die.

The speaker is the figure who appears as Samuel, already dead, and Saul hears him in a consultation with a medium. Saul was afraid of the Philistines, and God was not answering him. Some believe it was truly Samuel, and others that it was an apparition. The text stresses that Saul disobeyed God and lost the kingdom.

For today: disobeying God has consequences, yet He remains just. When you are afraid, do not seek answers in forbidden places. Come to God with sincerity, and obey Him today.
exp.16:47:
This verse says that when Goliath started forward to attack, David did not stay waiting or pull back. He ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him. The verse uses the word "ran" for David's movement, so no further explanation is needed here. Goliath is the Philistine warrior, the champion of the Philistine people.

The narrator tells this moment just after David told Goliath that God would give the victory, not the sword or the spear. David was a young shepherd, without armor for war, and he trusted that the battle belonged to God. That is why his words now show up in action: he advances with courage.

For today: when we trust God, sometimes it is time to take a step forward with courage instead of being frozen by fear. Praying and trusting do not rule out acting. We can face with faith that conversation, decision, or problem we have been avoiding for so long.
exp.16:45:
David is confident that the LORD will hand Goliath over to him that very day. He says he will strike the giant down and cut off his head. He also says the Philistine army's bodies will be left for the birds of the air and the creatures of the earth. In the end, the goal is that the whole world will know there is a God in Israel. "Cut off your head" means removing his head. "Strike you down" here means overcoming him.

David, a young shepherd, speaks in front of Goliath, the Philistine giant who mocked Israel's army and its God. Goliath had just threatened to leave David's body to the birds and the beasts, and David returns those very words. He does not trust in weapons, but in the name of the LORD.

For today: when you face a problem that seems enormous, do not rely only on your own resources. Place it in God's hands, act with courage, and seek to do what honors his name, not your own.
exp.7:7:
God tells Samuel that the people have always acted this way: from the day He brought them out of Egypt until today, they have abandoned Him and served other gods. Now they are doing the same thing to Samuel by rejecting him. "Just as they have done" means "just like they have always done," and "other gods" are the gods of other peoples.

The Lord speaks to Samuel, who is now old. The Israelites ask for a king like the other nations, and it grieves Samuel. God makes clear that the rejection is not so much against the prophet as against Him as their true King. Even so, He will allow them to have a king, but Samuel must warn them what it will cost them.

For today: sometimes we want something or someone else to give us security, instead of trusting God. Ask yourself where you are placing your trust. If this is hard for you, tell God honestly and ask Him to be first in your heart again.
exp.15:18:
Saul sent messengers to Jesse, David's father, asking him to send his son. He described David as "your son David, who is with the sheep," meaning the one who looks after the flock.

Here King Saul is speaking. He was troubled by an evil spirit, and his servants suggested he look for someone who could play music. One of them recommended David. Saul did not know that God had already chosen David in secret to be the future king. It is striking that David was out in the field, doing simple work, when he was sent for.

For today: God often prepares people through ordinary and little-seen everyday tasks. Be faithful in what you have been given to do today, even when no one notices; that way you will be ready when God opens a door.
exp.22:16:
Jonathan speaks to David and says, "Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command. Even my father Saul knows this is true." The phrase "lay a hand on you" means that Saul will never be able to reach or harm him.

The one speaking is Jonathan, Saul's son. David was hiding in the wilderness of Ziph because Saul was pursuing him to kill him. Jonathan went to find him to encourage him and strengthen his trust in God. Although he was the natural heir to the throne, he accepted that God had chosen David. We do not know in detail how Saul knew this, but the text suggests that he sensed it.

For today: we can be like Jonathan, encouraging others in their fear, reminding them that God carries out his plans, and setting aside pride and rivalry.
exp.24:6:
Here David, through his messengers, tells Nabal that he has heard it is time for shearing, a season of feasting and abundance. He reminds him that his shepherds stayed near David's men, and that David's men did not harass them, and that nothing of theirs went missing the whole time they were in Carmel.

David was living as a fugitive in the wilderness with his men. They had looked after Nabal's shepherds, and now David asks, courteously, for some provision. We do not know exactly what that protection looked like, but the text takes it for granted, and the servants can confirm it.

For today: when we have done good, it is right to ask with respect and humility, without demanding. And when someone has helped us, gratitude is a form of justice that honors God.
exp.24:10:
Nabal answers David's request with contempt. He asks why he should take his bread, his water, and the meat he has slaughtered for his shearers and give it to these men whose origin he does not know. In other words, he will not share his food with men he knows nothing about, that is, strangers to him. "Shearers" are the workers who cut the wool from the sheep.

Nabal, a rich man from Maon, speaks during the sheep-shearing feast. David, who was fleeing from Saul, had protected his flocks in the wilderness and asked for some food respectfully. Nabal despises him and does not even acknowledge what David had done for him. This kindles David's anger.

For today: generosity and gratitude guard us against pride. Before refusing help or answering harshly, let us think about the good we have received and treat others with humility.
exp.27:20:
The woman says she came to Saul and saw that he was deeply troubled. She reminded him that she had obeyed him and taken a great risk, and that she had done what he asked of her.

The speaker is the woman whom Saul sought out to consult Samuel, even though he himself had banned mediums from the land. She was in danger if she were found out. Saul had just heard his condemnation, and he was weak because he had not eaten all day. She speaks to him with compassion and offers him food. The Bible does not fully explain how Samuel appeared, and it is interpreted in different ways.

For today: do not wait until you are in despair to seek God. Turn to Him and to His Word early. And when someone suffers, help them with simple, kind gestures.
exp.8:23:
The cook picked up the leg and the meat attached to it and set it in front of Saul. Samuel told him that this portion had been set aside for him. He said it had been kept back for this occasion, from the time he had said he had invited the people. So Saul ate with Samuel that day.

Samuel was speaking at a sacrifice meal with about thirty guests. Saul had gone out to look for his father's lost donkeys and arrived where Samuel was. God had already told Samuel that he would send him the man who would be prince over Israel. This set-aside portion showed special honor, though Saul did not yet understand everything God would do through him.

For today: God may be preparing things for us long before we notice. We can trust that he guides our steps, even on ordinary days, and receive with humility and gratitude what he gives us.
exp.15:10:
Samuel asks Jesse whether these are all the sons he has. Jesse answers that there is still the youngest, but he is out tending the sheep. Samuel tells him to send for him, and says they will not sit down to eat until he arrives.

Samuel, the prophet, had been sent by God to the house of Jesse in Bethlehem to anoint a new king, since Saul had been rejected. God had already set aside the seven sons who were presented. Jesse had not even thought of David for this moment, and the text does not explain why; we only see that he left him out in the field.

For today: God does not look as people do, and sometimes he calls the one whom everyone overlooks. Do not belittle yourself or underestimate others; be faithful in small things, as David was with his sheep.
exp.28:8:
Here Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, tells David that he regards him as pleasing and trustworthy, as good as an angel of God. But he explains that the Philistine commanders do not want David to go into battle with them. "Commanders" here means leaders or rulers.

Achish speaks because David and his men were living among the Philistines, fleeing from King Saul. The Philistines were preparing to fight against Israel, and the other leaders distrusted David. Achish defends him, although in the end he sends him away. David says he wants to fight, but the Bible does not fully clarify his true intentions.

For today: sometimes others reject us or misunderstand us, even when our conduct has been good. We can keep a life of integrity and trust that God uses even closed doors to keep us from difficult situations.
exp.18:18:
This verse says that someone told Saul where David was: at Naioth, a place in Ramah. "When Saul was told" means that he received the news. Naioth seems to have been a site or group of dwellings near Ramah where Samuel was, though it is not known exactly what it was like.

Here the narrator of the story speaks. Saul, jealous, wanted to kill David. Michal, David's wife, had helped him escape, and David sought refuge with the prophet Samuel. But Saul found out and sent messengers to capture him. What follows shows that God protected David in a surprising way.

For today: even when it seems that troubles find us and surround us, God can care for us in unexpected ways. Let us seek refuge in Him and in wise people of faith, as David did with Samuel.
exp.24:2:
This passage introduces two very different people. Nabal was a wealthy man, but he was harsh and evil in his dealings. His wife Abigail was intelligent and beautiful, and she stood in sharp contrast to her husband. The text also says that Nabal was a Calebite, that is, a member of the family line of Caleb. Some scholars note that his name means "fool," but not all of them interpret it the same way.

Here the narrator is setting the stage for the story. Samuel has just died, and David is living in the wilderness. In describing Nabal and Abigail, the text foreshadows the conflict that comes when David asks for help and Nabal treats him badly.

For today: having a good family, money, or position does not guarantee a good character. Let us ask God for wisdom and a kind heart, and treat others with respect, as Abigail did.
exp.18:22:
So Saul went to Naioth in Ramah. But the Spirit of God came upon even Saul, and as he walked along, he began to prophesy until he reached Naioth in Ramah. This verse says that Saul arrived at Naioth in Ramah, looking for David. But before he got there, the Spirit of God came upon him, and he began to prophesy along the way. The word "prophesying" here is understood as speaking or praising under the impulse of God.

The account tells how Saul pursued David, and David had taken refuge with Samuel. Saul sent messengers three times, and every one of them ended up prophesying. Then he went himself. God protected David and stopped Saul's plans. Scholars understand in different ways what kind of prophecy this was, but the text shows that God acted on Saul without his choosing.

For today: no one can hinder God's purposes. If you are in the middle of an injustice, trust that God can care for you and work in unexpected ways.
exp.10:3:
The messengers from Jabesh came to Gibeah, the city of Saul, and relayed Nahash's threat to the people. Everyone wept aloud, with great grief. The phrase "they all wept aloud" describes crying out openly, without holding anything back.

The men of Jabesh-gilead were under siege by Nahash, king of Ammon, who wanted to gouge out their right eyes as a humiliation. They asked for seven days to look for help in Israel. The messengers spoke in Gibeah, and the people responded with weeping. But the weeping was not yet action. God would later move Saul to act.

When someone suffers, we should not be content with tears or lamentation alone. Weeping with the one who suffers is good, but we can also ask God to show us how to help, through prayer, time, words, or resources.
exp.24:35:
She came back to her house and found Nabal holding a feast fit for a king. He was in high spirits and very drunk. So she told him nothing until morning light. The wording "came back to" means "returned to" or "arrived where he was."

This is part of the story. Abigail had just gone out to meet David, who was coming in anger because Nabal, her husband, had refused his request for help. With food and wise words she prevented a massacre. Now she returns home, and the narrator shows the folly of Nabal, whose name means "fool."

For today: there are times to speak and times to wait. Abigail did not try to reason with someone drunk and unable to listen. She waited until he was sober. When a difficult conversation is necessary, it is wise to choose the moment carefully, so that what is said can really be heard.
exp.16:31:
David tells King Saul that no one should lose heart because of the giant Goliath. The phrase "let no one lose heart" means that no one should lose courage or nerve. David speaks of himself as Saul's servant and says that he himself will go and fight this Philistine.

David speaks after hearing that Goliath was defying the army of Israel and that everyone was afraid. He had asked several soldiers and was brought before Saul. David was young, and he had come to the camp to visit his brothers. His courage comes from the fact that Goliath was defying the people of the living God.

Today, when others are paralyzed by fear before a great problem, we can take a step of faith. It is not a matter of trusting our own strength, but of trusting that God is with us. Your courage can encourage others.
exp.2:7:
God called Samuel a third time. Once again the boy got up, went to Eli, and said, "Here I am, for you called me." This time Eli realized that it was the LORD who was calling the boy. The words "Here I am" are simply the reply "I am here," and "boy" refers to a young lad, perhaps quite small.

Samuel served in the sanctuary under the care of Eli, the aging priest. In those days the word of God was rare. Samuel did not yet know the Lord through his own experience, so he did not recognize his voice. Eli, though it took him a while, finally understood what was happening and was able to guide Samuel.

For today: God can speak to us, and sometimes we do not recognize him right away. We need to look for his voice in the Bible and also accept the help of mature believers, who can help us discern and respond to him with a willing heart.
exp.16:3:
The verse introduces Goliath, a Philistine warrior from the city of Gath, who steps out from the Philistine camp into the space between the two armies. The word "champion" names this kind of warrior, a fighter set apart to face the enemy in single combat, and "camp" refers to the place where the army is encamped. His height was six cubits and a span, roughly three meters by the most common calculation. Some ancient manuscripts say four cubits and a span, so the exact figure is debated.
