Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel and the Philistines stand facing each other, each on its own hill, with the valley between them. The author introduces Goliath to show the enormous threat that had paralyzed Israel and to prepare for David's arrival.

For today: problems can seem like giants and leave us paralyzed. Before giving up, let us remember that God is greater than any threat, and ask him for the courage to take the next step.
exp.14:10:
God says that he regrets that he made Saul king. The reason is that Saul has turned away from following him and has not carried out his instructions. Samuel was distressed, and he cried out to the Lord all that night.

God speaks, and he speaks to Samuel. God had commanded that the Amalekites be completely destroyed, but Saul and the people kept the best of the livestock and their king, Agag. When the Bible says that God regrets something, it does not mean that he made a mistake. It expresses his deep grief at the disobedience. Christians understand this in different ways.

Obeying God halfway is disobeying him. Today we can ask him to help us obey him sincerely, even in what costs us. And like Samuel, we can bring to him in prayer what grieves us.
exp.4:4:
It says that, after what happened to the statue of Dagon, the priests and everyone who entered his temple in Ashdod stopped stepping on the threshold, that is, the step at the entrance. Even in the writer's time they still kept this custom. The words "to this day" mean that the custom was still being followed when the book was written.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who explains the origin of a custom. The Philistines had placed the ark of God beside their idol. Dagon fell twice before the ark, and the second time he was left with his head and hands cut off on the threshold. Scholars do not agree on whether that custom was a sign of respect or of fear.

For today: idols, whether things or people, cannot stand before God. It is worth asking ourselves what has taken their place in our hearts, and placing it in the Lord's hands.
exp.16:28:
Here David answers his brother's harsh accusations with a simple question: "What have I done now?" It is like saying, "What wrong did I just do?" Then he asks, "Was it not just a question?" meaning, "Was I not only asking about what was being said?"

David had just asked the soldiers about the reward for defeating Goliath. His oldest brother, Eliab, became angry and accused him of pride and bad intentions. David had been sent by his father to bring food to his brothers. Some understand Eliab's reaction as jealousy or shame.

When someone attacks us without reason, we can respond with calm, without fighting. David did not defend himself with anger and went on with what God had placed in his heart.
exp.0:19:
This verse tells us that Hannah became pregnant and, in due time, gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel and explained the reason: "Because I have asked for him from the LORD." The phrase "in the course of time" points to the natural passing of the months until the birth.

Hannah had suffered for years from the sadness of having no children. At the temple in Shiloh, with a heavy heart, she asked God for a son, and the priest Eli sent her away with a blessing. The text says that the LORD "remembered her." The narrator speaks here, and he stresses that the child's name recalls the answered prayer.

Today we can do what Hannah did: bring our requests to God honestly, and when we receive an answer, remember it and thank Him for it in a concrete way.
exp.25:23:
David's words in this verse are both a statement and a prayer. He says that just as he valued and spared Saul's life that day, he hopes the Lord will value his life and rescue him from all trouble. "Valued" means held in high regard. "Trouble" means distress, hardship or danger. David asks God to bring him through all of it.

David is speaking to Saul, the king who was hunting him to kill him. That night David went into the camp and could have killed Saul while he slept, but he did not, because Saul was the Lord's anointed king. Now he shows Saul the spear as proof of his innocence and places his future in God's hands.

For today: when someone treats you badly, do not take revenge. Do what is right, treat others with respect, and leave your defense in God's hands, trusting that He cares for you.
exp.13:47:
Saul fought bravely and defeated the Amalekites, rescuing Israel from the raiders who had been plundering them. The verse tells us that he won the battle and freed the people from their attackers.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. He summarizes Saul's military victories at the beginning of his reign, before introducing his family and his general Abner. He shows that God used Saul to give protection to the people. Later, the story reveals that Saul failed to obey God, and so this success does not tell the whole of his story.

For today: achievements and strength do not replace obedience. We can thank God for what He allows us to accomplish, but it is wise to keep asking ourselves whether we do it with a heart that is faithful to Him.
exp.17:6:
The verse tells how the women of Israel sang and danced, taking turns in the song: "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands." The phrase "as the women danced" describes their festive celebration, and "thousands" and "tens of thousands" are a way of praising the victories.

The women came out from all the towns to meet the army after David had defeated the Philistines. Their song was a popular celebration, and it likely used poetic parallelism, without intending to offend Saul. But Saul took it as a comparison that left him in second place. The text shows that from that day he began to look at David with suspicion.

For today: when someone beside us receives recognition, we can choose between rejoicing or letting envy grow. Ask God for a grateful heart, one that celebrates the gifts of others without feeling diminished.
exp.7:10:
Samuel tells them what a king will do with them. He will take their sons to serve him: some will serve his chariots, some will ride his horses, and some will run ahead of his chariots as guards. "Manner" here means the customs or the way the king will act, not something that is fair. The "horses" are the animals the riders use.

Samuel speaks on God's command. The people of Israel asked for a king so they could be like the nations around them, and Samuel felt rejected. God told him to listen to them, but to warn them clearly. It was a warning, not an approval, of what that decision would cost.

Today we can learn to think about the price of what we desire. Before asking for something simply because others have it, it is wise to pray and ask what it will require of us, and what place we are giving God in that decision.
exp.19:6:
If Saul says, "Good," then your servant is safe, but if he is enraged, you will know he has evil intentions. Saul's reaction will serve as a sign. If he answers calmly, David will be safe. But if he becomes angry, that will show he has already decided to harm him. The phrase "evil intentions" means that his ill will is completely settled. Here David calls himself "your servant," speaking with humility.

David speaks with Jonathan, Saul's son and his faithful friend. David is fleeing because Saul wants to kill him, but he is not sure how serious the situation is. So he proposes a test: not to attend the New Moon feast and to see how the king reacts to his absence. Jonathan doubted that his father would go so far, and for that reason they agree to this plan.

Today it teaches us not to act only out of fear or naivety. When a situation is difficult, we can wisely look for clear signs, ask advice from a trustworthy friend, and pray so that we decide with prudence.
exp.9:6:
When these signs have come true, Saul should act with confidence and do what the occasion demands, meaning whatever presents itself before him. The reason is that God is with him, meaning God goes along with him.

Samuel speaks with Saul shortly after anointing him in private as the future king of Israel. He gives him several signs to confirm that God has chosen him, among them meeting a group of prophets. Saul doubted himself, so Samuel encourages him. Some understand "do as the occasion demands" to mean acting according to the circumstance; others take it to mean that Saul should wait for God's guidance, as verse 8 indicates.

For today: when God shows you that He goes with you, do not be paralyzed by fear. Take the step that lies before you, with humility and prayer, and trust that He guides you.
exp.20:12:
He said that David changed his behavior before the men of Gath. He pretended to be mad: he scratched marks on the gate doors and let his saliva run down into his beard. The verse itself says he changed his behavior, so there is no need to explain that his speech changed too. The phrase "in their hands" means that he did this while they had him under their control.

The narrator tells that David was fleeing from King Saul and came to Gath, a Philistine city, where the servants of Achish recognized him as the famous warrior. David was very much afraid that they would kill him, and for that reason he feigned madness. Psalm 34 and Psalm 56 are traditionally connected with this episode, although not all scholars agree on the details.

This passage shows that even a man of faith can feel fear and act with human awkwardness. When you are afraid, do not stay silent: cry out to God, as David did in his psalms, and trust that He can care for you even in your weakest moments.
exp.6:9:
This verse tells how, while Samuel was offering the burnt offering (a sacrifice that was burned completely in honor of God), the Philistines came forward to attack Israel. Then the LORD thundered loudly against them. The Berean wording says He threw them into such confusion that they fled before Israel, so the enemy was thrown into disorder and driven back before Israel.

The narrator describes what happened at Mizpah, where Israel had gathered to turn back to God and put away their idols. The Philistines saw that gathering and went out to attack. The Israelites were afraid and asked Samuel to keep crying out to God for them. The victory came in answer to that prayer, and not through Israel's military strength.

For today: when you feel afraid or find yourself in trouble you cannot solve, return to God with humility and cry out to Him. He will not always answer with thunder, but the Bible teaches that He hears and helps His people.
exp.26:8:
He says that whenever David attacked a territory, he left no man or woman alive. He would take the flocks and herds, the donkeys, camels, and clothing, and then return to Achish, the Philistine king. "Attacked" is the word used for the raids, and the clothing taken could be the goods and spoils gathered from the places he struck.

The narrator tells how David was living in Ziklag, fleeing from Saul. He attacked ancient enemies of Israel, such as the Amalekites, but led Achish to believe he was attacking Judah. To hide this, he left no survivors who could tell the truth. The text describes these events without approving them, and the Bible does not say here that God commanded them.

For today: even a man chosen by God can take paths of fear and deception. When we are under pressure, let us not justify lying or violence. Let us seek God and his guidance before we act.
exp.23:2:
This verse tells us that Saul gathered three thousand chosen soldiers from all over Israel and set out to look for David and his men. He went through the high rocky places where wild goats lived, that is, rugged, elevated terrain. "Chosen" here means selected for their strength.

The narrator of the book is speaking. Saul, Israel's first king, had just returned from fighting the Philistines, and he learned that David was in the wilderness of Engedi. Although David had done him no harm, Saul saw him as a threat to his throne and pursued him with a huge army.

When someone pursues us or treats us unjustly, we can remember that God sees everything. David was at a disadvantage, but he did not lose his composure. Trusting God helps us avoid responding with revenge.
exp.29:13:
Here the young Egyptian tells David what his band of Amalekites did. "We raided" means they attacked by surprise and carried off whatever they could. They struck the Negev of the Cherethites (who were Philistines of the coast), the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb. At the end he says they burned Ziklag, the town where David lived with his people.

It is an Egyptian slave speaking, sick and abandoned by his master three days earlier. David finds him in the field, feeds him, and asks him questions. In this way David learns who carried off his families and that Ziklag was destroyed. This detail, given almost without intending to, leads him straight to the enemy camp.

God can use the smallest and most forgotten people to show us the way. David was kind to a weak stranger, and that opened the door to the answer he needed. Today, treating with kindness someone no one attends to can bring blessings we do not expect.
exp.21:7:
Saul accuses his servants of having all conspired against him. He complains that none of them told him that his son Jonathan had made a covenant with David, "the son of Jesse." He says that none of them felt sorry for him, and that none of them told him his own son had stirred up his servant against him to lie in wait, as is the case today.

King Saul speaks in Gibeah, spear in hand, surrounded by his officers from the tribe of Benjamin. David has fled, and Saul, filled with jealousy and suspicion, sees traitors everywhere. His accusation seems to come more from fear than from proven fact, and his words reveal self-pity.

For today: when fear and envy take hold of us, we begin to see enemies where there are none. It is wise to bring those fears to God and to wise people before we accuse others.
exp.18:11:
It says that Michal, David's wife, lowered him from the window, and he ran away and got clear of those who were chasing him. "Lowered" means she let him down from up high. "Escaped" means he managed to save himself.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul, the king, was jealous of David and wanted to kill him. He had sent messengers to watch the house so they could seize him in the morning. Michal, who was Saul's daughter, warned David of the danger and helped him get away, putting herself at risk in the process. Many believe this episode is connected to Psalm 59, although that is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God often looks after us through people who act with courage and love at the right time. We can thank those who have helped us in this way, and be willing to help others when they are in danger, trusting that God guides the way.
exp.29:28:
David sent part of the plunder to the people in Racal, to the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and to the Kenites. The names here refer to peoples and regions in the south of Judah, and they are part of a longer list of places that received gifts.

The author tells what David did after defeating the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the families. David recovered everything and gained a great deal of plunder. Some of his men did not want to share it, but David said it should be divided among everyone. Then he sent gifts to the friends who had helped him while he was fleeing from Saul. We do not know exactly where Racal was.

Today we can learn to be thankful and generous. When God gives us something good, it is not only for us. We can remember those who supported us in hard times and share with them.
exp.19:8:
Jonathan answers David emphatically: "Never!" He promises that if he were to find out that his father had evil intentions against David, he would certainly tell him. "Evil intentions" here means harmful plans, and "had" in the sense of having already settled on them.

David speaks to Jonathan because he fears that King Saul wants to kill him. He asks him to find out Saul's attitude during the New Moon feast. Jonathan, Saul's son, is David's loyal friend, and the two made a covenant before God. That is why David trusts him, and Jonathan does not hesitate to promise his help, even though it puts him in tension with his own father.

Today it teaches us the value of sincere loyalty. A good friend tells the truth, even when it is difficult, and protects the other person. Think of someone who trusts you and look for a concrete way to support them honestly this week.
exp.2:17:
Samuel told Eli everything God had revealed to him, and he hid nothing. Eli replied, "He is the LORD; let Him do what is good in His eyes."

God had spoken to Samuel, a young man who served in the sanctuary, to announce judgment on Eli's household for failing to restrain his sons. Eli, now an old man, insisted that Samuel hold nothing back. Samuel, though he was afraid, was honest. Eli acknowledged that God has the authority to act.

Today we can learn from both of them. Like Samuel, we should speak the truth with respect, even when it is hard. Like Eli, we can accept correction with humility, trusting that God is just, without becoming defensive or looking for excuses.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that the boy Samuel served the LORD at the sanctuary, wearing a linen ephod. "Ministering" means that he served or helped with the tasks of worship. The linen ephod was a simple garment, something like an apron or vest, worn by those who served in the presence of God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Earlier, the sons of Eli were mentioned, who despised the offerings and abused their office. With that contrast, the text shows Samuel, a boy who served with reverence. Afterward it is told that his mother, Hannah, made him a small robe each year and brought it to him.

For today: even if you are young, or are in a setting where others do not take holy things seriously, you can serve God with simplicity and faithfulness in the small things that fall to you to do.
exp.25:20:
Saul admits, "I have sinned." He asks David to come back and promises never to harm him again, because David spared his life that day. He acknowledges that he acted like a fool, without wisdom, and that he made a grave error. "You considered my life precious" means that David valued him and showed him care.

Here Saul, the king, speaks after David, while hiding in the cave of the camp, could have killed him as he slept, chose not to lay a hand on him. David has just challenged him over his unjust pursuit. Saul had said similar things before (24:17; 15:24), and his later conduct shows that his repentance did not last. The Bible does not tell us how sincere he was at that moment.

For today: saying "I was wrong" is a good start, but true repentance is proven by lasting change. Let us ask God to give us a humble heart that corrects its course and does not only speak.
exp.24:4:
David sent ten of his young men up to Carmel, a region in the south of Judah, to go to Nabal. He instructed them to greet Nabal in David's name. The men David sends are his servants or young men in his service.

David is in the wilderness, fleeing from King Saul, with a group of men who need food. He learns that Nabal is shearing his sheep, a time of festivity and plenty. David and his men had looked after Nabal's shepherds, and now he approaches with respect to ask for help. The text presents Nabal as a harsh man, and Abigail as a wise woman.

For today: when you need to ask for something, begin with respect and good treatment. A kind greeting does not guarantee that you will be answered well, but it shows your character and opens the way to peace.
exp.24:27:
Abigail asks David to forgive what she calls her servant's offense, meaning the foolish behavior of her husband Nabal. She assures him that the LORD will surely establish a lasting dynasty for him, with descendants who will rule and a kingdom that will endure. She says he fights the LORD's battles and asks that no evil be found in him as long as he lives.

Abigail, Nabal's wife, is the one speaking. Nabal had insulted David and his men, and David was marching out armed to destroy her household. Abigail goes out to meet him with food and supplies and tries to calm his anger. With tact and humility, she reminds him of God's purpose for his life so that he will not stain his future with revenge.

For today: when someone wrongs you, before you act in anger, remember what God wants to do in your life. Leaving vengeance in God's hands protects you from carrying guilt that you would later regret.
exp.25:19:
David asks Saul not to kill him, so that his blood will not fall to the ground far from the presence of the LORD. He says that the king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, something very small and insignificant. He also compares himself to someone who hunts a partridge through the mountains, a bird that wears itself out by running away.

David speaks to Saul in the wilderness of Ziph. He had just spared Saul's life once again, although he could have killed him while he slept. Saul pursued him out of envy and fear. David presents himself humbly, but he also defends his innocence and trusts that the LORD is the judge between them.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not respond with revenge. Speak with truth and humility, and leave the matter in God's hands. He sees everything and knows how to do justice in his own time.
exp.19:0:
David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came to find Jonathan. He asks him three questions in a row: what he has done, what his wrong is, and how he has sinned against Jonathan's father, who is trying to kill him. The word "iniquity" here means a guilt or wrong, and the verse uses it in that sense.

David is speaking, and he has already been anointed as the future king. King Saul, out of jealousy, was pursuing him. Shortly before this, David had been with the prophet Samuel in Ramah. Jonathan, Saul's son, was his faithful friend. David feels confused and innocent, and he looks for someone he can trust.

Today, when someone attacks us without reason or we feel misunderstood, we are not alone. We can seek a wise and trustworthy friend to unburden ourselves and ask for counsel, and we can also bring our distress to God with sincerity, as David did.
exp.13:15:
The watchmen of Saul, who were in Gibeah in Benjamin, saw something strange in the Philistine camp: the troops were scattering in every direction, moving back and forth and coming apart. The watchmen are the lookouts who keep guard from a high place. The phrase "melting away" describes the army coming undone and falling to pieces.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonathan and his armor-bearer had attacked a Philistine outpost alone, and God sent a great fear over the enemy camp. Saul's watchmen could only see the result, without yet knowing the cause. Soon afterward Saul discovered that Jonathan was missing.

For today: sometimes God works in ways we do not understand right away. A small act of faith can have great effects. Trust, and take a brave step, even when no one sees you.
exp.13:30:
This verse says that Israel defeated the Philistines that day, striking them down and pursuing them all the way from Michmash to Aijalon, a long distance. But the people were left very exhausted. The word "faint" describes extreme weariness, the kind that comes from not having eaten.

The narrator recounts what happened after Saul made a hasty oath: no one could eat until evening. Jonathan, who did not know of it, tasted some honey and his strength returned. He criticizes his father's command, saying the people would have fought better had they eaten. Here we see the cost of that command: victory, but with a worn-out people.

For today: before demanding something of others, let us consider whether it truly helps or only weighs them down. Seeking God with zeal is good, but it should be done with wisdom and compassion.
exp.17:17:
David answers Saul with humility when Saul offers him his daughter Merab in marriage. He asks, "Who am I, and what is my family or my father's clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?" He is saying that he does not feel worthy of such an honor, and he points to his own background and his modest family.

David speaks with King Saul, who offers to give him his daughter in marriage, but on one condition: that he fight the wars of the LORD. The text says that Saul, in reality, hoped the Philistines would kill David. David does not know that intention and answers with simplicity. Afterward, Merab is given to another man.

When you receive an honor or an opportunity, receive it with humility, without boasting. And if someone treats you with deceit, trust that God cares for you, as He cared for David.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that the people, from north to south, came to recognize that Samuel was a true prophet of God. The word "knew" in the verse means "recognized" or "understood." "Dan" and "Beersheba" were the cities at the two ends of the land, so the phrase means "all Israel." The word "confirmed" here means shown to be genuine, someone whose words came true and whom people could trust.

It is the narrator who speaks. Earlier, God had given Samuel, while he was still young, a hard message for the priest Eli, and Samuel told it to him without hiding anything. Because God fulfilled what Samuel said, the people began to trust him. This happens at a time when the word of God was rare in Israel.

For today: faithfulness is recognized over time. Try to speak the truth with humility, even when it costs you, and live in such a way that your words and your actions deserve trust.
exp.27:22:
It says that Saul at first refused to eat. But his servants, together with the woman, urged him until he gave in and agreed. "Urged" here means they pressed him with gentle insistence to accept.

Saul had just visited the medium of Endor and had received from Samuel a terrible message: he would lose the battle and die. He had fallen to the ground, drained of strength, and had gone a full day without eating. The woman, grateful that he had not punished her, offers him food. Saul is broken and desperate.

When we are exhausted or discouraged, we sometimes turn away help. God often uses ordinary people to care for us. Let us learn to accept the support of others humbly, and also to offer it with tenderness.
exp.4:10:
The people of Ekron, frightened, called together all the rulers of the Philistines. They asked that the ark of the God of Israel be sent away and returned to its own place, so that it would not kill them or their people. The verse describes a deadly confusion that had spread through the city, and it says that the hand of God was very heavy upon it, meaning that the punishment was growing more severe.

The Philistines had captured the ark in battle and had carried it to Ashdod and then to Gath. In each city, suffering followed. Now in Ekron, the people speak with fear. They believed the ark was the cause, and the text presents these events as the hand of God at work.

For today: we cannot treat God as an object we use for our own convenience. With humility, let us acknowledge his holiness and, instead of resisting him, seek his forgiveness and his guidance.
exp.24:8:
This verse says that the young men sent by David arrived where Nabal was and told him all of this message from David, repeating it fully. After they had spoken, they stopped and waited for his answer. The "young men" are David's attendants, and "waited" means they paused, giving Nabal time to respond.

David was hiding from Saul in the wilderness, and his men had looked after Nabal's flocks without harming them. It was sheep-shearing time, a season of feasting and plenty. That is why David respectfully asked for some help. The messengers spoke "on behalf of David," that is, as his representatives. Nabal's reply, which comes next, was harsh and scornful.

For today: when you have to ask for something or speak with someone difficult, do it with clarity and respect, and then know how to wait without pressing. We cannot control how others will respond, but we can control how we speak.
exp.19:36:
This verse tells us that the young servant reached the place where Jonathan's arrow had landed. Then Jonathan called out to him: "Isn't the arrow beyond you?" In this verse, "the boy" is the servant who ran to fetch the arrow, and Jonathan's call is simply a shout to tell him where it had gone.

Jonathan speaks to his servant, but in reality he is sending a coded message to David, who was hiding nearby. Saul, Jonathan's father, was seeking to kill David. Jonathan and David had agreed on this signal: if the arrow fell far away, David must flee because he was in danger. The servant understood nothing.

For today: loyal love sometimes calls for prudence and courage. Jonathan risked his own position to protect his friend. Ask yourself whom you can care for faithfully, even when it costs you something, and act with wisdom.
exp.8:16:
When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, "Here is the man of whom I spoke." The phrase "he shall rule" means that he will govern or hold authority over the people.

God had told Samuel a day earlier that He would send him a man from the tribe of Benjamin to be anointed as leader. Samuel was a prophet and a judge. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys and did not know what God was preparing. The text says that God had heard the cry of His people, who were oppressed by the Philistines.

For today: God can work in the middle of ordinary life, even when we do not notice it. Trust that He hears your cry and directs your steps, even in common tasks, and stay attentive to what He may want to show you.
exp.3:21:
She says that the glory has departed from Israel, because the Philistines had captured the ark of God. The word translated "departed" does not mean wounded but carried away or sent into exile, like someone going into exile.

She is the wife of Phinehas, who is dying in childbirth. That same day Israel lost the battle, her father-in-law Eli and her husband died, and the ark was captured. She does not find comfort even in the birth of her son, and she names him Ichabod, a name usually understood as "no glory" or "where is the glory?". Scholars debate its exact meaning.

For today: God's presence does not depend on objects, buildings, or traditions. These may help us, but they do not replace God. Place your trust in God himself, and seek a living faith, not merely a religious one.
exp.19:32:
Saul, in a fit of rage, hurled his spear at his own son Jonathan to kill him. With this, Jonathan understood that his father was determined to kill David.

Jonathan had just defended David at a new moon feast. Saul saw David as a threat to his family's throne. When Jonathan asked, "What has he done?", Saul gave no reasons, only violence. In this way it became clear that there was no room for dialogue.

For today: there are moments when anger shuts the ears and reason no longer gets in. If you defend what is right, do it with courage but also with prudence, and do not rest in the illusion that everything will work itself out. Ask God for wisdom to see the reality clearly and to act with love and firmness.
exp.15:1:
Samuel tells God that he is afraid: if King Saul finds out what he is about to do, Saul will kill him. God answers that he should take a young cow from the herd and say, "I have come to sacrifice to the LORD."

Samuel speaks with God after Saul has been rejected as king. God sends him to Bethlehem to secretly anoint one of Jesse's sons as the new king. The sacrifice was real, and Samuel truly was going to offer it. God gives him a wise way, without any lie, to protect his life and carry out his plan. Many scholars read it this way, though some debate the matter.

For today: you can speak to God about your fears with honesty, as Samuel did. He does not scold you; he gives you the next step, with wisdom and patience.
exp.27:11:
It says that when the woman saw Samuel, she cried out in a loud voice. Then she spoke to Saul and said to him, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!" "Cried out in a loud voice" means she shouted strongly, out of fright or surprise.

Saul, king of Israel, was afraid before the Philistine army. God was no longer answering him, so he went in disguise to look for a woman who consulted the dead, something the law of God forbade. She was frightened because the appearance was different from what she expected. Scholars disagree about whether it was truly Samuel or something else, but the text presents it as Samuel.

For today: when we feel fear and it seems that God is silent, let us not look for answers in forbidden paths. Rather, let us return to Him with humility, pray, and listen to His Word, even when the answer is slow in coming.
exp.9:24:
Samuel explained to the people "the rights of kingship," that is, the rules and the duties of the king and of the people. Then he wrote them on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD, probably in a sacred place, near the sanctuary.

Israel had just asked for a king, and Saul was presented publicly. Samuel, prophet and judge, speaks so that the new reign would not be a power without limits. Scholars do not know exactly what that writing said, but it shows that the king too was under God's authority.

Today it reminds us that all authority, in the home, the church or the workplace, must submit to God and to clear principles. If you have any leadership, exercise it with humility and accountability.
exp.15:2:
God tells Samuel to invite Jesse to the sacrifice. There God will show him what to do. The word "invite" is what the verse says here. The instruction means that Samuel will anoint for God the one God indicates. Samuel does not yet know who it will be; he only has to wait for God's direction.

God speaks to Samuel, who was grieving over Saul, the rejected king. God has already chosen a new king from among the sons of Jesse. Samuel fears that Saul will kill him, so God gives him a plan: go with a young cow and offer a sacrifice. The sacrifice was real, and it served as an occasion to gather Jesse's family.

For today: God often shows us only the next step, not the whole road. We can obey what we already know and trust that He will guide us afterward, even when we feel afraid or do not understand the full plan.
exp.13:0:
One day, the verse says, Jonathan, the son of King Saul, spoke to the young man who carried his armor: "Come, let us cross over to the Philistine outpost on the other side." An outpost is a group of enemy soldiers stationed in one place. But Jonathan did not tell his father.

The narrator of the book speaks here and introduces Jonathan. Israel was at war with the Philistines, and Saul's army was small, about six hundred men. The verses that follow show Saul sitting still under a pomegranate tree while Jonathan acts. The Bible does not explain why he did not tell his father; some think he wanted to avoid a "no," but that is an interpretation.

For today: when you see something that God places on your heart to do, take a step of faith, but with humility and prayer. Doing something brave is not the same as acting in secret; seek wise counsel before you decide.
exp.10:5:
He says that when Saul heard the threat against the people of Jabesh, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he burned with great anger. The word "rushed" here means that the Spirit took hold of him and drove him forward with power. The phrase "when Saul heard" simply means "upon hearing."

The narrator tells what happened when Saul was returning from the field with his oxen. The people of Jabesh Gilead were threatened by Nahash, king of the Ammonites, and they were asking for help. The people were only weeping, but Saul, already chosen as king, responded. His anger does not seem selfish, but rather an indignation over God's people in danger. Some readers see here the Spirit equipping a leader for a specific moment.

Today, indignation can be good when it moves us to defend the weak and act with justice. Let us ask God to guide our anger, so that it does not destroy, but serves and protects.
exp.16:20:
This verse describes the scene of the battle. Israelites and Philistines had lined up for combat, arrayed in formation against each other. "Arrayed against each other" means that each force had its ranks drawn up facing the other, ready to fight.

The narrator places us in the Valley of the Terebinth (or of Elah). David has just arrived with supplies for his brothers, sent by his father Jesse. Everything seems about to become a battle, but the text shows a standoff: the armies looked at each other without charging. This sets up the appearance of Goliath and the challenge that will change the story.

For today: sometimes we live through long tensions, with fear and no progress. David came to do something simple, carry food, and there God put him in the right place. Be faithful in small things; God can use them in great ways.
exp.9:18:
Samuel tells them that by asking for a king they have rejected God himself. God had saved them from all their troubles and afflictions, yet they answered, "No, set a king over us." Rejected means refused or looked down upon. The clans are the family groups into which each tribe was divided. Now Samuel orders them to present themselves before the LORD, tribe by tribe.

Samuel speaks at Mizpah, where he had gathered all Israel. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt and delivered them from other oppressing kingdoms. The people had already asked for a king (1 Samuel 8), and now the king is chosen by lot, beginning with the tribe of Benjamin. Saul is singled out, though he does not appear right away.

For today: when we feel we need something more secure than God, let us remember how he has cared for us before. Trusting in him, even when we have human plans, protects us from placing our hope in the wrong place.
exp.14:0:
Samuel reminds Saul that the LORD sent him to anoint Saul as king over Israel, God's people. Because of this, Samuel asks Saul to listen carefully to the words of the LORD that are about to come.

Samuel speaks as the prophet and judge of Israel. Before giving a hard command from God, he reminds Saul that his reign depends on God. Saul is king because God allowed it, and so he must obey. The orders that follow about the Amalekites are harsh, and scholars understand them in different ways. Here the emphasis is on listening and obeying.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself whether you are truly listening to God or only looking to confirm what you already want to do. Read his Word with humility and obey what you understand.
exp.3:13:
The verse says that when Eli heard the loud sound of people crying out, he asked what the noise of this tumult meant. A tumult is a great uproar, many voices raised at once. Then the man came in hurriedly and told Eli what had happened.

Eli was a priest at Shiloh, and by now he was very old and nearly blind. Israel had fought against the Philistines, and the ark of God was out on the battlefield. Eli was waiting beside the road with a trembling heart, anxious for the ark. The city had already cried out on hearing the news, and Eli, unable to see, could only ask what was going on.

When we fear bad news, we can recognize ourselves in Eli: his heart was troubled over what mattered to God. Today we can bring our worries to God honestly, and ask him to help us put first what matters to him.

sum.29:
When David and his men came back to Ziklag, they found the city burned and their wives, sons, and daughters taken captive. David strengthened himself in the LORD his God, inquired of the LORD, pursued the Amalekites, and recovered everything that had been taken.

Afterward he insisted that the plunder be divided equally, even with the men who had stayed behind exhausted, and he sent a share to the elders of Judah.
sum.2: God calls Samuel at night, and the young man, not recognizing the voice, runs three times to Eli, until Eli teaches him to answer: "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening." God announces judgment on Eli's house, and Samuel tells him about it honestly. God was with him, and all Israel knew he was a faithful prophet.
sum.28: The Philistines gather at Aphek to fight against Israel, and David goes along with King Achish. But the Philistine commanders distrust David and insist that he leave, out of fear that he might turn against them in the battle. Achish praises David, but he sends him away, and David returns early to Philistine territory.
sum.8: Saul sets out with a servant to look for his father's lost donkeys, and when they cannot find them, they go to consult the prophet Samuel. God had already told Samuel that this young man from the tribe of Benjamin would be the leader of his people. Samuel honors him at the feast and sets him apart to give him a message from God.
sum.26: David feared that Saul would someday kill him, so he fled with his six hundred men into Philistine territory, and King Achish gave him the city of Ziklag. From there he raided neighboring peoples, but he deceived Achish by telling him that he was attacking Judah, and Achish believed him. The text shows David's fear and his questionable decisions, without either approving or condemning them.
sum.10: Nahash the Ammonite threatened Jabesh Gilead with a cruel condition, and Saul, moved by the Spirit of God, gathered all Israel and delivered them. After the victory, Saul pardoned his critics and acknowledged that the Lord had given the salvation. Then the people confirmed him as king at Gilgal with joy.
sum.1: Hannah prayed and praised God because he brings down the proud, lifts up the poor, and watches over those who are faithful to him. While the boy Samuel grows up serving God, the sons of Eli abuse the offerings and the people, and God announces judgment on Eli's family and promises to raise up a faithful priest.
sum.23: David had Saul in his hands inside a cave and, instead of killing him, only cut off the edge of his robe, because he respected the anointed one of God. He then showed Saul that he was not his enemy and left the judgment in God's hands. Saul wept, admitted that David was more righteous, and asked him to look after his family.
sum.15: God sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a new king from among the sons of Jesse, and he teaches that God does not look at outward appearance but at the heart. He chooses David, the youngest, who tends the sheep, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him. Meanwhile, Saul is tormented, and David soothes him by playing the harp.
sum.9: Samuel anointed Saul in private and told him of signs that would take place that very day. The Spirit of God came upon him, changing him, and he prophesied among the prophets. Afterward, at Mizpah, Samuel rebuked the people for asking for a king, and God pointed to Saul, who had hidden himself. Some cheered for him, but others looked down on him, and he kept silent.
sum.18: Saul wants to kill David, but Jonathan defends him, and then Michal helps him escape at night. David flees to Samuel in Ramah, and when Saul pursues him, the Spirit of God stops him among the prophets. In this way, God protects David against the king's threat.
sum.13: Jonathan and his armor-bearer, trusting that for the LORD it is no hard thing to save by many or by few, attack the Philistines, and God sends panic and victory to Israel. But Saul's hasty oath wears the people out and almost costs Jonathan his life, and the people rescue him.
sum.24: David asks Nabal, a rich but harsh man, for help, and Nabal insults him, so David sets out with his men intending to take revenge. Abigail, his wise wife, brings food and begs David not to shed blood without cause, and he listens to her. Afterward God strikes Nabal down, and David takes Abigail as his wife.
sum.3: Israel lost a battle to the Philistines and brought the ark of the covenant out to the fighting as if it were a good-luck charm, but they were defeated again. Thirty thousand men died, Eli's sons were killed, and the ark was captured. When Eli heard the news, he died. His daughter-in-law gave birth, and she named the boy Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel."
sum.22: David consults God, rescues the city of Keilah from the Philistines, and then learns that Saul is coming to trap him, so he flees with his six hundred men. Jonathan encourages him and renews his covenant with him. Saul almost catches up with David, but a Philistine attack forces him to turn back, showing God's care over David.
sum.17: Jonathan loved David as he loved himself and made a covenant with him, while David succeeded in everything he did and all the people loved him. Saul, filled with jealousy and fear because the LORD was with David, tried to kill him with a spear and then sent him to fight against the Philistines. But David came through successfully and married Michal.
sum.0: Hannah, a woman without children and with a wounded heart, prayed with tears at Shiloh and promised to dedicate to God the son she might be given. God heard her prayer, and Samuel was born. When the boy was weaned, Hannah kept her promise and gave him over to God at the house of the LORD.
sum.16: The Philistines challenge Israel with the giant Goliath, and everyone is afraid. David, a young shepherd, trusts in the living God and faces him with a sling and a stone, without armor. In this way he defeats the giant and teaches that victory comes from the LORD, not from the sword or the spear.
sum.14: God commands Saul to completely destroy the Amalekites, but he and the people spare King Agag and the best of the livestock. Samuel teaches him that obeying God is worth more than sacrifices, and he announces that the kingdom will be taken away from him. Saul confesses his sin, but Samuel never sees him again and mourns for him.
sum.11: Samuel, now an old man, takes his leave before the people and shows that he has always acted with integrity. He reminds them how God rescued them again and again, and that asking for a king was a mistake. God sends thunder and rain, the people repent, and Samuel encourages them not to be afraid but to serve God with all their heart.
sum.5: After seven months of plagues, the Philistines send the ark back to Israel with gifts of gold, and two cows carry it on their own all the way to Beth Shemesh, showing that the LORD was at work. But some of the people there looked inside the ark and died, and the people understood that God is holy and must be treated with reverence. The figure of 50,070 is widely debated.
sum.27: When the Philistines attacked, Saul was gripped by fear, and since God did not answer him, he went looking for a medium in Endor, even though he himself had banned such practices. Samuel appears and tells him that he will lose the kingdom and die, along with his sons, because of his disobedience. Saul is devastated, but the woman takes care of him and gives him a meal.
sum.20: David flees from Saul and comes to Nob, where he lies to the priest Ahimelech in order to receive holy bread and the sword of Goliath. Doeg, a servant of Saul, sees all of this. Then David escapes to Gath, feels fear, and pretends to be insane so that King Achish will let him go. The Bible here shows his fear and his human decisions.
sum.4: The Philistines carried the ark of God into the temple of their god Dagon, but the statue fell and was smashed to pieces in front of the ark. Then a plague struck Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron, and the people asked for the ark to be sent away. The chapter teaches that God cannot be compared with idols.
sum.30: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa, and Saul and his three sons die. Saul takes his own life so that he will not fall into the hands of the enemy. The Philistines display his body, but the brave men of Jabesh-gilead rescue it, bury it with honor, and fast for seven days.
sum.7: As Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel, but they were corrupt. They took bribes and twisted justice. So the elders of Israel came to Samuel and asked him for a king to rule over them, like all the other nations. Samuel was displeased by their request, but the LORD told him that the people had not rejected Samuel, but had rejected God as their king. Samuel warned the people about how much a king would cost them. Still, they refused to listen and insisted that they wanted a king. In the end, God allowed them to have one.
sum.19: David flees from Saul and asks his friend Jonathan for help. Jonathan promises to warn him if his father plans to kill him. At the New Moon feast, Saul becomes furious, tries to kill Jonathan with a spear, and makes clear his hatred for David. Jonathan warns David by means of arrows, and the two friends say goodbye in tears, faithful to their covenant before God.
sum.6: After twenty years of sorrow, Israel repents: they put away their idols, fast at Mizpah, and confess their sin. When the Philistines attack, Samuel offers a sacrifice and cries out to God, and the LORD defeats them with thunder. Samuel sets up a stone called Ebenezer, which means "Thus far the LORD has helped us."
sum.25: The Ziphites betray David, and Saul searches for him with three thousand men. At night, David and Abishai enter the camp and find Saul asleep, but David refuses to kill the Lord's anointed. He takes only Saul's spear and water jug. Saul admits his wrongdoing, and David trusts that God will deliver him.
sum.21: David flees to the cave of Adullam, where his family joins him along with about four hundred men who were in distress, and he leaves his parents in the care of the king of Moab. Saul, consumed by suspicion, has the priests of Nob killed through Doeg, and only Abiathar escapes. David feels responsible and offers him protection.
sum.12: Saul faces the Philistines, and when he sees the people growing frightened and deserting him, he offers the burnt offering without waiting for Samuel. Samuel rebukes him for not obeying the LORD and tells him that his kingdom will not last. Israel is left weak and without weapons, and obedience to God matters more than acting in a hurry.
